title: Unified Hallucination Fuzzing for Multimodal Large Language Models
summary: Hallucination remains a persistent challenge for Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs), severely limiting their reliability in high-stakes applications. Existing evaluations, predominantly based on static benchmarks, suffer from narrow taxonomical coverage and rapid performance saturation, failing to reflect model robustness in evolving real-world scenarios. To bridge this gap, we present a systematic evaluation framework integrating a comprehensive benchmark with self-evolving stress testing. First, we introduce UniHall, a fine-grained dataset grounded in a unified taxonomy spanning Object, Instruction, and Knowledge dimensions. Second, to address benchmark saturation, we propose Self-Adaptive Multimodal Fuzzing (SAMF), a self-adaptive framework that employs evolutionary mutation strategies to explore the boundaries of model hallucinations. Crucially, to ensure reliable assessment of dynamic inputs, SAMF incorporates a structured metric suite driven by an ensemble of multi-modal oracles. Our extensive experiments reveal that state-of-the-art MLLMs exhibit significant performance degradation under fuzzing compared to conventional settings, exposing a dissociation between reasoning capabilities and factual grounding. Furthermore, we identify a helpfulness-hallucination trade-off, where reinforcement learning alignment inadvertently exacerbates sycophancy in instruction-following tasks. The framework, code and benchmark are available at https://github.com/LanceZPF/EvalHall.

AI.tldr: They propose UniHall, a unified hallucination taxonomy and dataset for multimodal LLMs, plus SAMF, a self-adaptive multimodal fuzzing framework that stress-tests models using evolutionary mutations and multi-modal oracle metrics, revealing severe robustness issues and a trade-off between helpfulness and hallucination.
AI.motivation: Hallucinations in multimodal LLMs remain common, undermining their reliability in high-stakes use. Existing hallucination benchmarks are static, narrow in coverage, and quickly saturate, so they fail to show how robust models are in changing real-world conditions. The authors want a more comprehensive, fine-grained, and dynamically extensible way to evaluate hallucinations in multimodal models.
AI.method: They build (1) UniHall, a hallucination evaluation dataset organized under a unified taxonomy with three main dimensions—Object, Instruction, and Knowledge—providing fine-grained labels. (2) They design Self-Adaptive Multimodal Fuzzing (SAMF), which uses evolutionary mutation strategies on multimodal inputs and instructions to automatically generate challenging, hallucination-inducing test cases. SAMF runs models on these fuzzed inputs and uses a structured metric suite powered by an ensemble of multimodal oracles (other models/tools) to detect and score hallucinations and reliability under dynamic conditions.
AI.result: Experiments on state-of-the-art multimodal LLMs show that performance drops significantly under SAMF fuzzing compared with standard, static benchmark settings. This indicates that current models are far less robust than static scores suggest and that their reasoning skills do not reliably translate into factual grounding. They also empirically observe that RL-based alignment that aims to increase helpfulness can increase sycophantic behavior and hallucination in instruction-following tasks.
AI.conclusion: Static hallucination benchmarks are insufficient for assessing robustness of multimodal LLMs. A unified, taxonomy-based dataset plus a self-evolving fuzzing framework with multimodal oracle metrics (UniHall + SAMF) can expose deeper weaknesses, including a separation between reasoning and factual accuracy and a trade-off between helpfulness and hallucination. Their released framework and resources are intended as standard tools for future hallucination robustness evaluation in multimodal models.

title: DocAtlas: Long-Document Understanding as Mutable-State Interaction
summary: Long-document understanding requires models to find and combine evidence across many pages, layouts, tables, figures, and charts. Existing retrieval-augmented systems usually select evidence from a static index before generation, while recent agentic systems add multi-turn tool use but often rely on frozen proprietary backbones whose behavior is set by prompts. We present DocAtlas, a system that treats long-document understanding as a mutable-state information-seeking process. We instantiate DocAtlas as a mutable document harness: an external environment that determines what document information is searched, read, stored, reviewed, and shown to the model at each step. Given a document and question, the harness exposes search, reading, note-taking, and review tools, maintains a hierarchical tree and note store, and updates both as the agent records evidence. DocAtlas combines self-improving retrieval, selective evidence access, and active working memory under a fixed context budget. The same harness supports inference-time use with large VLMs and end-to-end reinforcement learning for compact VLM agents. With GPT-5.4, DocAtlas reaches 71.4\% on MMLongBench-Doc, exceeding the human-expert reference of 65.8\%. A Qwen3.5-4B VLM trained with end-to-end RL in the DocAtlas environment reaches 63.7\%, compared with a 54.4\% direct-input baseline, showing that mutable document-harness design can improve compact document agents by a large margin.

AI.tldr: DocAtlas is a mutable document-harness system that treats long-document understanding as an information-seeking process with tools for search, reading, note-taking, and review, enabling both large and compact vision-language models to more effectively retrieve and use evidence within a fixed context budget.
AI.motivation: Long-document understanding is difficult because models must locate and combine evidence spread across many pages, diverse layouts, and modalities (tables, figures, charts). Existing retrieval-augmented methods rely on static pre-generation retrieval, and agentic systems often depend on non-trainable proprietary backbones controlled only by prompts. There is a need for a more flexible, trainable framework that can adaptively explore documents and manage information over multiple steps under a limited context budget.
AI.method: The authors introduce DocAtlas, a mutable document harness conceptualized as an external environment in which a model acts as an agent. The harness exposes tools for searching within a document, reading specific content, taking notes, and reviewing accumulated evidence. It maintains and updates a hierarchical tree structure and note store as the agent gathers information. This design supports self-improving retrieval, selective access to evidence, and active working memory. DocAtlas can be used at inference time with large vision-language models and as an RL training environment for compact VLM agents, enabling end-to-end reinforcement learning over tool use and memory management.
AI.result: Using GPT-5.4 within the DocAtlas harness, the system achieves 71.4% accuracy on the MMLongBench-Doc benchmark, surpassing the human-expert reference score of 65.8%. Furthermore, a compact Qwen3.5-4B VLM trained end-to-end with reinforcement learning in the DocAtlas environment attains 63.7%, substantially outperforming a 54.4% baseline that directly processes the input without the mutable harness. These results demonstrate gains for both large and small models from the DocAtlas framework.
AI.conclusion: Treating long-document understanding as a mutable-state information-seeking process and operationalizing it through a document harness yields significant performance improvements. DocAtlas’s combination of self-improving retrieval, selective evidence access, and active working memory under a fixed context budget benefits both large proprietary VLMs at inference time and smaller, trainable VLM agents via reinforcement learning. The findings suggest that carefully designed mutable document environments are an effective way to build stronger, more efficient document-understanding agents.

title: WuYuEval: A Multi-Level Benchmark for Large Language Models in Solid Waste Management
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as technical assistants, but their competence in solid waste management (SWM) remains difficult to assess because existing benchmarks emphasize general knowledge rather than professional decisions under engineering, environmental, and policy constraints. We introduce WuYuEval, a multi-level benchmark for evaluating LLMs in SWM across foundational knowledge, domain reasoning, and expert decision-making. After quality auditing, WuYuEval contains a Foundation Module with 4,590 closed-ended multiple-choice questions across six task types and eight domain categories, together with an Expert Module with 247 scenario-based open-ended questions involving multi-objective optimization, constraint trade-offs, and system design. For expert tasks, we combine anchor-calibrated LLM-as-a-Judge scoring with Elo-based pairwise comparison. Across 33 LLMs, performance varied widely. The leading model reached 94.64\% accuracy on the Foundation Module, but average accuracy still fell from 84.14\% on easy questions to 42.50\% on hard questions, with lower performance concentrated in calculation, experimental design, urban planning, and open-ended expert tasks. Reasoning-oriented Thinking modes improve most matched model pairs after auditing, but the gains depend on baseline capability and are not uniformly positive. These results suggest that visible deliberation helps only when it remains anchored to units, assumptions, and engineering constraints; otherwise, it may drift from decisive answer boundaries. WuYuEval therefore provides both an evaluation resource and an empirical basis for developing SWM-oriented foundation models with professional reasoning chains and explicit constraint control.

AI.tldr: The paper presents WuYuEval, a specialized benchmark to evaluate large language models’ competence in solid waste management, spanning basic knowledge, domain reasoning, and expert-level decision-making.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM benchmarks focus mostly on general knowledge and generic reasoning, not on professional decisions that must respect engineering, environmental, and policy constraints. Solid waste management is a complex applied domain where LLM performance is unclear, and current tests don’t capture multi-objective trade-offs or system-level design choices that professionals face.
AI.method: The authors build WuYuEval, a multi-level benchmark for SWM. It has a Foundation Module with 4,590 multiple-choice questions over six task types and eight domain categories to test basic and intermediate knowledge. It also has an Expert Module with 247 open-ended, scenario-based questions targeting multi-objective optimization, constraint trade-offs, and system design. For scoring expert tasks, they combine an LLM-as-a-judge setup calibrated with anchors and an Elo-style pairwise comparison to rank model responses. They then evaluate 33 different LLMs, including variants with “reasoning-oriented” or “Thinking” modes, and compare performance across difficulty levels, task types, and prompting modes.
AI.result: Among 33 LLMs, scores span a wide range. The top model achieves 94.64% accuracy on the Foundation Module, yet average accuracy declines markedly from 84.14% on easy questions to 42.50% on hard ones. Weaknesses cluster in calculation-heavy problems, experimental design, urban planning aspects, and the open-ended expert tasks. Reasoning-oriented “Thinking” modes generally improve performance across many matched model pairs, but the benefits are uneven and depend strongly on the base model’s capability, with some cases showing no improvement or even degradation.
AI.conclusion: WuYuEval offers a domain-specific benchmark and empirical analysis framework for testing LLMs in solid waste management, highlighting significant gaps between current LLM performance and expert-level decision-making, especially under complex constraints. The findings indicate that visible chain-of-thought or “deliberation” only helps when reasoning remains grounded in correct units, assumptions, and engineering constraints; otherwise it can introduce drift and errors. The benchmark is positioned as both an evaluation resource and a guide for developing SWM-focused foundation models that feature robust professional reasoning chains and explicit control of constraints.

title: Search-G1: Grounded Search Agents via Representation-Based Intrinsic Rewards
summary: Search-augmented language agents should retrieve external information only when necessary and ground their answers in retrieved evidence. Existing external rewards provide either sparse outcome supervision or richer feedback from process annotations and LLM judges. Outcome rewards scale readily but cannot distinguish grounded retrieval from redundant search, whereas richer signals require costly annotation or inference during training. Internal rewards based on policy-side signals such as entropy, likelihood, or information gain are graded and inexpensive to evaluate, yet mainly reflect model confidence rather than evidence grounding. We propose Search-G1, a representation-based intrinsic reward framework that measures the operational grounding of an agent's answers through two intervention-calibrated readouts. A prompt-state readout predicts closed-book sufficiency, whose complement defines policy-relative retrieval necessity; an answer-commit readout estimates evidence reliance from answer-stage sensitivity to evidence deletion. Together, they provide additional credit to correct searched trajectories when retrieval is estimated necessary and the answer is evidence-sensitive, favor correct direct answers when closed-book knowledge suffices, and penalize repeated search. After calibration, reward scoring requires neither process annotations nor LLM-as-judge inference during policy optimization. Because reinforcement learning changes policy representations, Search-G1 periodically refits both readouts on trajectories from the latest checkpoint, allowing the reward to co-evolve with the policy. Experiments across multiple search-based question-answering benchmarks and two model scales show that Search-G1 improves the grounding--search-cost trade-off, producing shorter response-side trajectories at competitive task accuracy. Code is available at https://github.com/Rosy0912/Search-G1.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Search-G1, an intrinsic reward framework that encourages language agents to retrieve information only when necessary and to ground their answers in retrieved evidence, improving the trade-off between grounding and search cost.
AI.motivation: Search-augmented language agents often either over-search or fail to ground their answers properly. Existing external rewards are either sparse and unable to distinguish useful from redundant retrieval, or require expensive process annotations or LLM judges. Internal rewards are cheaper but primarily measure confidence rather than true evidence grounding. The authors aim to design a scalable, fine-grained reward signal that directly reflects when retrieval is needed and whether answers genuinely rely on retrieved evidence.
AI.method: The authors propose Search-G1, a representation-based intrinsic reward framework with two intervention-calibrated readouts. (1) A prompt-state readout predicts whether the model can answer a question correctly in closed-book mode; its complement defines when retrieval is necessary relative to the current policy. (2) An answer-commit readout estimates how much an answer depends on retrieved evidence by measuring sensitivity to evidence deletion at the answer stage. These readouts are trained via calibration interventions and then used to shape rewards: giving extra credit to correct answers when retrieval is estimated necessary and the answer is evidence-sensitive, rewarding direct correct answers without retrieval when closed-book suffices, and penalizing redundant repeated searches. During reinforcement learning, because the policy representation drifts, both readouts are periodically refit on new trajectories from the latest checkpoint so that the intrinsic reward remains aligned with the evolving policy.
AI.result: In experiments on several search-based QA benchmarks and across two model sizes, agents trained with Search-G1 achieve a better balance between evidence grounding and search cost. They produce shorter response-side trajectories (i.e., fewer search and reasoning steps) while maintaining competitive task accuracy compared to baselines using outcome-only rewards or more expensive supervision. This demonstrates that representation-based internal rewards can effectively guide retrieval behavior without expensive external annotations or LLM-judge calls.
AI.conclusion: Search-G1 offers a scalable way to train search-augmented language agents to retrieve only when needed and to ground their answers in retrieved evidence. By using representation-based readouts that are periodically recalibrated during RL, the framework provides informative intrinsic rewards without relying on costly external supervision. The approach improves the grounding–search-cost trade-off and suggests that internal, intervention-calibrated signals are a promising direction for aligning language agents’ search behavior with principled notions of retrieval necessity and evidence reliance.

title: Towards an Argumentative Foundation for Evaluative AI
summary: Evaluative AI (EAI) has been recently proposed as a way to support human decision-making, not by producing a single recommendation, but by presenting competing hypotheses together with evidence for and against each. In this position paper, we advocate (computational) argumentation as a particularly suitable paradigm to provide a formal, computable foundation for forms of EAI that are explainable and contestable, setting the ground for a long-term research agenda towards distributed and human-centred EAI systems.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes using computational argumentation as a foundation for Evaluative AI that supports human decision-making by presenting competing hypotheses and their supporting and opposing evidence, aiming for explainable and contestable, human-centred, and distributed AI systems.
AI.motivation: Traditional AI decision support often provides single recommendations without adequately exposing alternative options, underlying reasons, or conflicts, limiting transparency, explainability, and users' ability to contest or scrutinize outcomes. Evaluative AI (EAI) has been introduced to address this by offering multiple hypotheses and their evidence, but it needs a rigorous formal and computational basis to be reliable, scalable, and systematically explainable.
AI.method: This is a position paper rather than an empirical or technical paper. The authors conceptually argue that computational argumentation frameworks (e.g., abstract and structured argumentation) are well-suited as a formal basis for EAI. They outline how argumentation can represent competing hypotheses as arguments, encode supporting and attacking evidence as relations, and enable algorithmic evaluation and comparison of hypotheses within an explainable, contestable framework. They also sketch how such an approach can support distributed and human-centred systems.
AI.result: The paper does not present experimental results; instead, it presents a conceptual mapping between EAI requirements (explainability, contestability, handling competing hypotheses) and the capabilities of computational argumentation. It identifies benefits, challenges, and open problems, and articulates directions for developing argumentation-based EAI architectures and interaction mechanisms for human decision-makers.
AI.conclusion: Computational argumentation is a promising paradigm to underpin Evaluative AI systems that go beyond single recommendations, enabling the presentation and comparison of competing hypotheses with explicit pro and con evidence. This foundation can make EAI systems more explainable, contestable, and aligned with human decision-making processes, and it opens a long-term research agenda toward distributed, human-centred EAI infrastructures.

title: Scaling Inherently Interpretable Language Models
summary:
Interpretability is often treated as a tax on capability: language models are trained as opaque systems, then explained after the fact, with methods whose reliability is difficult to establish. In this work, we challenge this premise. Rather than reverse-engineering a model, we make interpretability a constraint of the training pipeline, optimized alongside the language modeling objective. Across three orders of magnitude of compute, on both autoregressive and diffusion language models, interpretability scales with capability rather than against it. Surprisingly, model representations become more disentangled and aligned with human-understandable concepts with scale.
  We instantiate the training-time recipe with Steerling-8B, a diffusion language model with a causal attention mask. For any group of generated tokens, Steerling-8B attributes the output to relevant input tokens, human-understandable concepts, and training data. This enables closed-loop intervention: diagnose an output through its concept or feature attribution, retrieve similar training data, and correct the behavior through concept steering without retraining. Steerling-8B remains competitive with open peer models trained on substantially 2-16x more compute, suggesting a different scaling paradigm: interpretability can be designed into training, and it improves with scale.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes making interpretability a core training objective for language models instead of a post-hoc add-on, showing that interpretability can scale with capability. They introduce Steerling-8B, a diffusion language model trained with built-in attribution and steering mechanisms that remains competitive with larger models trained on more compute.
AI.motivation: Most current language models are opaque: they are trained solely for performance and then analyzed using post-hoc interpretability tools whose fidelity is uncertain. This creates a perceived tradeoff where more capable models are harder to understand or control. The authors aim to challenge this tradeoff by asking whether interpretability can be embedded directly into the training process such that it improves, rather than degrades, as models scale.
AI.method: The authors incorporate interpretability as an explicit constraint in the training pipeline, optimized jointly with the language modeling objective, for both autoregressive and diffusion language models. They conduct scaling experiments across three orders of magnitude of compute to study how interpretability behaves with scale. They instantiate their approach in a concrete model, Steerling-8B, a diffusion language model with a causal attention mask, equipped with mechanisms for attributing outputs to input tokens, intermediate human-understandable concepts, and training data. They design the system to support closed-loop interventions (diagnose via attribution, retrieve similar data, and steer concepts) without full retraining.
AI.result: Empirically, the authors find that as they scale compute, model interpretability improves along with model capability: internal representations become more disentangled and better aligned with human-understandable concepts. Steerling-8B can attribute its generated tokens to specific input tokens, identified concepts, and related training examples. It supports effective concept steering interventions to correct undesirable behaviors. Performance-wise, Steerling-8B is competitive with open peer models that used 2–16x more compute, indicating that this interpretability-constrained training does not come at a major capability cost and may confer efficiency benefits.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that interpretability does not need to be a performance tax; instead, it can be integrated into the core training process and actually scales positively with model capability. By demonstrating Steerling-8B, the authors argue for a new scaling paradigm where models are designed from the outset to expose faithful attributions over inputs, concepts, and training data, enabling efficient closed-loop debugging and steering. This suggests that future large language models can be both powerful and inherently more transparent and controllable if interpretability is treated as a first-class training objective.

title: Flow-by-Flow:Content-Judgment Bypass for Governing AI Output in High-Loss Domains
summary: Prior work showed that human-in-the-loop oversight becomes structurally untenable in high-loss domains when AI output velocity V exceeds human cognitive capacity C_max. The operative constraint, however, is not V alone but V x L, where L denotes per-item cognitive load. L consists of triage, judgment, and response, which respond asymmetrically to AI capability improvement. Triage cost does not decline as models become more capable, because semantic indeterminacy is inherent in general-purpose design. Response cost is invariant to accuracy improvements. Only judgment cost faces downward pressure, and this pressure often operates by inducing omission rather than genuine reduction. Capability improvement therefore restructures L rather than reducing it. Governance mechanisms based on evaluating whether AI output is correct either delegate that evaluation to AI and inherit hallucination risk, or delegate it to humans and face the V x L ceiling. We propose Flow-by-Flow, a governance paradigm that controls supervisory load without evaluating content. A cognitive cost score based on formal, countable features imposes nonlinear costs on high-volume production, while an institutional capacity cap keeps processing volume within C_max. We derive four design invariants for any content-judgment-bypass exceedance pathway: no content judgment, no scalable consumption of examiner capacity, identity-bound per-application friction, and no batch clearance. One reference implementation is discussed to show that these invariants are jointly satisfiable, while its practical difficulties are explicitly acknowledged. An illustrative Monte Carlo analysis across 1,000 parameter draws suggests that composite multi-metric flow control outperforms supervision reinforcement alone in 90.8% of trials.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that human oversight of high-velocity AI systems fails because the true constraint is human cognitive load (velocity × per-item load), and proposes a new “Flow-by-Flow” governance paradigm that limits output via cognitive-cost scoring and capacity caps without judging content.
AI.motivation: As AI systems generate outputs at increasing speed and scale in high-loss domains, relying on humans to check whether each output is correct becomes impossible: humans either cannot keep up (velocity exceeds cognitive capacity) or must delegate checking to AI, reintroducing hallucination and error risk. Existing governance frameworks mostly assume we can keep evaluating content quality, but they ignore how per-item cognitive load decomposes and how capability gains actually shift, rather than reduce, that load. The authors are motivated to find a governance mechanism that remains workable as AI scale rises, without assuming scalable human content judgment.
AI.method: The authors first provide a conceptual and structural analysis of human cognitive load in AI oversight, decomposing it into triage, judgment, and response. They examine how each component scales with AI capability, arguing that only judgment can be partially reduced and often via omission. They then formalize a constraint based on output velocity times per-item load relative to maximum cognitive capacity. Building on this, they design a “Flow-by-Flow” paradigm that uses a cognitive cost score derived from formal, countable features of AI outputs and workflows, combined with institutional capacity caps, to constrain throughput. They further derive four design invariants that any governance scheme must satisfy if it wants to bypass content judgment. Finally, they implement a reference system consistent with these invariants and run a Monte Carlo simulation across many parameter sets to compare composite multi-metric flow control with supervision reinforcement alone.
AI.result: Conceptually, the paper shows that capability improvements in AI do not remove the V × L bottleneck for human oversight because triage and response costs remain nondecreasing and judgment cost reductions are limited and often illusory. Formally, it derives four invariants for any governance pathway that avoids direct content judgment: (1) no content judgment, (2) no scalable consumption of examiner capacity, (3) identity-bound friction for each application, and (4) no batch clearance. The reference implementation demonstrates that a system satisfying all four invariants is possible, though operationally challenging. In simulation, a Monte Carlo analysis over 1,000 parameter draws finds that composite multi-metric flow control outperforms reinforcement of traditional supervision mechanisms in 90.8% of cases, suggesting that flow-based controls are generally more effective for managing oversight load.
AI.conclusion: Human-in-the-loop content evaluation cannot scale in high-loss, high-velocity AI deployments because the real constraint is human cognitive capacity applied to velocity times per-item cognitive load. AI capability gains mainly reconfigure, rather than shrink, this load and cannot resolve the structural bottleneck. Governance mechanisms that rely on checking correctness must either offload judgment to AI—accepting hallucination risk—or hit a hard ceiling in human oversight capacity. The proposed Flow-by-Flow paradigm offers a viable alternative by regulating the volume and structure of AI outputs using cognitive cost scores and capacity caps without inspecting content. The four derived invariants provide design constraints for any such system, and preliminary simulation evidence indicates that composite, multi-metric flow control is typically more effective than simply reinforcing human supervision, though practical implementation challenges remain and require further work.

title: Embedding Initialization for Unseen Low-resource Languages in Multilingual NMT: A Case Study on Limbum-English Translation
summary: Multilingual neural machine translation models such as NLLB-200 cover 200 languages but leave thousands unsupported, including most Grassfields Bantu languages of Cameroon. When fine-tuning these models for an unseen language, practitioners must choose a proxy language token, yet no principled method exists for this selection. We implemented an embedding initialization strategy where a language token is the average of embeddings from multiple typologically related languages already in the mod el. We evaluate this approach on Limbum-to-English translation using a parallel corpus of 8,837 sentence pairs from New Testament text and a bilingual dictionary. We compare models: NLLB-200 zero-shot (chrF2++ = 12.5), a Transformer trained from scratch (chrF2++ = 14.5), NLLB-200 fine-tuned with a Swahili proxy token (chrF2++ = 47.3), and NLLB-200 with our averaged embedding initialization (chrF2++ = 46.7). We find that the multi-language initialization achieves performance comparable to the best single-language proxy. Both NLLB-200 variants improve over the from-scratch baseline by over 32 chrF2++ points. These results show that multilingual transfer is the dominant factor in extremely low-resource Bantu translation while eliminating the need for heuristic proxy selection. However, all systems fail to preserve tonal diacritics, highlighting an open challenge. We make our dataset and code available to support further research.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates how to effectively fine-tune a multilingual NMT model (NLLB-200) for an unseen, extremely low-resource language (Limbum) using a principled language-token initialization based on averaging related language embeddings, and shows that multilingual transfer dominates performance while proxy choice can be systematized.
AI.motivation: Many multilingual NMT models support hundreds of languages but still exclude thousands of low-resource ones, such as most Grassfields Bantu languages of Cameroon. When adapting these models to an unseen language, practitioners must choose a proxy language token in an ad hoc, heuristic way, with no principled or tested methodology. There is a need to both extend coverage to these languages and reduce guesswork in proxy selection while understanding how much multilingual transfer helps in extremely low-resource settings.
AI.method: The authors propose an embedding initialization strategy for unseen language tokens in NLLB-200. Instead of reusing a single proxy language token (e.g., Swahili), they construct the new language token embedding as the average of embeddings from multiple typologically related languages already in the model. They then fine-tune NLLB-200 on Limbum-to-English using an 8,837-sentence parallel New Testament corpus plus a bilingual dictionary. They compare: (1) NLLB-200 zero-shot on Limbum, (2) a Transformer trained from scratch on the same parallel data, (3) NLLB-200 fine-tuned using Swahili as a single proxy token, and (4) NLLB-200 fine-tuned using the proposed averaged multi-language initialization. chrF2++ is used as the main evaluation metric, and tonal diacritic preservation is analyzed qualitatively/quantitatively.
AI.result: Zero-shot NLLB-200 performs poorly on Limbum (chrF2++ = 12.5). A Transformer trained from scratch modestly improves to 14.5, demonstrating the difficulty of the setting. Fine-tuning NLLB-200 with a Swahili proxy token yields a large improvement (chrF2++ = 47.3), showing strong benefits from multilingual transfer. The proposed averaged embedding initialization achieves chrF2++ = 46.7, statistically comparable to the best single-language proxy. Both NLLB-200 variants outperform the from-scratch baseline by more than 32 chrF2++ points. However, all approaches systematically fail to preserve tonal diacritics in Limbum, indicating a major unresolved issue.
AI.conclusion: Multilingual transfer from a large model like NLLB-200 is the key driver of performance in extremely low-resource Bantu translation, far outweighing architecture or from-scratch training approaches. A principled multi-language embedding initialization for unseen language tokens can match the best carefully chosen single proxy language, thereby removing the need for heuristic proxy selection. Yet, the inability of all tested systems to handle tonal diacritics remains a significant challenge. The authors release their Limbum-English dataset and code to facilitate further work on low-resource, tonal, and Bantu languages in multilingual NMT.

title: Determinization in Structure Theories: A Unified Framework via Closure, Comparability, and Joint Admissibility
comment: Formal framework paper on canonicalization and determinization in structure theories; version v2.16.4; 29 pages
summary:
We develop a formal framework for constructing canonical interpretations from plural structure theories. A structure theory is a triple T = (Σ, A, I) consisting of a signature, axioms, and an inference policy, whose admissible interpretation family collects all globally consistent assignments of structural conclusions.
  We distinguish three levels of canonicalization: closure stabilization (per-seed convergence), global completion (seed-independent convergence), and determinization (a unique admissible interpretation). Non-determinism is classified into epistemic plurality (Type E) and structural plurality (Type S), with a refined Type S-strong subclass characterized by the absence of common upper bounds.
  Two canonicalization mechanisms arise: operator-based completion and selector-based construction. We provide sufficient structural conditions under which these mechanisms exist, and show that pure inference-based completion reduces to a saturated closure operator under positive, non-retractive rules with an additional soundness condition. For Type E theories, closure stabilization is established, while full determinization depends on a global confluence property that remains open. For Type S-strong theories, determinization is achieved via canonical selection.
  We further show that multi-level canonicalization forms a structurally non-commutative system via staged operators, and provide a conditional classification theorem reducing theory-intrinsic mechanisms to closure or selection. The framework also applies to LLM-assisted reasoning, where hallucination can be viewed as unsupported canonicalization.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a general logical framework that turns non-deterministic “plural” structure theories into more canonical, deterministic interpretations, classifies types of non-determinism, and shows when and how various canonicalization mechanisms exist.
AI.motivation: Many logical and structural theories allow multiple admissible interpretations (plurality), which complicates reasoning, automation, and applications like LLM-assisted inference. The authors want a general way to (a) describe such plural theories, (b) understand why non-determinism arises, and (c) systematically convert them into canonical (ideally unique) interpretations when possible, thereby improving predictability and soundness of reasoning systems.
AI.method: They formalize a “structure theory” as a triple T = (Σ, A, I) of signature, axioms, and inference policy, and define its admissible interpretation family as all globally consistent assignments of structural conclusions. Within this setting, they define three levels of canonicalization (closure stabilization, global completion, determinization) and a typology of non-determinism (Type E epistemic, Type S structural, and S-strong). They then construct two general canonicalization mechanisms: (1) operator-based completion via closure operators and (2) selector-based construction via canonical selection functions. They prove sufficient structural conditions on T under which these mechanisms exist, show that under positive, non-retractive rules and a soundness condition pure inference gives a saturated closure operator, and analyze when each type of plurality can be reduced by these mechanisms. They also investigate algebraic properties of composing canonicalization stages and derive a classification theorem relating intrinsic canonicalization to closure vs. selection, and discuss how the framework models LLM-assisted reasoning.
AI.result: The paper shows that: (1) three precise levels of canonicalization can be defined (per-seed convergence, seed-independent convergence, and uniqueness of interpretation); (2) non-determinism in structure theories splits into epistemic (Type E) and structural (Type S), with S-strong capturing cases lacking common upper bounds; (3) two generic canonicalization mechanisms exist—operator-based completion and selector-based construction—and they exist under stated structural conditions; (4) for theories with positive, non-retractive, sound rules, inference-based completion is equivalent to a saturated closure operator; (5) all Type E theories enjoy closure stabilization, though full determinization requires a strong global confluence property that is not yet fully characterized; (6) Type S-strong theories can be determinized via canonical selection; and (7) multi-level canonicalization is structurally non-commutative, and intrinsic canonicalization mechanisms can be conditionally classified as arising from closure or selection. They also identify how the framework interprets LLM hallucination as a form of unsupported canonicalization.
AI.conclusion: The framework provides a unified, structural account of how plural structure theories can be made more canonical, explaining and classifying different sources of non-determinism and showing when they can be resolved by closure-like operators or selection functions. It clarifies that canonicalization typically proceeds in stages that do not commute, that epistemic and structural plurality behave differently with respect to determinization, and that for important classes of inference policies canonical interpretations correspond to saturated closures. The results both systematize canonicalization in abstract logical settings and suggest principled ways to understand and constrain canonicalization-like behavior in applied systems such as LLM-assisted reasoning, where hallucinations correspond to illegitimate canonicalization steps.

title: SurveyReview: A Reviewer-Aligned Benchmark for Survey Evaluators
summary: The rapid advancement of large language models has transformed survey writing from a months-long manual effort into an automated process. As generation scales, reliable evaluation becomes the bottleneck, and LLMs are increasingly used as survey evaluators. However, existing approaches largely rely on off-the-shelf LLM-as-a-judge methods without systematic alignment to human reviewers, and there remains a lack of systematic frameworks for quantifying alignment with human reviewers. To address this gap, we propose SurveyReview, a reviewer-aligned, multi-dimensional benchmark and dataset for survey evaluation. We collect and annotate 675 survey papers with 1,630 review reports. We structure authentic peer-review reports by converting free-form comments into four-dimensional scores (Readability, Criticalness, Comprehensiveness, Structure) paired with supporting rationales. We further release standardized train/test splits and an evaluation protocol to measure alignment between automatic evaluators and human reviewers. To validate the benchmark, we develop SurveyAlign, a strong baseline evaluator by fine-tuning Qwen3-32B with LoRA on our annotated data, augmented with external knowledge for knowledge-intensive dimensions. On the test set, SurveyAlign substantially improves reviewer alignment over prompt-based judging with GPT-5.2, reducing average MSE from 2.28 to 1.38 and MAE from 1.15 to 0.69 across all four dimensions. Our contributions are twofold: (1) we establish the first multi-dimensional, reviewer-aligned dataset with a reproducible evaluation framework for survey reviewing; (2) we develop a strong baseline evaluator that substantially improves alignment with human reviewers, providing a competitive reference for future research. Our code and data are available at https://surveyreview.github.io

AI.tldr: Introduces SurveyReview, a benchmark and dataset to align LLM-based survey evaluators with human peer reviewers, plus SurveyAlign, a fine-tuned model that better matches human review scores than prompt-based GPT-5.2.
AI.motivation: As LLMs automate survey paper generation, evaluation becomes the bottleneck. Current LLM-as-a-judge methods for survey evaluation are not systematically aligned with human reviewers and lack a framework to quantify this alignment. There is a need for a standardized, multi-dimensional benchmark and methodology to measure and improve how well automatic evaluators match human peer reviews.
AI.method: The authors construct SurveyReview by collecting 675 survey papers and 1,630 authentic peer-review reports. They transform free-form review comments into four numerical dimensions—Readability, Criticalness, Comprehensiveness, and Structure—each paired with textual rationales. They provide standardized train/test splits and an evaluation protocol for measuring alignment (e.g., via MSE and MAE) between automatic evaluators and human reviewers. To validate the benchmark, they develop SurveyAlign by fine-tuning the Qwen3-32B model using LoRA on this annotated dataset, incorporating external knowledge sources for knowledge-intensive aspects of evaluation.
AI.result: SurveyAlign, evaluated on the SurveyReview test set, substantially improves alignment with human reviewers compared to prompt-based GPT-5.2 judges. Specifically, it reduces average mean squared error from 2.28 to 1.38 and mean absolute error from 1.15 to 0.69 across the four evaluation dimensions. This demonstrates both the value of the benchmark and the effectiveness of model fine-tuning on reviewer-aligned data.
AI.conclusion: SurveyReview provides the first multi-dimensional, reviewer-aligned benchmark and reproducible evaluation framework specifically for survey paper reviewing, enabling systematic study of LLM-as-a-judge alignment with human peers. The proposed baseline, SurveyAlign, shows that targeted fine-tuning on structured peer-review data meaningfully improves alignment, offering a strong reference point and resources (code and data) for future work on automatic survey evaluation.

title: Emotion in an active inference model of human driving
summary: Active inference has emerged as a principled framework for modeling adaptive behavior by balancing goal-directed action with uncertainty reduction. It has been successfully applied across biological and artificial systems, including recent work on human driving. However, existing active inference models of driving have yet to address an important determinant of behavior in traffic: affective state, which significantly influences decision-making. Prior work in non-traffic domains has explored active inference agents in which emotions are represented along the axes of valence and arousal in the circumplex model. However, this work has been limited to simplified settings with discrete state spaces. In this work, we propose an expanded formulation of valence and arousal that can be extracted from a more complex active inference model of driving with continuous states. In particular, we condition affective estimates not only on the current state but also on predicted future outcomes. We evaluate the proposed approach in two interactive driving scenarios and show that the resulting emotion signals correspond to affective patterns reported in similar scenarios.

AI.tldr: The paper extends active inference driving models by integrating continuous valence–arousal emotion estimates, conditioned on both current and predicted future states, and validates them in interactive driving scenarios.
AI.motivation: Existing active inference models of driving capture goal-directed behavior and uncertainty reduction but ignore affective state, despite its known impact on traffic decisions. Prior affective active inference work uses valence–arousal representations only in simplified, discrete settings, which is inadequate for realistic, continuous driving environments. The authors aim to bridge this gap so that computational driving models better reflect human-like emotional influences on behavior.
AI.method: The authors develop an expanded formulation of valence and arousal within a continuous-state active inference model of driving. Emotion estimates are derived not only from the agent’s current inferred state but also from predicted future outcomes under the generative model. They apply this formulation to interactive driving scenarios, where an active inference agent interacts with other vehicles, and compute continuous valence–arousal signals from the model’s inferences and predictions.
AI.result: In two interactive driving scenarios, the computed valence–arousal trajectories show patterns that qualitatively match affective responses reported by humans in comparable situations (e.g., stress or negative valence in risky interactions, relief or positive valence after successful maneuvers). This suggests that the proposed affective formulation yields plausible emotion-like signals in realistic driving tasks.
AI.conclusion: By integrating a continuous valence–arousal representation into a richer active inference driving model and conditioning it on both present and anticipated outcomes, the paper provides a more psychologically grounded account of how emotions may shape driving behavior. The results indicate that such affective active inference models can reproduce realistic emotional patterns in traffic scenarios, supporting their potential use for modeling, analyzing, or designing human-centered driving systems.

authors: Venkata Naga Sai Vishnu Rohit Pulipaka
title: Evaluating Dedicated Monolingual and Joint Multilingual Causal Models for Dravidian Languages
summary: Dravidian languages, mainly Tamil, Telugu, Kannada, and Malayalam make up only a small part of the data used to train multilingual language models, so it's not clear how much per-language ability these models actually keep. I have trained five GPT-2 architecture models from scratch to compare four monolingual models (one each for Tamil, Telugu, Kannada, and Malayalam, each with its own 32K-vocabulary subword tokenizer) against one multilingual model sharing a 64K-vocabulary subword tokenizer across all four languages. All the 5 models are trained on cleaned CC-100, Wikipedia, and Samanantar data. I have tested the models on perplexity, bits-per-byte, tokenizer efficiency, and fine-tuning results which are compared against mGPT. The monolingual models outperform mGPT on sentiment classification and named entity recognition, and their tokenizers proved more efficient than the shared multilingual model across all the languages tested.

AI.tldr: The paper compares monolingual and multilingual GPT-2-style models for Dravidian languages, showing monolingual models and their tokenizers perform better than a shared multilingual model and mGPT on several metrics.
AI.motivation: Dravidian languages are underrepresented in multilingual language model training data, making it unclear how well such models actually support each language. The authors aim to quantify and compare per-language capabilities and tokenizer efficiency for these low-resource but widely spoken languages.
AI.method: Train five GPT-2 architecture models from scratch on cleaned CC-100, Wikipedia, and Samanantar corpora: four monolingual models (Tamil, Telugu, Kannada, Malayalam) each with its own 32K subword vocabulary, and one multilingual model with a shared 64K subword vocabulary across all four languages. Evaluate them on perplexity, bits-per-byte, tokenizer efficiency, and downstream fine-tuning tasks, and compare with an existing multilingual model (mGPT).
AI.result: Monolingual models achieve better performance than the multilingual model and mGPT on sentiment classification and named entity recognition; their language-specific tokenizers are more efficient than the shared multilingual tokenizer for all languages.
AI.conclusion: For Dravidian languages, language-specific GPT-2 models with dedicated tokenizers provide superior performance and tokenization efficiency compared to a shared multilingual model and mGPT, suggesting that tailored monolingual models are beneficial for underrepresented languages in multilingual setups.

title: Training Variable Long Sequences with Data-Centric Parallel
summary: Training deep learning models on variable long sequences poses significant computational challenges. Existing methods force a difficult trade-off between efficiency and ease-of-use. Simple approaches use static configurations that cause workload imbalance low efficiency, while complex methods introduces significant complexity and code change for new models. To break this trade-off, we introduce Data-Centric Parallel (DCP). Its core principle is to let the data itself drive the runtime. It achieves this by dynamically adjusting direct runtime settings (e.g., parallel size, gradient accumulation, recomputation) based on each batch's sequence length. Empirical results demonstrate that our method achieves up to a 2.88$\times$ speedup on 32 H200 GPUs. Designed for generalization, it can be integrated into any model with 10 lines of code. We anticipate this simple yet effective approach will serve as a robust baseline and facilitate future advancements in distributed training for variable long sequences.

AI.tldr: They propose Data-Centric Parallel (DCP), a simple runtime mechanism that dynamically adapts parallelism and training settings to each batch’s sequence length, achieving large speedups for training models on variable-length sequences with minimal code changes.
AI.motivation: Training deep learning models on inputs with variable sequence lengths is computationally challenging because current solutions either use static configurations that cause workload imbalance and poor hardware utilization, or rely on sophisticated, model-specific techniques that require substantial code modification and engineering complexity. The authors want a method that is both efficient and easy to integrate into existing models.
AI.method: They introduce Data-Centric Parallel (DCP), which makes the data characteristics—in particular sequence length—drive the parallel training runtime. For each batch, DCP dynamically adjusts key runtime hyperparameters such as data/sequence parallel size, gradient accumulation steps, and activation recomputation settings. This adaptivity aims to keep computational load and memory usage balanced across batches and devices, while remaining model-agnostic and requiring only small code changes (around 10 lines) to integrate into arbitrary models.
AI.result: Empirical evaluation on up to 32 H200 GPUs shows that DCP can achieve as much as a 2.88× training speedup compared to baselines, indicating significantly improved efficiency for training on variable-length sequences while maintaining correctness.
AI.conclusion: DCP offers a practical, general, and easy-to-use approach for efficient distributed training on variable-length sequence data by allowing batch-wise dynamic adjustment of parallelism and runtime configurations. Because it is simple to integrate and yields substantial speedups, the authors argue it should serve as a strong baseline and enabler for future improvements in this area.

title: The No-Meaning Falsity: The Structural Impossibility of the Arbitrary Sign in Classical Arabic
summary: This paper investigates whether the postmodern claim of unrestricted semantic indeterminacy, and its foundational Saussurean axiom of the arbitrary sign, are compatible with the structural architecture of Classical Arabic. We develop a formal mathematical model of Arabic non concatenative morphology in which lexical meaning is determined by the interaction between an invariant root and a morphosyntactic pattern. Within this framework, we establish a Morphological Correspondence Theorem, demonstrating that every lexical item is uniquely generated by a root pattern pair, and a Semantic Localization Theorem, proving that lexical meaning is determined at the derivational level prior to surface realization. To address Saussurean weaker notion of relative arbitrariness, we formalize it via conditional Kolmogorov complexity, defining arbitrariness algorithmically as the no rule property. We prove that general relative arbitrariness is formally undecidable, while Arabic relative arbitrariness is decidable and provably less than 1 for its motivated signifiers (Levels W and M), establishing a strict system complexity asymmetry over Indo-European languages.

AI.tldr: The paper tests postmodern and Saussurean claims about radical arbitrariness of the sign against the structure of Classical Arabic, using formal morphology and algorithmic information theory to show that Arabic exhibits constrained, decidable, and partly non-arbitrary sign–meaning relations.
AI.motivation: To challenge or refine the postmodern and Saussurean thesis that the relation between signifier and signified is wholly or maximally arbitrary, by examining a non-Indo-European language (Classical Arabic) whose root-and-pattern morphology may structurally encode meaning in ways that reduce arbitrariness. The authors aim to provide a rigorous, formal test case that can reveal whether such philosophical-linguistic claims are universally valid or language-specific, and to quantify degrees of arbitrariness using tools from mathematical linguistics and algorithmic complexity theory.
AI.method: The authors construct a formal mathematical model of Classical Arabic’s nonconcatenative (root-and-pattern) morphology, where lexical items are generated by combining an invariant consonantal root with a morphosyntactic pattern. Within this model, they prove (1) a Morphological Correspondence Theorem ensuring a one-to-one mapping between lexical items and specific root–pattern pairs, and (2) a Semantic Localization Theorem showing that lexical meaning is fixed at the derivational stage, before surface phonological realization. To formalize Saussure’s notion of relative arbitrariness, they use conditional Kolmogorov complexity and define arbitrariness as the absence of generative rules (the “no rule property”). They then investigate the decidability and degree of such arbitrariness for Arabic and for (implicitly) Indo-European languages, comparing system complexity and motivation levels of signifiers.
AI.result: They show that in their model each Classical Arabic lexical item is uniquely determined by a specific combination of root and morphosyntactic pattern (Morphological Correspondence Theorem), and that the semantic content of a word is already fixed at this derivational stage (Semantic Localization Theorem). Using conditional Kolmogorov complexity, they demonstrate that in the general case relative arbitrariness of sign–meaning relations is formally undecidable, but for Arabic, because of its structured root-and-pattern system, relative arbitrariness becomes a decidable property. Furthermore, for the subset of “motivated signifiers” (Levels W and M) in Arabic, the quantified measure of arbitrariness is strictly less than 1, implying a systematic, non-maximally arbitrary relationship between form and meaning. This yields a provable asymmetry in system complexity between Classical Arabic and Indo-European languages, with Arabic exhibiting a more constrained, motivated morphology–semantics interface.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that the strong postmodern and Saussurean thesis of unrestricted or maximal arbitrariness of the linguistic sign is incompatible with the structural and semantic organization of Classical Arabic. The formal model and theorems show that Arabic’s nonconcatenative morphology enforces a unique mapping between roots, patterns, and lexical items, and that meaning is localized at the derivational level, resulting in a partially non-arbitrary and algorithmically decidable sign system. By quantifying arbitrariness via Kolmogorov complexity, the authors argue that Classical Arabic has a lower degree of arbitrariness and higher structural motivation in its signifiers than typical Indo-European languages, challenging the universality of postmodern and Saussurean claims and highlighting language-specific constraints on semantic indeterminacy.

title: The Knowing-Saying Gap: When Probes See Errors that Confidence Misses
summary: Linear probes detect corrupted context in language models with near-perfect accuracy, yet this does not translate into reliable failure prediction. The result is a dissociation with direct implications for deployment monitoring. Across multi-hop arithmetic chains, probes that detect corruption turn out to be uninformative about final answer correctness; models forced into structured confidence formats collapse to two values with indistinguishable error rates; and probe persistence across hops fails to separate correct from incorrect outcomes, refuting our pre-registered "persistence beats peak" hypothesis. This pattern of knowing but not saying generalises across model families including reasoning models. As a real-time monitor, probe-based interventions are sharply model and error-type dependent: branch-and-pick is net-positive across models and uniquely non-breaking on Llama-3.1-8B (4 rescued, 0 broken), while reprompt and replace-prior break correct traces at roughly the rate they rescue wrong ones. Probe-based monitoring is a necessary complement to verbalised confidence, but no single intervention dominates, and the deployable answer is model-aware, error-type-aware routing.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that linear probes can very accurately detect when intermediate reasoning in language models is corrupted, but this signal does not reliably predict whether the final answer is wrong, so monitoring and interventions must be model- and error-type-specific rather than relying on a single probe-based strategy.
AI.motivation: As language models are deployed in real settings, we need reliable ways to detect when they are going wrong. Linear probes on internal representations look promising because they can detect corrupted intermediate states with high accuracy, suggesting they might serve as real-time monitors or failure predictors. However, it is unclear whether this internal knowledge actually translates into reliable signals about final answer correctness or supports robust interventions across models and error types.
AI.method: The authors study multi-hop arithmetic reasoning chains in several language model families, including specialized reasoning models. They train linear probes on internal activations to detect corrupted context at different reasoning steps. They then evaluate how well these probes predict final answer correctness, including tests of a pre-registered hypothesis that the persistence of probe-detected corruption across hops would outperform peak corruption in predicting failure. They also constrain models to structured confidence formats to analyze the relationship between expressed confidence and error rates. Finally, they design and test several probe-based interventions—branch-and-pick, reprompt, and replace-prior—as real-time monitoring strategies, measuring how often these interventions rescue incorrect traces vs. break correct ones across models.
AI.result: Linear probes can almost perfectly detect corrupted intermediate context, but this signal largely fails to predict whether the final answer is correct. Probes that detect corruption provide little information about answer correctness; structured confidence outputs collapse to just two confidence values with similar error rates; and corruption persistence across reasoning hops does not distinguish correct from incorrect answers, falsifying the pre-registered “persistence beats peak” hypothesis. The dissociation between internal detection (knowing) and outward behavior (saying) is observed across different model families, including reasoning-oriented models. For intervention strategies, branch-and-pick is consistently net beneficial and uniquely non-breaking on Llama-3.1-8B (rescuing 4 wrong traces and breaking none), whereas reprompt and replace-prior disrupt correct reasoning about as often as they fix incorrect reasoning.
AI.conclusion: Linear probes reveal that models internally register corrupted context, but this internal signal does not straightforwardly translate into reliable failure prediction or uniform monitoring strategies. Probe-based signals and verbalized confidence are complementary but individually insufficient for robust deployment monitoring. No single probe-based intervention is universally superior; effective, deployable monitoring must be tailored to the specific model and error types, using routing strategies that choose among interventions in a model-aware and error-type-aware manner.

title: Jako Tako or Fluent? Presenting PoVisLE: A Polish Vision-Language Evaluation
summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) have achieved strong performance on tasks such as image captioning, visual question answering, and image-to-text generation. However, they are predominantly trained on English-centric data, which limits their ability to handle culturally grounded visual understanding and leads to failures in interpreting region-specific meanings, symbolic content, and context-dependent visual cues. Existing benchmarks for cultural competence are often template-driven and focused on surface-level recognition, making them insufficient for evaluating deeper linguistic and pragmatic understanding in culturally situated settings. We introduce PoVisLE, a monocultural vision-language benchmark for Polish designed to evaluate culturally grounded multimodal understanding under a grounded evaluation paradigm, where language is interpreted in interaction with visual context. The dataset contains 1,117 images and 2,366 manually annotated VQA pairs. Overall, our dataset provides a controlled and challenging resource for assessing culturally grounded vision-language understanding beyond surface-level recognition.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces PoVisLE, a Polish monocultural vision-language benchmark to evaluate culturally grounded multimodal understanding beyond surface-level recognition.
AI.motivation: Most existing vision-language models are trained on English-centric data, limiting their ability to interpret culturally specific visual cues, symbols, and contexts. Current cultural competence benchmarks are template-based and focus on shallow recognition, failing to test deeper linguistic, pragmatic, and culturally situated understanding. There is a need for a benchmark that captures culturally grounded multimodal understanding in a non-English context, specifically Polish.
AI.method: The authors construct PoVisLE, a monocultural Polish vision-language benchmark under a grounded evaluation paradigm. They collect 1,117 images relevant to Polish culture and manually annotate 2,366 visual question answering (VQA) pairs, where the language must be interpreted in interaction with the visual context. The benchmark is designed to test deeper, culturally grounded reasoning rather than just surface-level recognition.
AI.result: The outcome is a curated dataset comprising 1,117 images and 2,366 manually annotated Polish VQA pairs. Empirical performance numbers are not given in the abstract, but the dataset is presented as controlled and challenging for evaluating cultural grounding in VLMs.
AI.conclusion: PoVisLE offers a focused resource for assessing and advancing vision-language models’ abilities to perform culturally grounded understanding in Polish settings, moving evaluation beyond template-driven, surface-level recognition to deeper multimodal, context-sensitive reasoning.

title: NL2SHACL-Bench: A Benchmark Suite for Natural Language to SHACL Translation
summary: SHACL is a core technology for validating the conformance of RDF knowledge graphs (KGs). Yet, authoring SHACL shapes requires technical expertise that most domain experts lack. Translating natural language requirements into SHACL (NL2SHACL) would lower this barrier. However, there is no dedicated benchmark for NL2SHACL, and evaluating generated shapes requires methods beyond string comparison, as semantically equivalent shapes can differ in serialisation and structure. To tackle these challenges, we present NL2SHACL-Bench, a benchmark suite for natural language to SHACL translation. Using NL2SHACL-Bench, we evaluate four state-of-the-art large language models (LLMs) for this task. Our results show that current LLMs are highly capable of generating syntactically valid SHACL, but still struggle to produce semantically equivalent constraints for complex logical and structural patterns. This indicates that NL2SHACL-Bench provides a meaningful basis for measuring advances in the NL2SHACL state of the art.

AI.tldr: They introduce NL2SHACL-Bench, a benchmark for translating natural language requirements into SHACL constraints, and show that current large language models can generate valid SHACL syntax but often fail on complex semantic constraints.
AI.motivation: Creating SHACL shapes to validate RDF knowledge graphs is difficult for non-technical domain experts. Automatically translating natural language requirements into SHACL (NL2SHACL) could make SHACL more accessible, but there is no dedicated benchmark to evaluate such systems and simple string-based evaluation fails because semantically equivalent SHACL shapes can look different. A robust benchmark and evaluation methodology are therefore needed.
AI.method: The authors design and release NL2SHACL-Bench, a benchmark suite specifically for the natural language to SHACL translation task. They then use this benchmark to systematically evaluate four state-of-the-art large language models on their ability to generate SHACL from natural language, employing evaluation procedures that go beyond surface string matching to assess syntactic validity and semantic equivalence of the produced shapes, including for complex logical and structural constraints.
AI.result: Experiments on NL2SHACL-Bench show that all evaluated LLMs are generally good at producing syntactically correct SHACL shapes, meaning the generated code parses and follows SHACL syntax. However, their performance drops when dealing with more complex logical combinations and structural constraints, where the models often fail to capture the intended semantics present in the natural language requirements.
AI.conclusion: NL2SHACL-Bench effectively exposes current limitations of LLMs in capturing complex SHACL semantics even though they handle syntax well. This demonstrates that the benchmark is a useful tool for tracking progress on the NL2SHACL task and can guide future research toward methods that better encode and reason about the logical and structural nuances of SHACL constraints.

title: On the use of foundation models in cognitive science
summary: A host of recent studies have evaluated the cognitive and developmental alignment of Foundation Models (FMs). These investigations include evaluations of their correspondence to adult performance across a range of cognitive domains, as well as whether aspects of model training track children's cognitive development. However, using FMs as candidate cognitive models poses significant methodological and conceptual challenges. A key question underlies this effort: under what conditions does behavioral alignment justify treating FMs as explanatory models of cognition? In this paper, we articulate a four-stage inferential framework for evaluating FMs as cognitive and developmental models: adapting human experimental tasks to model-compatible formats, specifying linking hypotheses that map model outputs to human measures, evaluating behavioral correspondence, and comparing across candidate models or manipulations. We clarify the role of linking hypotheses in mapping model outputs to human behavioral measures, identify challenges that constrain alignment claims, and propose principles for theory-driven and comparative evaluation. Throughout, we argue that behavioral fit alone is insufficient. Alignment becomes scientifically meaningful only when embedded within explicit theoretical commitments, theory-diagnostic tasks, and systematic contrastive evaluation across candidate models.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a structured framework for when and how behavioral alignment between Foundation Models (FMs) and humans can support claims that FMs are cognitive or developmental models, emphasizing that behavioral fit alone is not enough.
AI.motivation: Many recent studies compare Foundation Models to human cognition and development, but there is confusion and inconsistency about when such behavioral similarities actually justify treating FMs as explanatory models of the mind. The authors aim to bring conceptual and methodological clarity to these efforts so that claims about cognitive alignment are scientifically meaningful rather than superficial.
AI.method: The paper develops a four-stage inferential framework for using FMs as cognitive and developmental models: (1) systematically adapting human experimental tasks into formats suitable for FMs; (2) making explicit linking hypotheses that map model outputs to human behavioral measures; (3) rigorously evaluating behavioral correspondence between models and humans; and (4) conducting comparative analyses across different models or experimental manipulations. The authors analyze each stage, discuss typical pitfalls, and propose principles for better theory-driven evaluations.
AI.result: The authors show that many existing alignment studies implicitly rely on underspecified or unjustified linking hypotheses and task adaptations, which weakens their cognitive claims. They demonstrate, conceptually and via examples, how different choices at each stage can change conclusions about alignment, and they offer a more disciplined approach for designing, interpreting, and comparing FM–human alignment studies.
AI.conclusion: Behavioral alignment between FMs and humans is not, by itself, sufficient evidence that FMs are good models of human cognition or development. Such alignment becomes scientifically informative only when it is grounded in explicit theoretical commitments, clear and justified linking hypotheses, carefully designed, theory-diagnostic tasks, and systematic comparisons across alternative models and manipulations. The proposed four-stage framework is intended as a methodological guide to make FM-based cognitive modeling more rigorous and interpretable.

title: Dynamic Coalition Formation and Communication Pricing in Skill-Based Agentic AI Systems
summary: Modern agentic AI systems combine multiple large language model agents with heterogeneous skills, yet most architectures either fix communication in advance or allow full broadcast. Both can be inefficient because token cost, latency, redundancy, and error propagation increase with the number of active agents and communication links. We model agent selection and communication as a cooperative game with task-conditioned net utility $U(C\mid x)=V(C\mid x)-\sum_{i\in C}c_i$, separating coalition-level costs from agent activation costs. We propose a marginal-value activation rule and greedy router, extend the model to optimize communication edges with per-edge costs, and use estimated Shapley values to predict which agents are worth contacting before and during execution. We connect the problem to submodular maximization and prove two limited guarantees: a curvature-refined bound for a monotone, cardinality-constrained special case, and a tight $1/2$-approximation, with a correction for signed objectives, for an unconstrained non-monotone case via double greedy. Neither guarantee applies directly to the main router, which remains a heuristic. We also prove a Shapley-submodularity sandwich bound linking the error of marginal-value routing to a per-agent diminishing-returns quantity. In synthetic experiments, greedy routing achieves $99.5%$ of brute-force-optimal utility while activating $1.96$ of $8$ agents on average, compared with $38.8%$ for full broadcast. Performance is robust to activation cost and redundancy weight but falls to $66%$ under strong violations of submodularity or noisy value estimates. We distinguish the framework from Shapley pricing, hedonic coalition formation, and communication-graph pruning, and propose evaluation on real multi-agent LLM benchmarks.

AI.tldr: They propose a game-theoretic, submodularity-inspired framework and greedy routing heuristic to decide which LLM agents should communicate, reducing cost and redundancy while preserving utility.
AI.motivation: Existing multi-agent LLM systems often either fix communication paths or allow full broadcast among agents. Both approaches can be inefficient because as the number of agents grows, token usage, latency, redundant work, and error propagation also grow. The authors want a principled way to selectively activate and connect agents so that communication pays off in terms of task performance minus its costs.
AI.method: They model the set of active agents as a coalition in a cooperative game with a task-conditioned utility function that separates coalition value from per-agent activation costs. On top of this, they define a marginal-value activation rule and a greedy router that incrementally selects agents and communication edges based on estimated gains in utility. They extend the model to include per-edge communication costs and leverage Shapley values to estimate each agent’s contribution and decide whom to query, both before and during task execution. Using submodular maximization theory, they derive approximation guarantees for simplified routing variants (monotone cardinality-constrained and unconstrained non-monotone with double greedy). They also prove a Shapley-submodularity sandwich bound to relate routing error to a notion of diminishing returns at the agent level.
AI.result: Synthetic experiments show that the proposed greedy routing nearly matches brute-force optimal utility (99.5%) while only activating about 1.96 out of 8 agents on average, in contrast to a full-broadcast baseline that achieves only 38.8% of optimal utility. The method remains effective under varying activation costs and redundancy penalties but degrades to about 66% of optimal utility when submodularity assumptions are strongly violated or value estimates are noisy.
AI.conclusion: The work introduces a cooperative-game and submodularity-based framework for selective agent activation and communication in multi-agent LLM systems, with a practical greedy router guided by marginal values and Shapley estimates. While the core router is still heuristic and theoretical guarantees cover only restricted cases, the synthetic results suggest substantial gains in efficiency and utility over naive full broadcast. The authors argue that their approach is distinct from related concepts such as Shapley pricing and hedonic coalition formation and recommend evaluating it on real-world multi-agent LLM benchmarks.

title: "Many Are My Names": The Anatomy of the Assistant and Its Personas via Sparse Autoencoders
summary: How a language model internally represents who is speaking, the Assistant, an assigned roleplay persona, or a narrated story character, remains underexplored. We study speaker representations using a dataset of user-expressed emotional text and corresponding model responses. We decompose three generation settings (Assistant, Roleplay, and Story) into sparse autoencoder features extracted at turn-boundary and pronoun-token positions and selected through a filtering pipeline for different depths. We characterize each surviving feature through its steering effects and activation distribution. Our main finding is that the Assistant and roleplay personas are not independent alternatives: personas retain the Assistant-associated feature core while progressively differentiating from it across layers, starting from operational machinery towards behavioral and stylistic features. Meanwhile, generated story characters lack the Assistant-associated core. Both Story and Roleplay can be distinguished from the Assistant with Immersive Simulation Mode. However, the Assistant can sometimes enter or slowly drift into it even in the default setting.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes how language models internally represent different kinds of speakers (Assistant, roleplay personas, and story characters) by examining sparse autoencoder features associated with these modes of generation.
AI.motivation: While language models can act as assistants, roleplay personas, or story narrators, it is unclear how they internally distinguish or conflate these speaker types.
