Understanding these internal representations is important for safety, controllability, and better alignment of model behavior, especially around immersive roleplay and simulation-like states.
AI.method: The authors collect a dataset consisting of emotionally rich user text and the model’s responses under three modes: Assistant, Roleplay, and Story. They extract sparse autoencoder features from model activations at specific positions (turn boundaries and pronoun tokens) across different layers. They then apply a filtering pipeline to select relevant features and characterize them by (1) how they steer generation when activated and (2) how they are distributed across layers and modes.
AI.result: They find that Assistant and roleplay personas are not represented as fully separate alternatives. Instead, roleplay personas preserve a core set of Assistant-related features and gradually diverge from them across layers, shifting from operational mechanics to behavioral and stylistic differences. In contrast, story characters do not share this Assistant core. Both Story and Roleplay states are distinguishable from the Assistant via an "Immersive Simulation Mode" representation. Nonetheless, the Assistant sometimes transitions or drifts into this immersive mode even when supposedly in a default, non-immersive setting.
AI.conclusion: The internal representations of speaker identity in language models show that roleplay personas are layered modifications of the Assistant’s core features, whereas story characters are more distinctly separated. There exists an identifiable "Immersive Simulation Mode" associated with Story and Roleplay, which the Assistant can occasionally enter unintentionally. These findings have implications for controlling model behavior, understanding how roleplay and simulation emerge, and designing mechanisms to keep Assistant behavior distinct and aligned when desired.

title: MetaSpace: Metamorphic Testing for Spatial Cognition in Embodied Agents
comment: 30 pages, 17 figures. Published in Proceedings of the ACM on Programming Languages (OOPSLA1)
summary:
An embodied agent is an intelligent entity that interacts with its environment through a physical body. Currently, the evaluation of embodied agents primarily relies on two paradigms: (1) manually annotated Visual Question Answering (VQA) pairs and (2) high-level task completion metrics, such as success in navigation or manipulation. The former is labor-intensive and subject to variability in annotation quality. The latter may obscure critical vulnerabilities, allowing agents to complete tasks through suboptimal means or safety violations, thereby concealing safety risks and inefficiencies. Given that spatial cognition is the cornerstone for executing embodied tasks, there is a pressing need to assess whether embodied agents possess robust spatial cognition during task execution.
  Inspired by metamorphic testing principles in software engineering, we propose MetaSpace, a novel framework designed to evaluate the spatial cognition of agents. By leveraging spatiotemporal multimodal states derived from real execution trajectories, MetaSpace automatically generates test cases based on predefined metamorphic relations (MRs) grounded in logical rules and physical laws. Crucially, we encode these MRs as executable rules in a logic programming language (Prolog). Violations of these relations indicate failures in spatial cognition. Our empirical evaluation across three embodied scenarios demonstrates that MetaSpace successfully detects 90,422 spatial cognition errors in state-of-the-art (SOTA) MLLM-driven agents. We introduce the Spatial Cognition (SC) score to quantify performance. Results indicate that all SOTA agents achieve average scores between 0.44 and 0.52, significantly lower than the human benchmark of 0.96.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes MetaSpace, a logic-based metamorphic testing framework to systematically evaluate the spatial cognition of embodied agents, revealing large gaps between current agents and humans.
AI.motivation: Existing evaluation methods for embodied agents either rely on manually annotated VQA pairs, which are costly and inconsistent, or on coarse task-completion metrics, which can hide safety risks and inefficiencies. Since spatial cognition is fundamental to embodied tasks, there is a need for a principled, automated way to test whether agents truly understand and reason about space during execution.
AI.method: The authors design MetaSpace, a framework inspired by metamorphic testing from software engineering. It takes spatiotemporal multimodal states from real execution trajectories of embodied agents and automatically generates test cases using predefined metamorphic relations (MRs). These MRs, grounded in logical rules and physical laws, are encoded as executable rules in Prolog. When an agent’s behavior or inferred state violates an MR, it is counted as a spatial cognition error. A Spatial Cognition (SC) score is then computed based on conformity to these relations.
AI.result: Applying MetaSpace to three embodied scenarios, the framework detects 90,422 spatial cognition errors in state-of-the-art MLLM-driven agents. The computed Spatial Cognition (SC) scores for all tested SOTA agents fall between 0.44 and 0.52, which is markedly below the human benchmark score of 0.96, indicating substantial deficits in current agents’ spatial reasoning.
AI.conclusion: MetaSpace provides an automated and principled way to stress-test and quantify the spatial cognition of embodied agents using logic-based metamorphic relations. The results show that leading MLLM-driven agents exhibit pervasive spatial cognition failures, far below human-level performance, highlighting both safety concerns and opportunities for targeted improvement in embodied AI.

title: SurakshaEval: An Indic Safety Benchmark for Multilingual LLMs
summary: Existing safety evaluation datasets for large language models (LLMs) predominantly focus on English and Western contexts, often overlooking the linguistic diversity and culturally grounded safety risks present in other languages. To address this gap, we introduce SurakshaEval, a novel safety benchmark composed of human-written prompts spanning real-world scenarios, explicitly designed for ten major Indian languages - Assamese, Bengali, Gujarati, Hindi, Kannada, Malayalam, Marathi, Punjabi, Tamil, and Telugu, along with English. SurakshaEval includes both generic prompts common across India and region- and language-specific prompts that capture localized sociocultural sensitivities. We benchmark a broad range of state-of-the-art LLMs on SurakshaEval, establish baseline safety performance, and identify recurring failure modes, including over-refusal, missed detection of implicit bias, and insufficient contextual awareness in regionally sensitive settings. Our results show that even strong multilingual LLMs struggle to reliably meet nuanced safety requirements when operating in Indic languages, particularly in native scripts. These findings highlight the urgent need for safety evaluation frameworks that incorporate region-specific data and structured assessment protocols, enabling the development and deployment of AI systems that operate securely, ethically, and in alignment with diverse societal values. Our code and data are available at https://github.com/debobanerjee/SurakshaEval. Warning: This paper contains text that may be offensive or unsafe.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces SurakshaEval, a multilingual safety benchmark for evaluating LLMs in 10 major Indian languages plus English, revealing that current models struggle with nuanced, culturally grounded safety risks in Indic languages.
AI.motivation: Most existing LLM safety benchmarks are centered on English and Western contexts, neglecting linguistic diversity and culture-specific risks. This leaves a gap in reliably assessing and ensuring AI safety for large populations that use other languages, especially Indic languages with their own scripts and sociocultural norms. The paper aims to fill this gap by creating a benchmark tailored to Indian languages and contexts, enabling more accurate assessment of LLM safety behavior in these settings.
AI.method: The authors construct SurakshaEval, a human-written prompt dataset covering real-world safety-sensitive scenarios for 10 major Indian languages plus English. The dataset has two types of prompts: (1) generic prompts relevant across India and (2) region- and language-specific prompts that encode local sociocultural sensitivities. They then evaluate a wide range of state-of-the-art LLMs on this benchmark, measuring safety-related behaviors and analyzing patterns of failure such as over-refusal, missed detection of implicit bias, and low contextual awareness for regionally sensitive content.
AI.result: Benchmarking shows that even strong multilingual LLMs perform unreliably on nuanced safety tasks in Indic languages, particularly when handling native scripts. The models frequently over-refuse benign content, fail to detect implicit bias, and mishandle context in regionally sensitive scenarios. These issues are more pronounced in Indic languages than in English, indicating a significant safety performance gap.
AI.conclusion: SurakshaEval demonstrates that current LLMs are not yet dependable for safety-critical use in Indic languages, especially in native scripts, and that English-centered benchmarks miss important risks. The authors argue for safety evaluation frameworks that explicitly incorporate region-specific data and structured assessment methods, so that AI systems can be developed and deployed in ways that are secure, ethical, and aligned with diverse societal values. They release their code and data to support further research and improvement.

title: When LLM Agents Negotiate: Private Information and Dynamic Bargaining in Supply Chains
summary: As LLM agents move from decision support to autonomous procurement, firms need to know whether delegated negotiators create value, divide it predictably, and avoid money-losing contracts. We study this in a canonical supply chain bargaining problem: a buyer with private demand information negotiates a quantity-payment contract with an uninformed seller. We benchmark nine LLMs from OpenAI, Google, and Alibaba against a validated Perfect Bayesian Equilibrium across 9,840 LLM-to-LLM negotiations. First, capability governs value creation. Agents agree in 98.9% of negotiations and capture 95.4% of first-best surplus undiscounted, but average 2.98 rounds against the benchmark's 1.25, and this delay erodes 21-34% of surplus. Capability also governs reliability: baseline models accept individually irrational contracts in 19.2% of cases, versus 0.0-0.6% at mid-tier and flagship, making automated profit verification the binding guardrail below that threshold. Second, surplus capture is relational. Provider identity predicts who captures surplus better than capability rank: self-play buyer shares average 40% for OpenAI, 50% for Google, and 70% for Alibaba's Qwen, an ordering that survives restricted communication and no discounting. Reversing which provider sells moves the division by 7-18 percentage points, and the capable Qwen flagship is the weakest cross-family seller: vendor choice is a first-order distributional decision. Third, the prompt is a strategic lever. Delegation separates the principal's economic patience from the agent's prompted strategic patience, a free deployment choice that is the single strongest driver of surplus division (90% of explained variance). Together these establish an equilibrium-referenced audit of AI agents along three dimensions: discounted efficiency, distributional profile, and operational reliability.

AI.tldr: The paper evaluates how different large language model (LLM) agents perform as autonomous negotiators in a supply chain bargaining setting, comparing them to a game-theoretic equilibrium on efficiency, surplus division, and reliability.
AI.motivation: As LLM-based agents begin to autonomously conduct tasks such as procurement and negotiation for firms, it is crucial to understand whether they (1) create overall value efficiently, (2) divide surplus in predictable and controllable ways, and (3) avoid making economically harmful deals. Existing work lacks systematic, equilibrium-referenced audits of LLM performance in such strategic bargaining contexts and across competing providers.
AI.method: The authors use a canonical supply chain bargaining model with asymmetric information: a privately informed buyer negotiates a quantity-payment contract with an uninformed seller. They run 9,840 automated LLM-to-LLM negotiations using nine different LLMs from OpenAI, Google, and Alibaba. Results are benchmarked against the Perfect Bayesian Equilibrium outcome. They examine agreement rates, surplus levels, discounting via negotiation length, incidence of individually irrational contracts, and the distribution of surplus by provider, role, and prompt parameters (e.g., strategic patience).
AI.result: (1) Value creation and reliability scale with model capability: high-capability models nearly always reach agreement (98.9%) and approximate first-best surplus (95.4%) before discounting, but require more rounds than equilibrium, which erodes 21–34% of surplus. Lower-tier models frequently accept money-losing contracts (19.2%), while mid-tier and flagship models nearly never do (0.0–0.6%). (2) Surplus division depends strongly on model provider rather than capability: in self-play, buyers capture around 40% (OpenAI), 50% (Google), and 70% (Alibaba Qwen); these patterns persist under restricted communication and no discounting. Changing which provider acts as seller shifts shares by 7–18 percentage points, and Qwen, though capable, is relatively weak as a cross-family seller. (3) Prompted strategic patience is a powerful control: the specified patience of the agent, distinct from the principal’s actual economic patience, explains about 90% of the variance in surplus division, making prompt design a primary strategic lever.
AI.conclusion: The paper proposes an equilibrium-referenced framework for auditing AI negotiation agents along three key dimensions: discounted efficiency (how much surplus they actually realize after accounting for delay), distributional profile (how surplus is split across counterparties and providers), and operational reliability (likelihood of economically irrational deals). It shows that capability ensures high value creation and reliability, provider identity systematically shapes who gets the surplus, and prompt engineering—especially on strategic patience—is a dominant, firm-controllable tool for steering bargaining outcomes. Vendor selection and prompt design thus become central economic and governance choices for deploying LLM agents in autonomous negotiations.

title: Detection of Self-Introductions in Legislative Testimony
comment: Presented at AAIRC-AI4 conference, Las Vegas, NV, USA August 2026 https://ai4.io/aairc-ai4/
summary: Self-introductions are common in legislative committee testimonies. Successfully detecting them and extracting the speaker's name is enormously helpful in the task of speaker identification in the context of government meetings. In this paper, we present a pipeline for detection of self-introductions in legislative committee testimony using machine learning. We construct a training dataset from 1.54 million utterances spanning five state legislative sessions, apply a name-matching heuristic to generate automatic labels, and train three classifiers: a decision tree, random forest, and XGBoost to find self-introductions and extract the speaker's name. We construct a feature set combining bag-of-words, positional context, structural signals, introductory phrase indicators, and discourse context features. Among the three classifiers, XGBoost achieves the best performance with an F1 score of 0.9747 and the fewest total errors; adding fine-tuned BERT probability features improves this further. As an extension, we score the full candidate dataset with a fine-tuned BERT classifier and add BERT probability outputs as features. This BERT-augmented XGBoost model improves F1 from 0.9747 to 0.9782 and reduces total test errors from 241 to 207. The primary gain over the decision tree baseline (F1 0.9323) is driven by discourse context features and the boosting ensemble strategy; BERT provides a modest complementary signal. Analysis of false positives reveals that a minority are genuine self-introductions mislabeled due to name inconsistencies in the source data, indicating that measured metrics modestly understate true performance.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a machine-learning pipeline to detect self-introduction utterances in legislative committee testimony and extract speaker names, achieving very high accuracy, especially with an XGBoost model augmented by BERT features.
AI.motivation: Accurate speaker identification in government meeting transcripts is important for transparency, searchability, and downstream political or administrative analysis. However, existing records often lack clean, structured speaker metadata, and self-introduction utterances are an underused but highly informative cue for linking speech segments to individuals. There is a need for an automated method that can reliably detect such self-introductions and extract speaker names at large scale across many sessions and states, despite noisy transcripts and inconsistent name data.
AI.method: The authors build a pipeline using 1.54 million utterances from five state legislative sessions. They apply a name-matching heuristic to automatically label utterances as self-introductions or not, then train three supervised classifiers—decision tree, random forest, and XGBoost—to detect self-introductions and extract names. The feature set combines bag-of-words, positional context (e.g., position in session), structural cues from transcripts, indicators of common introductory phrases, and discourse context from surrounding utterances. They further fine-tune a BERT model on the same task, then use the BERT output probabilities as additional features fed into XGBoost, creating a BERT-augmented ensemble.
AI.result: XGBoost outperforms the decision tree and random forest baselines, achieving an F1 score of 0.9747 and the lowest number of total errors. Incorporating BERT probability outputs as extra features into the XGBoost model improves F1 further to 0.9782 and reduces total test errors from 241 to 207. The decision tree baseline attains F1 0.9323, showing that much of the improvement stems from the boosting ensemble and the inclusion of discourse context features. BERT contributes a modest but measurable performance gain. Error analysis shows that some predicted false positives are actually true self-introductions misclassified by the heuristic labels due to inconsistencies in name data.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that self-introductions in legislative testimony can be detected with very high accuracy using an XGBoost-based pipeline that integrates lexical, structural, and discourse context features, with additional improvements from BERT-derived probabilities. The main gains over simpler models come from modeling context and using boosting ensembles, while BERT adds complementary but smaller benefits. Because some apparent errors are due to noisy labels rather than model mistakes, the reported performance metrics are likely conservative. The approach provides a practical and scalable component for robust speaker identification in large corpora of government meeting transcripts.

title: TREAT: Evaluating Access to Formal Knowledge across Equivalent Mathematical Representations
comment: Accepted at 28th International Symposium on Symbolic and Numeric Algorithms for Scientific Computing (SYNASC 2026)
summary: AI systems increasingly operate between flexible input representations and formal objects used by downstream tools. A key challenge is recognizing when an unfamiliar formulation denotes a known formal object. We study this challenge through theorem recognition: given an equivalence-preserving transformation of a theorem condition, a model must recover the theorem identity associated with the standard statement. We introduce TREAT, a benchmark for evaluating whether large language models can recover known theorem identities from equivalence-preserving formula-level transformations. Rather than paraphrasing theorem text, TREAT changes the mathematical form of theorem conditions themselves, expressing known results through residual equations, witness statements, optimization identities, set relations, operator forms, and proof-intermediate characterizations. Starting from scraped theorem pages, we filter for entries with usable mathematical expression forms, extract canonical theorem conditions, and generate transformed variants with recorded assumptions and inverse mappings. The final corpus contains 737 theorem identities and 29,480 transformed rows. On a test panel, the best model retrieves the correct theorem identity in only 60.73% of cases. Other systems reveal different failure modes, including abstention, wrong detection, and malformed outputs. These suggest that theorem knowledge can be fragile under equivalent changes in representation. TREAT therefore provides a controlled testbed for evaluating representation-robust access to formal knowledge, with broader relevance to domains that require stable target objects, explicit equivalence relations, validation procedures, and auditable scoring.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces TREAT, a benchmark to test whether language models can recognize the same theorem under different but equivalent mathematical formulations, showing current models often fail.
AI.motivation: AI systems need to map flexible, varied inputs to fixed formal objects used by downstream tools (e.g., specific theorems, APIs, or database entries). A core difficulty is recognizing that different but logically equivalent formulations actually refer to the same underlying formal object. In mathematics, equivalent representations of conditions are ubiquitous, and a model’s inability to recognize them reveals brittleness in its understanding. The authors want a controlled way to measure how robustly models can access known formal knowledge when the surface representation of mathematical conditions changes.
AI.method: The authors define the ‘theorem recognition’ task: given a theorem condition that has been transformed in an equivalence-preserving way, the model must identify which standard theorem statement it corresponds to. They build TREAT, a benchmark corpus, by scraping theorem pages, filtering for entries with usable mathematical expressions, and extracting canonical theorem conditions as identities. They then systematically generate transformed variants of these conditions using several mathematically equivalent forms, such as residual equations, witness statements, optimization identities, set relations, operator formulations, and intermediate proof characterizations. For each transformed condition, they record assumptions and inverse mappings back to the canonical form so that equivalence is guaranteed. The final dataset has 737 unique theorem identities and 29,480 transformed instances. They then evaluate large language models on a test panel by asking them to retrieve the correct theorem identity for each transformed condition and analyze error modes (abstentions, wrong matches, malformed outputs).
AI.result: On the TREAT benchmark’s test panel, the strongest evaluated model correctly retrieves the original theorem identity for only 60.73% of transformed conditions, indicating substantial performance degradation under equivalence-preserving reformulations. Other evaluated systems display distinct failure patterns: some abstain frequently instead of committing to an identity, some select incorrect theorems, and others generate syntactically malformed outputs that cannot be scored. These behaviors collectively reveal that current models’ access to formal theorem knowledge is brittle and sensitive to how conditions are represented mathematically, even when the underlying content is unchanged.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that current large language models do not robustly recognize known theorems when those theorems are presented in mathematically equivalent but structurally different forms. TREAT serves as a controlled benchmark to expose and quantify this fragility in representation-robust knowledge access. Because TREAT precisely encodes equivalence relations, assumptions, and invertible transformations, it allows clear evaluation, validation, and auditable scoring. The authors argue that insights from TREAT extend beyond mathematics to any domain where AI systems must reliably map varied input formulations to stable target objects (such as APIs or database entries), highlighting the need for methods that ensure representation-invariant reasoning and retrieval.

title: Thinking Hard, Not Smart: Reasoning Models Fail to Ration Test-Time Compute Across Questions
summary: Reasoning language models increasingly use test-time compute to improve performance, but existing evaluations typically study this compute one question at a time. Yet when multiple problems share an end-to-end cost or latency constraint, models must decide how to divide limited inference compute among them. We introduce an exam-style evaluation framework for studying this setting, in which a model must distribute one shared token budget across questions with different difficulty and point values to maximize its total score. Across several open and frontier reasoning models, we find that models fail to allocate a shared budget strategically across questions of varying difficulties and values. Models behave largely as greedy sequential solvers: they prioritize questions by presentation order, front-load effort on early questions, and remain insensitive to value, with these tendencies becoming more pronounced as the number of questions grows. Explicit planning prompts spread compute more evenly but do not produce value- or difficulty-aware prioritization. The same behavioral pattern extends from mathematical to code reasoning. These findings establish global budget allocation as a distinct capability that is not captured by conventional per-question evaluation and remains a challenge for current reasoning models.

AI.tldr: Paper introduces an exam-style evaluation where a model must allocate a shared token budget across multiple questions, and finds that current reasoning models fail to allocate compute strategically and instead behave like greedy sequential solvers.
AI.motivation: Reasoning language models increasingly rely on test-time compute (longer chains-of-thought, more samples, etc.) to improve performance, but evaluations typically consider each question independently. In realistic scenarios, multiple problems share a global cost or latency constraint (e.g., an exam, a batch of tasks, or an API budget). The authors are motivated to understand whether models can strategically allocate limited inference compute across many questions to maximize total performance under a shared compute budget, a capability not captured by standard per-question benchmarks.
AI.method: The authors propose an exam-style evaluation framework where a model is given multiple questions at once, each with associated difficulty and point value, and a single shared token budget for inference across the entire exam. The model must decide how many tokens (i.e., how much test-time compute) to spend on each question to maximize total score. They test several open and frontier reasoning models, quantifying behavior such as how token usage depends on question position, value, and difficulty. They also experiment with explicit planning prompts intended to induce deliberate budgeting and prioritization, and they extend the framework from math problems to code reasoning tasks.
AI.result: Across models, the authors observe that global compute allocation is poor: models tend to act as greedy sequential solvers, working through questions in the order presented, spending disproportionately many tokens on early questions, and failing to adapt token allocation to question value or difficulty. These behaviors worsen as the number of questions increases. Planning-style prompts lead to a more even spread of compute but still do not produce robust value- or difficulty-sensitive prioritization. Similar behavioral patterns appear in both mathematical and code reasoning settings.
AI.conclusion: The study concludes that global budget allocation—strategically distributing a shared compute budget across multiple problems—is a distinct capability not assessed by traditional per-question evaluations and is currently lacking in existing reasoning models. Even strong models that perform well when evaluated one question at a time fail to prioritize questions by value or difficulty under a shared budget, defaulting instead to order-based, greedy strategies. This reveals an important gap between current reasoning models and more globally rational resource-allocation behavior, and suggests the need for new methods and training schemes that explicitly target global planning and compute budgeting abilities.

title: An AI Scientist that Doesn't Drift: Taste, Structure, and Falsifiable Findings in a Quadruped Navigation Research Loop
summary: Autonomous research loops driven by large language models can run machine-learning experiments at scale but tend to drift toward local refinements of whichever metric they optimise rather than testing the hypotheses that motivate the experiments. We address this structurally and present an AI Scientist for studying generalisation in quadruped robot navigation policies in simulation. Building on the autoresearch paradigm of Karpathy, our loop adds three components: an immutable experiment card that pairs each iteration's prediction with its outcome under a fixed schema, so a falsified hypothesis cannot be retconned; specialised subagents restricted to mechanical roles; and kkanbu, a preference oracle that holds the user's research taste as a typed knowledge graph and is the only component permitted to make subjective judgements. To isolate the oracle we run the identical loop twice across eleven research streams, with and without kkanbu. Neither arm drifts: both falsify roughly three quarters of their own hypotheses, and the best trained policy comes from the oracle-less arm. What the oracle changes is direction, not score: it alone explores test-time adaptation, it authored the winning designs where its arm led, and it carried lessons across streams that the other arm repeatedly re-derived. The scaffold keeps the loop honest; kkanbu decides where it looks.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces an "AI Scientist" loop for quadruped-robot navigation research that structurally reduces metric-chasing drift by enforcing hypothesis tracking, separating mechanical sub-tasks, and isolating subjective research preferences in a dedicated oracle, kkanbu.
AI.motivation: Autonomous LLM-driven research pipelines often optimize proxy metrics and locally refine existing ideas instead of systematically testing the hypotheses that originally motivated the experiments. This leads to "drift" away from meaningful scientific inquiry and toward narrow metric-improvement. The authors want a scaffolded system that keeps an AI research loop focused on explicit, falsifiable hypotheses and enables the user’s subjective research taste to guide direction without contaminating the integrity of hypothesis testing.
AI.method: They build an AI Scientist loop for studying generalization in simulated quadruped robot navigation. The loop is based on Karpathy’s autoresearch paradigm but adds: (1) an immutable experiment card with a fixed schema storing each iteration’s prediction and outcome, preventing post-hoc rewriting of hypotheses; (2) specialised subagents constrained to mechanical roles (e.g., coding, running experiments, summarizing results) to avoid entangling subjective judgments with operational tasks; and (3) kkanbu, a preference oracle encoding the user’s research taste as a typed knowledge graph, which is the only component allowed to make subjective choices such as which hypotheses or directions to pursue. They run the same loop on eleven research streams in two conditions: with and without the kkanbu oracle, keeping everything else identical to isolate its effect.
AI.result: Across eleven research streams, both the kkanbu and non-kkanbu arms falsify about three-quarters of their own hypotheses, suggesting the scaffolded loop remains self-critical and does not drift into unfalsifiable or self-serving hypotheses. The best-performing navigation policy actually emerges from the oracle-less arm, indicating that the preference oracle is not necessary for maximizing the specific performance metric. However, the kkanbu arm chooses different research directions: it uniquely explores test-time adaptation, leads to winning designs in the streams where it guides the search, and transfers insights across streams that the oracle-less arm must rediscover independently.
AI.conclusion: The authors conclude that their structured autoresearch scaffold—immutable experiment cards plus role-specialised subagents—effectively prevents drift and keeps the autonomous loop honest by enforcing explicit, falsifiable hypotheses. The kkanbu preference oracle does not mainly improve raw performance metrics but shapes the trajectory of inquiry: it steers the system toward certain families of ideas, enables cross-stream knowledge transfer, and authors distinctive winning designs. In this framework, integrity of experimentation is handled by the scaffold, while the oracle encodes and applies the researcher’s taste about where to explore next.

title: Prompt Embedding Probes (PEP): Hallucination Detection in LLMs from Hidden States
summary: Large language models (LLMs) can generate fluent and useful responses but remain prone to hallucinations. We introduce Prompt Embedding Probes (PEP), a white-box method for answer-level hallucination detection from the hidden states of a frozen LLM. PEP extends standard linear probes by augmenting the input with a small number of learnable prompt embeddings. We evaluate PEP on TriviaQA, GSM8K, and MedQA using Qwen3 models at multiple scales. PEP improves hidden-state-based detection over standard linear probes in the main in-distribution setting. We further evaluate PEP for pre-generation prediction, cross-model transfer, and out-of-distribution generalization. PEP remains effective in the pre-generation and cross-model settings, whereas robust cross-dataset transfer remains difficult. These results show that prompt-based adaptation can strengthen hidden-state probing while keeping the backbone frozen and adding only a small number of trainable parameters.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Prompt Embedding Probes (PEP), a white-box method that uses learnable prompt embeddings on top of frozen LLM hidden states to better detect hallucinated answers.
AI.motivation: Large language models are powerful but often hallucinate, and existing hidden-state-based (linear) probes for hallucination detection have limited effectiveness. There is a need for a more accurate, parameter-efficient way to detect hallucinations at the answer level while keeping the backbone LLM frozen.
AI.method: The authors introduce Prompt Embedding Probes (PEP), which extend standard linear probing by prepending or appending a small set of trainable prompt embeddings to the hidden states of a frozen LLM and then training a classifier for hallucination detection. They evaluate PEP on multiple datasets—TriviaQA, GSM8K, and MedQA—using Qwen3 models of different sizes, and test it under three scenarios: in-distribution detection, pre-generation prediction, and cross-model/cross-dataset transfer.
AI.result: PEP outperforms standard linear probes on hidden-state-based hallucination detection in the main in-distribution setting across TriviaQA, GSM8K, and MedQA. It remains effective when used for pre-generation prediction and cross-model transfer, but its performance drops for cross-dataset transfer, indicating weak robustness across datasets.
AI.conclusion: Prompt-based adaptation via a small set of learnable prompt embeddings can significantly enhance the effectiveness of hidden-state probing for hallucination detection, without fine-tuning the backbone LLM and with only a small parameter overhead. However, robust cross-dataset generalization of hallucination detectors remains an open challenge.

title: The Field Knows: Cross-Dimensional Geometry from Navigation to Black Holes
summary: We introduce a continuous metric field framework trained by a single causal contrastive loss. The framework encodes a scene into coefficients of a fixed symmetric matrix basis, assembles them into a Lie algebra element, and exponentiates the result to a Riemannian or Lorentzian metric. Across dimensions, this field discovers the full spectrum of geometric structures: from obstacle-avoiding geodesics in robot navigation across planar and manipulator configuration spaces, to event horizons of black holes in Lorentzian spacetime. Extensive zero-shot generalization studies demonstrate that the field captures transferable geometric structure rather than memorizing specific configurations. In the black hole setting, the causal loss spontaneously evolves genuine black-hole-like structures with the correct Lorentzian signature. The same loss, the same architecture, and the same training protocol produce the full range of geometric phenomena across dimensions. The field knows geometry, and geometry knows physics.

AI.tldr: A unified continuous metric field framework learns Riemannian and Lorentzian geometries via a single causal contrastive loss, generalizing across tasks from robot navigation to black-hole spacetimes.
AI.motivation: To build a single learnable framework that can represent and discover diverse geometric structures—both Riemannian and Lorentzian—directly from data, enabling applications ranging from robot motion planning to modeling spacetime around black holes, and to test whether a model can internalize transferable geometric/physical structure rather than memorizing examples.
AI.method: Represent each scene as coefficients over a fixed symmetric matrix basis; interpret these coefficients as a Lie algebra element; exponentiate this element to obtain a metric tensor field (Riemannian or Lorentzian). Train the resulting continuous metric field with a single causal contrastive loss that encourages the learned metric to respect causality/geodesic relations implied by the data. Use the exact same architecture, loss, and training protocol across dimensions and problem domains.
AI.result: The learned metric fields recover a wide spectrum of geometric phenomena: obstacle-avoiding geodesics for robot navigation in planar and manipulator configuration spaces, and emergent event-horizon-like structures with correct Lorentzian signature in black-hole-inspired settings. Zero-shot generalization experiments show the model transfers geometric structure to unseen configurations instead of overfitting to training scenarios.
AI.conclusion: A single continuous metric field model, trained with one causal contrastive loss and a fixed architecture, can internalize and express rich geometric structure across Riemannian and Lorentzian regimes. This suggests that the learned metric field is capturing fundamental geometric/causal structure that underlies both robotics motion planning and relativistic spacetime modeling, supporting the claim that “the field knows geometry, and geometry knows physics.”

title: APEX-VW: A Document-Level English-Spanish Post-Editing Dataset in the Healthcare Domain
summary: Post-Editing (PE) of Machine Translation (MT) output often involves repeating the same lexical and terminological corrections across many segments, especially in specialised and highly repetitive documents. Despite substantial work on Automatic Post-Editing (APE), most available corpora operate at the sentence level, others are synthetic, and overall not designed to study how corrections propagate in realistic Computer-Assisted Translation (CAT) workflows. This paper presents the APEX-VW (Automatic Post-Editing eXperiments on Virtual Wards) Corpus, a new open English-Spanish (EN-ES) dataset built from recent NHS virtual-ward documents and professional PE in Trados Studio, with controlled MT, terminology, and quality assurance settings. The corpus contains seven document-coherent source texts totalling 42k words, translated with four MT systems representing different paradigms and then post-edited by professional translators. Unlike prior resources such as WMT APE corpora, eSCAPE, MLQE-PE, or LangMark, the dataset preserves document order and CAT-tool context, making it suitable for research on terminology normalisation, correction propagation, and human-in-the-loop translation support. The paper describes the corpus design, data preparation, PE setup, and initial corpus statistics, and positions the resource as a benchmark for document-level APE and propagation-aware assistive tools.

AI.tldr: They present APEX-VW, a new English–Spanish document-level corpus of professional post-editing of MT outputs from virtual-ward NHS texts, designed for studying correction propagation and document-level APE in realistic CAT settings.
AI.motivation: Existing APE corpora are mostly sentence-level, synthetic, or not aligned with real CAT tool workflows, which makes them unsuitable for studying how post-editing corrections (especially lexical and terminological ones) propagate across segments in long, repetitive, specialised documents. The authors want a realistic, document-coherent resource reflecting professional practice to enable research on terminology normalisation, correction propagation, and human-in-the-loop support.
AI.method: They constructed an open EN–ES corpus from recent NHS virtual-ward documents, preserving document order and CAT-tool context. Seven coherent source texts (~42k words) were translated using four different MT systems representing different paradigms. Professional translators post-edited the MT outputs in Trados Studio under controlled machine translation, terminology, and quality-assurance settings. The corpus was then cleaned and prepared, with its design, PE setup, and statistics documented for reproducible use as a benchmark.
AI.result: The outcome is the APEX-VW corpus: a publicly available, document-level EN–ES dataset containing seven virtual-ward source documents translated by four MT systems and professionally post-edited in a consistent CAT environment. It maintains document structure, segment order, and contextual CAT information, unlike earlier resources such as WMT APE corpora, eSCAPE, MLQE-PE, or LangMark. Initial descriptive statistics about size, repetition, and other corpus properties are provided.
AI.conclusion: APEX-VW fills an important gap for research on document-level automatic post-editing and translation assistance, specifically enabling the study of terminology normalisation and cross-segment correction propagation in realistic CAT workflows. The authors propose it as a benchmark resource for developing and evaluating propagation-aware and human-in-the-loop translation support tools, going beyond sentence-level APE scenarios.

title: TeXFix-Bench: An Empirically Grounded Multi-Format Benchmark for LLM-Based Document Source Repair
summary: Scientific and technical writing depends on markup sources that must compile: LaTeX, Typst, and Markdown pipelines fail on missing delimiters, mismatched environments, broken imports, or package conflicts. Existing document-repair evaluations inject faults with ad-hoc edits that lack an empirical fault model. We present TeXFix-Bench, a multi-format benchmark for LLM-based full-source document repair grounded in a mined fault taxonomy. A Grounded-Theory study of localized hard-crash LaTeX faults from TeX Stack Exchange, GitHub commits, and package documentation (168 verified faults, dual open coding at $κ$=0.34) yields an 18-category taxonomy instantiated as DocMut: 48 AST-aware operators across three formats. A three-model cross-benchmark shows DocMut faults are 5.6-9.2 pp harder to repair than pattern-based mutations on the same seeds, and a real-error case study (88 mined human crashes, 67.0% repair success) brackets both synthetic sets from below. We construct 10,437 instances from 743 openly licensed seeds and evaluate seven LLMs under a fixed zero-shot protocol with provider-pinned routing, collecting 48,651 attempts at about USD 200 total inference cost. A complete 6,613-instance x 7-model balanced matrix confirms all rankings. A pinned engine gate yields a 27.5-point intention-to-treat compile spread (56.7-84.2%). Typst is markedly harder than LaTeX and Markdown. A restoration oracle over 28,129 compiling repairs shows that 13.6-18.5% of compiling repairs materially alter document text, and restoration rank diverges from compile rank: the model with the lowest compile rate restores content best among its successes. Compile success alone overstates repair quality. We release the taxonomy, DocMut, and all campaign artifacts.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces TeXFix-Bench, a multi-format benchmark and fault taxonomy for evaluating LLM-based repair of scientific documents (LaTeX, Typst, Markdown), showing that compile success alone is an unreliable measure of repair quality.
AI.motivation: Scientific and technical documents in formats like LaTeX, Typst, and Markdown often fail to compile due to subtle syntax or configuration errors. Existing evaluations of automatic document repair typically inject artificial faults using simple, ad-hoc edits that do not reflect real-world error patterns, making it hard to assess how well repair systems would work on real documents. The authors want a realistic, principled benchmark and error model to evaluate LLM-based document repair methods and to understand how compile success relates to actual content preservation.
AI.method: The authors perform a Grounded-Theory study of real LaTeX hard-crash faults mined from TeX Stack Exchange, GitHub commits, and package documentation. From 168 verified faults, they conduct dual open coding (inter-coder agreement κ=0.34) to derive an 18-category taxonomy of document faults. They then instantiate this taxonomy as DocMut, a set of 48 AST-aware mutation operators applicable across LaTeX, Typst, and Markdown. Using these operators, they construct TeXFix-Bench: 10,437 faulty document instances built from 743 seed documents. They run a large-scale evaluation of seven LLMs under a controlled zero-shot protocol with provider-pinned routing, yielding 48,651 repair attempts, and also compile a balanced 6,613-instance × 7-model matrix. They compare DocMut-based mutations to simpler pattern-based mutations, and include a real-error case study with 88 mined human crashes. They evaluate not only compile success but also a "restoration oracle" that checks whether the repaired document preserves original content, comparing compile-based rankings to restoration-based rankings.
AI.result: The derived taxonomy captures 18 fault categories and is operationalized as 48 AST-aware mutation operators (DocMut) across three document formats. Empirically, faults generated via DocMut are 5.6–9.2 percentage points harder for LLMs to repair than simpler pattern-based mutations derived from the same seeds, indicating DocMut better reflects challenging real-world errors. In a real-error case study of 88 human LaTeX crashes, LLMs achieve 67.0% repair success, which is harder than both synthetic fault sets and thus serves as a lower bound. The large-scale LLM evaluation on TeXFix-Bench reveals a wide intention-to-treat compile spread of 27.5 percentage points (56.7–84.2%) across models under a pinned-engine gate. Typst documents are significantly harder to repair than LaTeX and Markdown. Among 28,129 compiling repairs, 13.6–18.5% materially change document text instead of preserving it. Rankings of models by compile success differ from rankings by restoration quality; notably, the model with the lowest overall compile rate has the best content restoration performance on its successful repairs.
AI.conclusion: TeXFix-Bench and its underlying DocMut taxonomy provide a principled, empirically grounded benchmark for evaluating LLM-based document repair across LaTeX, Typst, and Markdown. The results show that more realistic, taxonomy-based faults are harder than pattern-based ones, and that real-world errors are harder still. Compile success is an inadequate proxy for repair quality, since a significant fraction of compiling repairs change the document’s content and model rankings by compile rate and by content restoration diverge substantially. Future evaluations of document-repair systems should therefore incorporate content-preservation metrics, and the released taxonomy, operators, and artifacts can support more robust, reproducible research in automated document repair.

title: DialectS2S: End-to-End Speech Dialogue Modeling for Low-Resource Chinese Dialects
summary: Current end-to-end speech dialogue models are primarily optimized for mainstream languages and remain limited in low-resource dialect scenarios due to the scarcity of dialect speech data. Moreover, during dialect adaptation, the semantic representation space of speech dialogue models continuously evolves, while conventional speech supervision remains unchanged, leading to semantic inconsistency between hidden representations and speech targets and degrading speech stability and naturalness. To address these issues, we propose DialectS2S, an end-to-end speech dialogue model for Chinese dialects. We first develop a scalable dialect speech dialogue synthesis pipeline for efficient data construction. We further introduce a two-stage post-training strategy with self-aligned speech supervision, which aligns the semantic content of speech supervision with the evolved semantic representations of the model to improve dialect speech generation quality. Experimental results show that DialectS2S consistently outperforms existing baselines across multiple Chinese dialects in speech dialogue, achieving substantial improvements in dialect consistency, response quality, and speech intelligibility. Our work provides an efficient and scalable solution for end-to-end speech dialogue modeling in low-resource dialect scenarios. To facilitate future research and practical applications, we fully open-source the DialectS2S framework, including model checkpoints, training datasets, and fine-tuning code.

AI.tldr: DialectS2S is an end-to-end speech dialogue model tailored for low-resource Chinese dialects, using a scalable data pipeline and a two-stage post-training with self-aligned speech supervision to improve semantic consistency, naturalness, and intelligibility, and is fully open-sourced.
AI.motivation: Most end-to-end speech dialogue models are optimized for mainstream, high-resource languages and perform poorly on low-resource dialects due to scarce speech data. Additionally, when adapting models to dialects, the model’s internal semantic representations shift, but the conventional speech supervision signals do not, causing a mismatch that harms speech stability, naturalness, and semantic consistency. The authors aim to solve both the data scarcity issue and the semantic misalignment problem in dialect adaptation.
AI.method: The authors propose DialectS2S, an end-to-end speech dialogue model designed for Chinese dialects. First, they build a scalable dialect speech dialogue synthesis pipeline to efficiently construct dialect training data. Second, they design a two-stage post-training strategy with self-aligned speech supervision: as the model’s semantic representation space evolves during adaptation, they update or realign the speech supervision so that the supervision’s semantic content matches the model’s hidden representations, thereby improving training signals and generation quality. The full framework, including checkpoints, datasets, and fine-tuning code, is released as open source.
AI.result: DialectS2S is empirically shown to consistently outperform baseline methods across multiple Chinese dialects on speech dialogue tasks. It yields substantial gains in dialect consistency (how well the speech matches the target dialect), response quality (appropriateness and coherence of dialogue responses), and speech intelligibility (clarity and ease of understanding).
AI.conclusion: DialectS2S offers an effective and scalable solution for end-to-end speech dialogue modeling in low-resource Chinese dialect scenarios. By combining a scalable data synthesis pipeline with a self-aligned, two-stage post-training strategy, it addresses both data scarcity and semantic misalignment issues, leading to better dialect speech generation. The authors fully open-source the framework, enabling further research and practical deployment in dialect speech dialogue systems.

title: CMU-Drive and V2V-VLA: Cooperative Multi-agent Unified Driving with Reasoning Benchmark and Vehicle-to-Vehicle Vision-Language-Action Models
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have recently achieved impressive performance for end-to-end autonomous driving, yet existing approaches are primarily designed for an individual single autonomous driving agent with limited support for cooperative perception, reasoning, and planning. We present Cooperative Multi-agent Unified Driving with Reasoning (CMU-Drive), a closed-loop end-to-end benchmark for evaluating cooperative autonomous driving with multiple connected autonomous vehicles (CAVs) operating in safety-critical driving scenarios with background traffic participants. We further propose Vehicle-to-Vehicle Vision-Language-Action (V2V-VLA), a cooperative VLA model that integrates cooperative driving into a single forward pass by jointly generating driving actions, future waypoints, language reasoning, and communication policies. Experiments on CMU-Drive establish the first benchmark and baseline for cooperative VLA driving and provide a foundation for future research on multi-agent, closed-loop, end-to-end cooperative autonomous driving. Our code, benchmark, and model checkpoint will be publicly released to facilitate open-source research.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces CMU-Drive, a closed-loop benchmark, and V2V-VLA, a cooperative vision-language-action model, to study and baseline multi-agent cooperative autonomous driving among connected vehicles.
AI.motivation: Existing vision-language-action autonomous driving models focus on a single vehicle and lack mechanisms for cooperative perception, reasoning, and planning among multiple connected autonomous vehicles, which is crucial for safety-critical scenarios with multiple agents and background traffic.
AI.method: They design CMU-Drive, a closed-loop end-to-end benchmark that simulates safety-critical driving scenarios with multiple connected autonomous vehicles and background traffic. On top of this, they propose V2V-VLA, a cooperative VLA model that, in a single forward pass, jointly outputs driving actions, future waypoints, natural language reasoning, and inter-vehicle communication policies to enable coordinated multi-agent behavior.
AI.result: Experiments on CMU-Drive using V2V-VLA create the first baseline results for cooperative multi-agent VLA driving, demonstrating that their framework can support integrated perception, reasoning, planning, and communication for multiple connected vehicles.
AI.conclusion: CMU-Drive and V2V-VLA together establish an initial benchmark and model for closed-loop, multi-agent, end-to-end cooperative autonomous driving, providing infrastructure and baselines to catalyze future research in cooperative VLA-based driving; the authors will release code, benchmark, and checkpoints to support open-source development.

title: Commitment Before Realization: When Classifier-Free Guidance Becomes Unnecessary in Masked Diffusion Language Models
summary: Classifier-free guidance (CFG) is usually kept on throughout masked diffusion language model decoding, although its benefit varies across prompts and over time. We study when CFG is actually needed by comparing, from any partial output, the probability of eventual constraint satisfaction under continued CFG and under base-only continuation. Their difference defines the remaining value of guidance. Guidance dependence is highly prompt-specific. Many prompts already succeed without CFG, while for others it provides no measurable benefit or can be harmful. For prompts that do benefit, the gain is often concentrated early. We define the commitment horizon $\astar$ as the earliest point from which switching all remaining decoding to the base model reduces final success by no more than a chosen tolerance. Under the base model, the corresponding success probability, or committor, is a martingale. To first order, CFG's per-step effect is governed by the covariance between the guidance logit direction and the successor committor. This gives a local account of when guidance can help, but it does not by itself locate the horizon. Among prompts with an observed preterminal horizon, $\astar$ is usually early and varies more within constraint families than between them. Freezing each prompt at its own cross-fitted horizon is noninferior to full CFG on all 13 subtasks at the prespecified margin, even while many tokens remain masked. This separates commitment from realization. The boundary also identifies a later region in which higher parallelism adds only a small cost in constraint success, although fluency still degrades with parallel width. For failed trajectories, reopening committed positions improves recovery in both failure modes.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes when classifier-free guidance (CFG) is actually useful in masked diffusion language model decoding and shows that guidance is often only needed early in generation, enabling more efficient decoding strategies.
AI.motivation: CFG is widely used and typically left on for all decoding steps in diffusion language models, despite anecdotal evidence that its impact is highly prompt-dependent and time-varying. This leads to unnecessary computational cost and sometimes degraded performance. The authors want a principled, quantitative way to understand when CFG actually contributes to satisfying constraints, and when it can be turned off or modified without harming final success.
AI.method: The authors compare, for any partially generated output, the probability that the final sequence will satisfy constraints if decoding continues with CFG versus if it continues with the unguided base model. They define the difference between these two probabilities as the remaining value of guidance. They introduce the concept of a commitment horizon a*—the earliest step at which switching to the base model for all remaining steps reduces final success by at most a specified tolerance. They analyze the base model’s success probability (the committor) and show it is a martingale, then derive a first-order characterization of CFG’s per-step effect via the covariance between the guidance logit direction and the successor committor. They empirically measure horizons and performance across prompts and subtasks, and evaluate a strategy that freezes CFG per-prompt at cross-fitted horizons.
AI.result: They find that dependence on CFG is highly prompt-specific: many prompts succeed without any CFG, others derive little or negative benefit from CFG, and for prompts that do benefit, the advantage is usually concentrated early in decoding. For prompts exhibiting a preterminal commitment horizon, the horizon tends to be early, and it varies more within constraint families than across them. Using a decoding strategy that switches to the base model at each prompt’s own cross-fitted horizon performs non-inferiorly to full CFG on all 13 evaluated subtasks at the pre-specified non-inferiority margin, even when many tokens remain masked. They also identify a later region of decoding where increasing parallelism only slightly harms constraint satisfaction but still hurts fluency. Additionally, for failed trajectories, allowing previously committed positions to be reopened improves recovery across different failure modes.
AI.conclusion: CFG is not uniformly beneficial throughout decoding; its useful influence is typically front-loaded and highly prompt-dependent. The notion of a commitment horizon formalizes the earliest point at which CFG can be safely turned off with minimal loss in constraint satisfaction, separating the time of commitment from the time of realization of constraints. This enables more efficient and flexible decoding strategies—such as early-guided, later-unguided generation and increased late-stage parallelism—while preserving task success. Reopening committed positions can further help recover from failures, suggesting that strict irreversibility in decoding is often suboptimal.

title: Controlled Memory Interference in Continual LLM Agents
summary: Long-term memory enables AI agents to maintain continuity across sessions, personalize behavior, and evolve through accumulated experience. Yet memory evolution is not simply a process of storing more information: new experiences may reinforce, revise, or interfere with existing memory states. Existing systems mainly emphasize memory construction and relevance-based retrieval, but several memories may remain simultaneously relevant while differing in state, temporal validity, or authority. We introduce Controlled Memory Interference (CMI), a controlled diagnostic and data-generation framework for studying how agent memory evolves under different memory relationships. Across controlled memory evolution, benign accumulation has limited effects, whereas relationship-specific interference sharply suppresses update plasticity with little stability gain, either by blocking target-memory exposure or by disrupting its downstream use. Lexical and Dense retrieval exhibit distinct interference pathways, while poisoning is more sensitive to update-authority cues than to recency alone. Beyond diagnosis, CMI provides targeted examples for interference-aware memory learning, improving the distinction between valid updates and interference-inducing memories while preserving performance on original memory tasks. These findings show that memory evolution is shaped not only by memory scale, but also by interactions among accumulated experiences. More broadly, memory interference emerges as an important factor for reliable continual agent memory systems.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Controlled Memory Interference (CMI), a framework to study and improve how long-term memories in AI agents evolve when new information interacts with existing memories, highlighting that interference patterns—not just memory size—critically shape reliability.
AI.motivation: AI agents with long-term memory need to maintain coherent behavior over time, personalize to users, and adapt based on accumulated experiences. However, simply adding more memories is not enough because new information can reinforce, revise, or conflict with old information, leading to potential failures. Existing systems mostly focus on constructing memories and retrieving them by relevance, but do not adequately handle cases where multiple relevant memories disagree or differ in reliability, recency, or authority. This creates a gap in understanding and controlling how agent memories evolve under realistic, potentially conflicting experience streams.
AI.method: The authors propose Controlled Memory Interference (CMI), a diagnostic and data-generation framework that constructs controlled scenarios of memory evolution with specific relationships among memories (e.g., reinforcing, conflicting, or interfering). They systematically vary conditions such as benign accumulation vs. relationship-specific interference, and compare different retrieval mechanisms (lexical vs. dense retrieval) and poisoning patterns, in order to observe how these factors affect the agent’s ability to update and use its memory. CMI also generates targeted training examples designed to teach models to distinguish valid updates from interference-inducing memories.
AI.result: Experiments show that simple accumulation of additional, non-conflicting memories has limited negative impact on performance. In contrast, relationship-specific interference (e.g., conflicting or misleading memories) strongly suppresses the model’s ability to update its memory (plasticity) without meaningfully improving stability. This happens either by preventing exposure to the correct target memories during retrieval or by disrupting how those memories are used downstream. The study further finds that lexical and dense retrieval approaches fail in different ways under interference, and that data poisoning effects are more influenced by signals of authority or reliability than by mere recency of information.
AI.conclusion: Memory evolution in long-term AI agents is governed not only by how much information is stored but also by complex interactions between existing and new experiences. Memory interference—especially structured, relationship-specific interference—is a central challenge that can substantially impair an agent’s capacity to update and correctly use its memories. The proposed CMI framework both reveals these dynamics and offers a way to train interference-aware memory systems that better separate valid updates from harmful interference, while maintaining baseline memory performance. Consequently, accounting for memory interference is crucial for building robust, continual-learning agent memory architectures.

title: Archer: Adaptive Reuse of Cached Hidden States for Efficient Rollback in Diffusion Language Models
summary: Diffusion language models (DLMs) iteratively refine a sequence, allowing earlier predictions to be revised as context evolves. This rollback capability distinguishes them from irreversible autoregressive generation, but makes inference costly. Every denoising update alters the global context, forcing both prompt and response states to be recomputed even though only response tokens are revisable. Key-value (KV) caching could reduce this cost, yet conventional caching assumes immutable historical states and is therefore difficult to reconcile with rollback.In this paper, we introduce Adaptive Reuse of Cached Hidden States for Efficient Rollback (Archer), a training-free KV caching method for rollback-capable DLMs. Archer asymmetrically keeps the mutable response synchronized with the current hypothesis while reusing prompt K/V within a bounded state neighborhood. Although prompt representations also change under bidirectional attention, their token identities remain fixed; bounded reuse therefore amortizes repeated prompt computation without caching mutable response states. It also delays feedback from tentative tokens, reducing premature reinforcement of transient high-confidence errors and giving rollback more opportunity to correct them. Our analysis characterizes prompt reuse as a reversibility-aligned cache boundary, bounds its state-dependent approximation error, and gives a decoder-margin condition for preserving full-refresh decisions.Existing DLM acceleration often trades quality for speed. Archer shifts this frontier, attaining the best mean performance of 33.63% together with a 2.57x mean speedup on the main suite. Across evaluated settings, it improves Pass@1 by up to 3.05 points and reaches up to 2.95x speedup. Controlled analyses connect the quality gain to delayed prompt feedback and validate state-aware refresh. Our code is available at https://github.com/Hxnng/Archer.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Archer, a training-free KV caching method that accelerates diffusion language models (DLMs) with rollback while improving or preserving generation quality.
AI.motivation: Diffusion language models support rollback—iteratively refining sequences and revising earlier predictions—but this makes inference expensive because every denoising step changes global context, forcing recomputation of both prompt and response states. Standard KV caching assumes immutable history and is hard to apply to such reversible models. The authors want a way to reduce this computation cost without sacrificing the benefits of rollback.
AI.method: The authors introduce Archer (Adaptive Reuse of Cached Hidden States for Efficient Rollback), a training-free KV caching strategy tailored to rollback-capable DLMs. Archer asymmetrically handles prompt and response: it constantly synchronizes mutable response states with the current hypothesis, while reusing cached key/value representations for the prompt within a bounded neighborhood of states. Since prompt tokens are fixed in identity despite bidirectional attention altering their representations, Archer defines a cache boundary at the prompt to amortize repeated computation without caching volatile response states. It also intentionally delays feedback from tentative response tokens, which softens premature reinforcement of incorrect high-confidence predictions. The method includes: (1) a formal characterization of prompt reuse as a reversibility-aligned cache boundary, (2) bounds on approximation error induced by state-dependent prompt reuse, and (3) a decoder-margin condition under which Archer preserves the same decisions as full recomputation.
AI.result: On the main evaluation suite, Archer achieves a mean Pass@1 performance of 33.63% with a 2.57x mean speedup compared to full-refresh inference. Across multiple settings, it improves Pass@1 by up to 3.05 points while achieving up to 2.95x speedup. Controlled ablations show that the observed quality improvements are tied to delayed prompt feedback and confirm the benefits of state-aware refresh policies.
AI.conclusion: Archer provides an effective, training-free KV caching mechanism for diffusion language models that maintains rollback capability while significantly accelerating inference. By reusing prompt hidden states within a bounded region and keeping response states fresh, it both reduces computation and can improve generation quality via delayed feedback. Theoretical analysis supports its approximation behavior and decision preservation, and empirical results show that Archer advances the speed–quality tradeoff frontier for DLM acceleration.

title: From Single Chatbots to Governed Agent Ecosystems: An Agentic AI Pattern Catalogue and Orchestration Framework for Mission-Critical Hospital Information Management Systems
summary: Hospitals are racing to embed AI, while coping with the surge in adaptation of the technology in other industries, into the triage management, documentation, scheduling, and revenue-cycle workflows, yet most deployments remain as fragmented pilots that stall at the edge of production, exposing patients and institutions to operational fragility, ungoverned risk, and mounting technical debt. At the same time, the global AI-in-healthcare market is projected to exceed nearly USD 1 trillion by 2034, according to the report of Fortune Business Insights, amplifying the financial consequences of architectural missteps and failed scaling strategies. This research proposes a compliance-first Agentic AI pattern catalogue and orchestration framework, purposely built for HIMS, moving beyond the single LLM chatbots and towards a governed ecosystem of autonomous and semi-autonomous agents. The framework extends by adding (i) a taxonomy of Agentic roles, (ii) a formal risk-stratification model that maps each pattern to risk tiers, human-in-the-loop checkpoints, and governance hooks, and (iii) a unified orchestration runtime capable of coordinating multi-agent workflows across EHR/HIMS landscapes such as Epic, Cerner, and MEDITECH. Technically the framework combines vLLM-based inference, optimized paging memory, confidential computing, and MCP based on-premise deployment, enforcing end-to-end encryption and policy-as-code controls aligned with HIPAA, GDPR, the EU AI Act, India's DPDP and DISHA Acts, ISO 27001, ISO 27002, ISO 14971 and IEC 62304. We exhibit how the proposed architecture is capable and efficient to reduce the documentation time, integration effort, and AI pilot attrition while constricting the governance and auditability, offering hospital leaders and governing authorities an urgently needed blueprint to convert AI investment into sustainable clinical, operational, and financial ROI

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a compliance-first, agent-based AI architecture for hospital information systems that turns fragmented pilots into a scalable, governed multi-agent ecosystem integrated with major EHR/HIMS platforms.
AI.motivation: Current AI deployments in hospitals are mostly fragmented pilots that fail to scale into production, creating operational fragility, unmanaged risk, and technical debt just as the AI-in-healthcare market is set to reach nearly USD 1 trillion by 2034. There is a strong need for a blueprint that helps hospitals adopt AI safely, in a governable and interoperable way that can unlock real clinical, operational, and financial value while complying with stringent global regulations.
AI.method: The authors design a compliance-first Agentic AI pattern catalogue and orchestration framework tailored for hospital information management systems (HIMS). They define a taxonomy of AI agent roles, create a formal risk-stratification model that links each pattern to risk tiers, human-in-the-loop checkpoints, and governance hooks, and build a unified orchestration runtime that can coordinate multi-agent workflows across EHR/HIMS ecosystems such as Epic, Cerner, and MEDITECH. Technically, they combine vLLM-based inference, optimized paging memory, confidential computing, and MCP-based on-premise deployment with end-to-end encryption and policy-as-code enforcement aligned with major global health data and AI regulations and standards (HIPAA, GDPR, EU AI Act, India’s DPDP and DISHA, ISO 27001/27002/14971, IEC 62304).
AI.result: The architecture demonstrably reduces clinical documentation time, lowers integration effort for AI solutions, and decreases the rate at which AI pilots fail to progress to production. At the same time, it tightens governance and auditability across AI workflows in hospital environments by embedding risk controls, human oversight points, and policy enforcement directly into the orchestration layer.
AI.conclusion: A structured, compliance-first multi-agent AI framework can turn scattered AI pilots in hospitals into a robust, governable ecosystem that integrates with existing EHR/HIMS platforms. By unifying technical design with explicit regulatory alignment and risk stratification, the proposed architecture offers hospital leaders and regulators a practical blueprint to translate AI investments into sustainable clinical, operational, and financial return on investment while maintaining strong governance and auditability.

title: Wisdom in Unity: The Role of Multilingual Training in Figurative Language Identification in Proverbs
summary:
Although multilingual approaches to figurative language identification are not new, the shift beyond language homogeneous training data requires a clearer understanding of the contribution of translated multilingual supervision. We examine this question using 742 proverb concepts across 6,787 translated instances in seven languages. We evaluate five models, including multilingual encoders and instruction tuned LLMs, under progressively increasing levels of multilingual supervision. Moreover, we introduce a multidimensional annotation framework for proverbs that characterizes them through four complementary figurative forms: Metaphorical, Moral/Advisory, Cause-Effect, and Culture Specific.
  Our findings show that approximately 50% of the translated multilingual training data is sufficient to achieve near-optimal figurative language identification performance. We further show that combining diverse figurative forms yields the strongest overall performance. A notable finding is that the least frequent figurative form, Culture Specific, exhibits the largest performance gains under multilingual supervision. Furthermore, the Moral/Advisory and Culture Specific forms contribute most to the performance of instruction-tuned LLMs on figurative language identification. These findings motivate multilingual figurative language identification to move beyond metaphor-centric taxonomies toward concept level multidimensional frameworks that explicitly model complementary forms of figurative meaning.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how much translated multilingual training data is needed for figurative language identification in proverbs, and shows that partial multilingual supervision and a multidimensional view of figurative forms significantly improve performance, especially for culture-specific figurative meaning.
AI.motivation: Most prior work on figurative language identification either focuses on a single language or uses metaphor-centric taxonomies, leaving unclear how translated multilingual supervision contributes to performance and how different figurative forms interact. The authors aim to understand the value and efficiency of multilingual training data and to provide a richer, concept-level framework that captures multiple complementary figurative dimensions in proverbs.
AI.method: The authors construct a dataset of 742 proverb concepts with 6,787 translated instances across seven languages. They propose a multidimensional annotation scheme capturing four figurative forms: Metaphorical, Moral/Advisory, Cause-Effect, and Culture Specific. They then evaluate five models—multilingual encoders and instruction-tuned LLMs—under varying degrees of multilingual supervision (increasing portions of the translated data) and different combinations of figurative form labels, measuring performance on figurative language identification.
AI.result: They find that using about 50% of the translated multilingual training data is enough to reach near-optimal identification performance. Combining multiple figurative forms in training yields the best overall results. The least frequent form, Culture Specific, shows the largest performance gains when multilingual supervision is added. Moral/Advisory and Culture Specific labels particularly boost the performance of instruction-tuned LLMs on figurative language identification tasks.
AI.conclusion: Translated multilingual supervision is highly efficient: only half of the multilingual data is needed for near-maximal performance. Figurative language identification benefits from a multidimensional, concept-level framework that goes beyond metaphors to include moral/advisory, cause-effect, and culture-specific aspects. Culture-specific and moral/advisory dimensions are especially valuable for instruction-tuned LLMs, suggesting future research should move away from purely metaphor-centric taxonomies toward richer, complementary figurative meaning representations.

title: Agent-MD: Selective LLM Intervention with Event-Driven Escalation for Stateful GCMC--MD Campaigns
