This technical survey synthesizes primary papers, official technical reports, and prior surveys to organize modern Mixture-of-Experts systems along five coupled dimensions: expert granularity, expert topology, routing freedom, the scope of load balancing, and execution structure. We describe eight architectural milestones as a dependency graph with six mainline developments and two orthogonal branches, rather than as eight successive generations. We then analyze individual systems through four control planes: Expert Topology, Routing, Balance, and Expert Parallelism. These planes specify which experts exist, which experts process each token, how aggregate load is controlled, and how selected computation is mapped onto physical devices. The framework connects algorithmic choices such as Top-k routing, shared experts, fine-grained experts, and dynamic expert composition with systems concerns including token dispatch, device placement, all-to-all communication, and communication-computation overlap. We conclude with equal-budget pretraining experiments, quality and systems metrics, and open research questions. The main trend is a shift from merely activating more sparse parameters toward decoupling semantic routing, computational budgets, and physical execution.

AI.tldr: Survey of modern Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures, proposing a unified framework to compare and analyze their design dimensions and system trade-offs.
AI.motivation: MoE models allow scaling parameter counts without proportional increases in per-token computation, but rapid, heterogeneous architectural evolution has led to confusion and lack of unified understanding. Existing descriptions as linear generations of models are inadequate to capture dependencies, design trade-offs, and systems implications.
AI.method: The authors synthesize primary MoE papers, official technical reports, and prior surveys to build a structured taxonomy of MoE designs. They organize systems along five key dimensions—expert granularity, expert topology, routing freedom, load-balancing scope, and execution structure—and define four control planes: Expert Topology, Routing, Balance, and Expert Parallelism. They then map notable MoE systems into this framework and analyze how algorithmic routing and expert design choices interact with systems issues like token dispatch and device communication.
AI.result: They identify eight major architectural milestones and represent them as a dependency graph with six mainline developments and two orthogonal branches instead of a simple chronological sequence. The framework reveals patterns in how algorithmic innovations (e.g., Top-k routing, fine-grained/shared experts, dynamic expert composition) co-evolve with systems techniques (e.g., all-to-all communication, device placement strategies, communication-computation overlap). They present equal-budget pretraining comparisons and report results on model quality and system performance metrics under different MoE design choices.
AI.conclusion: The survey concludes that the key trend in modern MoE development is moving beyond simply increasing sparsely-activated parameters toward decoupling three aspects: semantic routing decisions, computational budgets, and physical execution layouts. The proposed framework clarifies design trade-offs, highlights open research questions at the intersection of algorithms and systems, and provides a structured lens for future MoE architecture development.

title: GRACE: LLM-Grounded Semantic Metric Spaces for Scalable Mixed-Data Clustering
summary: Clustering mixed tabular data requires a unified metric space to bridge the inherent heterogeneity between continuous numerical measurements and discrete categorical symbols. Traditionally, algorithms rely entirely on dataset-internal statistics to estimate categorical relationships, which confines the learned metric to empirical co-occurrences and ignores conceptually obvious yet statistically unobserved affinities. Although LLMs offer external world knowledge, applying their text-centric reasoning to highly abstract tabular concepts presents significant challenges. Bridging this modality gap to construct a semantically complete metric typically requires embedding LLMs into iterative metric learning loops to dynamically optimize cross-modality representations. This incurs intractable computational overhead, forcing a compromise between semantic enrichment and scalability. Therefore, we propose GRACE, an LLM-grounded framework for scalable mixed-data clustering. GRACE shifts semantic acquisition to the attribute-value level via a multi-perspective LLM querying strategy, mapping heterogeneous values into knowledge-informed descriptions. Crucially, this one-shot grounding extracts general-purpose semantic representations that embed heterogeneous attributes into a unified space, decoupling expensive LLM invocation from iterative optimization. Furthermore, GRACE cross-validates these external semantics against dataset-internal statistical evidence to ensure alignment with the dataset-specific cluster structure. Ultimately, GRACE matches the scalability of conventional statistics-driven baselines while achieving superior clustering accuracy and conceptual interpretability over 11 competing methods. The source code is available at https://github.com/develop-yang/GRACE-GRACE-A

AI.tldr: GRACE is an LLM-grounded framework that creates a unified, semantically rich metric space for clustering mixed tabular data, while remaining as scalable as traditional statistical methods and outperforming them in accuracy and interpretability.
AI.motivation: Existing clustering methods for mixed tabular data rely purely on dataset-internal statistics to model relationships among categorical values, which limits the learned metric to observed co-occurrences and fails to capture obvious but unobserved semantic affinities. While LLMs can provide external world knowledge, directly integrating them into metric learning causes high computational cost due to iterative cross-modality optimization. The paper aims to leverage LLM semantics to enrich clustering metrics without sacrificing scalability.
AI.method: The authors propose GRACE, which performs one-shot grounding of attribute values using a multi-perspective LLM querying strategy. Instead of repeatedly calling the LLM during optimization, GRACE asks the LLM to generate knowledge-informed descriptions of heterogeneous attribute values at the attribute-value level. These descriptions are transformed into general-purpose semantic representations that embed continuous and categorical attributes into a unified metric space. GRACE then cross-validates and aligns these externally derived semantics with dataset-internal statistical evidence to ensure that the resulting metric reflects both world knowledge and the dataset’s own cluster structure.
AI.result: On mixed-data clustering benchmarks, GRACE achieves higher clustering accuracy and better conceptual interpretability compared with 11 existing methods, while maintaining scalability comparable to traditional statistics-driven baselines, due to its one-shot LLM grounding strategy that avoids iterative LLM calls.
AI.conclusion: LLM-grounded, one-shot semantic grounding at the attribute-value level can effectively construct a unified metric space for mixed tabular data, resolving the trade-off between semantic richness and scalability. By combining LLM-based external knowledge with internal dataset statistics, GRACE delivers superior clustering performance and interpretable clusters without incurring the heavy computational overhead typical of LLM-in-the-loop approaches.

title: LibraSpec: Dynamic Diffusion-Based Speculative Decoding via Marginal-Gain-Driven Optimization
summary: Speculative decoding accelerates large language model inference by drafting multiple tokens for parallel verification, with efficiency critically determined by the speculative length selected at each decoding round. Existing dynamic speculation methods select the speculation length by estimating how many tokens will be accepted, which is reasonable for autoregressive drafters that generates tokens sequentially. The recent wave of diffusion-based drafters, however, generates candidate blocks in parallel at substantially lower drafting cost, shifting the key question from how many tokens to generate to how many generated tokens are worth verifying. We therefore reformulate dynamic speculative-length selection as expected-speedup optimization and derive a marginal criterion that extends the speculative sequence only when its acceptance gain outweighs the additional verification cost. Building on this criterion, we develop \textit{LibraSpec}, a training-free and plug-and-play algorithm that iteratively determines the speculative length using drafter confidence scores. Theoretically, we prove that LibraSpec monotonically converges toward the optimal speculative length. Experiments across six target models, three diffusion-based speculative decoding methods, and math, coding, and chat benchmarks show consistent improvements under both greedy and sampling settings, achieving a further $0.5\sim1.5\times$ improvement over baselines and up to $8.49\times$ speedup over autoregressive decoding.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes LibraSpec, a dynamic speculative-length selection algorithm that optimizes speedup for diffusion-based speculative decoding, achieving up to 8.49× faster inference over standard autoregressive decoding.
AI.motivation: Speculative decoding speeds up LLM inference by drafting and then verifying multiple tokens per step, but its efficiency heavily depends on the chosen speculative length. Existing dynamic methods are tailored to autoregressive drafters, where tokens are generated sequentially and the main question is how many drafted tokens will be accepted. With newer diffusion-based drafters, which can generate token blocks in parallel at low cost, the bottleneck shifts to deciding how many of these cheap candidates are actually worth the more expensive verification, requiring a new length-selection strategy.
AI.method: The authors reformulate dynamic speculative-length selection as an expected speedup optimization problem. They derive a marginal decision rule: extend the speculative sequence only when the expected gain from additional accepted tokens exceeds the added verification cost. Based on this, they design LibraSpec, a training-free, plug-and-play algorithm that adaptively chooses the speculative length in each round using the drafter’s confidence scores. LibraSpec iteratively adjusts the length according to this marginal criterion and is proven to monotonically converge to the optimal speculative length.
AI.result: Across six different target language models, three diffusion-based speculative decoding methods, and benchmarks in math, coding, and chat tasks, LibraSpec consistently improves decoding efficiency in both greedy and sampling regimes. It yields an additional 0.5–1.5× speedup compared with prior speculative-decoding baselines and achieves up to 8.49× speedup relative to standard autoregressive decoding.
AI.conclusion: Dynamic speculative-length control must be rethought for diffusion-based drafters, focusing on the tradeoff between cheap parallel drafting and expensive verification. LibraSpec addresses this by optimizing expected speedup via a marginal cost–benefit rule, requires no retraining, and can be plugged into existing diffusion-based speculative decoders. Theoretical analysis and experiments demonstrate that LibraSpec converges to near-optimal speculative lengths and delivers substantial, consistent inference speedups.

title: Reason Wide, Not Deep: Amortizing the Reasoning Premium into Distilled Skills
summary: Reasoning modes of language models outperform their non-reasoning counterparts on multi-step agentic tasks, but pay a 3-6x premium in output tokens on every episode -- much of it spent re-deriving procedures that are shared across episodes of the same domain. We show this recurring cost can be amortized: a coding agent analyses a small corpus of existing trajectories from a training split and compiles a compact natural-language skill that is injected into the non-reasoning model's system prompt. Across four agentic benchmarks (ALFWorld, tau$^2$-bench telecom and retail, and SpreadsheetBench-Verified), skills recover 55%-100%+ of the reasoning gap for GPT-5.4-mini on held-out tasks -- exceeding the reasoning mode outright on two of four -- while emitting 2.7-6x fewer output tokens and zero reasoning tokens. Notably, reasoning traces are not a prerequisite: skills distilled from non-reasoning trajectories alone remain competitive with skills distilled from paired reasoning/non-reasoning corpora, with domain-dependent differences between the two sources. We interpret these results through a search lens: test-time reasoning is deep search inside a single episode, re-paid at every deployment, while corpus distillation is wide search across episodes, paid once. The two recover overlapping procedural knowledge, and width over cheap trajectories is often the better buy -- with the residual gap on some domains (telecom, SpreadsheetBench) delineating where genuinely per-instance deep search remains necessary.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes amortizing the token and reasoning cost of multi-step agentic LLM tasks by distilling reusable natural-language skills from past trajectories and injecting them into a cheaper, non-reasoning model’s prompt, recovering most or all of the performance of explicit reasoning modes with far fewer tokens.
AI.motivation: Reasoning modes in language models (e.g., chain-of-thought) significantly improve performance on multi-step, agentic tasks but incur a large computational and monetary overhead because they generate many extra tokens and repeatedly rediscover similar procedures across episodes. This recurring per-episode cost is inefficient for deployed agents that operate many times in the same domain. The authors are motivated to reduce this overhead by finding a way to reuse procedural knowledge across tasks, so that the benefits of reasoning can be retained without paying the reasoning token cost on every single episode.
AI.method: The authors introduce a corpus distillation approach. A coding agent first analyzes a small set of existing agent trajectories from a training split, potentially including both reasoning-mode and non-reasoning-mode traces. From this corpus, the agent synthesizes a compact, reusable, natural-language description of domain-specific procedures, which they call a “skill”. This skill is then injected into the system prompt of a cheaper non-reasoning model at test time, instead of running that model in reasoning mode. They evaluate this approach across four multi-step agentic benchmarks (ALFWorld, tau^2-bench telecom, tau^2-bench retail, and SpreadsheetBench-Verified), and compare (1) non-reasoning base models, (2) reasoning-mode models, and (3) non-reasoning models augmented with distilled skills. They also compare skills learned from reasoning traces, from non-reasoning traces alone, and from paired corpora to understand the contribution of each data source.
AI.result: Across the four agentic benchmarks, adding distilled skills to GPT-5.4-mini recovers between 55% and more than 100% of the performance gap between non-reasoning and reasoning modes on held-out tasks. On two of the four benchmarks, the skill-augmented non-reasoning model even surpasses the performance of the explicit reasoning mode. At the same time, this approach reduces token usage substantially, emitting 2.7–6 times fewer output tokens and no reasoning tokens at all. Furthermore, the authors find that skills distilled solely from non-reasoning trajectories are often competitive with those distilled from corpora containing explicit reasoning, though the relative advantage is domain-dependent.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that much of the benefit of test-time reasoning for multi-step agentic tasks can be captured through one-time corpus-level distillation of reusable procedures into natural-language skills. This amortizes the cost of search: instead of deep search within each individual episode (as in chain-of-thought reasoning), corpus distillation performs wide search over many trajectories once, then reuses the resulting skill description across episodes. The authors interpret the remaining performance gap in some domains (e.g., telecom, SpreadsheetBench) as indicating where genuine per-instance deep reasoning is still necessary, but they argue that, in many settings, wide search over cheap trajectories is a more efficient way to acquire procedural knowledge than repeated deep search at deployment time.

title: Can We Optimize the Performance-Carbon Emission Break-Even Point?: The Quest for Greener LLMs
comment: 13 Pages, 6 Figures, Submitted to ARR Cycle
summary: The carbon footprint of any deployed Large Language Model (LLM) accumulates during inference, where repeated use of the model substantially exceeds the one-time cost of fine-tuning. Yet most efficiency interventions target either pre-training scale or post-hoc compression. We ask whether folding a calibrated, differentiable energy surrogate into the fine-tuning objective can produce inference behavior that gains task accuracy at zero or near-zero carbon cost, a break-even configuration. We propose a joint loss mechanism with a per-model carbon-emission parameter, a linear surrogate over parameter norm, FLOP proxy, and a memory proxy, fit from on-hardware energy profiling. We fine-tune three architecturally distinct families: Gemma-2 2B, Llama-3.1 8B, and Qwen-2.5 14B, and evaluate inference F1 and CO$_2$ emissions on three MMLU subjects: abstract algebra, philosophy, and formal logic. We discover from several outcomes that the carbon term behaves as either harmful interference or beneficial regularization depending on the task structure. We position calibrated carbon-aware fine-tuning as a lightweight, drop-in regularizer with a non-empty but model and task-dependent break-even region. This is an ongoing work, and we will release our codebase soon.

AI.tldr: The paper explores integrating a calibrated carbon/energy surrogate directly into the fine-tuning loss of LLMs to reduce inference-time CO2 emissions without sacrificing task accuracy, showing that this "carbon-aware" term can act as either harmful interference or useful regularization depending on model and task, and identifying conditions where accuracy gains come at near-zero extra carbon cost.
AI.motivation: Deployed LLMs incur most of their carbon footprint during inference rather than during the one-time fine-tuning step, but most efficiency work focuses on pre-training scale reductions or post-hoc compression. There is little understanding of how to steer fine-tuning itself so that the resulting model behaves in an energy-efficient way at inference, ideally improving accuracy without increasing emissions. The authors aim to fill this gap by making the fine-tuning objective explicitly carbon-aware and studying the trade-off between performance and emissions in a controlled setting.
AI.method: The authors construct a differentiable carbon/energy surrogate and incorporate it as an additional term in the fine-tuning loss. The surrogate is a linear model over three proxies: parameter norm, a FLOP-based proxy, and a memory-usage proxy. Its coefficients are calibrated using on-hardware energy profiling so that the surrogate approximates real energy/CO2 cost. A per-model carbon-emission parameter controls the strength of this term. They then fine-tune three LLM families of different sizes and architectures—Gemma-2 2B, Llama-3.1 8B, and Qwen-2.5 14B—under this joint loss. Performance (F1) and estimated CO2 emissions during inference are evaluated on three MMLU subjects: abstract algebra, philosophy, and formal logic.
AI.result: Experiments reveal that the carbon-aware loss term does not act uniformly across tasks and models. In some cases it introduces harmful interference, degrading task performance or failing to reduce emissions meaningfully. In other cases it behaves like a beneficial regularizer, yielding similar or improved F1 scores while keeping CO2 emissions constant or nearly constant, achieving a break-even or near break-even configuration. They identify a non-empty break-even region where the added carbon term leads to accuracy gains at zero or negligible additional carbon cost, but the size and location of this region depend strongly on both the model architecture and the task domain.
AI.conclusion: Calibrated carbon-aware fine-tuning, implemented as a differentiable energy surrogate added to the training objective, can function as a lightweight, drop-in regularizer that sometimes yields better task performance without increasing inference-time CO2 emissions. However, its effects are highly model- and task-dependent, alternately acting as a helpful regularizer or as harmful interference. The work suggests that sustainable deployment of LLMs can be supported by explicitly carbon-aware objectives, but careful calibration and task-specific tuning are necessary. The study is ongoing and the authors plan to release their codebase for further exploration.

title: TelemetrySuffBench: Is Agent Telemetry Sufficient for Failure-Origin Diagnosis?
summary: Agent systems increasingly expose execution traces, yet telemetry that reveals a failure may still be inadequate for identifying where that failure originated. We introduce TelemetrySuffBench, a controlled benchmark that separates failure detection, fault-origin localization, and safe abstention under insufficient evidence. The benchmark constructs canonical multi-component traces with delayed-binding faults and renders them as paired coarse views, seven-factor telemetry masks, and exact-equal ambiguous origin pairs. We evaluate five frontier language models using unified protocols, explicit candidate sets, invalid-output accounting, subgroup analyses, and a frozen blind holdout. With full telemetry, origin-step Top-1 accuracy ranges from 33.8% to 97.2% across models. Metadata, OpenTelemetry-compatible, and OpenInference-compatible views retain 99.5% to 100% detection F1 while limiting origin-step accuracy to at most 0.5%, exposing a robust detection-localization gap. Factor ablations further show that removing decision content reduces origin-step accuracy to zero for every model, while provenance removal also causes large model-dependent losses. On rich ambiguous inputs that require abstention, evidence gating reduces unsupported unique-origin answers by 12.5 to 48.6 percentage points for three models, whereas two models still answer every case, revealing strong model dependence in safe abstention. Results on the frozen holdout reproduce the central pattern within the same generator family. These findings show that terminal status can support detection, whereas reliable causal attribution requires explicit decision-to-provenance links and abstention safeguards that remain effective across models. The dataset and benchmark implementation are available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/TelemetrySuffBench-E635/README.md.

AI.tldr: They build a benchmark (TelemetrySuffBench) to test whether telemetry from agent systems is sufficient not only to detect failures but also to localize where they originated, and to see if models can safely abstain when evidence is insufficient.
AI.motivation: In complex agent systems, execution traces and telemetry are increasingly available, but even when a failure is visible, it can be hard to tell which component or step actually caused it. This creates a gap between detecting that something went wrong and correctly attributing the cause, which is important for debugging, accountability, and safety. The authors want to systematically study how well current language models can detect failures, localize their origin, and abstain when the telemetry does not support a confident conclusion.
AI.method: The authors construct a controlled benchmark called TelemetrySuffBench consisting of canonical multi-component traces where faults are introduced with delayed binding so the point of failure and its origin can differ. They render these traces in several telemetry “views”: paired coarse views, seven-factor telemetry masks, and pairs where the true origin is intentionally ambiguous. They then evaluate five state-of-the-art language models using unified evaluation protocols that include explicit candidate origin sets, accounting for invalid outputs, subgroup analyses, and tests on a frozen, blind holdout set. They run factor ablations on the telemetry (e.g., removing decision content or provenance information) and also design rich ambiguous cases that require models to abstain unless evidence suffices, measuring how evidence gating affects unsafe guesses.
AI.result: With full telemetry, models’ Top-1 accuracy for identifying the origin step ranges widely, from 33.8% to 97.2%. Telemetry views compatible with metadata, OpenTelemetry, and OpenInference maintain almost perfect failure detection (99.5–100% F1) while keeping origin-step accuracy below 0.5%, showing a strong separation between detecting failures and localizing their cause. Factor ablations show that removing decision content drops origin localization accuracy to zero for all models, and removing provenance also results in large, model-dependent performance losses. In ambiguous cases designed to require abstention, applying evidence gating reduces unsupported unique-origin answers by 12.5–48.6 percentage points for three models, but two models still answer on every case, indicating a high degree of model dependence in safe abstention behavior. Similar patterns are observed on a frozen holdout set generated by the same family of generators.
AI.conclusion: TelemetrySuffBench reveals that while terminal status and limited telemetry are sufficient for highly reliable failure detection, they are not sufficient for trustworthy causal attribution of faults. Accurate origin localization requires explicit links between decision content and provenance information. Furthermore, safe abstention is not a given: models vary widely in their willingness to withhold answers when evidence is insufficient, so explicit abstention safeguards and evidence gating mechanisms are needed and must be robust across different models. The benchmark thus highlights a structural detection-localization gap and provides a controlled setting for evaluating and improving failure attribution and abstention in agentic systems.

title: Multilingual Emotion Neurons in Large Audio-Language Models
summary: Emotion is central to human communication, and its expression varies across languages. Large audio-language models (LALMs) achieve strong performance on multilingual speech tasks, yet it remains unclear whether they encode emotion through language-specific correlations or language-agnostic representations. We present the first neuron-level interpretability study of this question. We define Multilingual Emotion Neurons (MLENs) as functional units exhibiting stable emotional selectivity and aligned causal effects across languages, and introduce Consistency-Regularized Fusion (CR-Fusion) to identify them. Across four modern LALMs and 12 typologically diverse languages, emotion-sensitive neurons identified independently per language show minimal overlap, and additional monolingual identification data saturates quickly without isolating more transferable units, motivating identification from pooled cross-lingual evidence. Causal interventions demonstrate that MLENs identified by CR-Fusion provide more precise and transferable affective control than monolingual neuron sets in both zero-shot and low-resource settings. Leave-one-out ablations further reveal asymmetric transfer: individual identification languages, including low-resource ones, contribute non-redundant evidence, while several low-resource languages benefit most from the resulting cross-lingual transfer. Together, our findings provide the first causal, neuron-level account of how LALMs encode emotion across languages, and establish multilingual neuron identification as an effective mechanism for understanding cross-lingual affective behavior.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates how large audio-language models encode emotion across multiple languages by identifying and causally testing multilingual emotion neurons (MLENs).
AI.motivation: While large audio-language models perform well on multilingual emotional and speech tasks, it is unclear whether their representations of emotion are tied to specific languages or reflect language-agnostic, shared emotional structure. Understanding this at neuron level would advance interpretability and cross-lingual affective control, especially for low-resource languages.
AI.method: The authors introduce the concept of Multilingual Emotion Neurons (MLENs), neurons that show consistent emotional selectivity and causal effects across languages. They propose Consistency-Regularized Fusion (CR-Fusion), which identifies such neurons by pooling cross-lingual evidence and enforcing consistency of emotional behavior. They apply this to four modern LALMs over 12 typologically diverse languages, comparing neuron sets identified monolingually versus via CR-Fusion, and conduct causal interventions and leave-one-out ablations to assess control and transfer properties.
AI.result: Monolingually identified emotion-sensitive neurons show little overlap across languages, and adding more monolingual data quickly saturates without revealing more transferable units. In contrast, neurons identified via CR-Fusion (MLENs) enable more accurate and transferable control of emotional outputs in zero-shot and low-resource settings. Leave-one-out ablations show that each identification language contributes unique evidence, including low-resource ones, and that some low-resource languages gain the most from cross-lingual transfer enabled by MLENs.
AI.conclusion: LALMs encode emotion through neuron populations that can be shared across languages, but these are not discoverable via purely monolingual analysis. The proposed CR-Fusion method successfully uncovers MLENs that causally support precise, cross-lingual affective control, particularly benefiting low-resource languages. This establishes multilingual neuron identification as a powerful tool for explaining and steering cross-lingual emotional behavior in LALMs.

title: GraphThink: Graph-Enhanced LLM Thinking for Long-Horizon Embodied Task Planning
summary: Embodied agents using LLM-based planners often struggle with physical hallucinations, poor generalization to long-horizon tasks, and lack of environmental awareness. We propose GraphThink, a novel framework that integrates a task graph to provide structured knowledge for robust planning and a scene graph to maintain environmental memory for event-driven replanning. Specifically, the task graph guides LLM thinking through contextual prompting and iterative refinement, effectively mitigating planning hallucinations. Furthermore, within the GRPO framework, the task graph offers delicate reward design to train the LLM planner, enhancing long-horizon planning capabilities and improving generalization. Finally, an event-driven replanning module, powered by the scene graph, enables closed-loop environment awareness and error correction. GraphThink achieves state-of-the-art performance on the ALFRED benchmark. In particular, our high-level planner surpasses leading API-based LLMs on both the validation set and held-out long-horizon tasks, underscoring its robust zero-shot and few-shot capabilities. Additional evaluations further demonstrate strong out-of-distribution generalization to novel tasks and environments.

AI.tldr: GraphThink is a framework for LLM-based embodied agents that combines task graphs and scene graphs to reduce planning hallucinations, improve long-horizon generalization, and enable event-driven replanning, achieving SOTA on ALFRED and strong OOD generalization.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM-based planners for embodied agents often hallucinate impossible actions, fail on long-horizon tasks, and lack persistent awareness of the environment, which limits their robustness and generalization. The paper aims to provide a structured way to guide the LLM’s reasoning and maintain memory of environmental changes so that agents can plan more reliably and adapt to unexpected events.
AI.method: The authors introduce GraphThink, which uses: (1) a task graph providing structured, contextual knowledge that guides LLM reasoning via tailored prompts and iterative refinement, and also defines fine-grained rewards in a GRPO reinforcement learning framework to train the planner for long-horizon tasks; (2) a scene graph that stores environment state and supports an event-driven replanning module, allowing the agent to update its plan when the environment changes or errors occur. Together, these graphs form a closed-loop planning and replanning system for embodied agents.
AI.result: On the ALFRED benchmark, GraphThink attains state-of-the-art results. Its high-level planner outperforms strong API-based LLM baselines on both validation and held-out long-horizon tasks, showing superior zero-shot and few-shot planning. Additional experiments on novel tasks and unseen environments demonstrate robust out-of-distribution generalization.
AI.conclusion: Structured graph-based guidance for LLM planners—via task graphs for reasoning and reward shaping, and scene graphs for environmental memory and replanning—significantly reduces hallucinations and improves long-horizon, robust planning in embodied agents. GraphThink’s performance on ALFRED and OOD settings suggests that integrating symbolic graph structure with LLMs is an effective path toward more reliable embodied intelligence.

title: OmnilingualGAIA2: Evaluating the Multilingual Gap in Frontier AI Agents
summary: Agentic benchmarks aim to measure how well AI agents plan, search, execute, and recover within realistic multi-tool environments, but they are almost exclusively in English. As AI agents are globally deployed to a linguistically diverse user base, whether agentic competence measured in English transfers to other languages remains an open question. We introduce OmnilingualGAIA2, a machine-translated expansion (with partial human- expert validation) of the GAIA2 agentic benchmark, covering ten target languages spanning five writing systems, paired with a localised and human-calibrated multilingual verifier. Evaluating seven frontier and open-weight agents, we find a universal cross-lingual gap of 8.8-18.4 pass@3 points that is agent-asymmetric in magnitude, concentrates on tool-orchestration rather than quantitative reasoning, and does not close with model scale. A stratified error attribution decomposes the gap as predominantly model-driven (55%), with a bounded translation-contamination floor of only 6.4% of scenario-language pairs. Human-expert linguistic analysis further identifies morphological cue loss and amplified ambiguity as the primary failure mechanisms in non-Latin-script languages. Our results argue that multilingual agentic evaluation must become a standard part of the reporting protocol for globally deployed agents.

AI.tldr: The paper extends an English agentic benchmark into ten languages and shows that current AI agents systematically perform worse in non-English settings, mainly due to model limitations rather than translation noise.
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks for AI agents largely focus on English, despite real-world deployment to users speaking many languages. It is unknown whether strong performance on English agentic tasks (planning, tool use, recovery) transfers cross-lingually, which is critical for fair, safe, and reliable global use.
AI.method: The authors create OmnilingualGAIA2 by machine-translating GAIA2 tasks into ten target languages across five writing systems, with partial validation by human experts. They also build a localized multilingual verifier calibrated by humans. Seven state-of-the-art and open-weight agents are evaluated on this benchmark. They perform stratified error attribution to separate model-driven errors from translation-induced issues and complement this with human linguistic analysis of error patterns, especially in non-Latin-script languages.
AI.result: Across all tested agents, there is a consistent cross-lingual performance drop of 8.8–18.4 pass@3 points compared to English. This gap is asymmetric across agents, is more severe in tool-orchestration tasks than in quantitative reasoning, and does not diminish with larger model scale. Decomposition shows that about 55% of the gap is model-driven, while translation contamination accounts for only about 6.4% of scenario-language pairs. Linguistic analysis reveals key failure modes in non-Latin scripts, particularly loss of morphological cues and increased ambiguity in translated prompts.
AI.conclusion: Agentic competence measured only in English is not representative of performance in other languages, especially in complex tool-use settings. Since most of the performance gap is due to model limitations rather than translation artifacts, multilingual agentic evaluation should become standard practice when reporting capabilities of globally deployed AI agents.

title: When Is Benchmark Contamination Detectable? Information Limits and Power-Calibrated Audits
summary: Behavioral contamination detectors can return "no evidence" either because a benchmark is clean or because the audit has little power. We formalize this distinction for a benchmark in which an unknown fraction alpha of items was seen during training. With matched clean and seen controls, the behavioral channel is the sparse mixture Q_alpha = (1 - alpha) P_0 + alpha P_1, and an exact second-moment argument shows that detectability is governed by alpha * rho * sqrt(m), where rho^2 = chi^2(P_1 || P_0) measures behavioral separability. Any scalar detector reduces to its efficacy, ef = |E_1 f - E_0 f| / sqrt(Var_0(f)) <= rho, which can be estimated from controls before the audit is run. A separate sample-split certificate lower-bounds alpha distribution-free, without requiring an orientation assumption. Our empirical finding is two-sided. Frozen calibration efficacy predicts held-out power curves, with R^2 = 0.83-0.98 across six exact-permutation channels, but the efficacy-only Gaussian budget is miscalibrated at the small sample sizes it prescribes, failing in 9/9 gate-passing channels even though efficacy itself transports. The failure is in the inversion, not the calibration. A predeclared two-stage planner that simulates the deployed test repairs the budgets, is uniformly conservative, and abstains when its probe does not transport. The certificate is valid but vacuous at audit scale, and a five-seed paired injection study recovers the mechanism ordering verbatim > paraphrase > surface, in which the apparent answer-only signal is explained by baseline drift. We report the audit contract and its failures together: a non-rejection is interpretable only alongside the efficacy, budget, and validity gates that produced it.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes when and how behavioral tests can reliably detect training data contamination, showing that detection power depends on contamination rate, behavioral separability, and sample size, and proposing practical planning and certification tools while highlighting where current methods fail.
AI.motivation: Audits for training data contamination often conclude with "no evidence of contamination," but this can mean either true cleanliness or simply that the audit lacked statistical power. Practitioners lack clear, quantitative guidance on how powerful their tests are, how much data they need, and how to interpret non-rejections. The paper aims to formalize this distinction, provide power and budget calculations rooted in theory, and clarify what can and cannot be concluded from behavioral contamination detectors in realistic, small-sample audit regimes.
AI.method: The authors model behavioral contamination as a sparse mixture distribution Q_alpha = (1 - alpha) P_0 + alpha P_1, where P_0 and P_1 are the behavioral distributions for clean and seen items, and alpha is the (unknown) fraction of contaminated items. Using an exact second-moment (chi-squared) analysis, they show that detectability is controlled by alpha * rho * sqrt(m), where rho^2 = chi^2(P_1 || P_0) measures behavioral separability and m is the sample size. Any scalar detector is summarized by its efficacy ef = |E_1 f - E_0 f| / sqrt(Var_0(f)), which is provably upper-bounded by rho and can be estimated from control data. They also develop a distribution-free sample-splitting certificate that lower-bounds alpha without assuming any particular direction of the behavioral shift. Empirically, they test multiple "channels" (experimental setups) with exact permutation tests, compare predicted power curves from frozen calibration efficacy to realized power, and examine a two-stage planner that simulates the deployed test to set conservative budgets and abstention rules. A paired injection study with different contamination mechanisms (verbatim, paraphrase, surface) is used to validate mechanistic claims about where the signal comes from.
AI.result: Theoretical analysis shows that behavioral detectability scales as alpha * rho * sqrt(m), so small contamination rates or weak behavioral separability make detection impossible at realistic sample sizes. Efficacy ef is identified as a key one-dimensional summary of any scalar detector and can be estimated in advance; it tightly predicts empirical power curves, achieving R^2 between 0.83 and 0.98 across six permutation-based behavioral channels. However, a naive Gaussian power-budget calculation that only uses efficacy is badly miscalibrated at the small sample sizes it recommends: in nine out of nine channels that pass simple validity gates, the predicted budgets fail, even though efficacy itself "transports" from calibration to held-out audits. The issue lies in inverting the Gaussian model to solve for sample size, not in estimating efficacy. A predeclared two-stage planning procedure that explicitly simulates the intended test fixes the problem, producing conservative (safe) budgets and abstaining in cases where the calibration probe does not transfer to the audit. The distribution-free contamination certificate is provably valid but practically vacuous at audit scales, providing only very weak lower bounds on alpha. The injection study recovers the expected ordering of contamination mechanisms—verbatim > paraphrase > surface—and attributes an apparent answer-only signal to baseline drift rather than genuine contamination signal in the answers alone.
AI.conclusion: Behavioral contamination audits cannot be interpreted solely through hypothesis test outcomes; their meaning depends critically on the achievable efficacy, the sample-size budget, and validity checks on whether calibration conditions transfer to the audit. The paper provides a theoretical framework that links contamination rate, behavioral separability, and sample size, and identifies efficacy as a central quantity that can be measured before running an audit. Empirically, efficacy predicts power well, but Gaussian-budget inversions are unreliable in small-sample regimes, and distribution-free certificates, while valid, are too weak to be useful at realistic audit scales. A simulation-based, two-stage planning procedure offers a more reliable way to set conservative budgets and decide when to abstain. Overall, a "no evidence of contamination" result is only meaningful when reported together with the efficacy estimates, budget planning, and validation gates that underwrite it, emphasizing transparent audit contracts and explicit acknowledgment of where the methodology can fail.

title: Unsure but Certain: Uncovering the Representation-Confidence Gap in Diffusion Language Models
summary: Diffusion language models use broad context to create text, suggesting they might handle input noise better than standard models. Testing reveals this is only partially true. Internally, diffusion models detect text errors highly accurately. Externally, their reported certainty ignores this signal. As accuracy drops due to noise, confidence stays near its maximum and the ability to correctly rank answers degrades toward random chance. We call this mismatch the representation confidence gap. The visible concentration of high certainty scores is a misleading surface symptom. Standard math adjustments remove this concentration but fail to fix the underlying loss of ranking order. This ranking deficit favors standard models under noisy conditions and resists common remedies. Matching training recovers accuracy but not ranking, while score recalibration and input level error signals cannot reorder the final answers. However, the information needed to properly evaluate an answer survives in the hidden states. A lightweight extraction tool uses this signal to improve ranking. This approach is highly efficient because it leaves the base model completely frozen and requires zero additional text generation steps. We present this tool to prove the signal exists, while clearly noting its limits. Ultimately, certainty reliability is a more pressing limit than overall accuracy under noisy conditions.

AI.tldr: The paper finds that diffusion language models internally detect noisy text very well but their output confidence scores fail to reflect this, leading to unreliable certainty under noise. A simple method that reads hidden states can recover better answer ranking without retraining the model.
AI.motivation: Diffusion language models are believed to be more robust to noisy inputs because they use broad context, but this assumption had not been rigorously tested. The authors want to understand how well these models actually cope with noisy text, especially in terms of the reliability of their confidence scores and answer ranking. They aim to diagnose whether diffusion models are really preferable to standard models in noisy settings and to identify where robustness breaks down.
AI.method: The authors systematically inject noise into text inputs and compare diffusion language models to standard models along three axes: accuracy under noise, reported confidence (certainty) levels, and the ability to rank candidate answers correctly. They analyze internal representations to see whether the models detect errors at the feature level. They then test standard post-hoc fixes like mathematical score normalization, recalibration, training to match noisy conditions, and using input-level error signals to adjust output scores. Finally, they design a lightweight extractor that reads hidden states of the frozen diffusion model to produce improved ranking scores, without changing the base model or requiring extra generations.
AI.result: Experiments show that diffusion models internally recognize textual errors with high fidelity, but their external confidence scores remain near maximal even when accuracy falls due to noise. This creates a representation confidence gap: internal states know the input is corrupted, but the final scores do not. As noise increases, the model’s ability to properly rank answers decays toward random, despite still being very confident. Standard mathematical adjustments can smooth or spread out the confidence distribution but cannot restore correct ranking order. Matching training conditions improves accuracy somewhat but not ranking robustness, and neither score recalibration nor input-level error awareness can solve the ranking loss. However, reading hidden states with a small auxiliary tool recovers much of the lost ranking quality, demonstrating that the necessary evaluation signal is present but unused by the default scoring head.
AI.conclusion: The main limitation of diffusion language models under noisy input is not raw accuracy but the unreliability of their certainty estimates. These models develop strong internal representations that detect noise, yet their output confidence fails to leverage this information, leading to a representation confidence gap that harms answer ranking. Conventional fixes do not repair the ranking deficit. A simple hidden-state-based extraction mechanism partially closes this gap without retraining or extra inference steps, proving that the relevant signal is available. The work suggests that future research should focus on making certainty more faithful to internal representations, especially in noisy environments, if diffusion LMs are to be trusted in practical settings.

title: TongGuOCR: A Layout-Aware and Token-Augmented OCR Framework for Chinese Historical Documents
summary: Chinese historical documents preserve valuable cultural heritage, but many collections remain accessible only as scanned page images, preventing full-text retrieval, collation, and computational analysis. Optical character recognition (OCR) can bridge this gap, but accurate transcription remains challenging because historical documents often contain complex layouts, rare characters, and nontrivial reading orders. We propose TongGuOCR, a layout-aware and token-augmented OCR framework for Chinese historical documents. First, a Layout-Aware Preprocessing module constructs and refines locally coherent recognition blocks to preserve local context while reducing interference across regions. Second, a Token-Augmented Recognition module augments the transcription target at two complementary levels: character-level vocabulary expansion gives each rare glyph a direct one-token representation and shortens its decoding path, while line-to-line transition modeling injects discrete spatial displacement tokens that guide the decoder along complex reading paths without requiring precise coordinates. Experiments on two Chinese historical document OCR benchmarks show that TongGuOCR outperforms representative traditional task-specific OCR models, general-purpose multimodal large language models (MLLMs), and OCR-oriented MLLMs. On the more challenging M5HisDoc benchmark, TongGuOCR achieves 93.76 AR and reduces NED from 10.43 to 6.15 and RO-ED from 7.53 to 3.49 relative to the best competing score for each metric. An online demo is available at https://jzzh2004.github.io/TongGuOCR.

AI.tldr: TongGuOCR is a layout-aware, token-augmented OCR framework that significantly improves recognition accuracy for complex Chinese historical documents.
AI.motivation: Chinese historical documents are mostly available as scanned images, which prevents full-text search, collation, and computational analysis. Existing OCR methods struggle with these documents due to complex layouts, rare characters, and irregular reading orders, leading to low transcription accuracy. There is a need for an OCR framework tailored to these challenges to unlock the cultural and research value of such collections.
AI.method: The paper proposes TongGuOCR with two key modules: (1) A Layout-Aware Preprocessing module that segments pages into locally coherent recognition blocks, refining them to preserve local context while minimizing interference between regions; (2) A Token-Augmented Recognition module that enhances the decoding target in two ways: (a) character-level vocabulary expansion that assigns a unique, single token to each rare glyph to shorten its decoding path; (b) line-to-line transition modeling, which inserts discrete spatial displacement tokens to guide the decoder along complex and non-linear reading paths without relying on precise coordinate supervision.
AI.result: On two Chinese historical document OCR benchmarks, TongGuOCR outperforms traditional specialized OCR systems, general-purpose multimodal large language models, and OCR-focused MLLMs. On the more difficult M5HisDoc benchmark, it achieves 93.76 AR, and improves error metrics over the best existing methods: NED is reduced from 10.43 to 6.15, and RO-ED from 7.53 to 3.49.
AI.conclusion: TongGuOCR effectively addresses the specific challenges of Chinese historical document OCR—complex layouts, rare characters, and nontrivial reading orders—through layout-aware preprocessing and token-level enhancements. The framework substantially improves recognition quality over both traditional OCR and modern MLLM-based approaches, making large-scale, accurate transcription of historical Chinese texts more feasible. An online demo demonstrates its practical applicability.

title: Evidence-Calibrated Runtime Reconstruction for Agent Skills Across Heterogeneous Coding Agents
comment: 17 pages, 1 figure, 6 tables. Submitted to PROFES 2026. Code and artifacts: https://github.com/hellogxp/skill-runtime-intelligence
summary:
Agent Skills package reusable instructions and assets for tool-using language-model agents. Progressive loading creates failure boundaries poorly represented by session-, model-, or tool-centric traces: a Skill can be discovered but not activated, activated without instructions, or appear successful without an independently verified outcome. We present Skill Runtime Intelligence, a passive runtime-intelligence system that reconstructs supported Skill-lifecycle stages across heterogeneous harnesses while preserving unsupported stages as unknown. Its Run Panorama separates immutable events, deterministic relations, inferred diagnoses, and controlled outcomes with four evidence grades; optional trace import and OTLP/HTTP export support existing observability deployments.
  Across six frozen repository profiles, three coding agents, and seven clean or fault-injected conditions, all 126 executions preserve source worktrees and each correlates to exactly one source session. Yet adapters expose three distinct semantics: no Skill runs; complete runs but no failure-like events; or failure-like events in every operational-failure and clean session. In a seven-template diagnostic study, semantic aliases and Panorama localize the same six non-clean boundaries but differ in exact/status behavior; both Raw views emit a failure status on all 18 clean cases, while Panorama emits none. A known-rule graph conforms to 126/126 frozen contracts, whereas a second model completes only 228/378 calls. These observations motivate executable adapter qualification and show that event presence is not boundary fidelity, composite exact scores mask distinct errors, and model explanations must not overwrite deterministic facts.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Skill Runtime Intelligence, a system to analyze and diagnose the lifecycle of reusable “Skills” in tool-using LLM agents, revealing subtle boundary and observability issues that traditional traces miss.
AI.motivation: As agents start using reusable Skills that load progressively, existing observability tools (focused on sessions, models, or tools) fail to capture where and how Skill executions actually succeed or fail. Failures can occur at multiple lifecycle stages (discovery, activation, instruction use, and outcome verification), but current traces either conflate or miss these boundaries, making it hard to qualify adapters, evaluate agents, and trust explanations.
AI.method: The authors design Skill Runtime Intelligence, a passive runtime-intelligence layer that reconstructs the lifecycle stages of Skills using a Run Panorama abstraction. This Panorama separates raw immutable events, deterministic relations, inferred diagnoses, and controlled outcomes, each with four evidence grades. The system imports traces and exports via OTLP/HTTP to fit into existing observability pipelines. They then evaluate across six frozen code-repository profiles, three coding agents, and seven experimental conditions (clean and fault-injected) to study how different adapters encode Skill semantics and boundary events.
AI.result: In 126 runs, all executions preserve source worktrees and align with exactly one source session, but adapters show three incompatible semantics: (1) no Skill runs at all, (2) Skills run but without exposing failure-like events, and (3) failure-like events appear even in clean sessions. In a seven-template diagnostic study, both semantic aliases and the Panorama identify the same non-clean boundaries, but differ on status details; raw views wrongly emit failures on all 18 clean runs while Panorama correctly emits none. A known-rule graph adheres to all 126 contracts, while a second model fails 150 of 378 calls, evidencing significant discrepancies in behavior.
AI.conclusion: The study demonstrates that merely having events does not guarantee faithful representation of Skill boundaries, that aggregate exact-match scores can hide distinct classes of errors, and that model-generated explanations must not override deterministically inferable facts. These findings argue for explicit, executable qualification of adapters and structured runtime intelligence like Run Panorama to achieve reliable observability and evaluation of Skill-based LLM agents.

title: ZhuLong: Execution-Grounded LLM Agent for EDA Scripting with Offline API Self-Exploration
summary:
EDA scripting with tool-specific, often undocumented APIs remains a long-tail bottleneck that existing LLMs fail to address. This paper presents ZhuLong, an execution-grounded LLM coding agent for PyAether and SKILL that combines API retrieval, documentation inspection, and sandbox execution via unified MCP tools, augmented by an offline API self-exploration mechanism that infers undocumented API behaviors through counterfactual experimentation.
  We evaluate ZhuLong on EDA-Eval-PyAether, a benchmark of 158 real-world tasks with assertion-based execution, where the complete system achieves 78.5% Pass@1 in the commercial Empyrean Aether environment, substantially outperforming a pure LLM baseline (23.6%). Ablation studies identify sandbox execution as the dominant performance driver (41.2 pp drop when removed), with the self-exploration mechanism contributing an additional 3.2 pp accuracy gain and a 22.1% reduction in per-task tool calls. On 20 interactive tasks involving unsaved layouts and schematics, ZhuLong achieves 60.0% Pass@1 for PyAether and 50.0% for SKILL.

AI.tldr: ZhuLong is an execution-grounded LLM coding agent that automates EDA scripting for PyAether and SKILL using unified tools for API retrieval, documentation inspection, sandbox execution, and offline self-exploration, achieving large gains over pure LLM baselines on a new benchmark.
AI.motivation: EDA scripting relies heavily on tool-specific and often undocumented APIs, creating a long-tail bottleneck for automation and productivity. Existing LLMs struggle in this setting because they lack reliable access to these APIs and their behaviors, especially when documentation is sparse or missing. The authors aim to build an agent that can robustly understand and use such APIs in real EDA environments, improving code generation accuracy and reducing manual effort.
AI.method: The paper introduces ZhuLong, an execution-grounded LLM coding agent for PyAether and SKILL. ZhuLong uses unified MCP tools to (1) retrieve API information, (2) inspect documentation, and (3) perform sandboxed code execution to test and refine candidates. Additionally, it employs an offline API self-exploration mechanism that automatically probes undocumented APIs through counterfactual experiments, inferring their behavior from execution outcomes. The system is evaluated on a purpose-built benchmark and through interactive tasks in realistic environments.
AI.result: On the EDA-Eval-PyAether benchmark of 158 real-world tasks with assertion-based execution, ZhuLong reaches 78.5% Pass@1 in the commercial Empyrean Aether environment, far surpassing a pure LLM baseline at 23.6%. Ablations show that removing sandbox execution causes a 41.2 percentage point drop in accuracy, making it the main performance contributor. The self-exploration component further adds 3.2 percentage points in accuracy and reduces per-task tool calls by 22.1%. On 20 interactive tasks that involve unsaved layouts and schematics, ZhuLong obtains 60.0% Pass@1 on PyAether and 50.0% on SKILL.
AI.conclusion: Execution grounding, especially via sandbox execution, is crucial for effective LLM-based coding in EDA environments with opaque, tool-specific APIs. ZhuLong’s combination of unified tools for API interaction and an offline self-exploration strategy substantially improves task success and efficiency over pure LLM baselines. The results suggest that systematic experimentation on undocumented APIs can close much of the gap between human and automated scripting for real-world EDA workflows.

title: Instability of LLM Pre-Pretraining: It Doesn't Always Help. An Investigation on Multiple Languages
summary: Pretraining LLMs on artificial languages ("pre-pretraining") is a technique that could reportedly increase token efficiency by 33%, i.e., save up to 33% of training tokens needed to reach a certain performance. We validate this prior result for English on a larger set of natural languages across four language families, using two different tokenizers and varying model sizes. We also relate the observed gains (or losses) in token efficiency to quantified linguistic properties of the languages, such as sentence length, morphological richness, and features of dependency syntactic trees (tree depth, number of children, number of crossing dependencies). Our empirical results indicate that the reported gains depend heavily on the experiment setup and the choice of random seed, although we can confirm the trend of stable gains with 128-Dyck pretraining of small models with the Llama tokenizer for most of the examined languages. On a general note, we argue that multiple training runs should be carried out at least for a subset of experiments to avoid the community adopting unstable approaches.

AI.tldr: The paper evaluates pretraining LLMs on artificial languages (pre-pretraining) for token efficiency across many natural languages, finding that reported gains are unstable and highly setup- and seed-dependent.
AI.motivation: Earlier work claimed that pretraining on artificial languages like Dyck can reduce the number of tokens needed to reach a given performance by about 33%. This is attractive because training tokens are expensive, but that result was only shown for English and in a specific setup. The authors want to test whether the effect generalizes to more languages, understand what linguistic properties might explain the gains, and check the robustness of the method.
AI.method: They pre-pretrain models on artificial Dyck-style languages (e.g., 128-Dyck) and then continue training on real natural languages from four language families. They vary: (a) language (several across four families), (b) model size (small vs larger models), (c) tokenizer (at least Llama and another), and (d) random seeds. They systematically measure token efficiency, i.e., how many training tokens are needed to reach a certain performance level on downstream tasks, and correlate the observed gains or losses with quantified linguistic features such as average sentence length, degree of morphological richness, and syntactic dependency tree characteristics (depth, branching factor, crossing dependencies).
AI.result: They show that the originally reported 33% token efficiency gain is not a universal or stable outcome: the size and even direction of the effect varies substantially across languages, setups, and random seeds. For small models using the Llama tokenizer, they generally replicate that 128-Dyck pre-pretraining tends to yield stable token-efficiency gains for most languages studied, but outside that regime the benefits may shrink, disappear, or even reverse. They also find relationships between the measured linguistic properties and the magnitude of the gains, though these are not uniformly strong or consistent.
AI.conclusion: Pre-pretraining on artificial languages can help in some conditions (notably for small models with Llama tokenizer and 128-Dyck) but is far from a universally reliable method to save training tokens. The gains are sensitive to experimental details and random seeds, so claims of large token-efficiency improvements should be interpreted cautiously. The authors recommend that future work include multiple independent training runs—at least for a subset of conditions—to properly estimate variance and avoid the field converging on unstable or irreproducible practices.

title: REIN: Bridging the Gap between Reasoning and Reliability via Reflection and Abstention Alignment
summary: Large reasoning models (LRMs) are prone to hallucination, which undermines their reliability and poses challenges for safe deployment. Hallucinations in LRMs arise from two distinct failure sources: reasoning hallucination, where flawed inference steps propagate to an incorrect conclusion, and knowledge hallucination, where the model lacks the requisite factual knowledge to answer the query. To address reasoning hallucination, we propose REIN, an alignment framework that trains LRMs to produce a structured reasoning sequence, $\texttt{<think>} $$\rightarrow$ $\texttt{<reflection>} $$\rightarrow$ $\texttt{<answer>}$, enabling explicit self-reflection before committing to a final answer. To address knowledge hallucination, REIN introduces a reward mechanism that encourages explicit abstention (e.g., "I don't know") when none of the sampled reasoning chains yields a correct answer, allowing the model to refrain from unsupported predictions. Extensive evaluations on mathematical and commonsense reasoning benchmarks show that REIN consistently improves selective accuracy, reduces incorrect-but-self-endorsed responses, and maintains high coverage compared with competitive baselines. Notably, REIN achieves these gains within a single forward pass, without requiring process supervision, inference-time controllers, external search, or multi-round critiques. Experiments on multiple backbones show that REIN reduces the hallucination proxy by $58\sim72\%$ relative to the base models while maintaining $86\sim91\%$ average coverage, and improves selective accuracy on attempted questions by $6.6\sim14.2\%$.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes REIN, an alignment framework that reduces hallucination in large reasoning models by structuring their reasoning and encouraging abstention when unsure.
AI.motivation: Large reasoning models often hallucinate, producing confident but incorrect answers due to flawed reasoning chains or missing factual knowledge, which threatens reliability and safe deployment. There is a need for methods that both improve reasoning quality and allow models to abstain when they lack sufficient information, without complex multi-pass or externally controlled inference.
AI.method: The authors introduce REIN, an alignment framework that structures model outputs into a three-stage sequence: <think> (reasoning), <reflection> (self-evaluation of the reasoning and answer), and <answer> (final response). They train LRMs so that, given multiple sampled reasoning chains, the model learns to reflect on their validity and either select a correct answer or explicitly abstain (e.g., respond "I don't know") when no chain is reliable. REIN uses a reward mechanism that favors accurate selective answering and abstention in uncertain cases, and is implemented to operate in a single forward pass without process supervision, external search, or multi-round critique.
AI.result: On mathematical and commonsense reasoning benchmarks, REIN improves selective accuracy and reduces the rate of incorrect answers that the model still endorses, while maintaining high coverage of answered questions. Across multiple backbone models, REIN reduces a hallucination proxy metric by 58–72% compared to base models, keeps average coverage at 86–91%, and increases selective accuracy on attempted questions by 6.6–14.2%.
AI.conclusion: REIN effectively mitigates both reasoning and knowledge hallucinations in large reasoning models by combining structured self-reflection with incentivized abstention. It offers substantial reductions in hallucination rates and better selective accuracy without sacrificing much coverage or requiring expensive multi-step inference or external supervision, making it a practical alignment strategy for safer deployment of reasoning models.

title: IDRAAK: From Multi-Agent NLP to Few-Shot Prompting for Semantic Drift Detection in Technical Requirements
summary: Translating technical requirements across languages can introduce semantic drift, altering numerical constraints, polarities, modalities, or other specification-critical meaning. IDRAAK is presented as an interpretable framework for detecting such drift using a language-independent Semantic Requirement Representation (SRR), with six detection workflows evaluated, ranging from deterministic comparison to multi-agent verification and few-shot prompting. On 890 synthetic perturbations across 300 requirements from 10 engineering domains, a single LLM call with six few-shot examples achieves MCC=0.888 and F1=0.983, outperforming the evaluated structured and multi-stage alternatives. Further evaluation on PAWS-X (805 pairs, 5 languages) and XNLI (700 pairs, 7 languages) exposes complementary strengths and limitations of structured and LLM-based approaches. Deterministic SRR comparison performs strongly on technical requirements (F1=0.898) but poorly on general-domain text (F1=0.012), while structured evidence improves performance on adversarial paraphrases. Post-hoc Platt scaling further improves confidence calibration. The results demonstrate that increased agentic complexity does not necessarily improve semantic-drift detection and that simple few-shot prompting can provide a strong and efficient alternative.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces IDRAAK, a framework to detect semantic drift when technical requirements are translated between languages, showing that simple few-shot LLM prompting can outperform more complex, structured, or multi-agent methods.
AI.motivation: When technical requirements are translated across languages, subtle changes in meaning—such as numerical limits, polarity (allow vs. forbid), or modality (must vs. may)—can cause serious specification errors. Existing cross-lingual semantic similarity tools are not tailored to these fine-grained, safety-critical shifts. The authors aim to provide a robust, interpretable way to detect such semantic drift, especially for engineering requirements, where precision is crucial.
AI.method: They propose IDRAAK, built around a language-independent Semantic Requirement Representation (SRR) that abstracts requirements into structured meaning. On top of SRR, they design six detection workflows, from rule-based deterministic SRR comparison to more complex setups involving multi-agent LLM verification and few-shot prompting. They evaluate these workflows on a synthetic benchmark of 890 perturbed requirement pairs drawn from 300 original requirements in 10 engineering domains, and further validate them on public cross-lingual datasets (PAWS-X and XNLI). They also apply post-hoc Platt scaling to improve probability calibration of drift predictions.
AI.result: On the technical-requirement benchmark, a single LLM call with six few-shot examples achieves very strong performance (MCC=0.888, F1=0.983), outperforming more elaborate structured and multi-stage alternatives. Deterministic SRR comparison is competitive on the same domain (F1=0.898) but collapses on general-domain datasets like PAWS-X and XNLI (F1=0.012), showing limited generality. In contrast, incorporating structured evidence boosts robustness to adversarial paraphrases, and Platt scaling provides better-calibrated confidence scores. The comparative experiments on PAWS-X and XNLI highlight that structured and LLM-based workflows have complementary strengths and weaknesses depending on domain and text type.
AI.conclusion: The study shows that semantic drift in cross-lingual technical requirements can be effectively detected using a language-independent representation plus LLM-based workflows. Contrary to intuition, increasing agentic complexity (e.g., multi-agent or multi-stage pipelines) does not necessarily yield better detection than a well-designed, simple few-shot prompt. Deterministic SRR comparison offers interpretability and strong performance in narrow technical domains, while LLM-based methods generalize better but benefit from structured support and calibration. Overall, the work positions few-shot LLM prompting over SRR as a strong, efficient, and interpretable solution for cross-lingual requirement-consistency checking.

title: Locating Failure in Multi-Page Visually Rich Document Understanding: An Empirical Attribution
summary: Multi-page visually-rich document understanding (MP-VRDU) requires managing evidence that is sparse, spread across pages, and often exceeds a model's context window. Prior work has produced competing, largely untested claims about how these systems should be built. We attribute incorrect answers to three failure modes, representation, selection, and reasoning, and isolate each over a multi-page document understanding dataset by intervening on one while holding the others fixed. We find that vision is necessary but does not replace text extraction, that missing pages bound accuracy while distractors cost little, and that reasoners fail to integrate evidence across pages even when it is fully supplied. Prompting can shift reasoning behaviour substantially, improving some outcomes at the expense of others. We translate these findings into guidance for building such systems under a fixed compute budget.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes why multi-page visually-rich document understanding systems fail, categorizing errors into representation, selection, and reasoning, and derives practical design guidance under compute constraints.
AI.motivation: Existing MP-VRDU models face sparse, cross-page evidence and context window limits, and prior work offers conflicting, insufficiently tested design claims. The authors aim to rigorously understand where these systems fail and which components (vision, text extraction, page selection, reasoning) actually matter.
AI.method: They decompose the problem into three failure modes—representation, selection, and reasoning—and systematically intervene on each while keeping the others fixed. Using a multi-page document understanding dataset, they run controlled experiments such as providing perfect page selection, perfect evidence aggregation, or different input modalities (vision vs. text extraction) to isolate the impact of each component.
AI.result: The study finds: (1) Visual input is important but cannot replace OCR/text extraction; (2) Not having the relevant pages imposes a hard upper bound on accuracy, whereas adding distractor pages has relatively small impact; (3) Reasoning components struggle to integrate cross-page evidence even when it is explicitly provided; and (4) Prompt design can significantly alter reasoning behavior, improving some metrics while degrading others.
AI.conclusion: The authors conclude that effective MP-VRDU systems must combine vision with reliable text extraction, prioritize robust page selection to avoid missing relevant pages, and address limitations in cross-page reasoning. They provide practical recommendations for how to allocate compute across representation, selection, and reasoning modules when building such systems under a fixed compute budget.

title: Tevatron-Elastic: A Unified Abstraction for Training Elastic Retrievers and Rerankers
summary: A single model scale challenges the flexibility of a production retrieval system: some settings need it faster, others need a smaller index, and the right trade-off changes with the workload. In the context of information retrieval (IR), a transformer-based model can be made smaller in three ways---using fewer layers, passing fewer tokens through the upper layers, or producing a shorter embedding---and each way saves a different compute resource. These options have been studied one at a time, each as its own method with its own code and training setup, which makes them hard to combine or adapt to a new model. We present~\ours to bring all three under one simple abstraction: a single object names any size the model can run at, and a short schedule lists the sizes to train. Training then produces one checkpoint that serves all of those sizes, and at deployment the user picks any of them. The same abstraction covers both retrievers and rerankers and both encoder and decoder models, as it works through interfaces that Hugging Face transformers already expose; a new backbone is a configuration change, not new modeling code. Prior methods---Matryoshka embeddings, early exit, 2D~Matryoshka (e.g., Starbucks), and layerwise token compression---become special cases of our unified abstraction. The same interface also enables Matryoshka~LTC (MLTC), which jointly trains several token-compression ratios in one retriever checkpoint. To validate our framework, we train 20 checkpoints across three backbones and two tasks: the quality curves are smooth, one checkpoint costs little over a model trained for a single size, and a controlled study confirms the wallclock speedups. We release the framework and all checkpoints as a resource for building elastic retrieval systems.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a unified framework to make transformer-based retrieval models elastically scalable in speed, memory, and index size, producing one checkpoint that can run efficiently at many sizes and trade-offs.
AI.motivation: Production information retrieval systems face varying constraints: some applications need low latency, others need small index size or reduced compute, and workload patterns change over time. Existing techniques to shrink transformer-based retrievers—fewer layers, fewer tokens, or shorter embeddings—are studied and implemented separately, each with custom code and training recipes, which makes it difficult to combine them, maintain them, and port them to new backbones. There is a need for a general, flexible way to train and deploy models that can seamlessly operate at many size/speed/quality trade-off points.
AI.method: The authors propose a unified abstraction and training framework, denoted as \ours, that parameterizes model size along three axes: depth (number of layers used), token budget (how many tokens are processed in upper layers), and embedding dimension (length of the output representation). A "size" is represented as a single object, and training is driven by a schedule listing a set of these sizes. During training, the model is jointly optimized across all scheduled sizes so that one final checkpoint supports them all. The framework is implemented through generic interfaces already present in Hugging Face Transformers, so different backbones (retrievers, rerankers, encoders, decoders) can be used by configuration rather than custom code. The design subsumes prior methods such as Matryoshka embeddings, early exit, 2D Matryoshka (e.g., Starbucks), and layerwise token compression as special cases within the same interface. They also introduce Matryoshka LTC (MLTC), which jointly trains multiple token-compression ratios in a single retriever checkpoint.
AI.result: Across three backbone architectures and two IR tasks, they train 20 multi-size checkpoints.
