Empirical results show (1) smooth quality curves over the different size configurations supported by a single checkpoint, (2) that the training cost for a multi-size checkpoint is only slightly higher than training a model for a single fixed size, and (3) a controlled experimental study confirms the expected wall-clock speedups at smaller configurations. The framework is robust enough to implement both prior specialized methods and the new MLTC variant under one codebase.
AI.conclusion: The framework provides a practical, unified way to build elastic retrieval systems where a single trained checkpoint can be deployed at multiple operating points, trading off accuracy, latency, and resource usage as needed. By exposing these capabilities via standard Transformer interfaces and covering both retrievers and rerankers, it reduces engineering overhead, simplifies experimentation with different efficiency techniques, and offers the community reusable code and pretrained checkpoints for flexible IR deployments.

title: Directed Neuro-Symbolic Stochastic Execution for Verification of Distributed Parallel AI Programs
summary: Distributed parallel Artificial Intelligence (AI) programs expose reliability gaps that conventional testing cannot close: parallel executions are non-deterministic, and AI workloads bring high-dimensional inputs and non-linear operations that defeat fuzzing and symbolic execution in isolation. We present Directed Neuro-Symbolic Stochastic Execution (DNSSE), a hybrid testing framework that couples schedule prediction guided by a Large Language Model (LLM) with symbolic constraint solving and coverage-guided stochastic mutation. We model distributed AI executions as non-deterministic transition systems, specify correctness in linear temporal logic, and prove soundness, bounded completeness, and probabilistic completeness of the hybrid solver, together with an expected-cost analysis of LLM-guided schedule exploration. A scalable implementation on PyTorch and Ray detects 2.9% more concurrency bugs than the strongest baseline and raises average branch coverage from 68.6 % to 91.6 % across five realistic distributed AI benchmarks.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces DNSSE, a hybrid testing framework combining LLM-guided schedule prediction, symbolic execution, and stochastic mutation to systematically find concurrency bugs in distributed AI systems, improving bug detection and coverage over existing methods.
AI.motivation: Distributed parallel AI programs are hard to test because their executions are non-deterministic and their workloads involve high-dimensional, non-linear computations. Traditional testing, fuzzing, and symbolic execution alone are ineffective at uncovering concurrency bugs and providing high coverage in this setting, leaving reliability gaps in practical AI systems.
AI.method: The authors model distributed AI executions as non-deterministic transition systems and specify correctness using linear temporal logic. They design Directed Neuro-Symbolic Stochastic Execution (DNSSE), which combines: (1) an LLM that predicts promising execution schedules to explore; (2) symbolic constraint solving to reason about conditions and paths; and (3) coverage-guided stochastic mutation to diversify tests. They also provide formal proofs of soundness, bounded completeness, and probabilistic completeness, as well as an expected-cost analysis of LLM-guided schedule exploration. The framework is implemented on top of PyTorch and Ray.
AI.result: On five realistic distributed AI benchmarks, DNSSE detects 2.9% more concurrency bugs than the strongest existing baseline and increases average branch coverage from 68.6% to 91.6%, demonstrating both improved bug-finding capability and more thorough exploration of program behaviors.
AI.conclusion: DNSSE is an effective and theoretically grounded hybrid testing framework for distributed AI systems, overcoming key limitations of traditional and single-technique approaches. By combining LLM-guided schedule prediction, symbolic reasoning, and stochastic testing, it achieves higher bug detection and coverage, and its formal properties and empirical results support its practicality and scalability.

title: Deployable Per-Instance Multi-Layer Activation Steering for Large Language Models
comment: 43 pages, 24 figures, 30 tables. Under review at ACL Rolling Review (August 2026)
summary: Activation steering edits the behaviour of a frozen language model by adding a learned vector to its residual stream, and current practice fixes the injection layers globally per task. We argue that the best layers are an instance-level decision, and we make per-instance, multi-layer selection both well understood and deployable. On two open-weight 8B models and six binary persona traits, a per-instance oracle over layer subsets shows that the best layers vary from one input to the next: on most trait-model pairs, no fixed global layer set recovers the per-instance benefit. A greedy rule that ranks layers by single-layer marginal effect recovers nearly all of the oracle's benefit, but both must score candidate layers against the gold answer, so neither can run at deployment; the rule instead becomes the target a prompt-only predictor is trained to reproduce. Our deployable recipe needs no label at inference: a per-instance layer ranker read off the prompt embedding, a classifier that infers the steering direction, and an adaptive gate that scores short steered passes against that inferred direction and steers no more layers than necessary. The recipe recovers most of the oracle's lift (the bulk on the stronger model, a clear majority on the harder one), never drives any trait-model pair below its unsteered alignment baseline on average, and largely avoids the fluency collapse that strong global selection incurs at higher layer counts. A mechanistic account, "direction over magnitude", explains the behavioural flip under a mis-directed global set, the output collapse from steering too many layers, and the ceiling of unsteerable inputs.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes an instance-wise, multi-layer method for activation steering in language models to better control persona traits without harming fluency.
AI.motivation: Existing activation steering typically uses a fixed set of layers per task, assuming the same layers are optimal for all inputs. Empirically, this often leads to suboptimal alignment, fluency degradation, and brittle behaviour when steering is too strong or misdirected. The authors observe that the best layers for steering differ across inputs and traits, and want a principled, deployable way to select layers per instance without using labels at inference time.
AI.method: 1) Empirically evaluate an oracle that can choose, per input, the best subset of layers for activation steering using gold labels, showing large variance across inputs and traits. 2) Propose a greedy layer selection rule that ranks layers by their marginal steering effect, nearly matching the oracle, but still label-dependent. 3) Train a prompt-only predictor to approximate this greedy ranking, so that layer choice depends only on the input prompt. 4) Build a deployable pipeline with: (a) a per-instance layer ranker from the prompt embedding; (b) a classifier that predicts the desired steering direction (e.g., trait polarity); and (c) an adaptive gate that incrementally applies steering to ranked layers, checking alignment with the inferred direction and stopping once sufficient effect is reached. 5) Provide a mechanistic explanation (“direction over magnitude”) for when and why steering fails, oversteers, or cannot affect model behaviour.
AI.result: On two 8B-parameter open-weight LMs and six binary persona traits, the per-instance oracle shows that optimal steering layers vary substantially by input and trait, and no single fixed layer set can fully recover oracle performance. The greedy marginal-effect ranking closely matches the oracle’s performance. The final deployable recipe—using prompt-based layer ranking, a direction classifier, and adaptive gating—recovers most of the oracle’s performance gains: nearly all on the stronger model and a clear majority on the more difficult one. It also avoids reducing alignment below the unsteered baseline on average for any trait-model pair and greatly mitigates the fluency collapse seen when many globally fixed layers are steered.
AI.conclusion: Activation steering is more effective and reliable when layers are selected per instance rather than fixed globally. A practical, label-free deployment scheme can approximate an oracle selector by combining prompt-based layer ranking, direction inference, and adaptive gating, yielding substantial alignment improvements with minimal fluency loss. The “direction over magnitude” mechanistic account clarifies why misdirected or excessive steering harms outputs and why some prompts remain unsteerable, offering insight for safer and more controllable LM editing.

title: Guixu: Valuation-Driven Data Discovery for Autonomous AI Agents with On-Chain Attestation
comment: This paper has been accepted for presentation at VLDB 2026
summary: Autonomous agents increasingly rely on external data to complete downstream tasks such as model training and decision support. However, existing data discovery systems remain largely retrieval-oriented: they surface candidate datasets from heterogeneous sources, but provide limited support for estimating task-specific utility, selecting cost-effective datasets under budget constraints, or incorporating trustworthy feedback from prior usage. This paper presents Guixu, a valuation-driven data discovery system for autonomous agents. Guixu employs a three-phase valuation pipeline with proxy-label propagation and multi-round knapsack optimization for task-aware data valuation. Guixu integrates agentic payment protocol to enable budget-constrained data procurement workflows. Guixu leverages on-chain data market and attestation signals for verifiable data discovery. Our demonstration highlights how Guixu enables an agent to move beyond keyword-based dataset retrieval toward task- and budget-aware, trustworthy data discovery and procurement. Attendees can interactively explore the full workflow, from NL task specification and multi-source search to data valuation and verifiable transaction feedback.

AI.tldr: Guixu is a valuation-driven data discovery system that helps autonomous agents find, price, and purchase the most useful datasets for a given task under budget constraints, with verifiable feedback from prior use.
AI.motivation: Autonomous agents need external datasets for tasks like model training and decision support, but existing systems are mostly retrieval-based: they return candidate datasets via search or keyword matching without estimating how useful each dataset will be for a specific task, how to choose datasets under a fixed budget, or how to incorporate trustworthy feedback from previous usage or markets. There is a need for a data discovery framework that is task-aware, budget-aware, and able to leverage verifiable market and attestation signals.
AI.method: Guixu introduces a three-phase task-aware data valuation pipeline. It uses proxy-label propagation to estimate task-specific utility of candidate datasets, then applies multi-round knapsack optimization to select an optimal subset of datasets given budget constraints. It integrates an agentic payment protocol to automate budget-constrained data procurement workflows. It also connects to an on-chain data market and uses attestation signals to make the discovery and procurement verifiable and trustworthy. The system is demonstrated through an interactive workflow from natural-language task specification and multi-source search, through valuation, to final purchase with verifiable feedback.
AI.result: Guixu enables agents to go beyond keyword-based retrieval and perform data discovery that accounts for task relevance, economic constraints, and trust signals. In the demo, users can see end-to-end support: NL task specification, search over multiple sources, computed valuations, optimized dataset selection under a budget, and verifiable on-chain transaction and feedback integration. This shows that the system can operationalize valuation-driven, trustworthy data procurement for autonomous agents.
AI.conclusion: Guixu provides a practical, valuation-driven architecture for autonomous agents to discover and procure data that is aligned with their tasks and budgets while leveraging verifiable on-chain signals. It addresses key limitations of retrieval-only systems by integrating task-aware valuation, knapsack-based selection, automated payment, and trusted market/attestation feedback into a unified workflow, moving data discovery toward more economic- and trust-aware autonomy.

title: Explicit Boundary Markers for Subword Vocabularies
summary: Subword tokenizers represent many common words twice in space-using writing systems, once with a leading space and once without. The two entries have separate embeddings in models, so occurrences of one word are divided across rows that are trained independently, and the two forms need not even segment the string the same way: " together" may be a single entry while the same word without a preceding space is tokenized as "to|gether". Capitalization divides a word further, into as many as six forms. We introduce an alternative to standard whitespace conventions using an explicit word boundary marker, which prevents such duplication. Words are delimited by the boundary markers, and spaces between words are represented as pairs of such markers. Two shift codes do the same for title case and upper case, allowing one internal representation of a word to be re-used across different settings. Switching to this convention mitigates the duplicate-entry issue, but does not improve tokenization compression: for both vocabulary-learning algorithms, the best marker scheme stays within one percent of the baseline in characters per token, averaged across six languages. It does result in better language modeling performance. Every marker scheme tested downstream reaches lower bits per byte than the baseline, suggesting that duplication carries a cost that compression does not capture.

AI.tldr: Paper proposes explicit word boundary markers and case shift codes to remove duplicate subword entries caused by leading spaces and capitalization, maintaining compression while improving language modeling performance.
AI.motivation: In common subword tokenizers used for space-using writing systems, the same lexical word often appears multiple times in the vocabulary: once with a leading space and once without, and further split by capitalization variants. These variants have separate embeddings and can even be segmented differently, which wastes parameters, fragments training signal, and may hurt downstream performance. The authors want a tokenizer design that avoids such duplication while preserving or improving compression and model performance.
AI.method: The authors introduce an alternative whitespace and casing convention where an explicit word boundary marker delimits words, and spaces between words are represented via pairs of these markers. Additionally, two shift codes indicate title case and upper case, allowing one internal representation of a word to be reused across different capitalization contexts. They integrate these conventions into standard subword vocabulary-learning algorithms and systematically compare different marker schemes to a baseline tokenizer across six languages, evaluating both tokenization compression (characters per token) and downstream language modeling (bits per byte).
AI.result: Switching to explicit boundary and case markers removes the duplicate-entry problem (e.g., separate tokens for " word" and "word" or capitalized variants) without hurting compression: for both vocabulary-learning algorithms and across six languages, the best marker schemes are within about 1% of the baseline in characters per token. However, all marker schemes tested produce consistently better language modeling metrics than the baseline, achieving lower bits per byte, indicating improved modeling efficiency.
AI.conclusion: Explicit word boundary markers and case shift codes are a practical alternative to standard whitespace and capitalization handling in subword tokenization. They eliminate vocabulary duplication and parameter fragmentation, maintain near-identical compression efficiency, and yield better language modeling performance. This suggests that duplication in conventional tokenizers imposes a modeling cost that is not reflected in raw compression metrics, and that reusing a single internal representation across different word contexts and casings is beneficial.

title: KGCache: Amortized Subgraph Retrieval for KG Reasoning with LLMs
summary: Large language models can answer knowledge-intensive questions more reliably when they are grounded with knowledge graphs, but systems such as Think-on-Graph and Reasoning-on-Graph repeatedly query the same graph neighborhoods across different questions. In this work, we study this repeated retrieval in Knowledge Graph Question Answering~(KGQA) workloads and propose KGCache, an in-memory cache for one-hop knowledge graph neighborhoods. KGCache is designed to be compatible with both iterative traversal (ToG) and one shot planning (RoG) KGQA paradigms. KGCache is placed between the KGQA engine and the backend serving the KG, so repeated entity requests can be served from cache instead of issuing new KG queries. We evaluate KGCache on WebQSP and CWQ using LRU, LFU, and a trace-aware Oracle policy. Our analysis shows that both datasets contain substantial entity reuse among starting entities and entities reached during traversal. We also explore semantic caching for similar queries, which shows additional hit-rate gains on WebQSP and needs further accuracy testing on CWQ. Entity caching accelerates KG retrieval by up to $1.91\times$, while semantic-context caching achieves up to $1.06\times$ full-system speedup in the evaluated WebQSP configurations, with each hit being up to $3.73\times$ faster.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces KGCache, an in-memory cache for one-hop knowledge graph neighborhoods to reduce redundant KG retrieval in KGQA systems, improving retrieval speed and overall QA latency.
AI.motivation: Existing KGQA systems using large language models, such as Think-on-Graph and Reasoning-on-Graph, repeatedly query the same knowledge graph neighborhoods for different questions, leading to unnecessary latency and backend load. There is no systematic study or mechanism focused on exploiting this redundancy in practical KGQA workloads.
AI.method: The authors empirically study retrieval patterns in KGQA workloads on datasets like WebQSP and CWQ, identifying repeated entity and neighborhood access. They then design KGCache, an in-memory cache layer for one-hop neighborhoods positioned between the KGQA engine and the KG backend. KGCache supports both iterative traversal and one-shot planning paradigms, and is evaluated with different cache replacement policies (LRU, LFU, and an oracle policy). They further explore semantic caching that reuses results across similar queries, beyond exact-entity matching.
AI.result: Analysis shows substantial reuse of entities both as starting points and as intermediate nodes during traversal in KGQA workloads. With entity caching via KGCache, KG retrieval is accelerated by up to 1.91×. Semantic-context caching for similar queries brings additional cache hit-rate improvements on WebQSP and yields up to 1.06× full-system speedup, with cache hits serving requests up to 3.73× faster than uncached retrieval. Semantic caching on CWQ shows promise but requires further accuracy evaluation.
AI.conclusion: Redundant retrieval of knowledge graph neighborhoods is common in KGQA workloads and can be effectively exploited via a dedicated caching layer. KGCache, an in-memory one-hop neighborhood cache compatible with multiple KGQA paradigms, significantly accelerates KG retrieval and moderately speeds up end-to-end systems. Semantic caching across similar queries offers additional benefits but needs careful accuracy assessment, especially on more complex datasets like CWQ.

title: Conversation as Measurement in Clinical Encounters: Observable Phase Structure, Partially Observable Patient State
summary: Many modern AI systems analyze conversational traces to infer aspects of human interaction and state, implicitly assuming that such information is recoverable from conversation. We study observability: whether a target is recoverable from conversational transcripts alone. Observability is difficult to assess because transcripts may provide only a partial view of many targets, and large-scale analysis requires model-based annotation, making true limits of the conversational signal hard to distinguish from annotator error. We therefore study clinical encounters, where patient-reported outcome measures (PROMs) provide an external anchor for patient state, and visits follow broadly structured patterns. We study observability of patient state and conversational phase structure using 439 real-world clinical encounter transcripts spanning 134 hours, including 245 ENT transcripts paired with 273 PROM surveys. We operationalize patient state using PROM scores for voice, cough, and swallowing; phase structure using conversational phase segmentation. To make these analyses credible at scale, we use a PHI-compliant GPT-5 deployment for transcript annotation and conduct 40 hours of manual validation, reducing the risk that apparent limits of observability simply reflect annotator error. Our core finding is an observability asymmetry: phase structure is observable and useful for characterizing clinical encounter organization, while patient state is only partially observable, even in a setting designed to elicit patient symptoms and experiences, cautioning against transcript-only inference of human state.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates how much we can actually infer about patient state and conversation structure from clinical visit transcripts alone, finding that conversation phases are observable but patient health state is only partially observable.
AI.motivation: Modern AI often assumes human states and traits can be accurately inferred from text conversations, but it is unclear what is fundamentally observable from transcripts versus what is guesswork or model hallucination. Clinical encounters, with structured dialogue and external patient-reported outcome measures (PROMs), provide a unique setting to rigorously test these limits.
AI.method: The authors analyze 439 real-world clinical encounter transcripts (~134 hours), including 245 ENT visits linked to 273 PROM surveys. They define patient state using PROM scores on voice, cough, and swallowing, and define conversational structure via phase segmentation. They use a PHI-compliant GPT-5 system to annotate transcripts at scale and perform 40 hours of manual validation to separate genuine observability limits from annotation noise, then assess how well transcript-based signals recover patient state and phase structure.
AI.result: They find that conversational phase structure is reliably observable from transcripts and can be used to characterize how clinical encounters are organized. However, patient state derived from PROMs is only partially recoverable from transcripts, even in settings that are explicitly designed to surface symptoms and experiences.
AI.conclusion: There is a fundamental observability asymmetry in clinical dialogue: interaction structure (phases) is clearly visible in conversation text, but underlying patient state is only partially encoded. This challenges the common practice of inferring rich human state purely from conversational logs and suggests caution when deploying transcript-only AI systems for sensitive state inference tasks.

title: Self-Evolving Neuro-Symbolic Skills for Tool-Augmented Spatial Reasoning
comment: 25 pages, 9 figures, 10 tables; includes supplementary material
summary: Large vision-language models have achieved strong performance in multimodal reasoning, but they remain unreliable on fine-grained spatial tasks that demand both precise spatial perception and fine-grained geometric computation beyond end-to-end generation. Tool augmentation offers a natural solution, while existing methods either plan tool calls from scratch without explicit dependency constraints or rely on fixed pipelines that are redundant and generalize poorly across spatial tasks. An effective spatial reasoning agent should instead accumulate reusable experience and adaptively compose it for new problems. To this end, we propose NeSy-Spatial, a neuro-symbolic framework for self-evolving spatial skills. NeSy-Spatial abstracts tool interactions and geometric operations into typed executable atomic instructions and composes them into two complementary skill types: Tool-Use Skills for organizing tool execution and Geometry Skills for structured geometric reasoning. During inference, NeSy-Spatial retrieves and executes relevant skills in a closed-loop process. During evolution, it analyzes buffered successful and failed trajectories to refine skill structures and prune unreliable or inactive entries. Experiments on three spatial reasoning benchmarks show that NeSy-Spatial consistently improves reasoning accuracy with more precise tool utilization.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces NeSy-Spatial, a neuro-symbolic framework that improves large vision-language models on fine-grained spatial reasoning by learning reusable, composable spatial skills built from typed atomic instructions and tool interactions.
AI.motivation: Although large vision-language models perform well on multimodal reasoning, they are unreliable on tasks requiring precise spatial perception and detailed geometric computation. Existing tool-augmented methods either plan tool use from scratch without explicit dependency structure or use rigid, fixed pipelines that do not generalize across spatial tasks and can be redundant. There is a need for a spatial reasoning agent that can accumulate reusable experience and flexibly adapt it to new spatial problems.
AI.method: NeSy-Spatial defines a set of typed executable atomic instructions covering both geometric operations and interactions with external tools. These atomic instructions are composed into two types of higher-level, reusable skills: Tool-Use Skills that structure and sequence tool calls, and Geometry Skills that encode structured geometric reasoning patterns. At inference time, the system retrieves relevant skills and executes them in a closed-loop fashion, allowing feedback from intermediate results to influence subsequent steps. During an evolutionary phase, the framework analyzes both successful and failed reasoning trajectories stored in a buffer, using them to refine the internal structure of skills and to remove skills that are unreliable or rarely used.
AI.result: On three different spatial reasoning benchmarks, NeSy-Spatial yields consistent improvements in reasoning accuracy compared to baselines, primarily through more precise and effective use of tools for spatial and geometric computation.
AI.conclusion: By abstracting spatial reasoning into reusable neuro-symbolic skills and enabling their continual evolution, NeSy-Spatial makes large vision-language models more reliable and accurate on fine-grained spatial tasks. The framework demonstrates that structured, adaptive composition of tool-use and geometric reasoning skills can outperform ad hoc or rigid tool-augmentation pipelines for spatial reasoning benchmarks.

title: Position Bias in Ordinal Classification: A Systematic Evaluation
summary: Large language models are increasingly used for ordinal classification, yet semantically equivalent changes to prompt organization can alter their predictions. We conduct systematic experiments to characterize positional bias from label order, demonstration order, and demonstration placement. First, we apply the three probes to ten frontier LLMs on a common ordinal-classification task; every model is sensitive to all three positional sources, showing that the problem is pervasive. Second, we vary eight prompt-, task-, and model-level factors across five datasets; accuracy and stability are often misaligned, and only lower scale cardinality consistently improves both. Third, we compare pointwise, pairwise, and listwise inference, alternative aggregation and debiasing methods, and joint configurations; the tested corrections do not provide a reliable remedy, while a comparison-based listwise formulation offers the best balance but transfers unevenly across models and bias sources. These findings show that positional robustness depends on the full system configuration rather than the model alone. Ordinal-classification systems should therefore be selected jointly for predictive performance and stability.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how the position and ordering of labels and examples in prompts systematically bias LLMs on ordinal classification tasks, evaluates many factors and mitigation strategies, and concludes that robustness depends on the full system configuration, so systems must be chosen for both accuracy and stability.
AI.motivation: Large language models are widely used for ordinal classification (e.g., ratings, levels, ordered categories), but their predictions can change when semantically irrelevant aspects of the prompt are modified, such as the order of labels or where examples are placed. This instability threatens reliability and fairness and is poorly understood in a systematic way. The authors are motivated to rigorously measure and characterize these positional biases and to test whether simple design choices or post-hoc corrections can provide reliable robustness across models, tasks, and prompts.
AI.method: The authors design three controlled probes targeting distinct positional effects in prompts: (1) label-order bias (changing the order of ordinal labels), (2) demonstration-order bias (reordering few-shot examples), and (3) demonstration-placement bias (moving demonstrations within the prompt). They first apply these probes to ten frontier LLMs on a shared ordinal classification task to assess how pervasive the biases are. Then they expand to five datasets and systematically vary eight factors across prompt design, task properties (e.g., number of ordinal levels), and model characteristics, comparing accuracy with a stability measure across positional perturbations. Finally, they compare different inference strategies—pointwise, pairwise, and listwise ordinal formulations—as well as aggregation schemes and debiasing or correction methods, including joint configurations that combine multiple elements, to see which, if any, improve robustness without sacrificing accuracy.
AI.result: All ten evaluated LLMs exhibit sensitivity to label order, demonstration order, and demonstration placement, confirming that positional bias is widespread. When varying prompt-, task-, and model-level factors, the study finds that higher accuracy does not reliably coincide with higher positional stability; in many settings, models that are more accurate are also more sensitive to prompt reorganization. Among the examined factors, reducing the number of ordinal categories (lower scale cardinality) is the only one that consistently improves both accuracy and robustness. Experiments with different ordinal inference paradigms and correction methods reveal that common debiasing strategies and aggregation approaches do not offer a consistent, reliable fix. A comparison-based listwise formulation of ordinal classification attains the best average trade-off between performance and stability, but its benefits are uneven and do not generalize uniformly across different models or bias sources.
AI.conclusion: Positional biases in LLM-based ordinal classification are inherent and pervasive, arising not just from model internals but from the interaction between models, tasks, and prompt designs. Because accuracy and positional robustness often diverge, optimizing only for predictive performance can yield brittle systems whose outputs change under harmless prompt reordering. Simple mitigation techniques or ad-hoc corrections are insufficient; even promising approaches like listwise comparison help only partially and are not universally transferable. Therefore, practitioners should treat ordinal classification as a full system design problem: jointly selecting models, prompt formats, scale cardinality, and inference formulations, and explicitly evaluating both accuracy and stability under positional perturbations when deploying such systems.

title: SCOUT: Self-Checking and Recovery-Aware Tool-Thought Agents for Ultra-Long Egocentric Video Reasoning
summary: Ultra-long egocentric video understanding requires reasoning over temporally sparse evidence distributed across hours or days, challenging current multimodal models with limited context and the grounding of key video segments. While Chain-of-Tool-Thought (CoTT) agent systems enable iterative retrieval and inspection, they suffer from error propagation due to rigid zoom-in strategies that lack recovery mechanisms. In this work, we address these challenges through SCOUT (Self-Checking Chain-Of-Tool-thought), a recovery-aware agentic framework introducing an adaptive policy that evaluates intermediate tool observations and dynamically trades off exploitation (zoom-in) and exploration (region switching), enabling robust multi-hop reasoning over extremely long horizons. However, training such multi-turn tool-using agents remains challenging, as existing RL methods rely on sparse outcome-level rewards and lack supervision over extended decision trajectories, resulting in suboptimal credit assignment for long-horizon reasoning. To address this, we develop UPS-GRPO, an uncertainty-prioritized policy optimization method that concentrates exploration on high-uncertainty post-tool states while preserving sample efficiency. We further introduce a turn-level advantage decomposition that integrates outcome rewards with tool-grounded temporal alignment rewards for improved credit assignment. Experiments show that SCOUT achieves state-of-the-art results on ultra-long egocentric benchmarks, while remaining competitive on shorter-horizon long-video settings.

AI.tldr: Proposes SCOUT, a self-checking, recovery-aware agent framework for ultra-long egocentric video understanding, trained with a new uncertainty-prioritized RL method (UPS-GRPO) and turn-level credit assignment, achieving SOTA on ultra-long video benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Ultra-long egocentric videos span hours or days, with key evidence sparsely distributed. Existing multimodal models have limited context windows and struggle to ground and reason over such long horizons. Chain-of-Tool-Thought agents can iteratively retrieve segments but rely on rigid zoom-in strategies without effective recovery, causing error propagation. Existing RL training for such multi-turn agents suffers from sparse outcome rewards and poor credit assignment across long decision trajectories. There is a need for an agent framework and training method that can adaptively explore/zoom in and learn robust long-horizon reasoning over ultra-long videos.
AI.method: The paper introduces SCOUT, a Self-Checking Chain-Of-Tool-thought framework. SCOUT implements an adaptive policy over tool calls that evaluates intermediate observations and dynamically chooses between exploitation (zooming further into promising regions) and exploration (switching to new regions), enabling recovery from earlier mistakes. For training, the authors propose UPS-GRPO, an uncertainty-prioritized policy optimization method that focuses exploration on post-tool states with high uncertainty while maintaining sample efficiency. They also add a turn-level advantage decomposition that blends final outcome rewards with tool-grounded temporal alignment rewards, improving credit assignment across long multi-turn trajectories. The system is evaluated on ultra-long egocentric video benchmarks and compared to existing long-video reasoning methods and CoTT agents.
AI.result: SCOUT, trained with UPS-GRPO and the proposed advantage decomposition, achieves state-of-the-art performance on ultra-long egocentric video understanding benchmarks. It also remains competitive on shorter-horizon long-video tasks, indicating that the method scales down reasonably well. The experiments suggest improved robustness in multi-hop reasoning, better handling of error recovery, and more effective use of tool calls over extremely long temporal horizons compared to prior CoTT and long-video baselines.
AI.conclusion: Adaptive, recovery-aware agent policies and improved RL training signals are key to effective reasoning over ultra-long egocentric videos. By combining self-checking Chain-of-Tool-thought decisions with uncertainty-prioritized policy optimization and finer-grained credit assignment, SCOUT successfully mitigates error propagation and improves multi-hop reasoning over hours-long video streams. The approach establishes new state-of-the-art results on ultra-long egocentric benchmarks and demonstrates that principled agent design plus targeted RL can substantially advance long-horizon multimodal understanding.

title: Tied Trit-Planes: Constraining PTQTP to a Uniform Nine-Level Quantizer, with a Persistent Folded Format for Disk-Streamed Mixture-of-Experts Serving
summary: PTQTP decomposes LLM weight matrices into two ternary (trit) planes with two free per-group scales. Tying the scales to a fixed ratio of three collapses the decomposition into a single uniform nine-level quantizer, a known balanced-ternary identity. To our knowledge, at the time of writing, this work is the first to impose that identity as a constraint inside PTQTP's solver. The two trit planes then fold losslessly into one 4-bit code plane that we make the persistent serving representation: disk bytes, expert-cache bytes, and kernel input are the same 4.0625-bits/weight blocks, consumed in one integer dot pass. For this conjunction (ratio-3 nine-level code, CPU-SIMD kernels, SSD expert streaming, identical persistent bytes) we likewise found no precedent. We apply this to the routed experts of DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731, a 284B-A13B mixture-of-experts model, quantizing in one shot from the released MXFP4 expert weights and streaming experts from SSD on a 64 GB laptop. Against a 4.5-bit Q4_K baseline, measured one process per fixture with an expert-lossless anchor arm as reference control, the tied model matches the official serving API on 5/5 fixtures at step 0 (Q4_K: 4/5) and 12/14 captured continuation steps (11/14), scores 86 vs. 84 on a 100-item MMLU subset, decodes 6.7% faster in decode phase, and ships 9% smaller files: no detected fidelity difference at these small evaluation sizes, and every fixture-level difference between the arms traces to a single measured near-tie cell. The tied fit nevertheless shows higher weight-reconstruction error and worse perplexity, a measured dissociation between proxy metrics and reference fidelity. A cumulative trunk-ternarization ladder and bitwise-pinned aarch64/x86-64 kernels complete the report. All code, formats, and evaluation artifacts are open source in the fucina inference stack.

AI.tldr: They propose a ternary-based post-training quantization scheme that collapses two trit planes into a single 9-level code, enabling 4-bit-equivalent storage and efficient CPU/SSD serving for MoE LLM experts while preserving practical fidelity.
AI.motivation: Make large MoE models like DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731 more deployable on commodity hardware (e.g., 64 GB laptops) by reducing expert weight size and improving CPU/SSD serving efficiency without hurting end-to-end model fidelity, and to explore whether better-constrained quantization codes can outperform standard 4–5 bit baselines.
AI.method: Extend PTQTP to decompose weight matrices into two ternary planes with per-group scales, then impose a fixed 3:1 ratio between the scales so the composition becomes a uniform 9-level quantizer (balanced ternary). Encode those 9 levels into a compact 4.0625-bits/weight representation that is used consistently across disk, cache, and kernel input. Implement CPU SIMD kernels and SSD streaming that directly consume this format, and apply the scheme in one-shot to the routed experts of DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731 starting from MXFP4 weights. Compare against a Q4_K baseline and an expert-lossless control on various evaluation fixtures, including MMLU subset and decoding-speed benchmarks, and analyze discrepancies between proxy metrics (weight error, perplexity) and end-to-end fidelity.
AI.result: The tied-ratio nine-level scheme matches the official DeepSeek API on all 5/5 evaluation fixtures at step 0 (slightly better than Q4_K), and on 12/14 continuation steps (vs 11/14 for Q4_K), achieves similar accuracy on a 100-question MMLU subset (86 vs 84), decodes 6.7% faster during decoding, and yields 9% smaller expert files. All observable fidelity differences at the fixture level are negligible and trace to single near-tied cells, despite the method having higher weight reconstruction error and worse perplexity than baselines.
AI.conclusion: A balanced-ternary, ratio-tied PTQTP scheme can serve as an effective 4-bit-like quantization and serving format for MoE experts, providing smaller model size and modest speedups on CPU/SSD deployments without detectable loss in practical fidelity on small evaluations. The work also highlights that traditional proxy metrics like weight error and perplexity may not reliably predict end-to-end task fidelity. They provide a full open-source stack, including the quantization ladder and bitwise-stable kernels, to support reproducible deployment.

title: CyberAGENTS: Structured Autonomy for Agentic Gamified Learning in Cybersecurity
summary: Gamification is especially effective in learning domains requiring active problem-solving and iterative skill-building, such as cybersecurity education. Generative AI agents offer a path to delivering such experiences adaptively at scale, but introduce well-documented risks in educational settings: inconsistent behavior, hallucinated reasoning, and misalignment with pedagogical frameworks. Grounding these systems in learning science is therefore essential. We present \model, an agentic framework for gamified cybersecurity learning that enables structured autonomy through ontology-guided validation, schema-governed behavioral control, and competency-based progression. The system is organized around a competency-based progression model that structures topics by difficulty and prerequisite relationships, reflecting evidence-based principles of scaffolded instruction. The learning loop is decomposed into four specialized agents: challenge, support, evaluation, and reward, each governed by behavioral schemas that encode operational modes and progression logic, bounding agent autonomy without eliminating generative flexibility. A cybersecurity ontology validates all generated content prior to display, enforcing domain-consistent reasoning and safety constraints. We evaluate CyberAgents through classroom deployment with undergraduate students, complemented by expert evaluations from educators and domain specialists. Results indicate improved engagement, clearer feedback interpretation, and greater learner trust in AI-generated responses when behavioral schemas and ontology validation are active. Preliminary comparisons with an unconstrained configuration further support the role of structured control in stabilizing instructional behavior. These findings offer a blueprint for designing pedagogically grounded agentic gamified learning systems.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes CyberAgents, an agentic, gamified cybersecurity learning framework that constrains generative AI with ontologies and behavioral schemas to improve educational reliability and learner trust.
AI.motivation: Existing generative AI–driven gamified learning experiences in cybersecurity suffer from issues like hallucinations, inconsistent feedback, and misalignment with learning science. The authors aim to design an AI-driven system that is engaging and adaptive while remaining trustworthy, safe, and pedagogically grounded.
AI.method: They design CyberAgents, an agentic framework organized around a competency-based progression model. The learning process is split into four specialized agents—challenge, support, evaluation, and reward—each controlled via explicit behavioral schemas that specify modes and progression logic. A cybersecurity ontology validates all AI-generated content before it is shown to learners, checking for domain consistency and safety. They then deploy the system in undergraduate cybersecurity classes and gather data from both students and expert evaluators, also comparing configurations with and without schema and ontology constraints.
AI.result: Classroom deployment and expert evaluations show that activating behavioral schemas and ontology validation leads to higher student engagement, clearer understanding of feedback, and increased trust in AI responses. Early comparisons to an unconstrained baseline suggest the controlled framework produces more stable and reliable instructional behavior.
AI.conclusion: Structuring generative AI agents with competency-based progression, schema-governed behavior, and ontology-based validation can mitigate common risks of generative AI in education while preserving adaptive, gamified experiences. The CyberAgents framework can serve as a generalizable design pattern for building pedagogically grounded agentic learning systems, particularly in domains like cybersecurity that demand precise, safe, and scaffolded instruction.

title: Investigating Multimodal Informativity under Different Partner Visibility Conditions in Video-Mediated Dialogue
summary: Situated language use is multimodal and embodied. For example, gestures can carry information that is absent or underspecified in the speech signal, yet dialogue models typically rely on transcripts alone. We study how much referential information gestures and their combination with speech carry in multimodal dialogue under different partner visibility conditions. % We build models that identify the intended referent in a video-mediated referential communication game based on either the speech transcript, the skeletal representation of gesture, or both modalities. Our results show that gesture alone is predictive of the intended referent and that multimodal fusion is most beneficial when the transcript-based model is uncertain. Training-only alignment of learned representations with the referent image further improves the fusion model performance. % In a comparison with human interaction data, we further see pragmatic effects of interlocutor visibility on gesture production and informativeness as well as an entrainment effect in speech and multimodal, but not gesture, performance across rounds of repeated interaction. We thus make contributions to the technical modelling of multimodal information in human dialogue and the analysis of human interaction data via trained model representations.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates how gestures and speech together convey referential information in multimodal dialogue, and builds models to predict intended referents from speech, gesture, or both, showing that gestures alone are informative and that multimodal fusion with representation alignment improves performance and reveals pragmatic effects of partner visibility and interaction history.
AI.motivation: Most dialogue models rely solely on text transcripts, ignoring that real-world language use is multimodal and embodied. Gestures can add or disambiguate referential information, especially in situated communication and under different visibility conditions between interlocutors. There is a need to quantify how much information gestures carry, how they interact with speech, and how visibility and repeated interaction affect their use, both for improving multimodal dialogue systems and for understanding human communication behavior.
AI.method: The authors use a video-mediated referential communication game where one interlocutor must identify an intended referent. They construct models that, given the interaction data, predict the intended referent using (a) only the speech transcript, (b) only a skeletal representation of gestures, or (c) a fusion of both modalities. They explore a multimodal fusion approach and a training-only alignment of learned representations with the referent image to enhance performance. They also compare model behavior with human interaction data to analyze pragmatic effects of interlocutor visibility and entrainment across repeated interaction rounds.
AI.result: Gesture-only models can successfully predict the intended referent, demonstrating that gestures carry substantial referential information. Multimodal fusion of speech and gesture works best when the transcript-based model is uncertain, and aligning learned representations with referent images during training further boosts fusion performance. Analysis of human interaction patterns reveals that interlocutor visibility influences how gestures are produced and how informative they are, and that there is entrainment over repeated rounds in speech and multimodal performance, but not in gesture performance alone.
AI.conclusion: Gestures provide rich referential information that can be exploited computationally, and combining gestures with speech in dialogue models yields clear benefits, particularly in uncertain cases for text-only models. Representation alignment with referent images further strengthens multimodal performance. Human interaction analyses show visibility-dependent pragmatic adaptation and entrainment in communication behavior. The paper advances both technical modeling of multimodal dialogue and the empirical study of human multimodal interaction using trained model representations as analytical tools.

title: VDGR-RAG: Vectors, Directories, Graphs, and Reflection Are All You Need for Unified Reasoning over Hierarchical Enterprise Knowledge
summary: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) is essential for enterprise knowledge question answering (QA), particularly in domains with complex product documentation like telecommunications. However, existing RAG approaches largely overlook the holistic integration of diverse retrieval strengths, leading to inaccurate domain routing, poor utilization of hierarchical document structures, and consequently limited reasoning capabilities over enterprise knowledge. To address these limitations, we present VDGR-RAG, which integrates vector retrieval, directory-driven reasoning, graph traversal, and iterative reflection in a unified framework for accurate enterprise knowledge QA. Specifically, VDGR-RAG is an agentic GraphRAG system that first constructs a Hierarchical Heterogeneous Knowledge Graph ($\text{H}^2$KG) from document chunks to preserve both hierarchical directory structures and semantic relationships, and then employs a set of atomic tools for knowledge retrieval that can be freely composed to navigate the $\text{H}^2$KG: (1) a directory-enhanced routing tool that uses table-of-contents (TOC) structures to route user queries to appropriate domain-specific $\text{H}^2$KGs; (2) a multi-route retrieval tool that combines vector search, TOC-based agentic search, and graph search for comprehensive knowledge retrieval; (3) a directory backtracking tool that corrects knowledge localization biases; and (4) a dynamic reflection tool that iteratively plans the next retrieval phase. We conduct extensive experiments on our enterprise product documents across four wireless domains (e.g., energy saving and fault management). Experimental results demonstrate that our method significantly outperforms a variety of RAG baselines in terms of both knowledge retrieval recall and QA accuracy.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes VDGR-RAG, a RAG framework that unifies vector search, directory-structured navigation, graph traversal, and reflection to improve enterprise QA over complex product documentation, significantly boosting retrieval recall and QA accuracy.
AI.motivation: Existing RAG systems for enterprise QA struggle with complex, hierarchical documentation. They often treat documents as flat chunks, failing to leverage table-of-contents structures and rich cross-document relations, which leads to inaccurate domain routing, suboptimal retrieval, and weak multi-hop reasoning over enterprise knowledge. The authors aim to build a system that better matches the structure and semantics of enterprise documents while enabling more flexible, tool-based retrieval strategies.
AI.method: The authors introduce VDGR-RAG, an agentic GraphRAG framework built on a Hierarchical Heterogeneous Knowledge Graph (H^2KG). First, they construct H^2KG from document chunks, encoding both directory/TOC hierarchies and semantic relationships. Then they design atomic retrieval tools that can be composed by an agent: (1) directory-enhanced routing using TOC structures to select the right domain-specific H^2KG; (2) a multi-route retrieval tool that fuses vector search, TOC-based navigation, and graph search; (3) a directory backtracking tool to correct mislocalized retrieval by moving up/down the hierarchy; and (4) a dynamic reflection tool that iteratively plans subsequent retrieval phases based on intermediate results.
AI.result: On enterprise wireless product documentation across four domains (including energy saving and fault management), VDGR-RAG achieves higher knowledge retrieval recall and QA accuracy than multiple strong RAG baselines. The experiments show that combining heterogeneous retrieval routes over the H^2KG and using reflection-driven orchestration yields more accurate and complete evidence for answering questions.
AI.conclusion: Integrating vector retrieval, hierarchical directory reasoning, graph traversal, and iterative reflection into a unified agentic GraphRAG framework yields substantial gains for enterprise QA over complex product documentation. Modeling both the TOC hierarchy and semantic relations in a Hierarchical Heterogeneous Knowledge Graph enables more accurate domain routing, better knowledge localization, and improved reasoning, suggesting that future enterprise RAG systems should more tightly couple document structure, graph-based representations, and agentic retrieval strategies.

title: Same Question, Different Answer? Measuring and Mitigating Prompt Privilege for Equitable AI Access
summary:
Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly integrated into healthcare, education, public services, and everyday decision making. They should provide comparable assistance regardless of a user's literacy, communication style, or prompt-engineering expertise. However, existing research on prompt robustness primarily focuses on adversarial attacks, prompt injection, and prompt optimization, while overlooking whether semantically equivalent requests receive different responses simply because they are phrased differently. We refer to this accessibility challenge as "Prompt Privilege": users with greater prompting expertise systematically obtain better model performance despite expressing the same underlying intent.
  To address this problem, we present a unified framework for measuring and mitigating accessibility disparities in LLM interactions. We introduce Prompt Equity Score (PES), a quantitative metric for evaluating performance consistency across user populations, and Prompt Equity Transformer (PET), an LLM-based agent that automatically transforms user requests into semantically equivalent, accessibility-oriented prompts while preserving their intent. PET shifts prompt optimization from the user to the AI system, functioning as an intelligent accessibility layer between users and foundation models. Experiments on the MedQA benchmark demonstrate measurable prompt privilege, with statistically significant performance disparities between low-literacy and expert-prompting cohorts. Applying PET eliminates these disparities while preserving semantic fidelity, demonstrating that accessibility-oriented prompt normalization can improve equitable AI access. By introducing prompt privilege as a new dimension of AI accessibility and PET as a practical solution, this work advances system-centered accessibility and provides a foundation for more fair, trustworthy, and inclusive AI systems.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces the concept of “Prompt Privilege” in LLMs—where users with better prompt-engineering skills get better performance for the same intent—and proposes a metric (Prompt Equity Score) and a system (Prompt Equity Transformer) to measure and reduce these disparities, improving equitable access to LLM capabilities.
AI.motivation: LLMs are being deployed in high‑stakes and everyday domains, so their help should not depend on a user’s literacy, communication style, or prompt-engineering expertise. Yet most robustness work focuses on security (attacks, injections) or performance gains, not on whether semantically equivalent prompts from different users yield unequal outcomes. This creates an accessibility and fairness problem: people with less expertise systematically receive worse assistance even when expressing the same intent. The paper is motivated by the need to formally characterize this gap—termed “Prompt Privilege”—and to design mechanisms so that the burden of prompt optimization shifts from users to the AI system itself, thereby supporting more inclusive and trustworthy AI use.
AI.method: The authors (1) formalize “Prompt Privilege” as an accessibility disparity in LLM interactions; (2) define Prompt Equity Score (PES), a metric to quantify consistency of model performance across different user groups (e.g., low‑literacy vs expert prompters) given semantically equivalent intents; (3) propose Prompt Equity Transformer (PET), an LLM-based agent that transforms raw user inputs into semantically equivalent, accessibility-oriented prompts optimized for consistent performance; and (4) evaluate on the MedQA benchmark by constructing user cohorts with different prompting styles, measuring baseline disparities via PES, then inserting PET as an intermediate layer to normalize prompts and re-measuring performance and semantic fidelity.
AI.result: On the MedQA medical question-answering benchmark, the authors find clear evidence of prompt privilege: LLM performance differs significantly between low-literacy style prompts and expert-engineered prompts, despite equivalent underlying intent. Using Prompt Equity Score, they quantify statistically significant disparities between these user cohorts. When PET is deployed as a preprocessing layer that rewrites user prompts, these disparities are effectively removed or greatly reduced, while maintaining semantic equivalence between original and transformed prompts. Thus, PET normalizes prompt quality across users without sacrificing intent or answer correctness.
AI.conclusion: The study concludes that prompt phrasing alone can create systematic accessibility gaps in LLM performance, constituting “Prompt Privilege.” By introducing Prompt Equity Score and the Prompt Equity Transformer, the authors provide a concrete framework and practical mechanism for measuring and mitigating these inequities. PET demonstrates that shifting prompt optimization from end users to the system can enhance fairness and accessibility without degrading semantic fidelity. The work argues that prompt privilege should be treated as a core dimension of AI accessibility and that system-centered accessibility mechanisms like PET are essential for building more fair, trustworthy, and inclusive LLM-based systems in real-world domains such as healthcare and education.

title: Thought-Level Beam Search for Reasoning
comment: Gambit is a thought-level beam search algorithm that reallocates inference compute to high-quality reasoning traces, achieving up to +6.7% accuracy gains and 68.5% token reduction over pruning and parallel sampling under strict hardware constraints
summary: Test-time compute scaling is a primary driver of performance in large reasoning models (LRMs), but extreme inefficiency bounds current approaches, shifting the critical question from \emph{how much} compute to spend, to \emph{where} to allocate it. We formalize test-time reasoning as a constrained compute allocation problem over partial trajectories. Under a fixed hardware budget, existing paradigms fail to actively allocate the compute to the most promising partial progress: traditional parallel sampling treats traces independently and induces severe memory bottlenecks, while subtractive pruning starves hardware and fails to actively and sufficiently shift the output distribution. To overcome this dichotomy, we introduce Gambit, an inference algorithm that executes \emph{thought-level beam search}. By periodically pruning unpromising trajectories and immediately branching from high-quality prefixes, Gambit dynamically concentrates compute onto the most promising reasoning traces via a light-weight scorer probing hidden states while maintaining continuous high hardware utilization. Extensive evaluations across multiple models and benchmarks demonstrate that Gambit strictly dominates existing baselines. Under identical hardware constraints, our method yields up to a +6.7\% absolute accuracy gain on HMMT-24 and +3.3\% on AIME-25 over pruning baselines, delivers $>2\times$ higher throughput on trace completion, and reduces total token consumption by up to 68.5\% relative to standard parallel sampling.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Gambit, a test-time inference algorithm that reallocates compute across partial reasoning trajectories using thought-level beam search, achieving higher accuracy, throughput, and token efficiency than existing sampling and pruning approaches under the same hardware budget.
AI.motivation: Large reasoning models benefit from more test-time compute, but current approaches are inefficient: parallel sampling wastes memory and treats trajectories independently, while subtractive pruning underutilizes hardware and cannot effectively redirect computation to better reasoning paths. There is a need to formalize and solve the problem of how to actively allocate limited compute across partial reasoning traces to maximize performance.
AI.method: The authors formalize test-time reasoning as a constrained compute allocation problem over partial trajectories and propose Gambit, an inference algorithm performing thought-level beam search. Gambit periodically scores partial trajectories via a lightweight hidden-state-based scorer, prunes low-promise traces, and immediately branches from high-quality prefixes. This dynamic scheduling keeps hardware highly utilized while concentrating compute on the most promising reasoning paths, effectively reallocating test-time compute at the granularity of individual “thoughts.”
AI.result: Across multiple models and benchmarks, Gambit outperforms existing baselines under identical hardware constraints. It improves absolute accuracy by up to +6.7% on HMMT-24 and +3.3% on AIME-25 over pruning-based approaches, achieves more than 2× higher throughput for completing reasoning traces, and reduces total token generation by up to 68.5% compared with standard parallel sampling.
AI.conclusion: By casting test-time reasoning as a compute allocation problem and implementing thought-level beam search, Gambit avoids the inefficiency of parallel sampling and the underutilization of subtractive pruning. The method consistently delivers better accuracy, higher throughput, and significantly lower token usage under fixed hardware budgets, indicating that intelligent allocation of test-time compute across reasoning trajectories is a key lever for improving large reasoning model performance.

title: How Can Rhetoric Reward-Hack AI Reviewers? Dissecting Rhetorical Sensitivity in AI-Based Peer Review
summary: As large language models increasingly participate in scientific evaluation, we investigate a potential form of reward hacking: how rhetorical choices shape AI-review judgments when reported scientific content is preserved and how these effects vary across evaluation conditions. We construct a controlled corpus of 4,200 full-paper manuscripts derived from 120 anonymized ICLR 2026 submissions. Two LLM rewriters transform six rhetorical dimensions in opposing directions, and five LLM reviewers evaluate the resulting manuscripts under standard and strict protocols. We also test joint, recursive, and reviewer-guided rewriting. Our results show that rhetorical sensitivity is structured rather than uniform. Evidence framing and novelty stance produce the largest positive-negative contrasts in overall assessment, with scope framing forming a weaker second tier; the remaining dimensions have smaller or less stable effects. This hierarchy persists across human-assessed quality levels, but score movement depends strongly on the AI reviewer's original score: lower scores tend to rise, higher scores tend to fall, and directional contrasts are clearest in the middle ranges. More elaborate workflows do not reliably yield larger gains. Joint rewriting is strongly rewriter-dependent, reviewer guidance does not consistently outperform an unguided second pass, and repeated rewriting yields diminishing, configuration-dependent returns. Across conditions, the rewriter primarily determines the separation between opposing variants, whereas the reviewer determines the magnitude and sign of their score effects. Strict review lowers mean OA by 1.36 points without consistently changing rhetorical sensitivity. These findings identify when rhetorical presentation influences AI scientific review and motivate evaluation systems robust to content-preserving variation in scientific writing.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how different rhetorical styles, while keeping scientific content fixed, influence large language model (LLM) reviewers’ scores, revealing systematic rhetorical sensitivity and implications for robust AI-based scientific evaluation.
AI.motivation: As LLMs are increasingly used to review and evaluate scientific papers, there is a risk of “reward hacking,” where authors can strategically adjust wording and framing without changing substantive content to obtain better scores. Understanding whether, how, and under what conditions rhetorical choices affect AI reviewers is essential for building fair, robust evaluation systems and for anticipating new gaming strategies in scientific publishing.
AI.method: The authors start from 120 anonymized ICLR 2026 submissions and generate a controlled corpus of 4,200 full-paper variants by using two LLM-based rewriting systems to systematically modify six targeted rhetorical dimensions in opposite directions, while preserving underlying scientific content. Five different LLM reviewers then score these manuscripts under two protocols: a standard-review setting and a stricter setting. The study also explores more complex workflows, including joint rewriting (modifying multiple dimensions together), recursive rewriting (multiple passes), and reviewer-guided rewriting (where the reviewer’s feedback informs subsequent rewrites). The authors analyze how these manipulations affect overall assessments across score ranges and human-labeled quality levels.
AI.result: Rhetorical impact on AI reviews is structured and heterogeneous across dimensions. Evidence framing and novelty stance yield the strongest and most consistent positive vs. negative contrasts in overall assessment, with scope framing having moderate effects and other rhetorical dimensions showing weaker or unstable effects. This ordering of sensitivity holds across human-assessed quality levels. However, the direction and magnitude of score changes depend heavily on the AI reviewer’s original score: low scores tend to be boosted, high scores often decrease, and the clearest directional contrasts occur for mid-range submissions. More complex workflows—joint, recursive, or reviewer-guided rewriting—do not consistently produce larger gains; joint rewriting’s benefits depend heavily on the specific rewriter, reviewer-guided rewriting does not reliably outperform a second unguided pass, and repeated rewriting has diminishing, configuration-dependent returns. The choice of rewriter mainly controls how far apart opposing rhetorical variants are, while the choice of reviewer determines how large and in what direction these separations translate into score changes. Under strict review instructions, mean overall assessment scores drop by about 1.36 points, but the basic pattern of rhetorical sensitivity remains similar.
AI.conclusion: LLM-based scientific review is meaningfully influenced by rhetorical presentation even when substantive content is held constant, with particular vulnerability to how evidence and novelty are framed. These effects vary systematically with the reviewer model and the initial score range rather than being random noise, and more complex rewriting strategies do not inherently solve or exacerbate the issue. Tightening review protocols reduces overall scores but does not remove rhetorical sensitivity. The findings underscore the need to design AI evaluation pipelines and training objectives that are robust to content-preserving stylistic variations, and to recognize rhetorical reward hacking as a realistic concern in automated scientific assessment.

title: Legal Responsibilities Using Autonomous Agents For Artificial Intelligence
summary: Recent incidents involving Artificial Intelligence (AI) agents, which were reported escaping their containment `unintentionally' to gain unauthorized access, pose looming questions about who or what should be held legally responsible for resultant criminal or negligent damage. As the independent capabilities of agents expand, Promise Theory suggests a systematic method to resolve these questions, based on the Downstream Principle for causal influence. Responsibility can easily be expanded to include AI agents where tracing responsibility becomes impactical, and agents' freedoms to act can be limtied by policy choices.

AI.tldr: The paper explores legal responsibility for unintended harmful actions by autonomous AI agents using Promise Theory and the Downstream Principle to systematically assign responsibility and constrain agent behavior by policy.
AI.motivation: As AI agents gain more autonomy and have been reported to escape containment and cause unauthorized access or damage, there is growing uncertainty in law and policy about who or what should be held responsible—developers, deployers, users, or the agents themselves. Existing legal frameworks struggle with distributed, semi-autonomous causality, so there is a need for a principled way to assign responsibility in multi-agent AI systems.
AI.method: The paper applies Promise Theory—a framework where autonomous agents make and keep promises about their behavior—to the problem of legal and causal responsibility. Using the Downstream Principle, which traces causal influence from upstream to downstream agents, the authors construct a systematic approach to decomposing responsibility across human and AI agents. They examine how responsibilities can be assigned, traced, and limited via explicit promises and policy constraints on agent freedoms.
AI.result: The analysis shows that Promise Theory can be used to extend traditional concepts of responsibility to AI agents in a structured way. Responsibility can be propagated along chains of promises and interactions, allowing one to identify which human or AI agents are downstream of a harmful outcome and to what extent they bear responsibility. The framework demonstrates that, even when direct tracing of all actions becomes impractical, responsibility can still be allocated by designating and constraining roles in the promise network.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that responsibility in autonomous AI systems can be systematically managed and extended to AI agents themselves using Promise Theory and the Downstream Principle. Legal and policy frameworks can leverage this to define where responsibility resides, even when complex chains of interactions make exact causal tracing difficult. Moreover, by treating agent freedoms as configurable through policy, it is possible to prevent or mitigate harmful behaviors in advance, aligning AI deployments with legal and ethical expectations.

title: How Far Do Foundation Models Transfer to Infant Signals? A Cross-Dataset Transfer Audit with a Unified Need Ontology
comment: 18 pages, 7 figures. Under review at AAAI 2027
summary: Public infant cry corpora are small, label-incompatible, and almost always evaluated one corpus at a time. We ask what this practice hides and what fixes it. Across four cry corpora screened by a multi-level leakage audit (byte-level and embedding-level deduplication plus a within-corpus train-test near-duplicate audit), we probe four frozen encoders and a handcrafted baseline under a unified five-class need ontology and shared task formulations. The audit exposes what single-corpus evaluation conceals: within-domain macro-F1 swings by 0.57-0.80 for the same encoder, cross-corpus transfer is negative on average (negative-transfer ratio 0.19-0.35, significant in 18 of 30 directed cells, BH-FDR), and 349 content-identical clip groups carry conflicting metadata labels across corpus distributions. The same audit, however, reveals a consistent way forward. Transfer into the noisiest corpus is consistently positive in effect size at matched training size and after near-duplicate removal, offering a practical recipe for small, noisy corpora. Frozen probes saturate at modest label budgets, while stabilized fine-tuning wins with full labels; domain-adaptive pretraining significantly beats stabilized fine-tuning at 5-10-shot (the 1-shot advantage is not robust to optimization-seed variance) but shows no significant advantage at 50-shot or beyond. In the tested binary, shared-label settings, ontology-mapped joint training wins in all four encoder-by-target combinations, whereas naively merging unmapped labels costs up to 37 F1 points. We release the ontology, mapping code, and audit pipeline, turning incompatible cry corpora into a usable joint-training resource.

AI.tldr: Study audits and unifies multiple public infant cry corpora to evaluate encoders and transfer learning under a shared need-ontology, revealing large hidden variability, negative cross-corpus transfer, but also practical recipes for noisy small datasets and joint training via ontology mapping.
AI.motivation: Infant cry datasets are small, inconsistently labeled, and typically evaluated one corpus at a time, which may hide issues like label conflicts, data leakage, and poor cross-corpus generalization. The authors want to systematically reveal these hidden problems and propose methods that enable more reliable evaluation and better use of all available data.
AI.method: They perform a multi-level leakage and duplication audit (byte-level, embedding-level, and within-corpus near-duplicate checks) on four public infant cry corpora. They map the corpora to a unified five-class infant-need ontology and define shared tasks. Under this standardized setting, they probe four frozen audio encoders and a handcrafted baseline, compare probing vs stabilized fine-tuning vs domain-adaptive pretraining under varying label budgets (1–50+ shots), and test different strategies for combining corpora (ontology-mapped joint training vs naive label merging). Statistical significance is assessed (e.g., BH-FDR correction).
AI.result: Single-corpus evaluation hides major variability: within-domain macro-F1 for the same encoder can vary by 0.57–0.80, and cross-corpus transfer is generally negative (negative-transfer ratio 0.19–0.35, significant in 18/30 transfer directions). They uncover 349 groups of content-identical clips with conflicting metadata labels across corpora. Yet transfer into the noisiest corpus is consistently beneficial when training size is matched and near-duplicates removed. Frozen probes saturate quickly with small label budgets, stabilized fine-tuning is best with full labels, and domain-adaptive pretraining is superior in very low-shot (5–10-shot) but not at 50-shot+. Ontology-mapped joint training consistently outperforms separate training or naive label merging, while naive merging can reduce F1 by up to 37 points.
AI.conclusion: Common evaluation practices on infant cry corpora can be misleading due to leakage, label conflicts, and negative cross-corpus transfer. A rigorous multi-level audit plus a unified five-class need ontology exposes these issues and enables reliable joint use of heterogeneous corpora. For practitioners, the paper offers concrete recipes: leverage positive transfer into noisy corpora with deduplication, choose between probing, fine-tuning, and domain-adaptive pretraining based on label budget, and always use ontology-based label mapping rather than naive label merging. The released ontology, mappings, and audit pipeline convert previously incompatible cry corpora into a coherent joint-training resource.

title: The Authority Expectancy Effect in Multi-User Conflict
summary: We investigate how social authority (SA) signals interact with severity-based prioritization in large language models, operationalizing each axis as a model-elicited baseline -- the triage hierarchy and the SA hierarchy. Across four LLMs (Claude, Gemini, GPT, Grok) and three experimental phases -- resource allocation, fault attribution, and multi-turn dispute mediation -- we find that occupational authority, institutional documentation, and relational congruence can restructure model judgments in ways not captured by additive reweighting of authority cues. We formalize this pattern as the Authority Expectancy Effect (AEE) and characterize it through three properties observed across our conditions: it is reference-dependent, defined only relative to a pre-authority baseline; it involves evidential reinterpretation, in which identical content acquires different inferential implications depending on which party bears the SA signal; and it exhibits direction sensitivity, producing opposite outcomes depending on whether authority position and evidentiary cues align.

AI.tldr: Study of how signals of social authority affect prioritization decisions in LLMs beyond simple severity-based rules.
AI.motivation: To understand whether and how large language models change their judgment and prioritization when one party is marked as socially authoritative (e.g., by occupation or institutional backing), and to see if this effect is more complex than just giving extra weight to authority cues.
AI.method: Elicit two baselines from four LLMs (Claude, Gemini, GPT, Grok): a triage hierarchy (severity-based prioritization) and a social authority (SA) hierarchy. Run three experimental paradigms—resource allocation, fault attribution, and multi-turn dispute mediation—in which authority cues (occupation, institutional documentation, relational congruence) are systematically varied between parties. Compare model outputs with and without SA cues and analyze whether changes can be explained by additive reweighting or require a new formalization.
