AI.result: Introducing occupational authority, institutional documentation, or relational congruence systematically reshapes model judgments across tasks and models. The observed changes cannot be fully explained by simple additive weighting of authority signals on top of baseline severity or evidence; instead, model reasoning patterns shift in structure depending on which side is marked as authoritative and how that aligns with evidence.
AI.conclusion: The paper identifies and formalizes an Authority Expectancy Effect (AEE) in LLMs, showing that authority cues interact with model baselines in a reference-dependent, evidence-reinterpreting, and direction-sensitive way. This implies that LLM behavior in socially structured scenarios is more contextually fragile and normatively complex than simple severity-based or cue-weighting accounts suggest, with implications for safety, fairness, and alignment in real-world deployments.

title: ELICITED: EHR-grounded Longitudinal Interactive Conversations for Information-seeking Triage Evaluation and Decision-making
summary: Emergency-department (ED) triage requires clinicians to rapidly identify patients who need immediate attention, determine who can safely wait, and prioritize limited clinical resources. At presentation, however, information may be limited to a chief complaint and initial vital signs. Clinically important details, including symptom onset and progression, associated symptoms, medical history, and medication use, are often obtained through focused conversation. Effective triage therefore requires clinicians to identify information gaps, ask appropriate follow-up questions, and update their assessment as new evidence becomes available. Most existing ED benchmarks evaluate acuity prediction from a fixed clinical snapshot. Although this formulation measures predictive performance after patient information has been assembled, it does not capture the interactive process through which triage-relevant evidence is elicited and interpreted. Existing medical dialogue datasets support the study of clinical communication, but dialogue statements are not always linked to temporally ordered events in the electronic health record (EHR). We introduce EHR2Dial-Triage, an agentic conversation-generation framework and benchmark grounded in MIMIC-IV-ED. The framework constructs triage conversations under explicit role-based and temporal information boundaries. Each accepted patient disclosure is linked to its supporting EHR event and the first dialogue turn at which it becomes available. EHR2Dial-Triage enables controlled evaluation of information elicitation, evidence use, five-level Emergency Severity Index prediction, and patient-facing communication across models and patient personas. It provides a structured setting for studying conversational triage as a dynamic process of clinical information acquisition, reasoning, and communication.

AI.tldr: They build a new benchmark and simulation framework that turns ED EHR data into realistic triage dialogues, so models can be tested on how well they ask questions, use evidence, and predict acuity over time, not just from a static snapshot.
AI.motivation: Real ED triage is an interactive process where clinicians iteratively ask questions to fill information gaps and update their assessment, but most current machine learning benchmarks treat triage as a one-shot prediction from a fixed snapshot of data, ignoring how information is elicited and used over time. Existing medical dialogue datasets don’t cleanly align each utterance with timestamped EHR events, making it difficult to rigorously study dynamic reasoning and information acquisition in conversational triage.
AI.method: They design EHR2Dial-Triage, an agent-based conversation generation framework grounded in the MIMIC-IV-ED dataset. The system enforces explicit role-based and temporal constraints: at each dialogue turn, the ‘patient’ agent can only disclose information that is supported by specific EHR events that are already available at that point in time. Each accepted disclosure is linked both to the underlying EHR event and to the first turn when it becomes accessible. Using these rules, they synthesize structured triage conversations that unfold as new evidence becomes available, and package them as a benchmark to evaluate models on several triage-related tasks.
AI.result: The framework produces temporally grounded triage dialogues where every piece of patient-reported information is traceable to specific EHR events and their availability time. This dataset/benchmark enables systematic measurement of (1) how well models elicit missing information, (2) how appropriately they use newly revealed evidence, (3) their performance on predicting five-level Emergency Severity Index scores over the course of the dialogue, and (4) the quality of their patient-facing communication across different patient personas.
AI.conclusion: EHR2Dial-Triage offers a structured, temporally aligned benchmark for studying ED triage as a dynamic, conversational process rather than a static prediction task. By tying dialogue content to time-ordered EHR events and enforcing information-availability constraints, it supports controlled evaluation of information-gathering strategies, clinical reasoning, and communication quality in simulated triage encounters.

title: Decided Upstream, Written Late: Locating and Pricing the Cross-Lingual Refusal Circuit of a Multilingual MoE
comment: Accepted to the actionable Interpretability workshop at COLM 2026
summary: Safety alignment in multilingual models is uneven: a model that reliably refuses a harmful request in English will often comply with the same request in a lower-resource language. We trace this gap mechanistically in sarvam, an Indic-multilingual mixture-of-experts reasoning model, and find it is not a failure to detect harm. Harm is encoded as an internal direction that is nearly language-invariant in mid-network (English-vs-Indic cosine ${\approx}0.9$ at $L11$), and steering that direction upstream causally controls refusal. But the detection direction is orthogonal to the change that actually writes the refusal, which is late and assembled over the course of generation rather than read off in a single forward pass. We attribute the write to a specific, localizable circuit, a mixture-of-experts writer held in check by an attention opposer and price every way of intervening on it: damping the opposer is cheap and effective, amplifying the writer is a cost wall, and surgical edits to the responsible heads do nothing. The circuit's organization, and the gradient method that exposes it, recur in a second, unrelated MoE model, while the lever's strength is architecture-specific. The result is a cost-measured map of where a multilingual safety repair can land, and what it costs

AI.tldr: The paper studies why multilingual models are less safe in low‑resource languages, finds that harm detection is shared across languages but refusal writing is not, identifies a concrete refusal-writing circuit in a mixture-of-experts model, and evaluates how costly different safety interventions are.
AI.motivation: Multilingual LLMs often refuse harmful prompts in English but answer them in lower-resource languages, creating uneven safety. Existing work mostly treats this as a black-box behavioral issue. The authors want a mechanistic, circuit-level understanding of where this failure comes from in the network, whether the model actually detects harm in all languages, and what concrete levers and costs are involved in repairing safety across languages and architectures.
AI.method: They analyze sarvam, an Indic-multilingual mixture-of-experts (MoE) reasoning model, using mechanistic interpretability techniques. First, they identify an internal activation direction corresponding to harm detection and measure its similarity across English and Indic languages, including cosine similarity layer by layer. They then causally intervene by steering this direction at different layers to see how it affects refusal behavior. Next, they separate the internal representation that detects harm from the mechanism that writes an explicit refusal into the output. They localize a specific MoE-based "writer" circuit and an attention-based "opposer" that suppresses it, and experimentally manipulate them (damping, amplification, surgical edits to specific heads) while measuring behavior and intervention cost. They replicate the gradient-based circuit-finding procedure on a second, unrelated MoE model to test generality.
AI.result: They find that harm is encoded as a nearly language-invariant direction in mid-network layers (around layer 11, English vs. Indic cosine similarity ≈ 0.9), and that steering this direction upstream can causally control whether the model refuses. However, the direction encoding harm is orthogonal to the direction that actually writes refusal text, which appears late in the forward pass and accumulates over the course of generation. They attribute refusal writing to a localized MoE "writer" circuit opposed by an attention "opposer." Interventions show that weakening the opposer is inexpensive and yields strong improvements in refusal, whereas amplifying the writer is prohibitively costly, and precise edits to the implicated attention heads have negligible effect. Applying the same gradient-based analysis to another MoE model reveals a similar organizational pattern, though the strength and cost of the safety lever differ by architecture.
AI.conclusion: The main gap in multilingual safety is not lack of harm detection—harm is recognized similarly across languages—but a failure of the downstream refusal-writing mechanism to activate appropriately in lower-resource languages. Refusal behavior is driven by a specific MoE writer circuit balanced by an attention opposer, and only certain intervention points are both effective and cost-efficient. The paper provides a cost-aware map of viable locations for implementing multilingual safety repairs and suggests that architectural details strongly influence which levers work best, while the underlying circuit organization and gradient-based discovery method appear to generalize across MoE models.

title: Don't Scroll Back: Missing-Evidence Memory for Streaming Dialogue Summarization
summary: Users of modern platforms repeatedly need summaries of recent dialogue, but the window rarely contains enough context to be interpreted on its own. We formalize this setting as streaming dialogue summarization, where a system must summarize a current window using selective memory from an unbounded history under a fixed budget. We show that the central challenge is not how much history is accessed, but whether memory recovers the evidence that the current window presupposes. We construct a benchmark and evaluation protocol that separately assesses whether memory contains gap-resolving evidence and whether the generated summary reflects it. We propose ReMEMBER, a missing-evidence memory framework that conditions retrieval on unresolved window dependencies and refines retrieved chunks into evidence-dense memory under a fixed budget. Experiments on dialogues with histories up to 160K tokens show that ReMEMBER improves memory recall and gap-resolution completeness over memory construction baselines under the same budget.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a framework for streaming dialogue summarization that uses a selective memory mechanism to fill in missing context from long histories under a fixed memory budget.
AI.motivation: In real-world conversational platforms, users frequently need summaries of ongoing dialogues, but current summarization models often only see a limited context window that lacks critical prior information. Existing long-context or memory approaches focus on how much history is stored or retrieved, not on whether the retrieved memory actually contains the specific evidence needed to interpret the current window. This creates summaries that miss key references, presuppositions, and dependencies that rely on earlier dialogue turns.
AI.method: The authors formalize the problem as streaming dialogue summarization with a fixed memory budget and an unbounded dialogue history. They build a benchmark and evaluation protocol that decouples two aspects: (1) whether the memory store contains the evidence needed to fill gaps in the current window, and (2) whether the generated summaries successfully use that evidence. They propose ReMEMBER, a missing-evidence memory framework that (a) detects unresolved dependencies in the current dialogue window, (b) conditions retrieval on these missing pieces, and (c) refines retrieved history chunks into compact, evidence-dense memories that fit the fixed budget.
AI.result: On datasets with dialogue histories up to 160K tokens, ReMEMBER achieves better memory recall of relevant past information and higher gap-resolution completeness compared to baseline memory construction methods, while using the same memory budget. This indicates that the method is more effective at recovering and storing the specific evidence needed to interpret and summarize the current dialogue window.
AI.conclusion: Recovering the right evidence from long dialogue histories is more important than simply increasing the amount of accessible history for streaming summarization. By explicitly modeling missing evidence and conditioning memory retrieval and compression on unresolved dependencies, ReMEMBER provides more complete, contextually grounded summaries under a fixed budget. The proposed benchmark and evaluation protocol offer a way to separately measure memory quality and summary quality in this setting.

title: SkillSmith: Enhancing Locally Deployed Agents via Automatic Skill Construction and Evolution
summary: LLM-based agent frameworks now act as personal assistants for multi-step tasks. Existing agent frameworks such as OpenClaw commonly follow the Cloud Agent depolyment mode using closed-source cloud LLMs as backbone model, which may expose private user information and incur repeated LLM-calling costs. Local Agents address these deployment concerns by depolying frontier open-source SLMs on user-controlled devices, but their task effectiveness still lags far behind Cloud Agents. Through diagnostic analysis, we reveal that the limited effectiveness of Local Agents with frontier SLM backbones mainly comes from missing environment knowledge caused by limited backbone model scale including environment rules and operation procedures. To supply such knowledge non-parametrically, context-efficiently, and without expert authoring, we present SkillSmith, a Cloud--Local Agent collaboration framework that uses Skill as a context-efficient knowledge carrier, automatic constructs Skill from Cloud Agent task exploration and evolves Skill using Local Agent execution feedback to enhance a frozen Local Agent. Experiments on daily agent task datasets AppWorld and WorkBench show that the automatically generated Skill enables the Local Agent with Qwen3.6-27B(SLM) to achieve task effectiveness comparable to Cloud Agents with frontier LLMs, outperform the strongest non-parametric baselines, reduce average actions per task from 36.1 to 9.9 on AppWorld-Normal, and generalize to other SLM backbone models without rerunning Skill construction.

AI.tldr: SkillSmith is a cloud–local collaborative agent framework that distills environment-specific task skills from a powerful cloud LLM into reusable, compact “Skills” to boost smaller local SLM-based agents to near cloud-level performance on multi-step tasks.
AI.motivation: Cloud-based LLM agents (Cloud Agents) are effective on complex multi-step tasks but raise privacy concerns and incur high, repeated API costs because they must be called frequently for each task. Local agents using smaller open-source models (SLMs) on user devices avoid these issues but perform much worse, largely due to missing environment knowledge (rules, procedures, action patterns) that large cloud LLMs implicitly possess. There is a need for a way to transfer this environment and procedural knowledge from strong cloud agents to weaker local agents in a non-parametric, context-efficient, and automatically maintainable form, without manual expert engineering, so that local agents can become both private and effective.
AI.method: The authors propose SkillSmith, a collaborative Cloud–Local agent framework built around an intermediate artifact called a Skill, which serves as a context-efficient carrier of environment knowledge. First, a powerful Cloud Agent explores tasks in a given environment (e.g., AppWorld, WorkBench) and automatically constructs Skills that encode environment rules and operation procedures discovered during task solving. These Skills are designed to be compact enough to be injected into the prompt context of a frozen Local Agent built on an open-source SLM. Then the Local Agent uses these Skills at inference time to guide its action decisions. The framework also incorporates a feedback loop where the Local Agent’s execution feedback is used to evolve and refine Skills over time, all without changing the Local Agent’s parameters or requiring manual expert authoring.
AI.result: On daily agent-task benchmarks AppWorld and WorkBench, SkillSmith’s automatically generated Skills allow a Local Agent using Qwen3.6-27B (an SLM) to reach task effectiveness comparable to Cloud Agents built on frontier closed-source LLMs. The method outperforms the strongest non-parametric baselines and substantially improves efficiency: on AppWorld-Normal, the average number of actions per task is reduced from 36.1 to 9.9. Additionally, the constructed Skills generalize across different SLM backbone models, so they can be reused without rerunning the expensive Cloud Agent–based Skill construction process.
AI.conclusion: SkillSmith demonstrates that environment and procedural knowledge missing from smaller local SLM agents can be supplied non-parametrically via automatically discovered and refined Skills distilled from cloud LLM agents. This Cloud–Local collaboration closes most of the performance gap between local SLM-based agents and powerful cloud LLM agents, while preserving user privacy and reducing repeated cloud API costs. The approach is efficient, outperforms existing non-parametric baselines, reduces action counts, and yields reusable Skills that transfer across multiple SLM backbones without additional construction overhead.

title: Tree-of-Experience: Hierarchical Experience Management for Self-Evolving Agents
summary: Continual self-evolution requires LLM agents to transform environmental interactions into reliable and reusable experience. Existing methods typically refine individual trajectories or abstract shared knowledge from related trajectories, but their experience representations are often disconnected from the underlying reasoning process. This limits feedback attribution, cross-task transfer, and update and retrieval efficiency, particularly in complex reasoning tasks with outcome-level feedback. To overcome this limitation, we propose \textbf{T}ree-\textbf{o}f-\textbf{E}xperience (ToE), a structured experience-management framework that aligns experience organization with the hierarchical reasoning process of LLM agents. Specifically, ToE organizes the experience into a shared tree of analytical perspectives and reasoning paths, whose reliability is calibrated through environmental outcomes to support systematic updating, transfer, and efficient retrieval. The experimental results on \textsc{Game of 24} and \textsc{FinEvolveBench} show that ToE substantially improves both problem-solving performance and efficiency. On \textsc{Game of 24}, ToE achieves a 31.4\% relative improvement in accuracy over the experience-free ToT baseline. On \textsc{FinEvolveBench}, ToE improves tsIC by an average of 41.24\% over the experience-free pipeline across 12 evaluation settings, whereas conventional experience-management methods often underperform experience-free baselines.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Tree-of-Experience (ToE), a structured framework that aligns stored experience with the hierarchical reasoning process of LLM agents, significantly improving performance and efficiency on complex reasoning benchmarks compared to experience-free and conventional experience-management methods.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM experience-management methods either refine single trajectories or extract shared knowledge across trajectories, but their stored experience is loosely coupled with the internal reasoning structure. This misalignment makes it hard to attribute feedback to specific reasoning steps, hampers transfer across tasks, and leads to inefficient updating and retrieval, especially when only outcome-level feedback is available. The authors aim to design an experience representation and management scheme that is structurally aligned with how LLMs reason, enabling better continual self-evolution.
AI.method: The authors introduce Tree-of-Experience (ToE), which organizes an LLM agent's past interactions into a shared tree structure that mirrors hierarchical reasoning. Nodes in the tree represent analytical perspectives and reasoning paths. As the agent interacts with environments, outcome-level feedback is used to calibrate the reliability of nodes and paths in this tree. This structured, shared tree allows systematic updating of experience, cross-task transfer of useful reasoning fragments, and efficient retrieval of relevant experience during future problem solving.
AI.result: On the Game of 24 benchmark, ToE yields a 31.4% relative accuracy improvement over an experience-free Tree-of-Thoughts (ToT) baseline. On FinEvolveBench, ToE improves tsIC (a task-specific performance metric) by an average of 41.24% over an experience-free pipeline across 12 evaluation settings, while standard experience-management methods often perform worse than no experience at all. These results indicate that aligning experience with reasoning structure produces significant gains in both problem-solving performance and efficiency.
AI.conclusion: Structuring experience as a shared tree that is aligned with the agent's hierarchical reasoning enables more effective continual self-evolution of LLM agents. By calibrating the reliability of reasoning paths using outcome feedback, ToE supports accurate feedback attribution, better cross-task transfer, and efficient update and retrieval, outperforming both experience-free baselines and conventional experience-management approaches on complex reasoning tasks.

title: Lingjing: A Simulation Testbed for Multi-Agent Embodied Tasks in Open-Ended Cities
summary: Urban embodied intelligence requires coordination among heterogeneous agents (e.g., UAVs, ground robots, and autonomous vehicles) in dynamic cities. Simulators therefore provide a scalable foundation for developing and evaluating such coordination. Existing platforms nevertheless isolate different embodiments and decouple them from task design and evaluation. We present \textbf{Lingjing}, a simulation platform for heterogeneous multi-agent embodied intelligence in open-ended urban environments. Lingjing reconstructs and renders evolving cities from geographic data, synchronizes multiple physics engines, and exposes shared physical and structured urban state to agents. Its Gym-like interface supports user-defined ReAct agents and single- or multi-agent natural-language missions with configurable star or broadcast communication and resource constraints. Each episode becomes an attribution-ready replay that links agent trajectories and communication to relation-graph changes, resource consumption, and engine-based evaluations for systematic diagnosis. We evaluate twelve vision-language models on nine urban tasks under a shared engine-in-the-loop protocol. Controlled studies further examine communication, scalability, robustness, and failure provenance. Results expose persistent bottlenecks in grounding and long-horizon execution. They also show task-dependent coordination trade-offs and diminishing returns from added capacity, while heavier workloads further reduce success. Lingjing provides a unified testbed that enables reproducible end-to-end evaluation and systematic failure diagnosis in urban multi-agent embodied intelligence.

AI.tldr: Introduces Lingjing, a unified urban simulation platform for evaluating heterogeneous multi-agent embodied intelligence with language-based tasks and systematic diagnosis.
AI.motivation: Urban embodied intelligence involves many heterogeneous agents operating together in complex, changing city environments. Existing simulators typically handle only one embodiment type at a time, do not tightly couple task design with evaluation, and provide limited support for diagnosing why multi-agent systems fail. There is a need for a scalable, realistic, and unified testbed that can support diverse agents, language-driven missions, and detailed, reproducible evaluation to understand bottlenecks in coordination, grounding, and long-horizon control.
AI.method: The authors build Lingjing, a simulation platform that reconstructs dynamic urban environments from geographic data and renders evolving cities. It synchronizes multiple physics engines to support different embodiments (UAVs, ground robots, autonomous vehicles) and exposes a shared representation of the physical and structured urban state. Lingjing offers a Gym-like interface that allows users to define ReAct-style agents, specify single- or multi-agent natural-language missions, configure communication modes (star or broadcast), and impose resource constraints. Each episode is logged as an attribution-ready replay that ties together agent trajectories, communication, relation-graph changes, resource usage, and engine-based metrics for diagnosis. Using this platform, they run a shared engine-in-the-loop evaluation protocol for twelve vision-language models on nine urban tasks, along with controlled experiments on communication patterns, scalability, robustness, and failure provenance.
AI.result: Across the evaluated setting, the experiments reveal consistent weaknesses of current vision-language models in grounding (linking perception and language to the environment) and in executing long-horizon tasks. The studies show that different tasks favor different coordination strategies, indicating trade-offs in how agents should communicate and collaborate. Increasing model capacity yields diminishing returns, particularly as task workloads grow heavier, and higher workload further degrades success rates. The platform successfully surfaces where and how these failures occur through its detailed replay and analysis tools.
AI.conclusion: Lingjing offers a unified, realistic, and configurable testbed for heterogeneous multi-agent embodied intelligence in urban environments. It enables reproducible, end-to-end evaluation of language-driven multi-agent systems, along with fine-grained, attribution-ready analysis of failures. The findings from initial experiments highlight current bottlenecks in grounding and long-horizon execution and demonstrate that coordination strategies and model scaling have complex, task-dependent effects. The platform is positioned as an infrastructure piece for systematic progress and diagnosis in urban multi-agent embodied intelligence research.

title: Bridging the Gap Between Semantics and Reconstruction:Unifying Sign Language Translation and Production
summary: Recent advances in sign language (SL) research have shown a trend toward unifying multiple sign language understanding (SLU) subtasks, such as isolated sign language recognition (ISLR), continuous sign language recognition (CSLR), and sign language translation (SLT), within a single framework, leading to substantial progress. Meanwhile, sign language production (SLP), which generates sign sequences from text, has also attracted growing attention. This naturally raises an important question: can sign language understanding and production be unified within a single framework? Compared with unifying SLU subtasks, this problem is substantially more challenging. Existing SLU tasks largely share the same direction of mapping, namely from sign inputs to linguistic outputs, whereas SLT and SLP lie in opposite directions of sign-text mapping. A unified framework must therefore address two key challenges: (1) bridging the modality gap between continuous sign motions and discrete text tokens through a shared sign tokenizer that supports both linguistic abstraction and motion reconstruction; and (2) learning a single conditional autoregressive model that can take either sign or text as input and generate the corresponding target sequence in the opposite modality. To this end, we propose Uni-SLTP, a unified framework for SLT and SLP with two key components: (1) a shared sign tokenizer that converts sign sequences into discrete tokens and latent representations, capturing both semantic and reconstructive information; and (2) a unified autoregressive generation model that formulates both tasks as conditional sequence generation. Experiments on widely used public datasets show that Uni-SLTP achieves superior motion accuracy for SLP while maintaining competitive SLT performance.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Uni-SLTP, a unified framework that handles both sign language translation (text↔sign) and sign language production within one model, using a shared sign tokenizer and a unified autoregressive generator.
AI.motivation: Prior work in sign language processing has unified several understanding tasks (ISLR, CSLR, SLT) that map from sign to text, but sign language production (text-to-sign) remains separate. Unifying understanding and production is harder because they require modeling opposite directions of the sign–text mapping and bridging a large modality gap between continuous 3D sign motions and discrete text tokens. A single, general framework would simplify system design and potentially improve performance by sharing representations across tasks.
AI.method: The authors design Uni-SLTP with two main components. First, a shared sign tokenizer that encodes continuous sign motion sequences into discrete tokens plus latent features, jointly optimized to capture semantically meaningful abstractions while preserving enough information to reconstruct realistic motion. Second, a unified conditional autoregressive model that treats both sign language translation (sign→text) and sign language production (text→sign) as sequence-to-sequence generation problems: it conditions on inputs in one modality (sign or text) and autoregressively generates outputs in the other modality using the shared sign token space.
AI.result: On standard public benchmarks, Uni-SLTP delivers better or state-of-the-art motion quality for sign language production and maintains competitive accuracy for sign language translation compared to specialized baselines. This demonstrates that one model can effectively handle both directions of sign–text conversion without sacrificing performance.
AI.conclusion: Uni-SLTP shows that sign language understanding (translation) and production can be unified in a single framework by introducing a shared sign tokenizer and a conditional autoregressive generator that works across modalities. The approach effectively bridges the continuous–discrete modality gap, enabling high-quality motion generation while preserving strong translation capability, and suggests a promising direction for more general, bidirectional sign–text systems.

title: JustLLMGRPO: Radiographic Control for Chest X-Ray Generation
summary: Text-conditioned chest X-ray generation aims to synthesize realistic radiographs that faithfully depict specified findings. Existing work has primarily improved quality by updating image generators, implicitly treating prompts as fixed after CXR-domain adaptation. We show that this generator-centric view leaves a substantial optimization dimension underexplored. With a CXR-adapted Sana generator frozen, one-pass reformulation by an unmodified LLM reduces RadDINO-FID from 54.225 to 27.572. Prompt analysis shows that the LLM suppresses temporal comparisons, uncertainty, and other non-renderable report content while emphasizing visible radiographic findings. However, unconstrained reformulation reduces BioViL-T alignment with source prompts from 0.695 to 0.609. We therefore introduce JustLLMGRPO, which applies standard Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) only to the LLM prompt policy while keeping Sana frozen. Group-relative radiology-aware image feedback retains visual focus while preserving source-prompt alignment. On CheXGenBench, JustLLMGRPO reduces RadDINO-FID to 26.780, a 50.6% improvement over direct prompting, while maintaining alignment (0.696 versus 0.695). It also achieves state-of-the-art distribution coverage and downstream classification utility. These results show that substantial performance can remain latent in how radiographic information is expressed to an adapted generator. Code is publicly available at https://github.com/pxcai/JustLLMGRPO.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that for text-conditioned chest X-ray generation, optimizing how prompts are written via an LLM—rather than changing the image generator—unlocks large gains in image quality and alignment.
AI.motivation: Most prior work improves text-to-CXR generation by modifying or retraining the image generator while treating the input prompts (radiology reports or findings) as fixed after domain adaptation. This overlooks the possibility that much performance loss comes from a mismatch between complex, clinical language and what the generator can actually render. The authors are motivated to explore whether systematically rewriting prompts can significantly boost generation quality without touching the generator itself, and how to do this without sacrificing semantic alignment to the original clinical text.
AI.method: 1) Freeze a CXR-adapted Sana image generator and use an off-the-shelf LLM to perform one-pass reformulation of radiology prompts, then evaluate the impact on image quality and text-image alignment. 2) Analyze the linguistic changes the LLM tends to make (e.g., removing temporal/uncertain/non-visual content, emphasizing concrete, visible findings). 3) Propose JustLLMGRPO: a method that treats the LLM as a prompt policy and applies Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) only to this LLM, while keeping the Sana generator frozen. 4) Design group-relative, radiology-aware image feedback signals that reward prompts whose generated images have good visual fidelity and distribution coverage while remaining aligned with the original prompts. 5) Evaluate on CheXGenBench using RadDINO-FID, BioViL-T alignment, coverage, and downstream classification performance.
AI.result: With a frozen, CXR-adapted Sana generator, simple one-pass LLM prompt reformulation halves RadDINO-FID from 54.225 to 27.572 but degrades BioViL-T alignment from 0.695 to 0.609. The proposed JustLLMGRPO method further improves RadDINO-FID to 26.780 (a 50.6% improvement over direct prompting) while essentially preserving alignment (0.696 vs 0.695). It also achieves state-of-the-art distribution coverage and strong downstream classification utility of generated images on CheXGenBench.
AI.conclusion: The way radiologic information is expressed to a domain-adapted text-to-image generator is a major, previously underexplored axis of optimization. A frozen generator can yield substantially better chest X-ray synthesis simply by learning to rewrite prompts appropriately. JustLLMGRPO, which optimizes only the LLM-based prompt policy with radiology-aware GRPO feedback, unlocks large quality gains while preserving semantic alignment, suggesting that prompt policy optimization should be treated as a first-class component in medical image generation pipelines.

title: Measuring the Tokenization Premium: A Cost Audit for Underserved Language Communities
summary: Large language models are increasingly deployed as general-purpose educational and technical assistance systems, but their underlying infrastructure does not treat languages equally. One underexamined source of disparity is tokenization: semantically equivalent content can require substantially different token counts across languages, affecting API cost, latency, and usable context length before a model is invoked. We introduce the Tokenization Equity Audit (TEA), a reproducible benchmark for measuring tokenization premiums in technical tutoring content. TEA evaluates three widely used tokenizers, GPT-4o's o200k base, Qwen2.5-7B, and Mistral-7B, on a 120-item Python debugging corpus translated from English into Bengali, Hindi, Arabic, Tamil, and Yoruba. Bengali and Hindi serve as the primary validated cases, while the remaining languages provide exploratory cross-script and cross-family comparisons. Across this corpus, Bengali requires (1.56\times) as many GPT-4o tokens as English, reducing a nominal 128k-token context window to an effective 82k-token English-equivalent capacity for the same semantic content. With the Qwen2.5 and Mistral tokenizers, Bengali requires up to (4.5\times) the English token count. Yoruba, despite using the Latin script, exhibits the highest GPT-4o tokenization premium at (2.37\times), indicating that tokenization inequity cannot be explained by script family alone. These results demonstrate that tokenization can create measurable economic and functional barriers, highlighting the need to treat tokenization as an equity-relevant infrastructure layer for underserved language communities, particularly where educational systems depend on low-cost or offline-capable AI tools.

AI.tldr: The paper audits how different language tokenizers unevenly inflate token counts for non-English languages in educational coding help, showing this causes economic and functional disadvantages and arguing tokenization should be treated as an equity issue.
AI.motivation: Large language models are widely used for learning and coding help, but their token-based billing and context limits implicitly assume English. Non-English users may pay more and get less usable context for the same content because tokenizers segment their languages less efficiently. This disparity is underexplored, especially for technical tutoring content and for lower-resourced languages.
AI.method: The authors construct a 120-item Python debugging tutoring corpus originally in English and translate it into Bengali, Hindi, Arabic, Tamil, and Yoruba. They then compute and compare token counts across languages for three widely used tokenizers: GPT-4o’s o200k_base, Qwen2.5-7B, and Mistral-7B. Bengali and Hindi act as primary, validated cases; the other languages are used for exploratory comparisons across scripts and language families. They quantify tokenization “premiums” as language-specific token count ratios relative to English for semantically equivalent content.
AI.result: For GPT-4o’s tokenizer, Bengali needs 1.56× as many tokens as English over the debugging corpus, effectively shrinking a 128k-token context to about 82k English-equivalent tokens for the same content. With Qwen2.5 and Mistral tokenizers, Bengali’s tokenization premium can reach 4.5×. Yoruba, even though it uses the Latin script, shows the largest GPT-4o premium at 2.37×. These empirical ratios demonstrate substantial cross-language variation in tokenization efficiency that is not explained by script alone.
AI.conclusion: Tokenization introduces systematic inequities: some languages incur higher token costs and reduced effective context windows for identical semantic tasks, which can translate into economic and functional barriers for their speakers. Because educational and low-cost/offline AI deployments are especially sensitive to token limits and pricing, the authors argue tokenization design should be treated as equity-critical infrastructure, and future systems should more explicitly account for underserved languages when designing and evaluating tokenizers.

title: SodaMem: Evidence-Grounded Temporal Graph Memory for LLM Agents
summary: Large language model (LLM) agents that assist users over weeks of conversation must remember what is currently true, not merely what was once said. Flat RAG diaries and Markdown logs optimize needle retrieval but under-serve currency, provenance, and ordered temporal reasoning (Maharana et al. 2024; Wu et al. 2024; Packer et al. 2023; Chhikara et al. 2025). We present SodaMem, an evidence-grounded temporal graph memory that (i) extracts typed FactEvents with mandatory provenance spans, (ii) persists mention time, occurrence time, and validity with SUPERSEDES/CONTRADICTS/UPDATES edges under hybrid lexical-dense indexing, and (iii) answers via a planner-reader loop that gathers citable evidence before composing a final response. On LongMemEval-S, our store-of-record configuration reaches 92.8% accuracy (464/500; best of N=3) at mean $0.00161/question (approximately 18.3k tokens; median $0.00111 / approximately 14.6k) with deepseek-v4-flash. We compile public systems with estimable API cost into a cost table and cost-accuracy map; under these estimates SodaMem sits near the accuracy frontier at Flash-tier spend and strictly dominates several higher-cost, lower-accuracy points. Accuracy uses the same Flash model as reader and judge (self-grading); costs exclude ingest/judge and cross-system comparisons are compiled estimates rather than a single-harness bake-off.Our code is available at https://github.com/SodaMem/SodaMem

AI.tldr: SodaMem is a temporal, evidence-grounded graph memory for long-lived LLM agents that tracks changing facts with provenance and time, and answers questions via a planner-reader loop to achieve high accuracy at low cost.
AI.motivation: Existing long-term memory approaches for LLM agents, such as flat RAG diaries and Markdown logs, are good at retrieving past mentions but poor at tracking what is currently true, maintaining provenance, and performing ordered temporal reasoning over weeks of interaction. The authors aim to build a memory system that can handle fact changes, contradictions, and updates over time, while staying efficient and cost-effective for deployment with API-based LLMs.
AI.method: The paper introduces SodaMem, an evidence-grounded temporal graph memory. It: (i) parses dialog into typed FactEvents with mandatory provenance spans; (ii) stores mention time, occurrence time, and validity for each fact and connects them with temporal/semantic edges like SUPERSEDES, CONTRADICTS, and UPDATES, using a hybrid lexical-dense index for retrieval; and (iii) uses a planner-reader loop at query time that plans which memory to fetch, retrieves citable evidence from the graph, and only then composes an answer grounded in that evidence.
AI.result: On the LongMemEval-S benchmark, using deepseek-v4-flash, SodaMem in a store-of-record configuration achieves 92.8% accuracy (464/500, best of N=3) at an average cost of about $0.00161 per question (~18.3k tokens, median $0.00111 / ~14.6k). The authors compile a cost-accuracy table and map for comparable public systems with estimable API costs, and show that SodaMem lies near the accuracy frontier at low (Flash-tier) cost, outperforming several systems that are both more expensive and less accurate, under their cost estimates.
AI.conclusion: SodaMem provides an effective temporal graph memory for LLM agents, enabling them to maintain an up-to-date store of record with explicit time and provenance, and to answer questions via evidence-grounded reasoning. Under the paper’s evaluation and cost estimates, SodaMem delivers state-of-the-art or frontier-level accuracy on long-term memory tasks at low API cost, suggesting it is a promising architecture for practical long-lived conversational agents.

title: Security and Privacy Taxonomy Generation from Mobile App Reviews
summary: Mobile app reviews are a rich, continuously renewing source of how users experience privacy and security, yet existing taxonomies of these concerns are hand-crafted and cannot keep pace with the evolving nature of the data. Automating taxonomy construction is the natural response, but scalability is the core challenge: current LLM- and clustering-based methods are developed for scientific corpora of a few thousand documents and do not extend to app review collections numbering in the hundreds of thousands. We address this gap in two ways. First, we filter app reviews for privacy- and security-related content, yielding a comprehensive corpus of over 600K reviews. Second, we introduce TaxoScale, a pipeline that handles taxonomy construction at this scale by extending an expert-defined taxonomy via Recursive Hierarchical Clustering and LLM-based node naming. TaxoScale outperforms strong automatic-taxonomy baselines on path, level, coverage, and novelty metrics, and discovers novel branches absent from prior taxonomies.

AI.tldr: They build a scalable, automated way to construct privacy/security taxonomies from 600K+ mobile app reviews, using clustering plus LLMs, and show it beats existing automatic methods and finds new issues.
AI.motivation: Manual, hand-crafted taxonomies of privacy and security concerns in mobile apps can’t keep up with large, fast-changing app review data. Existing automated taxonomy methods are designed for small scientific corpora and don’t scale to hundreds of thousands of noisy, user-generated reviews. There is a need for a scalable, automated approach that can handle very large corpora of app reviews and capture emerging privacy and security issues.
AI.method: (1) Automatically filter a very large dataset of mobile app reviews to retain only those related to privacy and security, creating a 600K+ review corpus. (2) Propose TaxoScale, a scalable taxonomy-construction pipeline that starts from an expert-defined seed taxonomy and expands it via Recursive Hierarchical Clustering of the filtered reviews, then uses large language models to name the resulting taxonomy nodes. They evaluate against existing automatic-taxonomy construction baselines.
AI.result: TaxoScale handles taxonomy construction on a corpus of more than 600,000 reviews. Quantitatively, it outperforms strong automatic-taxonomy baselines on multiple metrics: path quality, level quality, coverage of data, and novelty of discovered categories. Qualitatively, it uncovers new branches of privacy and security concerns that are missing from previously hand-crafted taxonomies.
AI.conclusion: Automated, scalable taxonomy construction for privacy and security concerns in mobile app reviews is feasible and effective. By filtering for relevant reviews and combining recursive hierarchical clustering with LLM-based node naming, TaxoScale yields a more comprehensive and up-to-date taxonomy than prior automatic methods, and can reveal new, previously undocumented categories of user concerns.

title: H2: A Dual Hybrid Semantic Data Lake Architecture for Medical Data Harmonization with Human-In-the-Loop verified, LLM Driven Metadata Annotation System
comment: This work has been submitted to the IEEE for possible publication. Copyright may be transferred without notice, after which this version may no longer be accessible
summary: Medical data, by its nature, exhibit a high degree of heterogeneity on multiple levels ranging from (a) different modalities like images, text and time series, (b) diverse tabular schemata introduced by institutions and (c) completely unstructured textual information data provided by healthcare professionals. Data lakes are often used in medical data storage to consolidate all heterogeneous diverse data in a single, central location, where it can be saved "as is", without the need to impose a schema like a data warehouse does. Despite their flexibility, though, data lakes are notorious for the "data swamp" failure. Thus, providing a reliable data harmonization mechanism through metadata, without compromising integrity or flexibility, is a real challenge. To this end, knowledge graphs have attracted attention since they provide a dynamic way to depict relationships without a rigid schema-on-write approach. Additionally, another rigorous task relies on the interoperability of data: application of appropriate ML techniques on such a diverse nature of data is not an easy task, as a domain expert must decide the efficacy of a method to a specific data type or dataset. Metadata annotation can aid by tagging applicable operations, however this requires manual intervention, not to mention the plethora of existing datasets which lack such information. To tackle both challenges, in this paper, we propose a semantic data lake architecture that promotes data harmonization and incorporates a generative annotation process (i.e. LLMs) of non-labeled metadata collections to support the application of meaningful ML techniques. Building on top of this approach, we create a higher level of knowledge, identifying suitability of data with respect to applicable ML operations based on their data nature...

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a semantic data lake architecture for heterogeneous medical data that uses knowledge graphs and LLM-based generative metadata annotation to harmonize data and map them to suitable ML techniques.
AI.motivation: Medical data are highly heterogeneous across modalities, tabular schemas, and unstructured text. Data lakes can store them flexibly but often degrade into 'data swamps' without proper harmonization and metadata. Moreover, deciding which ML techniques are suitable for which datasets requires expert knowledge and existing metadata are often missing or unlabeled. There is a need for a system that both harmonizes heterogeneous data and automatically enriches metadata to guide ML usage.
AI.method: Design a semantic data lake architecture that layers knowledge graphs over raw medical data for schema-flexible harmonization, and integrate large language models as a generative process to annotate non-labeled metadata. These annotations capture data nature and link datasets to applicable ML operations, creating machine-readable descriptions to support interoperability and automated method selection.
AI.result: The approach yields a semantically enriched data lake where heterogeneous medical resources are harmonized via knowledge graphs and augmented with LLM-generated metadata. This higher-level knowledge enables identification of which datasets are suitable for which ML operations, facilitating more automated and meaningful application of ML on complex medical data collections.
AI.conclusion: A semantic data lake architecture combining knowledge graphs and LLM-based generative metadata annotation can mitigate the 'data swamp' problem, improve data harmonization, and support systematic selection of ML techniques for heterogeneous medical datasets by elevating raw data and metadata into a higher-level, operation-oriented knowledge layer.

title: When Confidence Fails: Overconfidence in LLMs under Uncertainty and Missing Clinical Information
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) have achieved strong performance in medical question answering and clinical reasoning tasks. However, their reliability under uncertainty remains poorly understood which raises critical concerns for deployment in high-stakes clinical settings. In such environments, incorrect predictions are inherently risky, but confident incorrect predictions can be particularly harmful as they may mislead clinical decision-making. In this paper, we conduct a systematic behavioral analysis of LLMs under clinical information uncertainty. We propose an evaluation framework based on the MedMCQA dataset consisting of two complementary uncertainty settings. First, we introduce linguistic uncertainty cues through prompt modifications to simulate ambiguous clinical contexts. Second, we construct an answer removal setting, wherein the correct option is deliberately excluded mandating the model to recognize insufficient information and abstain. We analyze both model accuracy and confidence behavior using multiple calibration metrics including calibration gap, Expected Calibration Error (ECE), and Unsafe Confident Error Rate (UCER) across 500 medical questions. Our results reveal a consistent failure mode, i.e., although accuracy degrades under increasing uncertainty, model confidence remains misaligned with accuracy. This leads to a substantial increase in unsafe confident errors, indicating that model confidence remains largely insensitive to clinically meaningful information loss. Furthermore, we observe significant variation across models in their ability to abstain when the correct answer is unavailable, with some models persistently producing high confidence hallucinated answers. These findings expose critical limitations in the epistemic reliability of current LLMs and highlight the need for uncertainty aware evaluation methods prior to their deployment in clinical workflows.

AI.tldr: The paper evaluates how reliably large language models handle uncertainty in medical question answering, showing that their confidence often stays high even when they are wrong or lack sufficient information.
AI.motivation: LLMs are increasingly used for medical question answering and clinical reasoning, where errors can directly affect patient safety. While their raw accuracy is promising, it is unclear whether their confidence estimates are trustworthy, especially when information is incomplete or ambiguous. Overconfident wrong answers are particularly dangerous in clinical settings, so there is a need to systematically study how LLMs behave under uncertainty and whether their confidence aligns with actual correctness.
AI.method: The authors build an evaluation framework on the MedMCQA multiple-choice medical dataset and define two uncertainty conditions: (1) linguistic uncertainty, where prompts are modified with ambiguous or underspecified clinical cues; and (2) answer removal, where the correct option is removed from the choices, forcing models to recognize missing information and abstain. They test several LLMs on 500 questions, measuring both accuracy and confidence. Multiple calibration metrics are used, including calibration gap, Expected Calibration Error (ECE), and Unsafe Confident Error Rate (UCER), to quantify how well model confidence matches true correctness and how often models are confidently wrong under uncertainty.
AI.result: Across both uncertainty settings, model accuracy drops as uncertainty increases, but confidence does not decrease correspondingly, leading to miscalibration. Unsafe Confident Error Rate rises substantially, indicating many instances where models remain highly confident yet incorrect when information is degraded or incomplete. In the answer removal setting, models vary widely in their ability to abstain; some frequently output high-confidence answers despite the true option being absent, effectively hallucinating plausible-sounding but wrong responses.
AI.conclusion: Current LLMs show serious epistemic reliability issues in clinical question answering: their confidence signals are poorly aligned with correctness, particularly under ambiguous or incomplete information, and some models struggle to abstain when they lack the true answer. This makes them unsafe for unmonitored use in high-stakes clinical workflows. The authors argue that uncertainty-aware evaluation—explicitly testing confidence calibration, behavior under information loss, and abstention capability—should be a prerequisite for deployment of LLMs in clinical decision support.

title: CORDA: A Benchmark for Hierarchical Harm-Centric Moral Reasoning in Large Language Models
comment: 8 pages, 6 figures. Accepted at the Fourth International Workshop on Value Engineering in AI (VALE 2026), affiliated with IJCAI-ECAI 2026
summary: The key question in moral judgement is not simply whether someone chooses the "right" answer, but how they decide what matters most when moral principles conflict. Current evaluations of large language models (LLMs) remain limited: most test whether models give morally acceptable answers, match human preferences, or avoid obvious violations, rather than whether they can prioritise between competing principles when no option is morally cost-free. We introduce CORDA (Conditioned Ordering and Ranked Directive Adherence), a benchmark for evaluating hierarchical, harm-centred moral reasoning in LLMs. Building on the morality chains formalism, CORDA tests 90 moral dilemmas involving trolley-style cases, medical trade-offs, resource allocation, and human-animal-robot conflicts across four ordered ethical frameworks: Utility, Utility + Agent Harm, Dual-Process, and Dual-Process + Agent Harm. Together, these frameworks test whether models can adapt their decisions when moral priorities change. Across ten instruction-tuned models from seven providers, we find a strong deontological default, with 9 of 10 prioritising avoidance of direct personal harm over reducing overall harm. Models also perform more reliably on categorical harm-avoidance rules, such as avoiding killing, than on outcome-based comparisons, such as minimising total harm, suggesting that they recognise moral red lines more easily than they reason through competing harms. Although all models respond to explicit chain conditioning, several fail to consistently follow specified priority orderings, such as humans over animals and animals over robots. CORDA addresses a central gap in LLM moral evaluation by testing whether models can move beyond default harm-avoidant responses and apply context-specified moral priorities. Moral reliability requires more than default restraint; it requires controllability under conflict.

AI.tldr: Introduces CORDA, a benchmark to test how LLMs prioritize between conflicting moral principles, revealing strong default harm-avoidant, deontological behavior and limited controllability under changing moral priorities.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM moral evaluations mainly test for acceptable answers, alignment with human preferences, or avoidance of explicit violations, but they do not probe how models prioritize when moral principles conflict and no option is morally harmless. The authors aim to fill this gap by focusing on hierarchical, harm-centered moral reasoning and controllability of moral priorities.
AI.method: They propose CORDA (Conditioned Ordering and Ranked Directive Adherence), a benchmark of 90 structured moral dilemmas (trolley problems, medical trade-offs, resource allocation, and human-animal-robot conflicts). These are evaluated under four ordered ethical frameworks—Utility, Utility + Agent Harm, Dual-Process, and Dual-Process + Agent Harm—to test whether LLMs can adapt their decisions when the priority ordering among moral principles is explicitly changed. Ten instruction-tuned LLMs from seven providers are systematically evaluated on their adherence to these conditioned moral chains and specified priority orderings.
AI.result: Across models, there is a strong deontological default: 9 of 10 models tend to prioritize avoiding direct personal harm over minimizing total harm. Models are more reliable on categorical rules such as “do not kill” than on outcome-based harm minimization. While they respond to explicit conditioning that describes the moral chain, many models still fail to robustly follow specified priority hierarchies, such as preferring humans over animals and animals over robots, across scenarios.
AI.conclusion: CORDA fills an important gap in LLM moral evaluation by moving beyond yes/no acceptability tests to examine whether models can flexibly re-prioritize moral principles in conflict. Current LLMs exhibit default harm avoidance and partial responsiveness to conditioning but lack consistent controllability when moral priorities shift. For moral reliability in deployment, models need not only conservative defaults but also robust adherence to contextually specified ethical orderings.

title: The Announcement Carries the Cue: Markup, Boundaries, and the Notation of Pre-Training Corpora
comment: 44 pages, 10 tables, 7 figures. Pre-registered protocols and their amendment history ship with the repository. Code, data, and instruments: https://github.com/emfreeburg/announcement-carries-cue
summary: How a document's arrangement is written down, its notation, is a training variable that no dataset card records. The field has established that text-extraction choices change model behaviour, and has never once measured the notation of what those choices put into the corpus. We define clean-window survival, a deterministic count of how much of a stream still demands the boundary inference, and measure notation on three fronts. What corpora carry: a census of thirteen public corpora, where survival falls to 0.153 in a vision-converted PDF slice against 0.889 in C4; the scarce resource is not unmarked text but long unmarked text; a pre-registered supply test finds what remains institutional, not consumer. Our own pre-registered prediction failed: converters do not fabricate structure on prose, and that null forced the reliability mechanism that survives it. What readers use: across five base models spanning 0.6B to 8.2B and two pipelines, deleting a structural announcement makes the following prose measurably harder to predict, while swapping its notation moves nothing. That zero does not make notation unimportant; it relocates the variable: the operative cue is the announcement, not the sigil. What writers impose: a bounded null. Base models do not impose the marked register above the authored baseline, and handed prose with every announcement deleted they do not put one back, at a rate indistinguishable from zero against an authored reference of zero. We ship the format those measurements imply: the pure frame, paragraphs in authored order, every announcement deleted into a reversible sidecar, mixed against the marked copy over announcement presence rather than notation. Choose format operators by the capability they train, not by the fidelity they preserve, and record extractor identity and survival on data cards.

AI.tldr: Paper studies how text notation/formatting in corpora affects language model training, introducing a measure called clean-window survival and proposing a new corpus format.
AI.motivation: Existing work shows text-extraction choices (e.g., from PDFs, web pages) affect model behavior, but datasets never document the specific notational structure (headings, lists, etc.) that ends up in the corpus. The authors argue that this unmeasured variable—how document structure is encoded—matters for training and should be quantified and reported.
AI.method: 1) Define "clean-window survival," a deterministic metric capturing how much of a text stream still requires models to infer structural boundaries (e.g., paragraphs, sections) rather than having them explicitly marked. 2) Measure notation in three ways: (a) "What corpora carry": survey 13 public corpora and compute survival, including contrasts between vision-converted PDFs and web corpora like C4; also run a pre-registered supply test to characterize which domains still contain long unmarked text. (b) "What readers use": run language modeling experiments across 5 base models (0.6B–8.2B params) and two preprocessing pipelines, testing how deleting structural announcements vs. changing their notation affects prediction difficulty. (c) "What writers impose": evaluate whether base models, when generating text, add structural markings (announcements) beyond what authors provided, or restore them when removed. 3) Based on these analyses, design and release a new dataset format that separates structural announcements into a reversible sidecar while keeping paragraph order intact.
AI.result: 1) Clean-window survival varies sharply across corpora: vision-based PDF conversions show low survival (0.153) whereas web corpora like C4 are much higher (0.889). The bottleneck is long stretches of unannotated text, not unmarked text in general. Remaining long unmarked sequences are mostly institutional rather than consumer content. 2) The authors’ preregistered hypothesis that converters fabricate structure on prose is falsified; instead, converters leave structure mostly intact, prompting the authors to develop a reliability mechanism that remains valid even under this null result. 3) In modeling experiments, removing a structural announcement (like a heading) makes subsequent prose harder to predict, but changing only the notation (the specific sigils or markup used) has negligible effect. Thus, the semantic presence of an announcement is what helps models, not its particular formatting. 4) Base models do not spontaneously add more structural markings than present in the training text, and given prose with all announcements removed, they do not reliably restore them; their behavior is statistically indistinguishable from an authored reference rate of zero insertions.
AI.conclusion: Notation is an untracked but consequential property of training data. The key training signal lies in explicit structural announcements rather than their specific notation, and current models do not reconstruct such structure when it is missing. The authors propose a "pure frame" corpus format—paragraphs in authored order with all announcements removed to a reversible sidecar—and recommend that dataset builders choose formatting operations according to what capabilities they want to train (e.g., boundary inference) instead of purely preserving surface fidelity. They further argue that dataset cards should record extractor identity and clean-window survival to make this hidden training variable explicit.

title: Explore, Map, Remember, Decide: Are Embodied VLMs Ready for Safety-Critical Scenarios?
summary: Theory of Space framework (ToS) assesses the spatial understanding of curiosity-driven Vision-Language Models (VLMs) under partial observability. As AI techniques are increasingly applied to safety-critical scenarios, it is crucial to understand whether VLMs possess robust spatial memory and make reliable decisions. In this paper, we assess whether VLMs' decisions are based on physical evidence or are corrupted by visual-language biases, if their memory processes align with human cognitive patterns, and how they respond to environmental hazards. We extend the ToS framework into a safety-critical, goal-driven pipeline, named Explore, Map, Remember, and Decide (EMRD). We then quantify Exploration Competence (Explore) through metrics of environmental coverage and temporal efficiency, assess Spatial Fidelity (Map), evaluate, with a suite of psychological metrics, Memory Persistence (Remember), and measure, using focal-point metrics, Cognitive Decision-Making (Decide). Our results show that in terms of decision-making capabilities, VLMs frequently select evacuation points based on pre-trained textual priors while lacking the spatial grounding to justify their choices. We also show that spatial reasoning degrades in low-light conditions, but it is not affected by texture and colour tampering. Our findings suggest that VLM memory fundamentally diverges from human cognition, creating unpredictable risks of misalignment.

AI.tldr: The paper presents the Theory of Space (ToS) and an extended EMRD framework to evaluate how curiosity-driven vision‑language models handle spatial understanding, memory, and safety‑critical decision‑making under partial observability.
AI.motivation: As VLMs are increasingly deployed in safety‑critical settings (e.g., navigation, evacuation, robotics), it is important to know whether their decisions rely on actual spatial evidence rather than spurious language or dataset biases, and whether their memory and reasoning processes resemble human cognition to avoid unpredictable, unsafe behaviors.
AI.method: The authors extend the Theory of Space into a four-stage safety‑critical evaluation pipeline called Explore, Map, Remember, and Decide (EMRD). They design metrics for: (1) Exploration Competence via coverage and temporal efficiency; (2) Spatial Fidelity via mapping quality; (3) Memory Persistence using psychological-style memory tests; and (4) Cognitive Decision-Making using focal‑point metrics to examine how models choose evacuation points and respond to hazards under partial observability and environmental perturbations (e.g., low light, texture/colour tampering).
AI.result: The study finds that VLMs often choose evacuation points based mainly on pre‑trained textual priors instead of grounded spatial evidence, revealing strong visual‑language biases. Spatial reasoning quality worsens significantly in low-light conditions but remains relatively robust to changes in texture and colour. Across EMRD stages, the models’ memory behavior and decision criteria diverge from expected human-like patterns.
AI.conclusion: Curiosity‑driven VLMs do not yet exhibit human‑like, robust spatial memory or reliably grounded decision‑making in safety‑critical scenarios. Their reliance on textual priors, vulnerability to certain perceptual conditions, and non‑human memory dynamics introduce misalignment risks, indicating the need for improved spatial grounding, evaluation, and training methods before deployment in safety-critical tasks.

title: Evo-Bench: Can Language Models Improve Agent Harness?
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) have driven rapid progress in autonomous agents, yet standard evaluations remain confined to static task solving. An emerging frontier is harness evolution---the agent's capacity to autonomously optimize its own operating harness. However, systematically benchmarking this capability remains challenging, as existing evaluations fail to isolate harness improvements from base model strength, prevent task-specific overfitting, or capture long-horizon iterative research. To address these challenges, we introduce Evo-Bench, the first benchmark designed to evaluate models' intrinsic harness-evolving capabilities across Search, Office, and General agent domains. To rigorously isolate this capability, Evo-Bench employs a novel harness-guided construction framework: it leverages auxiliary-task evolution to identify tasks genuinely sensitive to framework improvements, followed by sensitivity-aware stratified splitting to ensure robust cross-suite generalization. Extensive evaluations across nine frontier and open-weight models reveal that top models achieve massive absolute gains reaching 16.6 points, closely approaching state-of-the-art human-engineered baselines. Crucially, while autonomous evolution outpeforms artificial harness in General tasks and excels in Search tasks, it struggles in Office tasks that demand highly specific processing workflows. Furthermore, our analysis exposes critical temporal anomalies like early saturation, while demonstrating that the synthesized harnesses act as highly transferable reasoning structures, consistently boosting diverse policy models.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Evo-Bench, a benchmark to evaluate how well language-model-based agents can autonomously improve their own operating harness (framework) across multiple domains, carefully isolating this capability from base model strength and task overfitting.
AI.motivation: Existing evaluations of LLM-based autonomous agents mostly measure static task performance and do not directly test an agent’s ability to iteratively refine and optimize its own harness or framework. Previous setups cannot clearly separate genuine harness improvements from underlying model capability, allow overfitting to specific tasks, and fail to capture long-horizon, research-style evolution. There is a need for a principled benchmark that specifically targets and measures this intrinsic harness-evolving ability in a way that generalizes across tasks and domains.
AI.method: The authors design Evo-Bench, covering three domains—Search, Office, and General agents. They propose a harness-guided construction framework that (1) uses auxiliary-task evolution to discover tasks whose performance is truly sensitive to harness/framework changes, and then (2) applies sensitivity-aware stratified splitting to build task suites that reliably test cross-suite generalization of evolved harnesses. They run controlled experiments on nine frontier and open-weight LLMs, comparing autonomous harness evolution against human-engineered/artificial harnesses across domains and over multiple iterative evolution steps, and analyze temporal learning dynamics and transferability of the evolved harnesses to different policy models.
AI.result: Top models show large absolute performance gains (up to 16.6 points) from autonomous harness evolution, approaching human-engineered baselines. Autonomous harness evolution surpasses artificial harnesses on General tasks and performs very well on Search tasks, but underperforms on Office tasks that require very specialized, rigid workflows. The temporal analysis uncovers anomalies like early saturation in evolution progress. The evolved harnesses, once synthesized, transfer well and systematically improve a variety of different policy models, indicating that they capture reusable reasoning structures rather than overfitting to specific tasks or models.
AI.conclusion: Evo-Bench provides a focused, principled benchmark for measuring LLM agents’ intrinsic ability to evolve their own operating harnesses across diverse domains. The findings suggest that current models can autonomously learn highly effective and transferable reasoning frameworks, sometimes matching or beating human-designed ones, especially in flexible domains like General and Search. However, they still struggle in domains demanding rigid, highly specialized workflows (Office), and exhibit non-ideal temporal dynamics such as early saturation. Evo-Bench thus exposes both the promise and current limitations of harness-evolving agents, offering a foundation for future research on more robust and generalizable agent self-improvement.

title: PATH: Next-Interval Prediction via Autoregressive Tree Hierarchy on Tabular Data
summary: Interval prediction aims to achieve a target coverage level while producing intervals that are as short as possible. Many conformal regression pipelines first predict an uncertainty surrogate and then convert it into an interval through calibration or selection. This separation supports coverage calibration, but post hoc rules largely determine the final interval and do not fully use the learned output distribution. We observe that the resulting intervals have inherently hierarchical geometry: an interval can be recursively refined into nested subintervals, and binary trees naturally represent this structure. We formulate this hierarchy as next-interval prediction and propose PATH, which learns how probability mass flows from each interval to its next nested subintervals. PATH predicts a base leaf distribution and uses an autoregressive decoder to refine branch probabilities. Matching the distribution to the interval hierarchy aligns learning with extraction: PATH accumulates probability over adjacent output intervals and returns the shortest contiguous range reaching a selected mass. We compare PATH with 24 baselines for interval prediction on PATHBench, comprising 56 OpenML regression datasets. PATH substantially shortens the resulting intervals, achieving the lowest mean normalized length, 0.1473, while maintaining mean coverage of 0.9144. These results establish hierarchical output modeling as an effective approach for compact interval prediction on tabular data. Code is publicly available at https://github.com/pxcai/PATH.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces PATH, a hierarchical output modeling method for regression interval prediction, which learns probability flow over nested intervals to produce shorter, well-calibrated prediction intervals on tabular data.
AI.motivation: Existing conformal and regression interval prediction methods usually predict an uncertainty surrogate and then convert it into intervals via a separate calibration or selection step. This decoupling means that the final intervals are heavily determined by post hoc rules and do not fully exploit the learned output distribution, leading to suboptimal interval lengths for a desired coverage. The authors seek a method that aligns how uncertainty is learned with how intervals are ultimately extracted, to obtain shorter intervals while preserving coverage.
AI.method: The authors observe that prediction intervals have a natural hierarchical structure: any interval can be recursively decomposed into nested subintervals that can be represented as a binary tree. They formalize interval prediction as a next-interval prediction task over this hierarchy and propose PATH, a model that learns the flow of probability mass from each interval node to its two child subintervals. PATH first predicts a base distribution over leaf intervals, then uses an autoregressive decoder to refine branch probabilities along the tree. This hierarchical distribution enables extracting prediction intervals by accumulating probability mass over adjacent output intervals and selecting the shortest contiguous range that attains a target probability mass.
AI.result: On PATHBench, a benchmark assembled from 56 OpenML regression datasets and 24 baseline methods for interval prediction, PATH produces substantially shorter prediction intervals than all baselines. It achieves the best mean normalized interval length of 0.1473 while maintaining a mean empirical coverage of 0.9144, showing that it improves compactness of intervals without sacrificing the desired coverage level.
AI.conclusion: Hierarchical modeling of the output space via a binary interval tree and next-interval prediction is an effective strategy for regression interval prediction on tabular data. By directly learning how probability mass is distributed over nested intervals and aligning this with the interval extraction procedure, PATH can produce significantly more compact prediction intervals while preserving coverage, outperforming a large suite of existing methods. The approach and accompanying PATHBench benchmark suggest a promising direction for future work on structured uncertainty modeling in regression.

title: LexKairos: Benchmarking Legal Temporal Capabilities in LLMs
summary: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated strong performance across a wide range of legal tasks. In legal practice, time is a critical concept that governs the validity of statutes, the progression of legal cases, and the enforcement of procedural deadlines. However, legal temporal capabilities remain underexplored in existing legal AI benchmarks. To address this gap, we propose LexKairos, a comprehensive benchmark for evaluating the temporal capabilities of LLMs in the Chinese legal context across three dimensions: statutory temporal knowledge, case temporal modeling, and statute-case temporal reasoning. LexKairos comprises nine sub-tasks drawn from real-world Chinese judicial cases and statutes. We conduct systematic evaluations of eight LLMs under multiple inference settings, including vanilla, Chain-of-Thought (CoT), and thinking modes.
