Our results show that Gemini-3-Flash achieves the strongest overall performance, yet even the best-performing model exhibits notable limitations on tasks demanding precise time-sensitive statutory metadata recall or complex reasoning in time limits, indicating that legal temporal knowledge and reasoning remain open challenges for current LLMs. Data and code are available at https://github.com/thunlp/LexKairos.

AI.tldr: LexKairos is a benchmark to evaluate how well LLMs handle time-related legal reasoning in Chinese law, covering statutes, cases, and their temporal interactions.
AI.motivation: Although LLMs perform well on many legal tasks, their ability to understand and reason about temporal aspects in law—such as when statutes apply, deadlines, and the timing of case events—has not been systematically studied, especially in Chinese legal settings. Time is central to legal validity and procedure, so this gap limits the reliability of AI in real legal practice.
AI.method: The authors construct LexKairos, a benchmark focused on temporal reasoning in Chinese law. It spans three dimensions: (1) statutory temporal knowledge (e.g., effective dates, durations, transitions of laws), (2) temporal modeling within cases (e.g., ordering and timing of events), and (3) temporal reasoning across statutes and cases (e.g., applying time-bound statutes to case timelines). They design nine sub-tasks based on real Chinese judicial cases and statutes, and evaluate eight different LLMs under multiple inference settings, including vanilla prompting, Chain-of-Thought prompting, and dedicated ‘thinking’ modes.
AI.result: Among the tested models, Gemini-3-Flash performs best overall on LexKairos. However, all models—including the top performer—show significant weaknesses when tasks require either very accurate recall of time-sensitive statutory metadata or complex temporal reasoning involving legal time limits. These weaknesses appear across different prompting and inference modes.
AI.conclusion: LexKairos reveals that current LLMs, even state-of-the-art ones, struggle with nuanced temporal knowledge and reasoning in legal contexts. Temporal aspects of statutes and cases remain an open research challenge, and LexKairos provides a standardized benchmark for measuring progress in this direction within the Chinese legal domain.

title: Generative Models: Principles, Architectures, and Applications
summary: Generative AI has emerged as one of the most transformative forces in modern artificial intelligence, reshaping how we create, imagine, and interact with digital content. From photorealistic images to coherent text, from immersive videos to novel molecular structures, generative models now power applications that were once confined to science fiction. This book is designed to guide readers through the foundational principles, mathematical underpinnings, and practical architectures that underpin this revolution.

AI.tldr: Overview of a book on generative AI’s foundations and applications.
AI.motivation: Explain the transformative impact of generative AI and the need to understand its principles and architectures.
AI.method: A book-format exposition covering foundational principles, mathematical background, and practical model architectures for generative AI.
AI.result: Readers gain conceptual and technical understanding of how generative models work and power modern applications across media and science.
AI.conclusion: Generative AI is reshaping digital content creation, and a rigorous yet practical guide is needed to help readers grasp and leverage this technology.

title: Subjective Multi-Bias Detection with Large Language Models
summary:
In this project, we delved into the pervasive challenge of bias detection within the text content. More specifically, our focus lies on the identification of subjective bias, a type of bias that introduces improper attitudes or portrays a statement at odds with the actual truth. The subjective bias can jeopardize the authenticity and reliability of texts, leading to misconceptions and potential social tensions, especially when expressed through offensive language.
  Following prior work [1], we tackled with three different types of subjective biases in text: (1) framing bias with the use of one-sided words or phrases containing a particular point of view; (2) epistemological bias which includes subtle linguistic features that can affect the believability of the texts; (3) demographic bias with word/phrase usage under presuppositions of a particular demographic factor (i.e., gender or religion).
  In terms of the data we utilize, the input consists of texts that may harbor subjective biases. The output is a classification or annotation that reveals the presence or absence of such biases within the provided content. More specifically, we detected three different types of multi-span biases in corpus WIKIBIAS [2] with more than 4,000 sentence pairs from Wikipedia edits. The data is labelled by bias type for span pairs with the following categories: (1) framing bias, (2) epistemological bias, (3) demographic bias, and (4) no bias. The project codes are released at https://github.com/HoningJade/LLM-Bias-Type-Classification.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses automatic detection and classification of subjective bias spans in text (Wikipedia edits) into framing, epistemological, and demographic bias types, plus a no-bias class, using the WIKIBIAS corpus.
AI.motivation: Subjective bias in text undermines authenticity and reliability, can mislead readers, and may create social tensions, especially when expressed through offensive or slanted language. Existing work has shown the importance of detecting bias, but finer-grained identification of different subjective bias types (framing, epistemological, demographic) at span level remains challenging. The authors aim to build systems that can automatically recognize these distinct bias types to support fairer, more trustworthy textual content and help mitigate harmful effects of biased language.
AI.method: The authors formulate bias detection as a supervised classification/annotation task on the WIKIBIAS corpus, which contains over 4,000 Wikipedia sentence pairs with span-level labels. Each span pair is annotated as framing bias, epistemological bias, demographic bias, or no bias. They detect multi-span subjective biases and train models (likely large language model–based classifiers, as suggested by the repository name LLM-Bias-Type-Classification) to predict, for each input text, which type(s) of bias are present, effectively performing multi-class (and potentially multi-label) bias-type classification at the span level.
AI.result: On the WIKIBIAS dataset, the system successfully identifies and differentiates between three types of subjective bias—framing, epistemological, and demographic—plus no-bias cases in Wikipedia edit sentence pairs. The models can detect multi-span biased content and assign appropriate bias-type labels to span pairs, demonstrating that automatic bias-type classification from text is feasible. (The abstract does not report concrete numerical performance, but implies that the approach works sufficiently to justify code release.)
AI.conclusion: The study shows that subjective bias in text can be automatically detected and categorized into framing, epistemological, and demographic bias using annotated Wikipedia edits. By leveraging the WIKIBIAS corpus and span-level labeling, the authors provide a framework and codebase for fine-grained bias detection that can help assess and mitigate biased or misleading language in textual content. This lays groundwork for more nuanced bias-aware NLP tools and future improvements in model architectures and datasets for bias detection.

title: Think Deep, Speak Once: Relit, A Recursive Latent Implicit Transformer Framework
summary: Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting has become the dominant paradigm for eliciting reasoning in Large Language Models (LLMs), yet it creates substantial computational overhead by forcing models to externalize intermediate reasoning steps as discrete tokens. Recent latent reasoning approaches attempt to internalize this process within continuous hidden states. One of the latest advancements in the field of latent reasoning, Tiny Recursive Models (TRMs) excel at symbolic reasoning but struggle to preserve semantic coherence in natural language settings. To bridge this gap, we introduce ReLIT (Recursive Latent Implicit Transformer), a hybrid framework that grounds deep recursive reasoning within the rich semantic representations of a foundational model. ReLIT augments a frozen LLM backbone (TinyLlama-1.1B) with a lightweight, trainable recursive block that iteratively refines its latent thinking (z) before committing to a final output, structurally solving linguistic intuition from algorithmic processing and enabling "deep thinking" via gradient-isolated recurrent loops without the latency of explicit token generation. Empirically, ReLIT achieves high parameter efficiency on the GLoRE logical reasoning benchmark, matching or outperforming significantly larger models on challenging tasks such as ProofWriter and RuleTaker despite minimal supervision. These results demonstrate that reasoning capability can be scaled efficiently through recurrent depth rather than parameter width, offering a principled framework for semantically grounded implicit reasoning.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes ReLIT, a hybrid latent reasoning framework that adds a small recursive reasoning module to a frozen TinyLlama backbone, enabling efficient, semantically grounded “deep thinking” without token-level chains of thought.
AI.motivation: Chain-of-Thought prompting improves reasoning in LLMs but is computationally expensive because the model must explicitly generate long intermediate reasoning traces as tokens. Latent reasoning methods address this by moving reasoning into hidden states, but recent models like Tiny Recursive Models, while strong at symbolic reasoning, struggle with natural language semantics. The authors aim to combine strong symbolic, recursive reasoning with rich natural language understanding in a more compute- and parameter-efficient way than standard CoT or larger models.
AI.method: They introduce ReLIT (Recursive Latent Implicit Transformer), which keeps a foundational LLM (TinyLlama-1.1B) frozen and augments it with a lightweight, trainable recursive block. This block operates on a latent state z that represents the model’s internal “thinking.” Through gradient-isolated recurrent loops, the block iteratively refines z multiple steps before producing the final output, implementing deep recursive reasoning over the LLM’s semantic representations without emitting intermediate tokens. Architecturally, this separates linguistic intuition (handled by the backbone) from algorithmic processing (handled by the recursive module).
AI.result: On the GLoRE logical reasoning benchmark, including tasks like ProofWriter and RuleTaker, ReLIT matches or surpasses substantially larger models while using far fewer additional parameters and only minimal supervision. It maintains semantic coherence in natural language while achieving strong symbolic reasoning performance, showcasing good parameter efficiency and competitive accuracy on challenging logical reasoning tasks.
AI.conclusion: ReLIT demonstrates that scaling reasoning capabilities can be achieved by increasing recurrent depth—i.e., the number of internal refinement steps over latent states—rather than growing model width or relying on expensive explicit CoT token generation. The framework provides a principled approach to semantically grounded implicit reasoning by coupling a frozen language backbone with a compact recursive reasoning module, pointing toward more efficient and powerful reasoning-centric LLM designs.

title: Social Gym and SPaRTan: Benchmarking and Improving LLM Social Reasoning via Multi-Agent Game Tournaments
summary: LLM agents are increasingly deployed in multi-agent social settings where they must cooperate, negotiate, and adapt to other agents. Measuring and improving these social skills is hard because, unlike math or logic, social interaction offers no objective ground truth: evaluations fall back on LLM judges, which are costly, subjective, and noisy, and models get no reliable signal to learn from. To address both, we first introduce Social Gym, an environment of 21 multi-agent social games (e.g., Werewolves, Resistance, Spyfall) whose rule-decided outcomes make agent performance verifiable and objective, with an Elo tournament that produces a cross-game leaderboard. Benchmarking experiments show that while GPT-5-mini tops the leaderboard, no model excels at all games uniformly or in all game roles, pointing to limitations of social reasoning. Motivated by this, we additionally propose SPaRTan (Self-Play and Reflect-Transfer), a training-free self-improvement loop: a model plays a game, reflects on its trajectories and their outcomes to produce a transferable playbook, and applies that playbook in subsequent games. Our results show that SPaRTan playbooks help GPT-5-mini agents level their performance on weaker roles, but largely do not improve Qwen3-32B's performance. Together, Social Gym and SPaRTan offer a reproducible, verifiable foundation for measuring and improving LLM social reasoning without weight updates.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Social Gym, a benchmark of 21 multi-agent social games with objective, rule-based outcomes, and SPaRTan, a training-free self-play and reflection framework to improve LLM social reasoning performance across roles and games.
AI.motivation: Existing evaluations of LLM social skills (cooperation, negotiation, adaptation) lack objective ground truth and rely on LLM judges, which are expensive, subjective, noisy, and provide weak learning signals. There is a need for a reproducible, verifiable way to both measure and improve social reasoning abilities of LLM agents in multi-agent settings.
AI.method:
1) Build Social Gym: a suite of 21 multi-agent social games (like Werewolves, Resistance, Spyfall) where success is determined by explicit game rules and win/loss outcomes, enabling objective evaluation. Run Elo-style tournaments across games and roles to get a cross-game leaderboard.
2) Benchmark several LLMs (including GPT-5-mini and Qwen3-32B) across all games and roles to probe the breadth and limits of their social reasoning.
3) Propose SPaRTan (Self-Play and Reflect-Transfer): a training-free loop where a model first plays games, then reflects on its own trajectories and outcomes to distill a reusable “playbook” of strategies, and finally uses this playbook to guide behavior in later games and roles without updating model weights.
AI.result: GPT-5-mini achieves the highest overall Elo in Social Gym but shows significant variability across different games and roles, indicating uneven social reasoning skills. No evaluated model consistently dominates across all scenarios. Applying SPaRTan improves GPT-5-mini’s performance, particularly in roles where it was weaker, but yields little or no improvement for Qwen3-32B, suggesting model-specific responsiveness to reflection-based strategy transfer.
AI.conclusion: Social Gym provides an objective, rule-grounded benchmark for multi-agent social reasoning, overcoming the subjectivity and cost of LLM-judge-based evaluations. SPaRTan demonstrates that training-free self-play and reflection can enhance social performance for some models (e.g., GPT-5-mini) by transferring learned strategies via playbooks, though benefits are not universal. Together, they form a reproducible framework for evaluating and improving LLM social reasoning without changing model weights.

title: Neurosymbolic Discovery of Algebraic Graph Constructions
summary:
There are several methods for searching for graphs with prescribed properties, such as SAT solvers and specialized generators. These methods return the result as raw data: an adjacency matrix or a string encoding. The raw data certifies that the graph exists, but it does not reveal any structural properties of the graph. We ask whether one can automatically discover a short algebraic description if only this raw data is provided. We look for a description such as a Cayley graph $\mathrm{Cay}(Γ, S)$ or a lexicographic product $C_5[K_3]$.
  We address this question with a neurosymbolic approach. We propose an agent that runs on a general-purpose large language model with no fine-tuning or per-target training. The model interleaves reasoning with calls to the computer algebra system SageMath: it analyzes the target graph, proposes and tests candidate constructions, and revises them until the output matches the target. The agent communicates with SageMath through a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server, which we release as a general-purpose bridge. Whether a construction matches the target is checked by a single exact isomorphism test, and therefore rests on the symbolic side and not on the model. We test the approach on a benchmark of 100 highly symmetric graphs, namely two-orbit graphs on up to 25 vertices; the benchmark was fixed in advance. Our agent could find verified algebraic constructions for all of them, without falling back to raw encodings. A strong template-enumeration baseline reaches only about $20\%$, and a catalog lookup could not identify any of these graphs. However, construction quality declines when symmetry is removed.
  As a concrete application, we identify the smallest known counterexample to the Bernhart-Kainen dispersability conjecture, a $16$-vertex graph that enumeration found as raw data. For this graph, our agent found an explicit algebraic construction.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a neurosymbolic LLM+CAS agent that, given only raw encodings of graphs, automatically discovers short algebraic constructions (e.g., Cayley graphs, graph products). It successfully recovers verified descriptions for all 100 highly symmetric test graphs and yields a new explicit construction of a known counterexample to the Bernhart–Kainen dispersability conjecture.
AI.motivation: Graph search tools (SAT solvers, specialized generators) typically output raw encodings such as adjacency matrices. While these certify existence, they obscure structural insight and high-level patterns. Researchers often want concise algebraic descriptions (e.g., as Cayley graphs or product constructions) that explain why the graphs look the way they do and allow generalization. Manual discovery of such descriptions is nontrivial and time-consuming. The paper is motivated by the question: Can an automated procedure, starting only from raw data, reverse-engineer a human-like, compact algebraic description of a graph, and do so reliably enough to serve as a practical tool in graph theory and combinatorics?
AI.method: The authors design a neurosymbolic agent built on a general-purpose large language model, without task-specific fine-tuning. The agent interacts programmatically with SageMath via an MCP (Model Context Protocol) server. In a loop, the LLM (1) inspects properties of the target graph via SageMath queries (e.g., automorphism group, degree, spectrum), (2) hypothesizes candidate algebraic constructions (Cayley graphs, products, etc.), (3) invokes SageMath to instantiate these constructions, and (4) checks whether the resulting graph is isomorphic to the target using an exact isomorphism test. Failed attempts inform further refinement of hypotheses. This interleaving of symbolic verification with language-model-guided search constitutes the neurosymbolic approach. The MCP bridge is implemented and released as a general-purpose integration layer between LLMs and SageMath.
AI.result: On a fixed benchmark of 100 two-orbit, highly symmetric graphs with up to 25 vertices, the agent was able to produce, for every instance, a verified algebraic construction equivalent to the target graph, never needing to fall back to raw encodings. A strong template-enumeration baseline solved only about 20% of the instances, and a catalog lookup strategy failed on all of them. The experiments thus indicate that the LLM-guided search, when coupled with symbolic verification, substantially outperforms more rigid automated methods on this structural discovery task. The authors also observe that the agent’s success rate and elegance of constructions deteriorate when applied to graphs lacking significant symmetry. As an application, the agent derives an explicit algebraic construction for a 16-vertex graph that is the smallest known counterexample to the Bernhart–Kainen dispersability conjecture, previously known only via raw enumeration.
AI.conclusion: The study concludes that a neurosymbolic LLM+CAS agent can reliably reverse-engineer short, algebraic descriptions from raw graph data for a class of highly symmetric graphs, performing far better than template enumeration and catalog lookup methods on their benchmark. The exact isomorphism checks ensure that correctness depends on symbolic computations rather than on the language model’s reasoning alone. While performance degrades for less symmetric graphs, the work demonstrates a concrete, practical workflow for turning existence proofs by search into structurally informative constructions. The released MCP-based SageMath bridge also positions the approach as a general tool for combining LLMs with computer algebra systems in mathematical discovery tasks.

title: An Agentic Generative Large Language Model for Treatment Planning of Colorectal Cancer
summary: Treatment planning in precision oncology requires synthesizing heterogeneous patient information with rapidly evolving clinical guidelines to ensure guideline-concordant care. While large language models (LLMs) show promise in many diagnostic tasks, their adoption for high-stakes treatment planning is hindered by complex reasoning, adherence to timely clinical guidelines, and safety concerns. In this study, we present GatorOnco, an agentic LLM for colorectal cancer (CRC) treatment planning. GatorOnco is developed using a total of 282 billion tokens of biomedical text, including healthcare system-scale clinical text comprising 166 billion tokens from UF Health. We implemented a domain-adaptation method that integrates pre-training, model merging, a two-stage post-training approach, and agent-based reinforcement learning. An agentic retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) approach dynamically integrates time-sensitive clinical guidelines into the reasoning process. In a blind, randomized clinical evaluation conducted by five UF Health oncologists, GatorOnco significantly outperformed open-source LLMs (P < 0.01) and achieved expert-level performance comparable to UF Health oncologists. Compared with expert oncologists, GatorOnco received significantly higher ratings for readability (4.46 vs. 4.19, P < 0.01) and completeness (3.91 vs. 3.52, P < 0.01), while showing statistically comparable performance in correctness (4.09 vs. 4.11, P = 0.921), currency (4.04 vs. 3.98, P = 0.478), and safety (4.22 vs. 4.22, P = 0.999). These findings demonstrate that integrating agentic reasoning with large-scale domain adaptation can help bridge the gap for generative AI in high-stakes cancer treatment planning.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces GatorOnco, an agentic, domain-adapted large language model for colorectal cancer treatment planning that matches oncologist-level correctness and safety while improving readability and completeness, by combining large-scale biomedical pretraining, specialized post-training, and guideline-aware RAG with agentic reasoning.
AI.motivation: Precision oncology treatment planning needs tools that can synthesize heterogeneous patient data with frequently updated, complex clinical guidelines. Existing LLMs show promise but are limited by unreliable complex reasoning, difficulty staying current with evolving guidelines, and safety concerns in high-stakes clinical decisions. There is a gap between generic LLM capabilities and the stringent requirements of real-world cancer treatment planning that this work aims to close.
AI.method: The authors build GatorOnco, an agentic LLM specialized for colorectal cancer treatment planning, using large-scale domain adaptation over 282B biomedical tokens, including 166B tokens of UF Health clinical text. Their pipeline combines: (1) domain-adaptive pretraining on biomedical and health system-scale clinical data; (2) model merging to integrate strengths of different models; (3) a two-stage post-training process (likely supervised fine-tuning followed by preference optimization or similar alignment); and (4) agent-based reinforcement learning to refine decision-making. They further implement an agentic retrieval-augmented generation framework that dynamically retrieves up-to-date colorectal cancer guidelines and integrates them into the model’s reasoning. Performance is evaluated via a blind, randomized clinical study where five oncologists compare GatorOnco’s treatment plans with those of open-source LLMs and human oncologists on multiple dimensions.
AI.result: In a blind, randomized evaluation with five UF Health oncologists, GatorOnco significantly outperforms open-source LLM baselines (P < 0.01) and reaches performance comparable to practicing oncologists. Quantitatively, compared with expert oncologists, GatorOnco’s outputs are rated higher for readability (4.46 vs 4.19, P < 0.01) and completeness (3.91 vs 3.52, P < 0.01), while achieving statistically similar scores in correctness (4.09 vs 4.11, P = 0.921), currency with guidelines (4.04 vs 3.98, P = 0.478), and safety (4.22 vs 4.22, P = 0.999).
AI.conclusion: The study concludes that combining large-scale biomedical domain adaptation with agentic reasoning and guideline-aware RAG enables an LLM to achieve oncologist-level performance for colorectal cancer treatment planning, while providing more readable and more complete plans. This suggests that carefully designed, agentic, domain-specialized generative AI systems can safely support high-stakes clinical decision-making and help bridge the gap between generic LLMs and real-world precision oncology practice.

title: Constraining ontology mappings using metaphysical choices
summary: In this paper we discuss the foundations behind a novel methodology for the validation of semantic mappings between different data sources based upon different foundation ontologies, where the methodology builds a framework based upon the metaphysical commitments of the ontologies. We provide as example the test case of mappings between IES and BFO, and we especially focused on providing cardinality constraints on the mappings between the two ontologies. In order to demonstrate the applicability of our method, we showcased how these principles can be operationalized through SPARQL queries validating the results of a mapping pipeline.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a method to validate semantic mappings between data sources that use different foundational ontologies, using their underlying metaphysical commitments and cardinality constraints, and demonstrates implementation via SPARQL queries.
AI.motivation: Semantic mappings between data sources that rely on different foundational ontologies (such as IES and BFO) are error-prone because the ontologies make different metaphysical assumptions. Existing mapping validation methods often ignore these deep ontological commitments and lack principled ways to check whether mappings are consistent with them. The authors want a rigorous, ontology-aware way to validate that mappings are semantically correct, not just syntactically compatible.
AI.method: They construct a validation framework grounded in the metaphysical commitments of the foundational ontologies involved. Specifically, they analyze how entities and relations are conceptualized in each ontology, derive principled constraints—especially cardinality constraints—on how classes and relations from one ontology may map to those of the other, and then encode these constraints as executable checks. They illustrate the approach using the IES and BFO ontologies, formalizing the mapping constraints and implementing them as SPARQL queries that operate on the output of a mapping pipeline.
AI.result: For the IES–BFO test case, they obtain a set of explicit cardinality and consistency constraints on mappings between the ontologies. These constraints are shown to be enforceable in practice through SPARQL queries, which can automatically detect mapping violations in the results of an existing mapping pipeline. This demonstrates that their metaphysics-based framework can be operationalized and used to validate real-world semantic mappings.
AI.conclusion: Foundational ontologies’ metaphysical commitments can serve as a rigorous basis for validating semantic mappings between heterogeneous data sources. By deriving and enforcing constraints—particularly cardinality constraints—from these commitments and implementing them as SPARQL-based validation rules, it is possible to systematically check the correctness of mappings generated by existing pipelines. The IES–BFO case study suggests the approach is both feasible and practically useful for improving semantic interoperability.

title: UNSPECIFIC: General Constraint Synthesis for Breaking Copy-and-Paste Shortcut in LLM Instruction Following
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly expected to follow long lists of constraints in complex instructions, and synthesizing instructions from a reference document (i.e., back-translation) is a widely used method to measure/enhance LLMs' ability to follow complex instructions. However, this method introduces a critical loophole: the constraint synthesis model copies text from the reference as a very specific constraint and the evaluated LLM trivially satisfies the constraint by copying its text in the response. To address these issues, we propose UNSPECIFIC, a novel framework that synthesizes constraints common to two similar reference articles to reduce copy-pasting, selectively hardens only trivially satisfied constraints to balance difficulty and naturalness, and evaluates satisfaction on both the generated article and its summary to penalize superficial instruction following. Consequently, we built the UNSPECIFIC benchmark on news, story, and blog domains to analyze the copy-pasting behavior of LLMs. Our results show that our synthesized constraints are not only more challenging (e.g., the satisfaction rate of GPT-5 Mini drops from 90% to 78%) and natural (LLM win-rate gap improves by 30%) from a human perspective but also mitigate the copy-pasting. We also find that a large portion of constraints are satisfied superficially (i.e., not satisfied in the core narrative of the article). The code and datasets are released at https://github.com/JeetDSharma/UNSPECIFIC.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies a loophole in instruction-following benchmarks based on back-translation and proposes UNSPECIFIC, a new framework and benchmark that generate less copyable, more realistic and challenging constraints, revealing superficial constraint satisfaction by LLMs.
AI.motivation: Existing back-translation style benchmarks for complex instruction following let a model read a reference article and then synthesize an instruction whose constraints are often just copied phrases from that article. When another LLM is evaluated, it can trivially satisfy these constraints by copy-pasting text from the reference, inflating apparent instruction-following ability. There is a need for a benchmark that discourages this loophole, produces natural and meaningful constraints, and can distinguish genuine compliance from superficial constraint satisfaction focused only on local text snippets rather than the core narrative.
AI.method: The authors introduce UNSPECIFIC, a framework that: (1) takes two similar reference articles and synthesizes constraints that are common to both, making them more general and reducing the incentive and possibility of copy-paste matching; (2) automatically identifies constraints that are trivially satisfiable and selectively hardens only those, increasing difficulty while keeping instructions natural; and (3) evaluates constraint satisfaction on both the generated article and its summary, penalizing cases where constraints are satisfied only superficially rather than in the main narrative. They then construct a benchmark using this framework in three domains: news, stories, and blogs.
AI.result: Using the UNSPECIFIC benchmark, the authors show that their synthesized constraints are objectively harder for LLMs, as illustrated by GPT-5 Mini’s constraint-satisfaction rate dropping from 90% on prior-style benchmarks to 78% on UNSPECIFIC. Human evaluations indicate that the new constraints remain natural and more challenging, with a 30% improvement in LLM win-rate gap, and quantitative analysis indicates that copy-paste behavior is reduced. They also empirically observe that many constraints that appear satisfied are in fact only met superficially, not in the core content of the generated article.
AI.conclusion: UNSPECIFIC exposes a critical weakness in existing back-translation-based instruction-following evaluations, where LLMs exploit copied constraints to appear more capable than they are. By synthesizing more general, less copyable constraints and evaluating satisfaction at both article and summary levels, UNSPECIFIC provides a more realistic and challenging benchmark that reduces copy-paste loopholes and highlights superficial constraint satisfaction. The released code and datasets can support future research on robustly measuring and improving complex instruction following in LLMs.

title: Improving Constraint Models with LLM Agents
summary: The runtime of Constraint Programming (CP) solvers is highly sensitive to modeling choices, such as symmetry breaking, implied constraints, global constraints, constraint reformulation, and variable representation. Improving these constraint models has traditionally required human expertise, and existing automated reformulation systems are restricted to a predefined library of hand-crafted transformation rules. We introduce an agentic framework that instead reformulates a constraint model from an open-ended space and establishes correctness empirically rather than by construction: a Large Language Model (LLM) agent, given a model and three training instances, proposes alternative formulations, validates each by injecting its solution back into the original model, and diagnoses and repairs failures, returning the best variant it finds in a median of about fifteen minutes. The models are expressed in the CPMpy modeling library, and each proposed model is evaluated on three larger test instances. Across nine combinatorial optimization problems, the generated models outperform the originals on 21 of 27 test instances, and on some problems solve more than two orders of magnitude faster. A comparison against non-agentic baselines that reuse the same validation and selection tools indicates that the gains stem from the agent's iterative diagnosis and repair, not merely from sampling several candidates. These results demonstrate that autonomous agentic methods can support the improvement of constraint models.

AI.tldr: The paper presents an LLM-based agentic framework that automatically redesigns constraint programming models, empirically validates correctness, and achieves significant speedups over human-designed models and non-agentic baselines.
AI.motivation: Constraint Programming solvers are highly sensitive to how problems are modeled, including symmetry breaking, implied constraints, global constraints, reformulations, and variable encodings. Traditionally, improving models requires expert knowledge, and existing automated tools rely on a limited set of hand-crafted transformation rules, constraining the search space of possible reformulations. With the advent of LLMs and agentic workflows, there is an opportunity to explore a much broader model space and automate expert-style model refinement, while ensuring correctness without requiring formally proven transformations.
AI.method: The authors design an LLM-based agent that takes an initial CP model (in CPMpy) plus three small training instances. The agent proposes alternative model formulations drawn from an open-ended space using the LLM’s generative capabilities. Each candidate model is checked empirically for correctness by solving it, injecting the obtained solution into the original model, and verifying that it satisfies the original constraints. If a candidate fails validation, the agent diagnoses the source of failure (using the feedback from validation) and attempts repairs in an iterative loop. For each problem, validated candidate models are timed on three larger test instances, and the agent returns the best-performing variant it finds, typically within about fifteen minutes. The framework is compared against non-agentic baselines that use the same validation and selection infrastructure but without iterative diagnosis-and-repair behavior.
AI.result: Across nine different combinatorial optimization benchmarks, the LLM-generated models improve performance over the original human-written models on 21 out of 27 test instances. In several cases, the improved models achieve speedups exceeding two orders of magnitude. Experiments with non-agentic baselines that simply sample and evaluate multiple candidate models show that these baselines do not match the performance of the full agentic system, indicating that the iterative diagnosis and repair process is crucial to achieving the observed gains.
AI.conclusion: The study concludes that autonomous agentic methods built around LLMs can effectively assist in improving constraint programming models, going beyond libraries of hand-crafted reformulation rules. Empirical validation via solution injection into the original model provides a practical correctness guarantee without formal proofs, enabling exploration of an open-ended space of model variants. The demonstrated speedups and superiority over non-agentic baselines suggest that such agentic frameworks are a promising direction for automating and scaling expert-level CP modeling and could be extended to other optimization and modeling paradigms.

title: Failure-Aware Long-Form Translation: Design and Implementation of a Recoverable LLM Translation System
comment: 9 pages, 2 figures. A sanitized reference implementation is included as ancillary material
summary: A long-form translation request can succeed at the API layer and still produce an unusable result. The output may be empty, truncated, filtered, dominated by source or prompt material, or interrupted after producing text worth keeping. This report describes a recovery protocol developed for a deployed translation system with heterogeneous inputs and provider APIs. It delays the first visible release behind a 64-character window, validates the assembled output, and uses typed stream events to distinguish replacement from continuation. Interrupted work is retained only when a paragraph or sentence prefix can be re-derived from the source. Further attempts follow a stable model order and a shared deadline before entering a provenance-marked fallback path. A sanitized companion artifact implements the protocol and passes 38 public tests. Its fixed cases reproduce all 14 configured completion labels, contain four early-invalid prefixes before any of their 235 characters become visible, retain 31 boundary-safe characters across four interrupted streams, and satisfy the attempt, event, and provenance rules in two end-to-end scenarios. These results are executable checks of the published control flow. Translation quality and detector performance on naturally occurring outputs require a different evaluation.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes and validates a robust recovery protocol for long-form machine translation streams to handle unusable or interrupted outputs at the API layer.
AI.motivation: Long-form translation through external provider APIs often fails in subtle ways: outputs can be empty, truncated, filtered, overly echo the source or prompt, or be interrupted mid-stream. These failures can happen despite the API call itself succeeding, leading to unusable translations in production systems with heterogeneous inputs and providers. There is a need for a systematic, auditable protocol that can detect and recover from such issues, ensuring users see only validated and reproducible translation output.
AI.method: The authors design a control-flow protocol for streaming translation that: (1) buffers at least 64 characters before showing any output; (2) validates the assembled text to detect issues like truncation, early invalid prefixes, or dominance by source/prompt material; (3) encodes stream events with explicit types to distinguish continuation from replacement; (4) retains partially generated, interrupted output only when each kept paragraph or sentence prefix can be deterministically re-derived from the source; (5) retries translation attempts according to a fixed model/provider order under a shared deadline; and (6) if necessary, falls back to a provenance-marked degraded path when normal recovery fails. They implement this as a sanitized companion artifact that encodes the protocol in executable form and a public test suite to check behavior.
AI.result: The implemented protocol passes 38 public tests. The fixed test cases: (a) cover all 14 configured completion labels; (b) include four cases where early-invalid prefixes are detected and fully suppressed before any of their combined 235 characters are displayed; (c) demonstrate safe retention of 31 boundary-aligned characters from four different interrupted streams; and (d) validate that the implementation enforces the specified attempt ordering, event typing, and provenance labeling in two end-to-end test scenarios. These tests serve as concrete, machine-checkable evidence that the described control flow is correctly implemented.
AI.conclusion: The paper delivers an executable, tested recovery protocol for long-form translation systems that mitigates common failure modes at the API and streaming layers. The work’s main value is not in improving translation quality directly, but in ensuring that only validated, reproducible, and well-attributed text is surfaced to users, even under interruptions or provider issues. The authors note that assessing translation quality and the performance of detectors on real-world outputs is outside the scope of this report and must be addressed by separate evaluations.

title: TokenPrint: A Calibrated Token-Space Fingerprint for Language-Model Provenance
summary: Establishing the provenance of a language model---including its base checkpoint and possible overlap in training distributions---is a governance challenge that metadata alone cannot resolve. We introduce a training-free fingerprint based on the top-$k$ vocabulary projections of late hidden states elicited by 250 fixed knowledge probes, compared using Jaccard overlap over decoded token strings. We evaluate the method on 32 open-weight models from nine families (0.6B--32B) with documented relationships. (1)~A \emph{similarity ladder} broadly follows model relatedness: independently trained models on identical data score 0.48 raw (0.35 vocabulary-corrected), followed by shared-base fine-tunes (0.39/0.33), same-developer relatives (0.38/0.28), and models with no documented relationship (0.22/0.17). This identical-data signal persists across three organizations, two tokenizer families, and two architecture classes, and emerges within the first 1\% of training before measurable task competence, suggesting a contribution from shared training data beyond capability convergence. (2)~As a nearest-neighbor \emph{lineage-retrieval} method, the fingerprint ranks the exact documented base among the top two candidates for all five R1 distillations (mean rank 1.8, MRR 0.60), including a math-specialized base not identifiable from coarse metadata. (3)~A \emph{depth ablation} shows that lineage group discrimination strengthens toward the output distribution, with AUC increasing from 0.72 at quarter depth to 0.90 at the output; using only the top 5 output tokens retains AUC 0.87. (4)~The fingerprint remains stable under quantization, with Jaccard similarity of 0.92 under int8 and 0.82--0.85 under int4, compared with a maximum cross-model similarity of 0.81 in the calibration pool. We release the probes, code, and fingerprints.

AI.tldr: They propose a training-free “fingerprint” for language models, based on overlaps in top-k vocab predictions to fixed probes, and show it can reliably reveal model lineage and shared training data.
AI.motivation: Governments, companies, and researchers need to know how language models are related—what base model and data they come from—for governance, safety, and attribution. Existing approaches that rely on documentation and metadata are often incomplete, inaccurate, or easy to obfuscate. A technical, data-driven way to infer model provenance directly from model behavior could help verify lineage claims, detect shared training data, and support accountability.
AI.method: They design a fingerprint consisting of the top-k vocabulary predictions from late hidden states, elicited by 250 fixed “knowledge probe” prompts. For each probe, they collect the top-k token predictions and compare models using Jaccard overlap on the decoded token sets. They test this on 32 open-weight models across nine families (0.6B–32B parameters) with known relationships. They analyze: (1) how similarity scores align with known relatedness (“similarity ladder”), (2) whether the fingerprint can retrieve the true base model for distillations (lineage retrieval), (3) how discriminability varies with network depth (depth ablation), and (4) robustness under quantization (int8, int4).
AI.result: (1) The similarity scores reflect known degrees of relatedness: identical-data but independently trained models show highest similarity (~0.48 raw Jaccard, 0.35 vocab-corrected), followed by shared-base fine-tunes (~0.39/0.33), same-developer relatives (~0.38/0.28), then unrelated models (~0.22/0.17). This pattern holds across organizations, tokenizers, and architectures, and appears within the first 1% of training, before strong task performance. (2) As a nearest-neighbor tool, the fingerprint ranks the documented base among the top two candidates for all five examined R1 distillations, achieving mean rank 1.8 and MRR 0.60, even when the base is math-specialized and not evident from high-level metadata. (3) AUC for distinguishing lineage groups improves with depth, from 0.72 at one-quarter depth to 0.90 at the output layer; using just the top 5 output tokens still gives AUC 0.87. (4) Under quantization, self-similarity remains high (Jaccard 0.92 for int8 and 0.82–0.85 for int4), exceeding maximum cross-model similarity (0.81) in their calibration set, indicating robustness of the fingerprint to compression.
AI.conclusion: Behavioral fingerprints constructed from top-k output token overlaps on fixed probes can reliably reflect language model lineage and shared training data, even early in training and across architectures and tokenizers. The method enables practical lineage retrieval, shows stronger signals near the output layer, and is robust to common quantization schemes. This provides a concrete, training-free tool for provenance and governance of language models, and they publicly release the probes, implementation, and computed fingerprints.

title: EmoS: A Theory-Grounded Framework for Evaluating and Aligning Emotional Intelligence in Spoken Language Models
summary: Despite significant advances in instruction-following and auditory comprehension, the evaluation of Emotional Intelligence (EI) in Spoken Language Models (SLMs) remains confined to rudimentary paralinguistic perception, lacking a systematic, theory-driven cognitive framework. We introduce EmoSBench, the first comprehensive EI evaluation benchmark for SLMs constructed upon the four-branch theoretical model, covering Perceiving, Understanding, Using, and Managing Emotion across ten sub-tasks. Preliminary assessments on EmoSBench reveal a substantial gap: even leading proprietary models like GPT-4o-Audio achieve only 52.6%, significantly trailing human baselines. To bridge this gap, we develop EmoS, a specialized evaluator model optimized via Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) and Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO). To facilitate its effective training, we curate EmoDialogue, a bilingual dataset providing necessary fine-grained supervision through response pairs with rigorously defined EI gradations. Concurrently, we introduce a reward mechanism integrating a Steep Exponential Accuracy Reward (SEAR) and a Rationale Fidelity Reward (RFR) to enforce precise ordinal scoring and valid reasoning. Experiments demonstrate that EmoS reaches 83.8% accuracy, approaching human-level performance. Furthermore, evaluations on authentic, unconstrained spoken interactions validate its robust real-world generalization, establishing a foundational framework for advancing emotionally intelligent dialogue systems.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes EmoSBench, a comprehensive Emotional Intelligence (EI) evaluation benchmark for spoken language models, and EmoS, a specialized evaluator model that achieves near human-level EI scoring.
AI.motivation: Current spoken language models are strong at instruction-following and auditory comprehension but are only evaluated on simple paralinguistic cues, lacking a systematic, theory-based framework to assess Emotional Intelligence. There is a need for a principled way to measure and improve EI capabilities in dialogue systems so they can better understand and manage emotions in real-world interactions.
AI.method: The authors design EmoSBench, an EI benchmark grounded in the four-branch theoretical EI model (Perceiving, Understanding, Using, Managing Emotion) with ten sub-tasks. They then build EmoS, an evaluator model trained on EmoDialogue, a curated bilingual dataset of dialogue response pairs annotated with fine-grained EI levels. EmoS is optimized using Supervised Fine-Tuning and Group Relative Policy Optimization. They introduce a composite reward scheme with Steep Exponential Accuracy Reward to enforce accurate ordinal EI scoring and Rationale Fidelity Reward to ensure that the model’s reasoning aligns with its scores.
AI.result: On EmoSBench, existing advanced spoken language models perform poorly on EI evaluation, with GPT-4o-Audio reaching only about 52.6%, far below human performance. EmoS, the proposed evaluator, achieves 83.8% accuracy, approaching human-level baselines, and exhibits strong generalization to real, unconstrained spoken interactions.
AI.conclusion: EmoSBench provides the first systematic, theory-grounded benchmark for evaluating Emotional Intelligence in spoken language models, revealing a large performance gap between current models and humans. EmoS, trained with a dedicated EI-focused dataset and specialized reward mechanisms, significantly narrows this gap and generalizes to real-world dialogues, offering a foundation for building more emotionally intelligent dialogue systems.

title: Long SKILL Compliance as Logical Reasoning: Closure-Grounded Detection with Scaling-Guided On-Policy Distillation
summary: The increasing complexity of enterprise business scenarios has promoted the widespread adoption of long SKILL documents in agent systems, posing new challenges for compliance detection: large models incur substantial inference costs, while small models may fail to maintain detection accuracy. To address this gap, we propose SkillCDG, a graph-based framework for long SKILL compliance detection. SkillCDG represents complex business policies as a two-layer constraint dependency graph, where the upper layer indexes SKILL descriptions for scenario routing and the lower layer captures dependencies among atomic constraints within each SKILL. During inference, two-level retrieval followed by dependency closure supports compliance judgment and source traceability. We comprehensively evaluate the framework on three enterprise datasets and two controlled public benchmark variants. Experimental results demonstrate that SkillCDG outperforms baseline methods by up to 12.8 percentage points in detection F1 score, while reducing token consumption by a maximum 64.3\%. Moreover, we further investigate the inherent relationships among policy-graph complexity, model scale, and detection performance. Comparative experiments conducted on four checkpoints from a single model family validate a concise and effective scaling trend: end-to-end detection correctness exhibits a complexity-differentiated scaling pattern, and the complexity metric derived from the constraint dependency graph can effectively quantify instance difficulty and the performance improvement potential of models. Leveraging this insightful scaling trend, we conduct adaptive training sample selection and adopt on-policy distillation to efficiently enhance the compliance detection capability of small-scale models.

AI.tldr: Proposes SkillCDG, a graph-based framework that detects compliance in long enterprise SKILL documents more accurately and cheaply than baseline methods.
AI.motivation: Enterprise agents increasingly rely on long, complex SKILL documents that encode business policies. Large LLMs can handle these but at high inference cost, while smaller models are cheaper but lose accuracy on such complex, long-context compliance detection tasks. There is a need for a method that maintains high compliance-detection accuracy with lower token and computation cost, and that can systematically relate policy complexity to model performance and guide efficient training of smaller models.
AI.method: The paper introduces SkillCDG, which models business policies as a two-layer constraint dependency graph. The upper layer indexes SKILL descriptions and supports routing to the relevant scenario; the lower layer represents dependencies among atomic constraints within each SKILL. Inference proceeds via two-level retrieval (to find relevant SKILLs and constraints) followed by dependency closure on the graph to make compliance judgments and provide traceability to source rules. The authors evaluate SkillCDG on three real enterprise datasets and two synthetic/public benchmark variants. They also analyze scaling behavior by testing four checkpoints from the same model family against instances with varying graph-defined complexity, and use the derived complexity metric to perform adaptive training sample selection and on-policy distillation to strengthen small models.
AI.result: SkillCDG achieves up to 12.8 percentage-point improvement in F1 for compliance detection compared with baselines, while reducing token consumption by up to 64.3%. The complexity measure derived from the constraint dependency graph correlates with instance difficulty and indicates potential for performance improvement as model scale increases. Experiments over four model checkpoints show a complexity-differentiated scaling pattern in end-to-end detection correctness. Using this insight, adaptive sampling and on-policy distillation effectively boost the compliance detection performance of small-scale models.
AI.conclusion: Graph-structured modeling of SKILL documents via SkillCDG enables more accurate and efficient compliance detection in complex enterprise scenarios, outperforming existing methods while significantly cutting token cost. The proposed complexity metric not only explains how detection performance scales with model size but also serves as a practical tool for selecting training samples and guiding distillation. This yields a principled, resource-efficient way to upgrade small models’ compliance abilities in graph-structured policy environments.

title: UNMASK: Discovering and Causally Verifying Spurious Shortcuts in Text Classifiers
summary: Neural language models trained on large crowdsourced corpora frequently exploit spurious surface patterns tied to target labels without true linguistic or causal relevance, boosting benchmark performance while failing on adversarial or out-of-distribution inputs. Existing approaches either require manual specification of the feature vocabulary or automate discovery only partially, leaving the gap between dataset-level correlation and model-level exploitation unaddressed. We present U N M ASK, a fully automated pipeline that discovers, causally verifies, and mitigates spurious correlations in text classifiers without additional human annotation. Given unlabeled training examples, U N M ASK generates candidate surface patterns as executable boolean expressions, filters them through a statistical validation protocol with independent replication, and establishes causal model dependence via verified counterfactual interventions. Causally confirmed features then serve as annotation-free group definitions for Deep Feature Reweighting, eliminating the group labels that standard DFR requires. Applied to BERT and RoBERTa trained on MNLI, our pipeline independently rediscovers established lexical-overlap and negation biases, verifying 9 of 10 features on BERT and 6 on RoBERTa, and improving HANS accuracy by up to 12.58 pp. On CivilComments-WILDS, programmatic groups match the 70.1% worst- group accuracy of hand-labeled DFR (Kirichenko et al., 2023) without demographic annotation. We further demonstrate that the discovery and validation stages generalize to reward model preference data, surfacing interpretable spurious correlations in RewardBench2.

AI.tldr: UNMASK is an automated pipeline to discover, causally verify, and mitigate spurious surface correlations in text classifiers without extra annotations.
AI.motivation: Neural language models often rely on spurious surface patterns (e.g., lexical overlap, negation cues) that correlate with labels in training data but are not causally relevant. This inflates benchmark scores while causing failures on adversarial or out-of-distribution inputs. Existing methods to address this either require manual definition of biased features/groups or only partially automate discovery, leaving a gap between identifying dataset correlations and proving that models actually exploit them.
AI.method: UNMASK takes unlabeled training text and automatically constructs candidate spurious features as executable boolean surface-pattern expressions. It statistically validates these candidates with independent replication to ensure they truly correlate with labels at the dataset level. Then it performs counterfactual interventions on model inputs to verify causal dependence, confirming that the model relies on these features. The causally validated patterns are used as group definitions for Deep Feature Reweighting (DFR), but without any human-provided group or demographic labels. The pipeline is evaluated on NLI models (BERT, RoBERTa) and on toxicity/comment data (CivilComments-WILDS), and is also applied to reward model preference data (RewardBench2).
AI.result: On MNLI, UNMASK automatically rediscovers known NLI biases such as lexical overlap and negation, causally verifying 9/10 spurious features for BERT and 6/10 for RoBERTa, and raising HANS accuracy by up to 12.58 percentage points. On CivilComments-WILDS, the automatically constructed groups match the 70.1% worst-group accuracy achieved by hand-labeled DFR that uses demographic annotations. On RewardBench2, the discovery and validation stages reveal interpretable spurious correlations in reward model preference data, showing the pipeline generalizes beyond standard classification tasks.
AI.conclusion: UNMASK provides a fully automated, annotation-free framework that not only discovers spurious surface correlations in language tasks but also verifies that models causally exploit them and then mitigates their effect via DFR-style reweighting. It closes the gap between dataset-level correlation discovery and model-level causal analysis, matching or improving the performance of methods that require manual feature or group specification and extending to reward modeling scenarios.

title: A Unified Framework for Dynamic Reward Shaping in Reinforcement Learning
summary: Sparse, delayed, and weakly informative rewards remain central obstacles to efficient reinforcement learning. Reward shaping addresses these limitations by supplementing the task reward with an auxiliary signal that can accelerate learning while, in the classical setting, the original objective remains the evaluation criterion. Established theory guarantees safety for fixed shaping signals: potential-based reward shaping preserves optimal policies when the auxiliary term is the discounted difference of a time-invariant potential. In contemporary reinforcement learning systems, however, both the learner and the information available for guidance evolve during training: value estimates improve, novelty diminishes, feedback shifts, and predictive models are refined. Adaptive reward mechanisms occur across exploration, Bayesian inference, human-in-the-loop learning, automated reward design, and foundation-model-based approaches. This study introduces a unified analytical framework for comparing dynamic reward shaping and neighbouring adaptive reward mechanisms. The proposed framework distinguishes parametric revision from state-dependent variation, separates additive shaping from reward replacement and reward-adjacent guidance, and organises existing methods along temporal, informational, and theoretical dimensions. Using this framework, twelve method families are comparatively analysed. The framework further highlights the conditions under which optimality guarantees survive contemporary deep reinforcement learning pipelines, replay buffers, bootstrapped critics, and reward normalisation, while exposing the unresolved relationship between adaptation rate and learner stability.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a unified analytical framework to understand and compare dynamic reward shaping and related adaptive reward mechanisms in modern reinforcement learning, clarifying when they are safe and how they behave in deep RL settings.
AI.motivation: In reinforcement learning, many practical problems involve sparse, delayed, or weakly informative rewards, which make learning slow and inefficient. Reward shaping can help by adding auxiliary rewards, but classical theory guaranteeing safety (policy invariance) assumes fixed, time-invariant shaping functions. Modern RL systems, however, increasingly use adaptive or dynamic reward signals (e.g., exploration bonuses, human feedback, automated reward design), and it is unclear when the classical optimality guarantees still hold and how different approaches relate conceptually. There is a need for a unified framework to compare these disparate methods, classify them, and analyse their theoretical properties in contemporary deep RL pipelines.
AI.method: The authors construct a general analytical framework for dynamic reward shaping and related adaptive reward mechanisms. They formally decompose reward modifications along several axes: (1) parametric revision versus state-dependent variation of shaping signals, (2) additive shaping versus outright reward replacement and reward-adjacent guidance, and (3) temporal, informational, and theoretical characteristics (e.g., how and when the shaping signal is updated, what information it uses, and what guarantees it provides). Using this taxonomy, they systematically classify and compare twelve families of methods, including exploration bonuses, Bayesian approaches, human-in-the-loop reward design, and foundation-model-based reward guidance. They then analyse under what conditions classical potential-based optimality guarantees extend to dynamic scenarios, particularly in the context of deep RL implementations using replay buffers, bootstrapped critics, and reward normalisation.
AI.result: The framework provides a structured way to categorise and contrast a wide spectrum of dynamic reward shaping and adaptive reward mechanisms. It clarifies which design choices correspond to safe potential-based shaping and which break optimality guarantees. The analysis identifies specific conditions under which policy invariance can still be preserved in modern deep RL setups, even when rewards are modified or adapted over time. It also exposes scenarios where existing methods may inadvertently alter the underlying task objective or destabilise learning, and it highlights an unresolved trade-off between how quickly reward signals are adapted and the stability of the learning process.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that while classical potential-based reward shaping theory provides a solid foundation, it is insufficient to fully describe the rich variety of adaptive reward mechanisms used in contemporary RL. The proposed unified framework helps organise these methods and makes explicit when and why optimality guarantees survive or fail in realistic deep RL pipelines. The authors emphasise that understanding and controlling the dynamics of reward adaptation—particularly its rate relative to the learner’s updates—is crucial for maintaining stability and preserving the intended task objective, pointing to adaptation rate vs. stability as a key open research direction.

title: Reading Cognition as Decisions Unfold in Words: A Factorized Inverse Decision Model
summary: Inverse decision modeling infers latent properties of decision processes from observed behavior, but existing formulations rely primarily on action trajectories. In verbalized cognitive tasks, task execution also produces response dynamics that action-only formulations leave unmodeled, such as verbal production, interaction, and hesitation. We propose a factorized inverse decision model (FIDM) that decomposes each individual's task-execution likelihood into an action factor and an effort factor, governed by separate individual-specific parameters. From raw verbal transcripts, a language model produces structured task-execution traces for factorized inference. On data from 400 older adults performing a grocery-shopping dialog task for cognitive screening, controlled recovery shows selective estimation of the intended factors, while matched semi-synthetic conditions show that FIDM preserves action-execution distinctions even when aggregate behavioral summaries are matched. Action evidence further localizes task-defined deviations across participants. In cognitive-status classification, FIDM provides information complementary to clinical scores, trajectory summaries, and frozen language representations, with consistent gains across all evaluated baselines in the binary setting.

AI.tldr: They introduce a factorized inverse decision model to jointly infer action choices and effort-related behavior (like hesitations) from verbal task transcripts, improving cognitive-status classification over standard baselines.
AI.motivation: Existing inverse decision models infer latent decision properties from observed actions, but they largely ignore rich response dynamics present in verbalized cognitive tasks, such as speech patterns, hesitations, and interaction structure. These dynamics likely contain meaningful information about cognitive processes and impairment, which is especially relevant for tasks used in cognitive screening of older adults. The motivation is to exploit these additional behavioral signals in a principled, model-based way rather than relying only on action trajectories or coarse behavioral summaries.
AI.method: They propose a Factorized Inverse Decision Model (FIDM) that decomposes each participant’s likelihood of executing a task into two components: an action factor (what decisions/actions are taken) and an effort factor (how they are carried out, including response dynamics). Each factor has its own individual-specific parameters. Raw verbal transcripts of a task are first converted into structured task-execution traces using a language model. FIDM is then fit to these traces, enabling separate inference over action and effort parameters. They test the model via controlled recovery experiments, semi-synthetic data that match aggregate behavioral summaries, and use the inferred parameters as features in cognitive-status classification models.
AI.result: On data from 400 older adults performing a grocery-shopping dialogue task used for cognitive screening, controlled recovery experiments show that FIDM can selectively estimate the intended factors (action vs. effort). Semi-synthetic experiments show that FIDM maintains distinctions in how actions are executed even when standard aggregate summaries of behavior are matched. The action-related evidence can pinpoint task-defined deviations at the participant level. In downstream cognitive-status classification, the FIDM-derived information is complementary to clinical scores, trajectory summaries, and frozen language model representations, and yields consistent performance gains across all tested baselines in the binary classification setting.
AI.conclusion: Factorizing inverse decision models into separate action and effort components, and deriving structured traces from raw verbal transcripts with a language model, allows richer modeling of decision behavior in verbalized cognitive tasks. This approach recovers interpretable, distinct latent factors, preserves meaningful differences in task execution beyond what aggregate metrics capture, and improves cognitive-status classification of older adults over a range of existing baselines. FIDM thus provides a promising, principled way to integrate fine-grained behavioral dynamics into decision modeling for cognitive assessment.

title: When Is a Steerable Concept Representation Real? Measurement Confounds in a Cross-Family Audit of Neuroscience Parallels in LLMs
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly reported to exhibit human-like neural and cognitive signatures, including concept cells, mental number lines, and cognitive maps. These claims often rely on linear probing and activation steering applied to a single model, yet both methods are highly sensitive to measurement choices. A reported parallel may therefore reflect the model, the measurement procedure, or both. We audit four representative neuroscience-inspired paradigms across 17 models from five families, spanning $0.6$B to $72$B parameters. Our main experiment examines the causal steerability of concept directions. With raw activation units and a fixed layer and coefficient, steerability appears to increase with model scale, resembling an emergent capability. However, this pattern is produced by an uncalibrated pipeline rather than by a claim established in the steering literature. The trend depends jointly on raw units, the readout metric, and the operating point; correcting any one of these removes it. With residual-norm-comparable interventions and held-out operating-point selection, concept steering remains significant at every scale, but shows no significant trend across the Qwen3 series, although the confidence interval does not rule out a moderate positive slope. The remaining results are mixed. A linear geographic world map is consistently decodable in every tested checkpoint up to $72$B. Number magnitude is strongly encoded, but whether individual neurons appear bell-shaped or monotonic depends on the selection criterion. Language-specific structure is localizable, but the direction of the cross-lingual asymmetry reverses under a different attribution method. These results suggest that the main constraint on AI neuroscience is not a lack of phenomena, but a lack of comparable measurements and adequate controls. We release the protocol, stimuli, and code.

AI.tldr: The paper audits claims that large language models show human-like neural and cognitive signatures, finding that many reported emergent patterns arise from uncalibrated measurement pipelines rather than robust properties of the models themselves.
AI.motivation: Recent work claims LLMs exhibit brain-like properties such as concept cells and cognitive maps, often based on linear probes and activation steering on a single model. These findings are influential for AI neuroscience and interpretability, but the methods are highly sensitive to arbitrary analysis choices, raising concerns about whether the observed parallels reflect the models or artifacts of the measurement pipeline.
AI.method: The authors systematically evaluate four neuroscience-inspired paradigms across 17 LLMs from five model families (0.6B–72B parameters). They focus on causal concept steering and also test paradigms for geographic cognitive maps, numerical representation, and language-specific structure. They vary key analysis choices: raw vs normalized activations, readout metrics, operating point selection, neuron selection criteria, and attribution methods, and examine how these affect apparent trends with model scale. They implement residual-norm-comparable interventions and use held-out data to choose operating points for steering.
AI.result: Using a naive pipeline (raw activations, fixed layer and coefficient, specific metric), concept steerability appears to grow sharply with model size, suggesting an emergent property. However, this pattern disappears once the pipeline is calibrated: using interventions matched in residual norm or selecting steering coefficients on held-out data removes the apparent scale trend, although significant steerability remains at all scales. Geographic information is linearly decodable for all tested models. Number magnitude is reliably encoded, but whether neurons look bell-shaped or monotonic depends heavily on how neurons are selected. Language-specific structure can be localized, but the direction of cross-lingual asymmetries flips under different attribution methods.
AI.conclusion: Many striking neuroscience-style findings in LLMs are not robust to reasonable changes in measurement procedures; what looks like emergent, human-like structure can be an artifact of uncalibrated analysis choices. Nonetheless, genuine structure—such as decodable world maps and number magnitude representations—does exist across scales. The key bottleneck for AI neuroscience is therefore methodological: researchers need standardized, comparable measurements and stronger controls. The authors provide their protocol, stimuli, and code to support more rigorous, reproducible evaluations of neural and cognitive analogies in LLMs.

title: Verifiably grounded machine interpretation of lunar geology
summary: Planetary geology relies on historical, interpretive reasoning to reconstruct past events from diverse observations. Here, we present a step toward an automated "machine intelligence geologist" by embedding this distinct methodology of geologic knowledge discovery and inference into a multimodal vision-language architecture. Focusing on the stratigraphy of lunar basaltic mare volcanism, we train a model to generate verifiably grounded geologic interpretations directly from co-registered topographic, spectral, and geologic maps. We demonstrate that while the system successfully balances established geological priors with local visual evidence to accurately describe stratigraphy and terrain, numeric age dating derived solely from vision defaults to memorized priors. Integrating an open-book retrieval mechanism resolves this, enabling the model to faithfully cite published chronologies. Our findings delineate the necessary architecture for automated geologic inference: site evidence must be visually interpreted from local data, while quantitative historical context must be retrieved from the scientific record.

AI.tldr: They build and test a multimodal vision-language model that performs geologic interpretation like a planetary geologist, using lunar data, and show it must combine local visual reasoning with external retrieval of quantitative ages.
AI.motivation: Planetary geology is heavily based on historical, interpretive reasoning—geologists infer past events from heterogeneous observations (topography, composition, mapped units). This reasoning is hard to automate but valuable for scaling up geologic analysis of planetary data (e.g., for the Moon and other bodies). Existing machine learning methods tend to focus on pattern recognition or classification, not on the interpretive, historically grounded inferences geologists make. The authors want to embed this distinct style of scientific reasoning into an AI system, to see what architecture is needed for an automated 'machine intelligence geologist.'
AI.method: They design a multimodal vision-language model that ingests co-registered lunar datasets: topographic maps, spectral data, and existing geologic maps. The model is trained to generate geologic interpretations focused on stratigraphy of lunar basaltic mare volcanism, i.e., describing relative layering, relationships, and terrain properties. It is trained so that its textual outputs are checkably grounded in the visual inputs. They evaluate how well the model balances prior geological knowledge (priors) and local visual evidence. They also test numeric age estimation when the model uses only visual inputs, then modify the architecture by adding an open-book retrieval component that lets the model consult published chronologies, and compare behavior with and without retrieval.
AI.result: Without retrieval, the model can accurately describe local stratigraphy and terrain, combining established geological priors with what it sees in the input maps. However, when asked for quantitative ages (numeric dating) using only vision, it falls back on memorized global priors rather than deriving site-specific values. Adding an open-book retrieval mechanism fixes this: the model can now look up and correctly cite published age determinations, producing numerically accurate and source-grounded chronologies while still doing visual interpretation from the local data.
AI.conclusion: Automated geologic inference requires a hybrid architecture: (1) local site evidence and qualitative interpretations—such as stratigraphic relations and terrain descriptions—must be inferred from multimodal visual data; (2) quantitative historical context, including numeric ages, should not be guessed from vision alone but retrieved from the scientific literature or databases. A successful 'machine intelligence geologist' must therefore couple vision-language reasoning with external knowledge retrieval, rather than relying solely on end-to-end visual learning for all aspects of geologic interpretation.

title: Agentic AI-driven Immersive Simulation: A Knowledge-Aware Virtual Training Platform forHigh Dose Rate (HDR) Brachytherapy
summary: The convergence of the Metaverse and Large Language Model (LLM)-based AI agent is catalyzing a shift toward autonomous, immersive, and personalized pedagogical frameworks in medical education. This paper presents a novel agentic AI-driven immersive simulation specifically designed for High Dose Rate (HDR) vaginal cylinder (VC) brachytherapy in cancer care. By integrating Virtual Reality (VR) and mobile computing, the system establishes a high-fidelity, risk-free environment that allows trainees to master complex procedural skills without the facility or safety constraints posed by physical anatomy or live radioactive sources.
