However, as adversarial transformations become more sophisticated, it becomes crucial to explicitly assess semantic preservation; otherwise, attacks that actually alter the underlying disinformation claim may be incorrectly treated as valid evasion. Future robust detection frameworks should thus combine iterative adversarial stress-testing with methods to verify that transformed content preserves the original semantic intent.

title: Metanormative Theory for RL-Based Moral Agents
comment: The 14th International Workshop on Engineering Multi-Agent Systems (EMAS 2026) held May 25-26, 2026 Co-located with AAMAS 2026 Paphos, Cyprus
summary: The overlapping disciplines of machine ethics and value alignment are concerned with designing artificial agents that are aligned with human values and that act in ethically acceptable ways. A recent trend in these disciplines is the use of reinforcement learning (RL) to design such agents, sidelining the philosophical literature that used to play a more central role. Against this backdrop, this paper pursues two goals. The first is to draw out ideas from recent work in metanormative theory that can be useful for designing artificial moral and value-aligned agents. The second is to examine the RL architecture through the lens of these ideas. This will give us clearer criteria for when an RL agent's behavior can be classified as moral, as well as a basis for evaluating and comparing different RL-based approaches to machine ethics and value alignment.

AI.tldr: Connects metanormative theory with reinforcement learning to better define and evaluate moral and value-aligned artificial agents.
AI.motivation: Recent work in machine ethics and value alignment increasingly relies on reinforcement learning methods while paying less attention to rich philosophical discussions about the nature of morality, norms, and value. This creates a gap: RL systems may perform well empirically but lack a principled account of what it means for their behavior to be genuinely moral or value-aligned. The paper is motivated by the need to re-integrate insights from contemporary metanormative theory into the design and evaluation of artificial agents so that their alignment is not just behavioral but also conceptually well-grounded.
AI.method: The paper is largely conceptual and theoretical. It surveys and extracts relevant ideas from recent metanormative theory—such as accounts of moral facts, reasons, normativity, and the nature of moral judgments—and maps these ideas onto components of RL architectures. It then analyzes standard RL setups (rewards, policies, value functions, learning objectives) through this metanormative lens, proposing criteria and distinctions for interpreting RL agents’ behaviors as moral or merely instrumentally optimized. The method is comparative and analytical rather than empirical or algorithmic.
AI.result: The paper yields a set of clarified criteria and conceptual tools for judging when the behavior of an RL agent can be meaningfully described as moral or value-aligned, rather than just reward-maximizing. It offers a framework to distinguish different senses of alignment (e.g., behavioral, motivational, and normative alignment) and applies this framework to existing RL-based approaches in machine ethics and value alignment. This enables more systematic evaluation and comparison of RL architectures in terms of their moral significance and limitations.
AI.conclusion: Metanormative theory provides important resources for understanding and designing morally significant artificial agents, and should not be sidelined in favor of purely RL-based engineering approaches. By interpreting RL agents through metanormative concepts, we can better specify what it would take for their actions to count as moral, clarify different types of value alignment, and expose limitations of current RL-based methods. The paper concludes that progress in machine ethics and value alignment requires ongoing dialogue between philosophy and technical RL research, with metanormative insights playing a central guiding role.

title: TCS-BENCH: Benchmarking State-of-the-Art Generative AI Theoretical Computer Science Research Ability
summary: We introduce TCS-Bench, a benchmark for evaluating Large Language Models (LLMs) on research-level Theoretical Computer Science (TCS) proof generation. TCS-Bench consists of theorem-proving tasks from papers published at top theoretical computer science venues (STOC, FOCS, and SODA). Each task provides the necessary context to derive a self-contained proof for a target result. We evaluate state-of-the-art models on this benchmark. We verify the correctness of generated proofs via a verification agent, and further benchmark the verifier against human-expert proof judgements on a set of target statements and generated proofs pairs. Our reference verifier achieves over 90% accuracy on the expert labeled set.

AI.tldr: The paper presents TCS-Bench, a benchmark for testing LLMs on research-level theoretical computer science proof generation, along with an automated verifier that aligns well with expert judgments.
AI.motivation: Current LLM benchmarks rarely target research-level theorem proving in theoretical computer science, especially using real results from top conferences. There is a need for a standardized way to measure and compare LLMs’ abilities to understand complex TCS context and produce correct, rigorous proofs, as well as to reliably verify those proofs at scale.
AI.method: The authors construct TCS-Bench from theorem-proving tasks extracted from STOC, FOCS, and SODA papers. Each task includes enough contextual material to allow generation of a self-contained proof of a specific target result. They then evaluate state-of-the-art LLMs on this benchmark and develop a verification agent that checks the correctness of the generated proofs. Finally, they benchmark this verifier by comparing its judgments with those of human TCS experts on a labeled set of statement–proof pairs.
AI.result: TCS-Bench is released as a collection of proof-generation tasks rooted in real TCS papers. When applying state-of-the-art LLMs to the benchmark, the authors obtain machine-generated proofs that can be automatically assessed by their verifier. The reference verification agent attains over 90% accuracy when its correctness judgments are compared to those of human experts on a labeled evaluation subset.
AI.conclusion: TCS-Bench provides a challenging, realistic benchmark for evaluating LLMs on research-level theoretical computer science proof generation. The accompanying verification agent is sufficiently accurate to serve as an automatic evaluator, showing strong agreement with expert judgments and enabling scalable, standardized assessment of model performance on complex proof tasks.

title: LatticeMind: A Conflict-Aware Memory Primitive for Multi-Agent Systems
summary: Multi-agent LLM systems often fail not for lack of candidate answers, but because they have no persistent mechanism for deciding which incompatible claim should currently be trusted. Majority vote, debate, and judge-based selection choose an output without recording which claim wins, which is contested, or why a later update supersedes it. We present \term{LatticeMind}, a conflict-aware structured memory that handles contradiction at write time. It maintains explicit item status, applies cheap symbolic conflict checks, and invokes LLM reconciliation only for unresolved semantic cases. On a label-blind ConflictBank evaluation that removes source-name hints, LatticeMind reaches 0.97 accuracy versus 0.61 for the strongest aggregation baseline, with the gap significant at $p<10^{-6}$ by paired McNemar test. Ablations show that removing the checker or the reconciler costs 12 to 14 points. On four secondary planning benchmarks the picture is mixed: LatticeMind beats naive merge on three of four, but does not replace deliberation methods on tasks rewarding iterative search.

AI.tldr: They propose LatticeMind, a structured memory for multi-agent LLM systems that explicitly tracks and resolves conflicting claims, significantly improving conflict resolution accuracy over standard aggregation baselines.
AI.motivation: Multi-agent LLM systems generate many candidate answers but lack a persistent, explicit mechanism to decide and remember which conflicting claim should be currently trusted and why. Existing approaches like majority vote or judge selection choose outputs without recording conflict structure or update rationale, limiting reliability and traceability.
AI.method: Introduce LatticeMind, a conflict-aware structured memory architecture for multi-agent LLMs. It stores items with explicit status labels, performs lightweight symbolic checks to detect and handle contradictions at write time, and only calls an LLM-based reconciliation process for semantic conflicts that symbolic rules cannot resolve. They evaluate it on ConflictBank, a label-blind benchmark where source names give no hints, and conduct ablations to isolate the roles of the symbolic checker and LLM reconciler. They also test on four planning benchmarks versus naive merge and deliberation-style baselines.
AI.result: On ConflictBank, LatticeMind achieves 0.97 accuracy compared to 0.61 for the best aggregation baseline, with the improvement highly significant (p<1e-6, paired McNemar test). Ablation experiments show that removing either the symbolic conflict checker or the LLM reconciler reduces accuracy by 12–14 percentage points. On four secondary planning benchmarks, LatticeMind outperforms naive merge in three out of four tasks, but does not consistently beat deliberation methods that rely on iterative search.
AI.conclusion: Conflict-aware structured memory with explicit status tracking and staged conflict resolution (symbolic checks plus LLM reconciliation) substantially improves reliability on contradiction-heavy tasks. However, while LatticeMind is useful as a memory and aggregation mechanism, it is not a full replacement for deliberative, search-based multi-agent methods in planning-style problems.

title: Mawqif-v2: An Arabic Benchmark Dataset for Cross-Target Stance Detection
summary: Publicly available Arabic datasets for target-specific stance detection remain limited, particularly for evaluating cross-target generalization. This paper presents the Mawqif-v2 Extension, consisting of 996 manually annotated Arabic tweets collected from three public targets: Women Driving, E-Cars, and Trimester System. Each tweet is annotated with stance, sentiment, and sarcasm labels following the original Mawqif annotation scheme. The released extension is intended as a held-out evaluation set for assessing model generalization to both semantically related and previously unseen targets, while the original Mawqif dataset is used for training and development. In addition, we establish baseline results using several Arabic and multilingual transformer models, as well as zero-shot large language models (LLMs), to facilitate reproducible evaluation. Together with the original Mawqif dataset, the Mawqif-v2 Extension provides a benchmark for evaluating cross-target generalization in Arabic stance detection.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Mawqif-v2 Extension, a manually annotated Arabic Twitter dataset designed as a held-out benchmark to evaluate cross-target generalization in stance detection models, with baseline transformer and LLM results provided.
AI.motivation: Arabic stance detection datasets are scarce, especially for studying how well models generalize their stance predictions to new or semantically different targets. Existing resources, including the original Mawqif dataset, are mainly used for in-target evaluation, limiting research on robust, cross-target stance detection in Arabic. The authors aim to fill this gap by providing an additional, dedicated evaluation set that supports systematic study of cross-target generalization.
AI.method: The authors extend the original Mawqif dataset by collecting 996 Arabic tweets on three public targets (Women Driving, E-Cars, Trimester System). They manually annotate each tweet for stance, sentiment, and sarcasm using the same annotation scheme as Mawqif. The original Mawqif data is designated for training and development, while the new extension is reserved as a held-out test set. They then train and evaluate several Arabic and multilingual transformer models, as well as zero-shot LLMs, to establish baseline performance for reproducible comparison.
AI.result: The work yields Mawqif-v2 Extension, a curated and consistently annotated dataset of 996 Arabic tweets covering three targets, each labeled with stance, sentiment, and sarcasm. Using this extension as a held-out test set, the authors report baseline results for multiple transformer-based models and zero-shot LLMs, demonstrating measurable performance on cross-target stance detection and providing reference scores for future studies.
AI.conclusion: Mawqif-v2 Extension, together with the original Mawqif dataset, forms a benchmark suite for evaluating cross-target generalization in Arabic stance detection. By offering a held-out test set with rich annotations and baseline model results, the paper enables more rigorous and reproducible research on robust stance detection models that can transfer across different targets in Arabic social media.

title: A Fair Objective for Human-Empowerment-Preserving AI: Desiderata, Design, and Likely Behavioral Consequences
comment: Slightly extended version of paper accepted for Algorithmic Decision Theory 2026
summary: This paper explores the idea of promoting well-being and safety in human-AI interactions by forcing AI agents explicitly to empower humans and to manage the power balance between humans and AI agents in a desirable way. Using a principled, partially axiomatic approach based on desirable properties, we design a parametrizable and decomposable objective function for AI systems that represents an inequality- and risk-averse long-term aggregate of human power. It can take into account models of human bounded rationality and social norms, and crucially, considers a wide variety of possible human goals. We prove how certain desiderata enforce particular functional forms and restrict parameter ranges. We exemplify the consequences of softly maximizing this metric in several paradigmatic situations and describe what instrumental sub-goals it will likely imply.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a formal objective function for AI systems that explicitly optimizes for human power and safety, aiming for inequality- and risk-averse promotion of human well-being in human-AI interactions.
AI.motivation: As AI systems gain capabilities, they can create power imbalances between humans and AI agents, risking loss of human control, unfair distributions of influence, and safety issues. Existing alignment and value-learning approaches often lack an explicit treatment of power dynamics, inequality, and human bounded rationality. The authors are motivated to develop a principled way to encode desirable properties of power distribution and long-term human welfare directly into AI objectives.
AI.method: The paper uses a principled, partially axiomatic approach: it specifies high-level desiderata for how an AI system should treat human power, risk, and inequality, and then derives constraints on the functional form of an objective function that aggregates human power over the long term. The resulting objective is parametrizable and decomposable, allowing it to incorporate models of human bounded rationality, social norms, and diverse human goals. The authors mathematically prove that certain desiderata force specific functional structures and limit the permissible ranges of parameters. They then analyze the behavior of AI systems that softly maximize this objective in several stylized or paradigmatic scenarios.
AI.result: The authors obtain a concrete class of objective functions representing a long-term, inequality- and risk-averse aggregate of human power, consistent with the stated axioms and desiderata. They show how requirements like aversion to concentration of power, robustness to human irrationality, and accommodation of multiple human goals narrow down the possible objective forms. Parameter ranges are derived that guarantee the desired theoretical properties. Through examples, they illustrate how an AI system optimizing this metric would manage power balances, respond to social norms, and choose instrumental sub-goals in different settings.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that it is feasible to formally encode and optimize for human-centered power dynamics in AI objectives, going beyond simple reward maximization or preference satisfaction. Their proposed inequality- and risk-averse power metric provides a structured way to encourage AI systems to empower humans, maintain desirable power balances, and respect bounded rationality and social norms. They argue that softly maximizing this metric leads to characteristic instrumental sub-goals that tend to promote safety and human well-being, and they propose the framework as a foundation for future design and analysis of human-AI interaction objectives.

title: ELBench: A Multi-Dimensional Benchmark for Education-Facing Large Language Models
summary: Large language models are increasingly deployed in education as tutors, teaching assistants, and content generators. These roles place demands that ordinary question answering does not: a usable education-facing model is supposed to be accurate, safe under sensitive prompts, instructionally useful, and aligned with pedagogical goals at the same time. Existing benchmarks evaluate these requirements largely in isolation, so none assesses education-facing suitability as an integrated profile. We introduce ELBench, the first benchmark to evaluate all four requirements (General Capability, Safety and Trustworthiness, Basic Education, and High-Level Cultivation) on the same models under a common protocol, combining curated public sources with newly synthesized safety and cultivation data. We evaluate nine models, seven frontier general-purpose systems and two education-specialized variants, and report three findings. First, module-level profiles are more informative than a single aggregate: the top six models are statistically indistinguishable on overall score, yet their module leaders differ substantially, and safety is anti-correlated with practical teaching (r = -0.83). Second, the Chinese-developed models lead the safety module, the most discriminative in the suite; this advantage is largest on region-specific normative content and narrows, but does not vanish, on universal-harm content. Third, the two education-specialized models lead neither education module, and on High-Level Cultivation all models share a systematic blind spot: on the structured judgment task they converge on the same non-reference option, favoring pedagogical style over fit to the stated goal, so the module scores uniformly low and does not separate models. This raises, but does not resolve, whether domain post-training keeps pace with frontier systems on education tasks.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces ELBench, an integrated benchmark to evaluate large language models for education-focused use, covering capability, safety, and pedagogical quality, and reveals trade-offs between safety and practical teaching as well as limitations of current education-specialized models.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM benchmarks mostly test abilities like general QA, safety, or educational quality in isolation. For real educational deployment, models must simultaneously be accurate, safe with sensitive prompts, and pedagogically effective and aligned with educational goals. There was no single, unified benchmark that holistically assesses these dimensions together for the same models under a common evaluation protocol, limiting our ability to judge their overall suitability as educational tools.
AI.method: The authors build ELBench, a benchmark that jointly evaluates four modules: (1) General Capability, (2) Safety and Trustworthiness, (3) Basic Education, and (4) High-Level Cultivation. They combine curated public datasets with newly synthesized data for safety and higher-order cultivation tasks. Using a common protocol, they evaluate nine large language models, including seven frontier general-purpose LLMs and two models specialized for education. They compute module-level and aggregate scores, analyze correlations (e.g., between safety and practical teaching ability), and examine specific task behaviors such as structured judgment in cultivation tasks.
AI.result: (1) Module-level evaluation reveals meaningful differences that overall scores obscure: the top six models have statistically indistinguishable aggregate scores, but different models lead different modules, and there is a strong negative correlation between safety and practical teaching performance (r = -0.83). (2) Models developed in China perform best on the safety module, which is the most discriminative part of the benchmark; their advantage is strongest on region-specific normative content and is smaller but still present on content involving universal harms. (3) The two education-specialized models do not lead in either educational module; particularly in the High-Level Cultivation module, all models perform poorly and similarly. On a structured judgment task, they systematically choose the same non-reference answer, prioritizing pedagogical style over alignment with the explicitly stated educational goal.
AI.conclusion: ELBench provides an integrated, multi-dimensional evaluation framework for judging the suitability of LLMs as educational tools. The results show that high overall performance masks important trade-offs, especially between safety and practical teaching utility, and that some region-specific models can be comparatively safer. However, current education-specialized models do not clearly outperform general-purpose frontier models on educational tasks, and all evaluated systems share a significant blind spot in higher-level cultivation tasks, where they tend to favor appealing teaching styles rather than goal-consistent instruction. This raises concerns about whether existing domain-specific post-training methodologies are keeping up with general LLM advances for real educational deployment.

title: FemWear: A Specialized Wearable Foundation Model for Women's Health
summary: General wearable foundation models are pretrained across broad sensor streams and populations, but are not designed around women's-health tasks. We introduce FemWear, a specialized wearable foundation model that parameter-efficiently repurposes a pretrained multimodal wearable backbone. FemWear retains the patch projection and Transformer encoder, training 239,236 parameters (1.11% of a 21.54M-parameter encoder) through low-rank residual adapters and causal task-family heads. It learns one shared longitudinal representation for menstrual, symptom, affective, sleep/recovery, autonomic, activity, and pregnancy-related outcomes. We evaluate six cohorts with 63 comparable primary metrics, including 33 from women's-health cohorts, while retaining the 32-task OpenMHC ability-retention benchmark. On a fixed participant split over three seeds, FemWear improved cycle-phase macro-F1 by 8.15% and reduced mean absolute error for cramps, mood symptoms, and sleep problems by 9.32%, 5.80%, and 9.43%, respectively. In a stricter 42-participant nested leave-one-participant-out audit, 24-hour onset, 72-hour onset, and cramps retained positive changes of 2.87%, 6.35%, and 2.19%; phase, mood, and sleep were neutral or negative, and no endpoint had a strictly positive corrected confidence interval. Capacity-matched experiments outperformed a latest-day multilayer perceptron but not shared-GRU or multi-gate mixture-of-experts baselines. Train-only calibration reduced onset expected calibration error by 84.2--88.2% with zero temporal-nesting violations. FemWear enables targeted transfer and coherent probability outputs for women's-health research, but does not establish universal performance dominance or clinical validity.

AI.tldr: FemWear is a parameter-efficient wearable foundation model adapted for women's-health tasks from a general multimodal wearable backbone, offering improved performance and calibration for several menstrual and symptom-related outcomes but without universal superiority or clinical validation.
AI.motivation: General wearable foundation models are trained on broad, mixed populations and tasks and are not optimized for the unique patterns and prediction problems in women’s health (e.g., menstrual cycle phase, symptom onset, pregnancy-related metrics). There is a need for a specialized model that can leverage large pretrained wearables backbones while focusing on women’s-health outcomes, maintaining performance on general tasks, and providing well-calibrated probabilistic outputs suitable for research and potential downstream clinical use.
AI.method: The authors propose FemWear, which repurposes a large pretrained multimodal wearable backbone using parameter-efficient fine-tuning. It keeps the patch projection and Transformer encoder from the original 21.54M-parameter model and trains only 239,236 parameters (1.11%) via low-rank residual adapters and causal task-family heads. FemWear learns a shared longitudinal representation across multiple outcome families (menstrual, symptom, affective, sleep/recovery, autonomic, activity, and pregnancy-related tasks). They evaluate it on six cohorts, with 63 primary metrics (including 33 from women’s-health cohorts) and measure its ability to retain performance on the 32-task OpenMHC benchmark. They also run capacity-matched baselines (MLP, shared-GRU, multi-gate mixture-of-experts) and perform train-only calibration to improve calibration metrics like expected calibration error while enforcing temporal nesting constraints.
AI.result: On a fixed participant split with three random seeds, FemWear increases menstrual cycle-phase macro-F1 by 8.15% and reduces mean absolute error for predicting cramps, mood symptoms, and sleep problems by 9.32%, 5.80%, and 9.43%, respectively, compared to the baseline. In a stricter 42-participant nested leave-one-participant-out evaluation, improvements for 24-hour onset, 72-hour onset, and cramps remain positive (2.87%, 6.35%, and 2.19%), while phase, mood, and sleep outcomes are neutral or negative, and no endpoint has a strictly positive corrected confidence interval, signaling limited statistical robustness. Capacity-matched experiments show FemWear surpasses a latest-day MLP baseline but does not outperform shared-GRU or multi-gate mixture-of-experts baselines. Train-only calibration reduces onset expected calibration error by 84.2–88.2% without temporal-nesting violations, indicating much better probabilistic calibration.
AI.conclusion: FemWear demonstrates that a parameter-efficient adaptation of a general wearable foundation model can produce a shared representation that improves several women’s-health prediction tasks and yields well-calibrated probabilities, while retaining performance on a broad OpenMHC benchmark. However, its gains are not universal—some tasks show neutral or negative changes, confidence intervals do not confirm strictly positive effects, and it does not consistently beat strong sequence-modeling baselines. As such, FemWear is presented as an enabling tool for targeted transfer learning and probabilistic modeling in women’s-health research, rather than a universally superior or clinically validated solution.

title: Pragmatic Attack Surface: Vulnerabilities of Implicit Context in Large Language Models
summary: In the era of large language models (LLMs), attackers often manipulate natural language to elicit unsafe or harmful outputs, creating a new natural language attack surface unique to LLM-based systems, where attacks directly exploit explicit linguistic cues in user prompts to bypass the safety mechanism of LLMs. However, such attacks can often be mitigated by existing safety alignment algorithms. On the other hand, human language is inherently grounded in pragmatics, necessitating typical context to interpret language, e.g., world knowledge, social norms. However, such contexts are often implicit because they are not directly expressed in human language and are not sufficiently leveraged in safety alignment, creating a fundamental mismatch between human language interpretation and safety alignment approaches. In this paper, we demonstrate that this mismatch exposes vulnerabilities in LLMs. We refer to this vulnerability as the pragmatic attack surface, which can be exploited to achieve high attack success rates. The experimental results demonstrate that our proposed approach outperforms baseline attack methods across various open-source and closed-source models by a substantial margin.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies and exploits a new “pragmatic attack surface” in LLMs, arising from the gap between how humans use implicit context and how LLM safety alignment works, and shows that attacks leveraging this can significantly outperform existing prompt-based attacks.
AI.motivation: Current LLM safety alignment mainly focuses on explicit linguistic features in prompts, yet human language understanding depends heavily on implicit pragmatic context such as world knowledge and social norms. This creates a mismatch: safety systems judge prompts mostly at the surface-text level, while humans interpret them using richer context. The authors are motivated to investigate whether this mismatch opens a new, underexplored vulnerability that attackers can systematically exploit, beyond standard jailbreaks and prompt manipulations.
AI.method: The authors conceptualize and formalize a new “pragmatic attack surface” where adversaries craft prompts that appear safe at the surface level but become harmful when interpreted with implicit pragmatic context. They design an attack framework that systematically embeds harmful intent into pragmatically implied meanings (e.g., relying on shared world knowledge or social norms) instead of explicit wording. They then implement concrete attack strategies following this framework and evaluate them against multiple state-of-the-art safety-aligned LLMs, both open-source and closed-source, comparing their performance to existing baseline attack methods.
AI.result: Empirical evaluations show that attacks exploiting the pragmatic attack surface achieve substantially higher attack success rates than traditional prompt-based attacks across a range of LLMs. The proposed methods consistently outperform baselines on both open-source and commercial closed models, indicating that current safety alignment techniques are not robust to these pragmatics-based attacks.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that there is a fundamental vulnerability in current LLM safety mechanisms stemming from their failure to adequately model and guard against pragmatic, context-dependent interpretations of language. This “pragmatic attack surface” allows adversaries to bypass safety filters even when explicit harmful cues are absent from prompts. The authors argue that future safety alignment must incorporate richer pragmatic and contextual reasoning, going beyond surface-level text analysis, to effectively mitigate these new kinds of attacks.

title: SuperLocalMemory 4.0: The Governed Memory Operating System for AI Agents
comment: 35 pages, 17 figures, 4 tables. Zenodo DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.21853302. Code: https://github.com/qualixar/superlocalmemory/releases/tag/v4.0.0
summary:
AI agents are becoming shared infrastructure, yet durable memory is commonly assembled from separate retrieval, governance, and operational components. We present SuperLocalMemory 4.0, a governed, local-first memory operating system for AI agents. The system combines dense semantic, BM25 lexical, temporal, Hopfield-associative, and spreading-activation retrieval through reciprocal-rank fusion; a governed learning and behaviour layer; bi-temporal recall; multi-scope personal, shared, and global memory; role-based access control; GDPR-oriented export and verified erasure; audit trails; and a deployment-context EU AI Act checklist.
  V4 introduces a reliability spine for its primary write path: generation-fenced admission, a policy registry, verifiable memory transactions with per-projection apply, verify, compensate, and erase owners, and hash-checkable completion manifests. The runtime is available through CLI, MCP, an HTTP daemon, a dashboard, editor integration, and framework adapters, and supports fully local, local-with-on-device-model, and provider-assisted modes.
  We evaluate eleven fault-injection and mechanism scenarios, each repeated 200 times. The released evidence bundle reports 2,200 of 2,200 deterministic repetitions upholding their scoped component properties. The governed write envelope measured 3.522 ms at p50 and 5.297 ms at p99, versus 1.835 ms and 2.569 ms for the ungoverned baseline, corresponding to in-process control-plane overheads of 1.687 ms at p50 and 2.728 ms at p99. These are scoped component and mechanism measurements, not an end-to-end multi-process or external retrieval-accuracy benchmark. The paper consolidates prior SuperLocalMemory work on privacy-preserving multi-agent memory, information-geometric retrieval, and the V3.3 Living Brain lifecycle.

AI.tldr: SuperLocalMemory 4.0 is a governed, local-first, reliability-focused memory OS for AI agents that unifies multiple retrieval modes, strong governance, and reliability mechanisms, with measured overhead but verified deterministic behavior under fault injection.
AI.motivation: As AI agents become shared infrastructure, their memory is often built from loosely coupled components for retrieval, governance, and operations, which can lead to reliability, compliance, and governance gaps. There is a need for a unified, local-first memory system that supports rich retrieval, strong governance (privacy, access control, GDPR, AI Act), and verifiable reliability guarantees in real deployments.
AI.method: The authors design and implement SuperLocalMemory 4.0, a memory operating system combining multiple retrieval strategies (dense semantic, BM25 lexical, temporal, Hopfield-associative, spreading-activation) via reciprocal-rank fusion, governed learning/behaviour, bi-temporal recall, and multi-scope memory (personal, shared, global). They incorporate role-based access control, GDPR-oriented export and verified erasure, audit trails, and an EU AI Act deployment checklist. V4 adds a “reliability spine” on the primary write path with generation-fenced admission, a policy registry, verifiable memory transactions with per-projection apply/verify/compensate/erase roles, and hash-checkable completion manifests. They expose the runtime via multiple interfaces and support several deployment modes (fully local, on-device, provider-assisted). For evaluation, they run eleven fault-injection and mechanism scenarios, repeating each 200 times (2,200 runs) to test scoped component properties and measure control-plane latency overheads of the governed write envelope vs an ungoverned baseline.
AI.result: Across 2,200 deterministic repetitions over eleven fault-injection/mechanism scenarios, all runs uphold their defined scoped component properties, indicating robust behavior of the reliability spine and governance mechanisms under injected faults. The governed write envelope introduces additional latency relative to an ungoverned baseline: 3.522 ms vs 1.835 ms at p50 and 5.297 ms vs 2.569 ms at p99, corresponding to control-plane overheads of 1.687 ms and 2.728 ms, respectively. These results are limited to component-level and mechanism-level behavior rather than full end-to-end or retrieval-quality benchmarks. The paper also unifies earlier results on privacy-preserving multi-agent memory, information-geometric retrieval, and lifecycle management.
AI.conclusion: SuperLocalMemory 4.0 provides a unified, governed, and reliability-focused memory OS for AI agents that integrates rich retrieval mechanisms with strong governance, auditability, and verifiable write-path reliability, at the cost of modest millisecond-level control-plane latency. Its deterministic behavior under fault injection and support for local-first, compliant deployments make it suitable as shared memory infrastructure for AI agents, while consolidating and extending prior SuperLocalMemory research on privacy, retrieval, and lifecycle management.

title: Se-DPO: Self-Evolving Token Credit for Direct Preference Optimization
summary: Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) aggregates token-level log-probability ratios via uniform summation, implicitly treating all tokens as contributing equally to the preference signal. However, the contribution of individual tokens to the preference signal varies. We introduce token credit, which modulates each token's KL regularization based on its contribution to the preference outcome. We derive that effective token credit is proportional to the magnitude of each token's implicit reward, and observe that this quantity evolves substantially during training. This implies that static token credit becomes increasingly misaligned as training progresses. In this work, we propose Se-DPO (Self-Evolving Token Credit for DPO), a live mechanism that derives token credit from the model's own evolving internal signals during DPO training. Since the reward signal varies in reliability across positions, Se-DPO calibrates token credit based on both the strength and the confidence of each token's contribution. Se-DPO requires no external models, adding only a lightweight calibration network with minimal computational overhead. Experiments show that Se-DPO improves over DPO by up to 9.8 points on AlpacaEval~2 and 12.2 points on Arena-Hard.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Se-DPO, a variant of Direct Preference Optimization that assigns dynamic, token-level credit based on the model’s evolving internal signals, leading to better alignment performance.
AI.motivation: Standard DPO uniformly aggregates token-level log-probability ratios, implicitly assuming all tokens contribute equally to the preference signal, which is unrealistic because different tokens impact the preference outcome differently. Static token credit or uniform weighting can become increasingly misaligned as training progresses, motivating a method that adapts token credit dynamically based on actual contribution to preferences.
AI.method: The authors introduce the notion of token credit that modulates each token's KL regularization according to its contribution to the preference outcome. They derive that effective token credit is proportional to the magnitude of each token's implicit reward and empirically show that this quantity shifts significantly during training. Building on this, they propose Se-DPO, which continuously re-estimates token credit from the model’s own evolving internal signals. Se-DPO uses a light calibration network to incorporate both the strength and the confidence of each token’s inferred contribution into position-wise credit, without requiring any external reward model.
AI.result: Se-DPO achieves substantial empirical gains over vanilla DPO, with reported improvements of up to 9.8 points on AlpacaEval 2 and 12.2 points on Arena-Hard, indicating better alignment and preference optimization performance.
AI.conclusion: Dynamic, self-evolving token credit improves DPO-based preference optimization by more accurately reflecting token-wise contributions to preference signals. Se-DPO’s lightweight, self-contained mechanism yields notable performance gains over standard DPO with minimal computational overhead, suggesting that adaptive token-level credit assignment is an effective and practical enhancement to preference optimization methods.

title: Your Prompt Is Not the Only Prompt: How Much Do LLMs Weight Structured-Output Schema Descriptions?
summary: Structured output, where an LLM populates a predefined JSON schema, has become a default mechanism for data labeling and information extraction, but it also introduces a second instruction channel through schema descriptions. We tested whether classification-label definitions are better placed in the system prompt, user prompt, or schema description using a single-field classification task with nonce labels across ten model configurations from two vendors. Schema descriptions did not consistently outperform prompt-based placement; for GPT-4.1 and GPT-5.4 without reasoning, schema placement underperformed system prompts by 11-13 percentage points. Yet schemas are not inert metadata: when prompts and schemas conflicted, incorrect schema instructions caused accuracy drops of 5-45 points, with Claude Haiku 4.5 falling from 52.5% to 7%, indicating that schema instructions can override prompt instructions, and GPT-5.5 falling from 100% to 73%. Further, adding a required intermediate reasoning field before the label field improved schema-only accuracy by 15-24 points when headroom existed, exceeding system-prompt-only performance in every case tested. The effect held even for Claude Sonnet 4.6 at medium reasoning, where extended thinking alone did not produce a comparable gain. This suggests that schema design can affect how effectively models use information encoded in field descriptions. Overall, these results indicate that schema influence is model-dependent. In practice, the system prompt remains a safe default for definitions, but the bigger discipline is maintaining a single source of truth and preventing prompt/schema drift. More importantly, schema design itself may be a stronger lever than instruction placement. Practitioners should treat prompts and schemas as a unified instruction surface and empirically validate both placement and field design for their target model.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how placing label definitions in different parts of an LLM setup (system prompt, user prompt, or JSON schema descriptions) affects classification accuracy, and finds that schema design and reasoning fields can strongly influence performance, often more than where instructions are placed.
AI.motivation: Structured JSON output is now a standard way to control LLMs for labeling and extraction, but this introduces an extra instruction channel in the schema itself. Practitioners lack clear guidance on whether label definitions should live in prompts or in schema descriptions, and how conflicts or schema design choices affect model behavior and reliability.
AI.method: The authors run a controlled single-field classification task using nonce (arbitrary) labels to avoid prior knowledge, across ten model configurations from two vendors. They systematically vary where the label definitions appear: system prompt, user prompt, or JSON schema field descriptions. They also create settings where prompts and schemas intentionally conflict to test precedence, and add a required intermediate reasoning field to examine whether structured reasoning within the schema improves accuracy. They compare performance with and without explicit reasoning across models and configurations.
AI.result: Schema descriptions do not reliably beat prompt-based definitions. For GPT-4.1 and GPT-5.4 without reasoning, putting definitions in the schema is 11–13 percentage points worse than in the system prompt. However, schema instructions are powerful: when they contradict prompts, wrong schema instructions can drop accuracy by 5–45 points; for example, Claude Haiku 4.5 falls from 52.5% to 7%, and GPT-5.5 from 100% to 73%, demonstrating that schemas can override prompt instructions. Adding a required intermediate reasoning field substantially boosts schema-only accuracy by 15–24 points where there is room to improve, surpassing system-prompt-only performance in all tested cases, and this benefit appears even when simply enabling more general “extended thinking” does not. Effects differ by model family and configuration.
AI.conclusion: Instruction placement across system prompts, user prompts, and schemas matters, but its impact is model-dependent. The system prompt is generally a robust default location for label definitions, yet the most critical practice is to avoid divergent or conflicting instructions across prompts and schemas and maintain a single source of truth. Schema design—especially incorporating explicit reasoning fields—can be an even more powerful lever than where definitions are placed. Practitioners should treat prompts and schemas as a unified instruction surface and empirically test both placement and schema field structure for their specific target models.

title: MDB-Link: Hierarchical Schema Linking for Multi-Database Text-to-SQL
summary: Traditional Text-to-SQL research and benchmarks assume a known target database, overlooking settings in which a query must be routed within a large, heterogeneous database collection. We therefore study schema linking in a multi-database setting, where the system must first locate the target database and then construct a compact, SQL-relevant schema for generation. We propose MDB-Link, a hierarchical schema-linking framework that retrieves question-relevant columns from a global index, aggregates retrieval evidence to shortlist databases, and uses a budget-aware large language model (LLM) for database reranking, table selection, and column grounding. With Qwen2.5-14B, MDB-Link outperforms LinkAlign on MMQA, Spider2-Snow, and BIRD-dev in database localization and column selection while producing schema subsets close in size to the gold schemas. Exact match improves from 16.88 to 51.41 on MMQA, 2.50 to 9.17 on Spider2-Snow, and 12.52 to 38.01 on BIRD-dev. MDB-Link also runs faster than LinkAlign and AutoLink, demonstrating the effectiveness of hierarchical schema reduction for downstream SQL generation.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces MDB-Link, a hierarchical schema-linking framework for Text-to-SQL over large collections of heterogeneous databases, improving database localization, schema selection, accuracy, and speed over prior methods.
AI.motivation: Most Text-to-SQL work assumes a single known target database, but real-world systems often have many heterogeneous databases where the correct one is not known in advance. In such multi-database settings, a system must first figure out which database (and which parts of its schema) are relevant to a natural language question. Existing benchmarks and methods overlook this database routing and compact schema construction step, limiting Text-to-SQL performance and scalability.
AI.method: The paper proposes MDB-Link, a hierarchical schema-linking framework. It first retrieves question-relevant columns from a global index built over multiple databases. Using the retrieval evidence, it shortlists candidate databases. Then, a budget-aware large language model is used to rerank these databases, select the most relevant tables, and ground specific columns to the question, effectively constructing a compact, SQL-relevant schema subset for the query. The approach is evaluated with Qwen2.5-14B and compared to prior schema-linking systems such as LinkAlign and AutoLink.
AI.result: With Qwen2.5-14B as the backbone LLM, MDB-Link achieves better database localization and column selection than LinkAlign on the MMQA, Spider2-Snow, and BIRD-dev benchmarks. It yields schema subsets whose sizes are close to the human-annotated gold schemas. On exact match SQL accuracy, MDB-Link improves from 16.88 to 51.41 on MMQA, from 2.50 to 9.17 on Spider2-Snow, and from 12.52 to 38.01 on BIRD-dev. It also runs faster than LinkAlign and AutoLink, indicating that the hierarchical schema reduction is efficient for downstream SQL generation.
AI.conclusion: MDB-Link effectively addresses the multi-database Text-to-SQL setting by jointly handling database localization and compact schema construction. Its hierarchical schema-linking design, based on global column retrieval and LLM-driven reranking and grounding under a budget, leads to large gains in exact match accuracy and runtime efficiency across several benchmarks. This suggests that careful schema reduction and routing are key components for scalable, real-world Text-to-SQL systems over large heterogeneous database collections.

title: OBLIVION: Workflow-Level Operational Skill Unlearning for Deployed Agents
summary: Large language model agents are becoming operational interfaces to files, memories, registries, and external tools. This deployment shift creates a new skill revocation problem: after a skill is removed from an explicit registry, an agent may still reconstruct it from residual carriers such as archives, transcripts, schemas, or memory entries. We study this problem as operational skill unlearning, where the goal is not parameter-level forgetting, but preventing a deployed agent from rebuilding a revoked skill through primitive tools. We introduce OBLIVION, a controlled benchmark and defense harness for revoked-skill resurrection. OBLIVION models each episode as a source-to-sink workflow, applies Cross-Surface Coherent Erasure to reduce residual carriers, and uses frozen workflow remediation near dangerous sinks. On the locked 88 attack episodes, the no-defense arm reaches formal attack success rate 1.0. OBLIVION reduces the rate to 0.114 and impact-weighted exposure to 0.115 while keeping locked utility at 1.0 and benign block rate at 0. In a separate skill-attack-derived sandbox, OBLIVION reduces attack success from 1.0 to 0.2 and impact-weighted exposure from 1.0 to 0.213 while preserving all utility controls. These results support workflow-level evaluation beyond checking explicit skill entries.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces OBLIVION, a benchmark and defense framework to prevent large language model agents from reconstructing revoked skills from residual artifacts in operational environments.
AI.motivation: As LLM agents are increasingly deployed as interfaces to tools, files, and memories, revoking a skill by removing it from a registry is not sufficient: the agent may still reconstruct the capability from leftover traces such as logs, archives, schemas, or memory. Existing unlearning work focuses on model parameters, not on deployed, tool-using agents. There is a need for a principled way to evaluate and defend against such "skill resurrection" in real workflows.
AI.method: The authors formalize the problem as operational skill unlearning and build OBLIVION, a benchmark and defense harness targeting revoked-skill resurrection. Each evaluation episode is modeled as a source-to-sink workflow that traces how information about a revoked skill might flow from residual sources to dangerous sinks. They apply Cross-Surface Coherent Erasure to systematically reduce or sanitize residual carriers (e.g., archives, transcripts, schemas, memory entries) across the workflow surfaces. Near potentially dangerous sinks, they use frozen workflow remediation, i.e., predesigned remediation behaviors that constrain what the agent can do when it approaches risky operations. The framework is tested on a locked set of 88 attack episodes and on a separate sandbox derived from skill attacks.
AI.result: Without defenses, their benchmark yields a formal attack success rate of 1.0 on the 88 locked attack episodes. With OBLIVION, the attack success rate is reduced to 0.114 and impact-weighted exposure to 0.115, while fully preserving locked task utility (1.0) and incurring no benign blocking (0). In a separate skill-attack-derived sandbox environment, OBLIVION reduces attack success from 1.0 to 0.2 and impact-weighted exposure from 1.0 to 0.213, again without degrading utility controls.
AI.conclusion: OBLIVION demonstrates that workflow-level modeling and defenses—through source-to-sink analysis, cross-surface erasure, and remediation near dangerous sinks—can substantially mitigate revoked-skill resurrection in tool-using LLM agents while preserving benign functionality. The work argues that evaluation of skill revocation must go beyond checking explicit skill registries and should instead consider the full operational workflow and residual information surfaces.

title: Measuring the Wrong Thing: Internal Harmfulness Scores Anti-Rank Successful Jailbreaks
summary: Internal safety scores judge a prompt before any text is generated, and they are validated by how well they separate harmful prompts from benign ones. That separation is then read as evidence that the score will also catch the attacks that succeed. Harmful intent is a property of the prompt. Jailbreak success is an outcome produced later by a particular target model, decoding policy, and judge. A filter tuned on a score that measures the wrong quantity spends its false positive budget on attacks that would have failed anyway. In this paper we audit that inference. Attention based measurements are usually read from prompt dependent locations, so a wrapper changes both the content being judged and the place the signal is taken from. We therefore introduce Active Attention Probing, which supplies a fixed content independent measurement coordinate. We pair every base goal with a plain and a wrapped version and generate real completions from the target models. On Llama, wrapping raises harmful generation from 0.05 to 0.27 while harmful intent AUROC falls from 0.936 to 0.803, so the attacks grow more dangerous while the prompts look safer to the score. Among wrapped harmful prompts the outcome AUROC is 0.220, which places the attacks that succeeded below the attacks that failed. Rare token, passive, and detector derived channels reproduce the reversal on the same matched design, and the reversal itself persists across three target models, seven attack families, and two independent judges. Distribution shift then degrades calibration and threshold transfer before it degrades ranking.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that commonly used internal safety scores can be systematically misled by prompt-wrapping attacks: as prompts are wrapped, models become more likely to generate harmful outputs while safety scores paradoxically rate the prompts as safer.
AI.motivation: Safety filters in language models often rely on internal, pre-generation scores that estimate how harmful a prompt is. These scores are validated by their ability to distinguish harmful from benign prompts, and it is implicitly assumed that this also predicts which attacks will actually succeed in causing harmful model outputs. The authors suspect this assumption is flawed, especially under prompt-wrapping attacks that change surface form without changing intent, and they aim to test how robust these internal scores are under such distribution shifts.
AI.method: The authors introduce Active Attention Probing, which reads attention-based safety signals from a fixed, content-independent measurement coordinate instead of prompt-dependent positions. They construct paired datasets where each harmful base goal appears in both a plain and a wrapped form. For each prompt, they generate real completions from target models (including Llama) under specific decoding policies and evaluate harmfulness with external judges. They compute AUROC metrics both for detecting harmful intent from prompts and for predicting harmful generation outcomes, and they repeat the analysis across multiple target models, attack families, and types of internal channels (rare token, passive, and detector-derived).
AI.result: On Llama, adding wrappers increases the rate of harmful generations from 0.05 to 0.27, meaning attacks become substantially more successful. At the same time, the AUROC for detecting harmful intent from prompts drops from 0.936 to 0.803, so the prompts appear safer according to the internal score. Within the subset of wrapped harmful prompts, the AUROC for predicting which prompts will actually lead to harmful outputs falls to 0.220, effectively ranking successful attacks as less risky than failed ones. Similar reversals occur for other internal channels and persist across three target models, seven jailbreak attack families, and two independent judges.
AI.conclusion: Internal safety scores that are calibrated to separate harmful from benign prompts can fail badly as predictors of actual jailbreak success under distribution shifts such as prompt wrapping. They may spend their false positive budget on attacks that would fail regardless, while missing those that succeed, and can even invert ranking among harmful prompts. This indicates that relying on such scores for thresholding or calibration is fragile: distribution shift harms calibration and threshold transfer before it visibly harms ranking, so robust safety defenses must account for these shifts and cannot assume that good intent-separation guarantees good outcome prediction.

title: Exploring LLM Capabilities for Situational Understanding and COLREG compliance on real-world maritime navigation scenarios
comment: Submitted and accepted to the IFAC WC 2026 as an invited session paper for track 7.2 Transportation and Vehicle Systems - Marine Systems
summary: Recently, Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown considerable capability for situational understanding, reasoning, and decision making in different domains, most notable in the automotive sector. Therefore, we explore current state-of-the-art LLMs as a tool for maritime navigation, which includes both codified rules in the Collision Regulations (COLREGs) and uncodified best practices summarized in the concept of ``Good Seamanship''. We construct a dataset consisting of 50 diverse, real-world navigation scenarios from AIS data, label scenarios with applicable COLREG rules, recommended actions, and the reasoning for the action. We explore a variety of different LLM architectures and sizes to determine their understanding of maritime navigation tasks as well as evaluate their reasoning capabilities in this domain. The results obtained indicate that the maritime navigation task remains difficult to solve without fine-tuning, even for larger online models.

AI.tldr: The paper evaluates how well state-of-the-art large language models can understand and reason about maritime navigation scenarios, finding that performance is still poor without fine-tuning.
AI.motivation: LLMs have shown strong situational understanding and decision-making ability in domains like automotive driving, but it is unclear whether they can safely and reliably handle the complex, safety-critical domain of maritime navigation governed by both formal rules (COLREGs) and informal best practices (Good Seamanship).
AI.method: The authors build a dataset of 50 diverse real-world maritime navigation situations derived from AIS data. For each scenario they annotate which COLREG rules apply, what actions are recommended, and the reasoning behind those actions. They then test different LLM architectures and sizes on these tasks to measure both decision quality and reasoning quality in this domain.
AI.result: Across models, including larger online LLMs, performance on correctly interpreting scenarios, applying COLREGs, and recommending appropriate actions is limited when used out-of-the-box, with frequent errors in both decisions and explanations.
AI.conclusion: Current general-purpose LLMs are not yet reliable tools for maritime navigation decision support without domain-specific fine-tuning or adaptation; maritime navigation remains a challenging benchmark for LLM situational understanding and reasoning.

title: How Do Large Language Models Judge Social Attraction? Evidence from Theory-Grounded Persona Ratings Across Multiple LLMs and Humans
comment: 9 pages, 2 figures, 2 tables. Includes technical supplement
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to perform subjective evaluations traditionally made by humans, yet their validity as social judges remains unclear. This paper examines whether LLMs can assess social attraction from theory-grounded persona profiles constructed from ten psychological and relational constructs and organized into three tiers: socially attractive, socially mixed, and socially unattractive. We examine LLM ratings in two studies and compare them with human judgments in a third study. In Study 1, 34 LLMs rated 12 profiles across three repeated runs. Although some models tended to give higher or lower ratings overall, they showed strong stability across runs, consistent three-tier ordering, and high agreement in relative profile ordering. Study 2 examined sensitivity to gender presentation using six matched name-and-pronoun profile pairs and a separate pronoun-only test with a gender-neutral name, finding no significant effects in either analysis. In Study 3, 198 human participants evaluated the six matched profiles from Study 2. Their ratings reproduced the three-tier structure and followed a profile ordering consistent with that of the LLMs. However, LLMs rated attractive profiles more positively and unattractive profiles more negatively than humans, while neither group showed a significant overall effect of gender presentation.

AI.tldr: The paper evaluates whether large language models (LLMs) can function as reliable social judges by rating social attraction from theory-based persona profiles, comparing their judgments with human ratings and testing for gender-related biases.
AI.motivation: As LLMs are increasingly used to replace or supplement human judgment in subjective, socially nuanced tasks (e.g., rating people, content moderation, recommender systems), it is crucial to know whether their evaluations align with human social perceptions and whether they introduce systematic bias, especially around socially sensitive traits like attractiveness and gender.
AI.method: The authors created 12 detailed persona profiles grounded in ten psychological and relational constructs, grouped into three intended tiers of social attraction: attractive, mixed, and unattractive. In Study 1, 34 different LLMs rated each profile three times to test stability, consistency with the intended tiers, and agreement across models. In Study 2, they probed gender sensitivity by constructing six matched profile pairs that differed only in name and pronouns (plus a pronoun-only variant with a gender-neutral name), then compared model ratings across male vs. female presentations. In Study 3, 198 human participants rated the same six matched profiles, enabling comparison of human and LLM rating patterns, tier structure, sensitivity to gender cues, and extremity of judgments.
AI.result: Across 34 LLMs, ratings were stable across repeated runs, preserved the intended three-tier ordering of profiles, and showed high agreement in the relative ranking of profiles. LLM ratings did not significantly differ by gender presentation for matched profiles, including in the pronoun-only test. Human participants reproduced the same three-tier structure and a profile ordering that closely matched the LLMs’ ordering. However, LLMs tended to produce more extreme judgments than humans, rating socially attractive profiles more positively and socially unattractive profiles more negatively, while both LLMs and humans showed no significant overall effect of gender presentation on social attraction ratings.
AI.conclusion: LLMs can act as consistent, theory-congruent social judges of attraction when given structured persona descriptions, largely mirroring human profile rankings and tier distinctions and showing no detectable gender bias in this setting. Nonetheless, they are more judgmentally extreme than humans, exaggerating positivity for attractive profiles and negativity for unattractive ones. This suggests LLMs may be suitable as scalable proxies for aggregate human judgments in some social evaluation tasks, but their tendency toward more polarized ratings and the constrained, profile-based setting warrant caution in generalizing to real-world social contexts.

title: Fair on the Surface? Benchmarking Hidden-Output Fairness Gaps in LLM Recommenders
summary: Fairness audits for LLM-based recommenders have largely focused on observable outputs, implicitly assuming that stable recommendations reflect stable internal processing. We challenge this assumption with FairGap, the first benchmark to jointly evaluate recommendation fairness at two levels: observable output shift (OBS) and hidden representation shift (IBS), measured through controlled counterfactual identity probes across gender, age, and race. Their relationship is summarized via Representation-Output Alignment (ROA), with quadrant diagnostics for identifying user-level hidden-output mismatch. Applied to six open-weight LLM families across three domains, FairGap reveals pervasive hidden-output decoupling: ROA rarely exceeds 0.22, and a non-negligible user population shows stable outputs despite substantial internal shifts, a mode that output-only audits cannot detect by design. Further, activation steering that reduces IBS by up to 8x simultaneously worsens OBS, demonstrating a fundamental tension between internal and output-level fairness that existing frameworks are unequipped to diagnose.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces FairGap, a benchmark that evaluates fairness in LLM-based recommenders at both the output and hidden-representation levels, revealing that stable recommendations can mask substantial internal bias shifts.
AI.motivation: Existing fairness audits for LLM-based recommender systems focus almost entirely on observable outputs, assuming that if recommendations do not change when a user’s sensitive attributes change, then the model’s internal treatment of those users is also fair and stable. The authors argue this assumption is flawed: LLMs might maintain similar outputs while their internal representations change significantly for different demographic profiles, hiding potential unfairness or bias that output-only audits cannot capture.
AI.method: The authors design FairGap, a benchmark that performs controlled counterfactual identity probes on user profiles, systematically varying gender, age, and race while holding other attributes fixed. They measure (1) observable output shift (OBS) in recommendations and (2) internal/hidden representation shift (IBS) in the LLM’s embeddings across these counterfactuals. They then define Representation-Output Alignment (ROA) to quantify how aligned internal changes are with output changes and use a quadrant diagnostic framework to categorize users by hidden–output mismatch. They further apply activation steering interventions to directly manipulate internal activations and observe the resulting effects on both OBS and IBS.
AI.result: Across six open-weight LLM families and three application domains, FairGap shows that hidden and output behaviors are often decoupled: ROA values are typically low (rarely above 0.22), indicating weak alignment between representation shifts and output shifts. A notable subset of users exhibits large internal representation changes despite almost unchanged recommendations, meaning traditional output-only fairness audits would incorrectly deem the system stable or fair. Additionally, when the authors use activation steering to reduce internal bias (IBS) by up to a factor of eight, the observable output disparities (OBS) actually worsen, exposing a trade-off between internal and output-level fairness.
AI.conclusion: The study concludes that fairness evaluations for LLM-based recommender systems cannot rely solely on observable outputs because such audits miss substantial mismatches between hidden representations and recommendations. FairGap demonstrates that internal and output-level fairness can be fundamentally in tension: efforts to equalize internal representations may inadvertently exacerbate output disparities. Therefore, future fairness frameworks must explicitly account for both levels, develop tools to detect hidden-output decoupling, and reconsider assumptions that stable outputs imply fair or stable internal processing.

title: REFRAMED: Towards Realistic Audio Description Generation for Movies
summary: Audio Description (AD) is a verbal narration of key visual content in videos, enabling access for visually impaired audiences. Unlike standard video captioning, AD is a structured editorial task: descriptions must be inserted into gaps in dialogue and must convey only what is needed to understand the narrative being told. However, existing approaches formulate AD generation in an artificial setting where both the content and timing of descriptions are pre-specified, reducing the task to clip-level captioning. They further rely on noisy transcription and alignment pipelines, and lack the rich parallel data required for modeling narrative context. We introduce a new formulation of AD generation in which models must jointly decide what to describe and when to do it. To support this, we present REFRAMED, a high-quality dataset of 2,023 videos that span 3,302 scenes from 206 movies, with professional AD transcripts (both American and British versions), professional subtitles and aligned screenplays. We also provide a manually curated challenge set that pairs full movies with multiple AD references, together with evaluation protocols that leverage dialogue gaps and multi-reference comparisons. Experiments with state-of-the-art AD systems and multimodal LLMs show that they outperform trivial baselines but fall far short of expert human performance. Our dataset and benchmark establish a new foundation for research on video understanding.

AI.tldr: They introduce a more realistic audio description (AD) generation task where systems must decide both what to describe and when, and release REFRAMED, a large high-quality dataset and benchmark; current models still lag far behind humans.
AI.motivation: Existing AD generation work simplifies the problem to clip-level captioning with pre-specified content and timing, relies on noisy pipelines, and lacks data that captures narrative context. This does not reflect the real editorial nature of professional AD, which must fit into dialogue gaps and focus on narrative-relevant visual content. There is a need for a realistic formulation and resources to study this task properly.
AI.method: They reformulate AD generation as a joint decision problem over what and when to describe, rather than assuming pre-aligned description segments. To support this, they construct REFRAMED, a dataset of 2,023 videos/3,302 scenes from 206 movies with professional American and British AD, subtitles, and aligned screenplays, plus a curated challenge set of full movies with multiple AD references. They define evaluation protocols that exploit dialogue gaps and multi-reference comparisons, and benchmark state-of-the-art AD systems and multimodal LLMs on these tasks.
AI.result: The resulting REFRAMED dataset is high-quality, large-scale, and captures realistic AD scenarios with rich narrative context and multiple professional references. In experiments, existing AD systems and multimodal large language models beat trivial baselines but still perform significantly worse than expert human describers on the new benchmark and challenge sets.
AI.conclusion: The work establishes a new, more realistic benchmark setting for audio description generation that better reflects its editorial nature. REFRAMED plus the proposed evaluation protocols provide a strong foundation for future research on video understanding and AD, highlighting substantial remaining gaps between automated systems and professional human performance.

title: Mitigating Over-Personalization in LLMs via Structured Memory
summary: Conversational assistants increasingly rely on persistent long-term memory to personalize responses across sessions. However, when stored user information is reintroduced into the model context, it can also influence responses in inappropriate or unrelated settings. We study two such failure modes in memory-augmented LLMs: cross-domain leakage, where memories from one life domain affect responses in another, and memory-induced sycophancy, where stored user beliefs make models more likely to agree with the user rather than respond truthfully. We apply a simple inference-time modification to how memories are presented to the model, without changing the model or the memory contents. Across seven models on PersistBench, we compare the commonly used all-in context format, where memories are injected as an unstructured list, with structured formats that partition memories by domain. This simple modification consistently reduces cross-domain leakage while preserving utility, with our strongest method reducing leakage by $8.8\%$ on average relative to the baseline.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates how the way long-term user memories are formatted in context affects undesired behaviors in memory-augmented LLM assistants, and proposes simple structured memory prompts that reduce harmful cross-domain influence without retraining models.
AI.motivation: Conversational assistants now use persistent long-term memory to personalize interactions across sessions. While this improves user experience, it also introduces new risks: information stored from one context can inappropriately affect model behavior in unrelated contexts, and stored user beliefs can push the model toward agreeing rather than giving truthful answers. There is a need to characterize and mitigate these failure modes without expensive retraining or changing memory contents, and to understand whether simple prompt-formatting interventions can control unwanted memory influence while keeping the benefits of personalization.
AI.method: The authors define and study two failure modes in memory-augmented LLMs: (1) cross-domain leakage, where memories taken from one life domain (e.g., health, work) improperly affect responses in another domain; and (2) memory-induced sycophancy, where user-belief memories make models more likely to agree with users over truth. Using PersistBench and seven different LLMs, they systematically compare a standard memory injection strategy—providing all retrieved memories as one flat, unstructured list in context (“all-in context”)—with alternative structured prompt formats. In these structured formats, retrieved memories are partitioned and labeled by domain, so the model sees an organized, domain-separated memory layout at inference time. The intervention is purely at inference: no model weights or memory contents are changed, only the way memories are presented in the prompt.
AI.result: Across all seven evaluated models and tasks in PersistBench, structuring the prompt by partitioning memories into domains consistently reduces cross-domain leakage compared with the all-in unstructured baseline, while maintaining utility on tasks where relevant memory use is beneficial. Their best-performing structured format yields an average reduction of 8.8% in cross-domain leakage relative to the standard all-in context method, indicating that prompt structure alone can meaningfully constrain undesired cross-domain influence of memories. Effects on memory-induced sycophancy are studied conceptually and empirically within this same framework, though the abstract emphasizes leakage reduction results most strongly.
AI.conclusion: Prompt-level structuring of long-term memories—specifically, partitioning them by domain when injecting them into the model context—can mitigate important safety and reliability issues in memory-augmented LLMs without requiring model retraining or changes to stored data. This simple inference-time change reduces cross-domain leakage while preserving the utility of personalization and memory use, demonstrating that careful memory formatting is a practical, lightweight control mechanism for deployed conversational assistants. The work underscores that how memories are represented to the model is as important as what is stored, and motivates further exploration of structured memory prompts for reducing sycophancy and other memory-related failure modes.

title: Cultivar: A Contrastive and Locale-Oriented Translation Benchmark for Investigating Contamination and Localisation Robustness
summary: Multilingual translation benchmarks are typically sourced in English and translated into other languages, treating language pairs as the unit of evaluation---a design that is prone to contamination over time and overlooks locale and cultural considerations. We therefore advocate for source-contrastive evaluation and instantiate it with Cultivar, a localised subset of FLORES, which enables locale-specific translation evaluation. When paired with unlocalised counterparts, performance discrepancy allows the probing of data contamination and localisation robustness. We benchmark 32 open-weight models and find that MT-specialised models are less robust, a few models potentially overfit FLORES, and models tend to translate US content better than that of other locales, regardless of language.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Cultivar, a localized subset of the FLORES benchmark, to enable source-contrastive, locale-aware multilingual translation evaluation and to detect data contamination and localization robustness issues in MT models.
AI.motivation: Existing multilingual translation benchmarks are usually created by translating English source texts into other languages and treating each language pair as the evaluation unit. This design is vulnerable to benchmark contamination over time (models seeing test data during training) and ignores important locale and cultural differences within the same language. These limitations make it hard to reliably evaluate modern multilingual translation systems, especially for locale-specific usage (e.g., US vs other country variants and cultures).
AI.method: The authors propose a source-contrastive evaluation setup, where the same or related content is localized for different locales and used as distinct evaluation sources. They instantiate this idea with Cultivar, a localized subset of the FLORES benchmark that includes locale-specific versions of content. By comparing model performance on localized vs unlocalized or US-centric content, they probe for (1) data contamination/overfitting to existing benchmarks like FLORES and (2) robustness of models to localization and cultural variation. They evaluate 32 open-weight machine translation models under this framework.
AI.result: Across 32 open-weight translation models, they find that models specialized for machine translation are less robust to localization variations than more general models, that some models show signs of overfitting or contamination with FLORES data, and that models generally perform better when translating US-localized content than content from other locales, even when the language is the same.
AI.conclusion: Cultivar and the proposed source-contrastive, locale-aware evaluation framework reveal systematic weaknesses and biases in multilingual translation models, including reduced robustness in MT-specialized systems, potential test set contamination, and a performance bias toward US-localized content. The work argues that future MT evaluation should move beyond simple language-pair benchmarks sourced from English and incorporate locale and cultural variation to more accurately assess real-world translation performance.

title: Query-Only Backdoor Attacks on Self-Evolving Skills via Trajectory Poisoning
summary: Agentic skills improve large language model (LLM) agents by encoding reusable procedures for complex tasks.
