However, manually authored skills often adapt poorly to long-horizon tasks and changing environments. To address the limitation, self-evolving skill systems have been developed to automatically construct and update skills from execution trajectories, shifting skill acquisition from external marketplaces to a trusted evolution pipeline. By replacing external skill acquisition with trusted internal construction, self-evolving skill systems reduce exposure to skill injection attacks that rely on direct skill manipulation. However, this skill evolution pipeline may introduce a new attack surface in which an attacker can indirectly steer skill evolution by inducing compromised trajectories through agent interactions. To demonstrate the threat, we propose Trajectory Backdoor Attack (TBA), a query-only attack that steers a trusted skill-evolution pipeline toward producing a backdoored skill. Specifically, we craft attacker-submitted queries to lead the agent to perform the target action and explicitly state the corresponding activation condition in the trajectory. We repeat the same condition-action pattern across diverse triggered tasks, while leaving clean queries unchanged, encouraging the evolver to consolidate the pattern as a reusable trigger-dependent rule into the evolved skill. Experiments on three benchmarks across two skill-evolution systems using four open- and closed-source backbone models demonstrate that TBA reliably implants conditional backdoors while preserving clean-task utility, matching or even surpassing direct skill injection. The results reveal a critical vulnerability in trajectory-driven skill evolution.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that self-evolving skill systems for LLM agents can be backdoored via query-only manipulation of their training trajectories, revealing a new security vulnerability.
AI.motivation: LLM agents are increasingly augmented with reusable, agentic skills, but manually designed skills do not scale to long-horizon, changing environments. Self-evolving skill systems that automatically learn skills from trajectories are emerging as a scalable, more secure alternative to downloading external skills. However, the security of this evolution pipeline itself has not been rigorously examined, and there is a need to understand whether attackers can exploit trajectory data to implant backdoors without direct access to the skill repository.
AI.method: The authors define a new threat model where an attacker can only submit queries to an LLM agent whose skills are evolved from its own execution trajectories. They introduce Trajectory Backdoor Attack (TBA), which constructs specially crafted queries that consistently cause the agent to execute a chosen malicious action under a clearly articulated trigger condition. These trigger-action pairs are embedded into many diverse tasks so that the skill-evolution mechanism will infer a reusable conditional rule and store it as a backdoored skill while normal (clean) queries remain unaffected. They implement TBA across three benchmarks, two trajectory-based skill-evolution systems, and four different LLM backbones (both open- and closed-source) to evaluate effectiveness and stealthiness.
AI.result: Across all evaluated settings, TBA successfully induces the skill-evolution pipeline to learn conditional backdoor behaviors while maintaining high performance on clean tasks. The attack’s success rate rivals or even exceeds that of more direct skill injection methods that modify skills explicitly. At the same time, overall utility degradation on non-triggered inputs remains minimal, making the backdoor hard to detect by standard performance checks.
AI.conclusion: Trajectory-based skill evolution, though seemingly safer than importing external skills, introduces a distinct and serious attack surface. An adversary with only query access can manipulate the trajectories used for skill learning and implant trigger-conditional backdoors into evolved skills. This finding implies that systems relying on self-evolving skills must incorporate additional defenses—such as trajectory sanitization, anomaly detection, or robust evolution algorithms—to prevent or mitigate trajectory backdoor attacks.

title: Structured Phonological Representations for Audio-Articulatory rtMRI Speech Classification
summary: Real-time MRI makes it possible to observe vocal-tract articulation during speech, but mapping these articulatory patterns to phonetic and phonological categories remains challenging. We investigate whether PhonoQ, an audio-based model trained to recognize structured phonological features, provides useful information for audio--articulatory modeling. Specifically, we extract representations from PhonoQ's Conformer module, whose training is shaped by supervision for manner, place, voicing, and vowel features. Using articulatory contours with synchronized audio-derived features, we compare WavLM-large and HuBERT-large baselines with models that incorporate PhonoQ-derived representations. Across unseen-speech and unseen-subject settings, these features improve macro-F1 for phonological targets including manner, place, voicing, vowel height, and vowel backness, and also improve fine-grained 39-phoneme classification. In a contour-only inference setting, audio-derived teacher supervision yields modest but consistent gains over contour-only training, indicating that phonological information from synchronized audio can be partially transferred to articulatory models. Finally, posterior analyses show interpretable surface-sensitive patterns consistent with flapping-like /t/ realizations, /t/-/r/ retraction or affrication, and nasal place assimilation.

AI.tldr: The paper evaluates whether phonologically supervised audio representations (from PhonoQ) help map real-time MRI articulatory data to phonological and phonetic categories, showing improved classification over strong self-supervised audio baselines and some transfer of phonological information to contour-only models.
AI.motivation: Real-time MRI can capture detailed vocal-tract movements during speech, but it is difficult to translate these continuous articulatory patterns into discrete phonetic and phonological labels (e.g., manner, place, vowel height). Existing audio representations (e.g., from self-supervised speech models) are not explicitly trained to encode phonological structure, potentially limiting their usefulness for articulatory-phonological modeling. The authors aim to see if an audio model trained with explicit phonological supervision (PhonoQ) can provide richer, more structured features that better bridge the gap between articulation and phonological categories, especially in challenging generalization settings like unseen speech and unseen speakers.
AI.method: The authors use synchronized real-time MRI articulatory contours and audio. They extract internal representations from PhonoQ’s Conformer module, which is trained with supervision to recognize phonological features such as manner, place, voicing, and vowel properties. These PhonoQ-based features are incorporated into models predicting phonological categories from articulatory contours, and compared against strong audio baselines using WavLM-large and HuBERT-large representations. They evaluate performance on multiple tasks: classification of phonological features (manner, place, voicing, vowel height, vowel backness) and more fine-grained 39-phoneme classification, under both unseen-speech and unseen-subject generalization regimes. They also test a contour-only inference setup where audio-derived features are used as teacher signals during training but not at test time, to probe whether phonological information can be transferred to purely articulatory models. Finally, they perform posterior analyses of model outputs to interpret how well the learned patterns align with known phonological surface phenomena.
AI.result: PhonoQ-derived representations improve macro-F1 scores over WavLM-large and HuBERT-large baselines for multiple phonological targets, including manner, place, voicing, vowel height, and vowel backness. The models also achieve better accuracy on fine-grained 39-phoneme classification. In the contour-only inference setting, supervision from the audio-based phonological teacher leads to modest but consistent performance gains compared to models trained solely on articulatory contours, indicating successful partial transfer of phonological information from audio to articulatory space. Posterior analyses of model outputs reveal interpretable, surface-sensitive phonological patterns, such as realizations consistent with /t/ flapping, /t/-/r/ retraction or affrication, and nasal place assimilation, suggesting that the system captures meaningful allophonic and assimilation processes.
AI.conclusion: Phonologically supervised audio representations from PhonoQ provide useful structure for bridging the gap between real-time MRI articulatory patterns and phonological/phonetic categories. Compared to strong self-supervised audio baselines, they yield better performance on phonological feature and phoneme classification tasks, generalizing to unseen speech and speakers. Moreover, phonological information encoded in synchronized audio can be partially transferred to purely articulatory models using teacher supervision, offering a path toward more phonologically informed articulatory modeling even when only articulatory data are available at test time. The learned models exhibit interpretable behavior that reflects known phonological processes, indicating that this approach captures linguistically meaningful articulatory-phonological mappings.

title: StructReward: Efficient Structured Process Rewards for Self-Correcting Multimodal Reasoning
comment: 9 pages, 3 figures. Yifan Li and Ruxin Sun contributed equally
summary: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has emerged as an effective approach for improving multimodal reasoning. However, most existing methods evaluate an entire response using a binary reward based only on final-answer correctness, thereby discarding the supervision available in intermediate reasoning steps. Process reward models offer finer-grained feedback, but they typically rely on separately trained verifiers, costly chain-of-thought annotations, or online judging by large language models (LLMs). In this work, we introduce StructReward, a compute-efficient framework that provides dense reinforcement signals through structured step-level reward alignment. StructReward represents each generated solution as a sequence of reasoning steps and aligns them with process-labeled reference steps using lightweight numerical, symbolic, and lexical matching rules. The aligned labels are aggregated into a dense process reward and combined with final-answer consistency and output-validity rewards through a gated Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) objective. We further recycle policy rollouts into complementary supervision for response comparison and reflective self-correction, rather than discarding them after policy updates. Separately, we use a strong LLM to rewrite sampled correct trajectories into reflection-oriented training instances, further strengthening the policy's ability to evaluate and refine its reasoning. Since reward computation is performed online without an additional learned verifier or external LLM judge, StructReward substantially reduces the computational overhead of multimodal reinforcement learning. Experimental results show that structured process supervision and rollout recycling provide an efficient path toward self-improving multimodal reasoning.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes StructReward, a compute-efficient reinforcement learning framework that provides dense, step-level rewards for multimodal reasoning by aligning generated reasoning steps with labeled reference steps, eliminating the need for separate verifiers or online LLM judges.
AI.motivation: Existing RL with verifiable rewards approaches mainly use a binary reward based on final-answer correctness, wasting rich supervision available in intermediate reasoning steps. Process reward models can exploit these steps but usually require expensive components such as separate verifiers, CoT annotations, or online judging by large LLMs, all of which introduce significant computational and annotation overhead. The authors aim to develop a method that captures fine-grained process supervision while remaining compute-efficient and not reliant on extra learned verifiers or external LLM calls.
AI.method: StructReward models each solution as a sequence of reasoning steps and aligns these generated steps with process-labeled reference steps using lightweight numerical, symbolic, and lexical matching rules. From this alignment, it derives dense step-level (process) rewards, which are then aggregated and combined with final-answer correctness and output-validity rewards within a gated Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) objective. Additionally, the method recycles policy rollouts as training data for response comparison and reflective self-correction instead of discarding them. A strong LLM is also used offline to rewrite correct trajectories into reflection-oriented examples, teaching the policy to evaluate and refine its own reasoning. All reward computation is done online via rules rather than via an extra learned verifier or external LLM judge.
AI.result: Experiments demonstrate that incorporating structured process-level supervision together with rollout recycling significantly improves multimodal reasoning performance in a compute-efficient manner. The approach shows that dense step-level rewards and self-reflective training can effectively enhance self-improvement in multimodal RL systems while greatly reducing the need for costly verifiers or LLM-based judges.
AI.conclusion: StructReward provides an efficient and scalable way to integrate fine-grained process rewards into multimodal reinforcement learning. By using structured step alignment, rule-based reward computation, and recycling of rollouts for reflective supervision, it achieves stronger multimodal reasoning with lower computational overhead, illustrating a practical path toward self-improving reasoning models without reliance on heavy external verifiers or online LLM judging.

title: PragMatch: Separating Pragmatic Incongruity from Cross-Modal Mismatch in Large Vision-Language Models
summary: Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) have demonstrated strong performance on multimodal benchmarks, yet it remains unclear whether they genuinely reason about relationships between images and text or rely on superficial correlations, known as shortcut learning. This question is particularly important for multimodal sarcasm detection, where successful prediction depends on recognizing pragmatic incongruity rather than treating sarcasm as simple image-text mismatch. We introduce PragMatch, a controlled benchmark of 3,000 image-text pairs derived from MMSD2.0, including original sarcastic examples and constructed literal and hard-negative pairs. We identify influential shortcut cues through systematic masking and evaluate their impact through targeted injection experiments. Our results show that LVLM predictions are sensitive to lexical, OCR-derived and stylistic cues, with injected surface signals causing substantial changes in model predictions despite unchanged underlying image-text relationships. Our findings reveal limitations in current LVLMs while PragMatch provides a systematic testbed for evaluating multimodal pragmatic reasoning beyond surface-level image-text alignment.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces PragMatch, a controlled benchmark to test whether large vision-language models (LVLMs) truly perform pragmatic, multimodal reasoning for sarcasm detection or rely on superficial shortcut cues, revealing current models’ over-reliance on surface lexical, OCR, and stylistic signals.
AI.motivation: Although LVLMs perform well on many multimodal benchmarks, it is unclear if they genuinely reason about the relationship between images and text or instead exploit superficial correlations (shortcut learning). This issue is especially critical in multimodal sarcasm detection, where recognizing sarcasm requires understanding pragmatic incongruity between modalities, not just detecting simple mismatches. Existing datasets and evaluations do not adequately isolate and test this deeper pragmatic reasoning, so the authors aim to create a controlled setup to probe and diagnose these capabilities and limitations.
AI.method: The authors construct PragMatch, a benchmark of 3,000 image-text pairs derived from the MMSD2.0 dataset. For each original sarcastic example, they create corresponding literal and hard-negative pairs to carefully control the underlying image-text relationships. They perform systematic masking experiments to identify which surface cues (e.g., specific lexical items, OCR text from images, stylistic patterns) most strongly influence LVLM predictions. They then run targeted injection experiments, adding or altering these cues while keeping the core image-text relationship the same, to measure how much these superficial changes sway model outputs.
AI.result: The experiments show that LVLMs’ sarcasm predictions are highly sensitive to surface-level features such as particular lexical cues, text extracted via OCR, and stylistic markers. Injecting these cues—without changing the underlying pragmatic relation between image and text—leads to large shifts in model predictions. This demonstrates that model decisions are driven substantially by shortcut cues rather than robust reasoning about multimodal pragmatic incongruity.
AI.conclusion: The study concludes that current LVLMs exhibit clear limitations in multimodal pragmatic reasoning and often rely on shortcut learning for sarcasm detection. PragMatch serves as a rigorous testbed to diagnose and quantify this behavior, enabling more precise evaluation of whether future models truly understand pragmatic relationships beyond surface-level image-text alignment. The benchmark is positioned as a tool to drive development and assessment of models with deeper multimodal reasoning abilities.

title: LLMVisor: A Real-Time Latency Attribution Model for Multi-Tenant LLM Serving
summary: As LLM inference shifts to multi-tenant GPU clusters, co-batching improves throughput but obscures per-tenant usage and limits control. Enabling fractional sharing of the inference engine requires a real-time, per-request attribution primitive that is accurate and light enough to run inside the scheduling loop. We present LLMVisor, a roofline-guided latency attribution model that captures the memory-bound and compute-bound phases via a concise piecewise-linear form over features proportional to FLOPs and memory I/O traffic. LLMVisor decomposes batch latency into additive, per-request shares and runs efficiently at microsecond scale. We evaluate LLMVisor across Llama 3.1-8B and Qwen 2.5-14B/32B on A100/H100 GPUs under varying tensor parallelism and workload mixes. Compared to a token-count baseline, LLMVisor attains near-perfect R-squared and reduces relative error by up to 2.5x and 3.3x at p90 and p99, respectively, for prefill, and by up to 3.5x and 4.4x for decode, despite batching variability and sequence divergence.

AI.tldr: LLMVisor is a lightweight, roofline-guided model that attributes batched LLM inference latency to individual requests accurately enough to be used inside the scheduler.
AI.motivation: In multi-tenant GPU clusters serving LLMs, providers rely heavily on co-batching to increase throughput. However, batching mixes multiple tenants’ requests, making it hard to know how much GPU time or latency each tenant actually consumed. Simple proxies like token counts are inaccurate, especially when requests diverge in sequence length and when batching patterns change over time. For fair billing, throttling, and scheduling, operators need a fine-grained, real-time attribution of latency and resource usage to each request, without incurring high overhead or requiring intrusive profiling.
AI.method: The paper introduces LLMVisor, a latency attribution model guided by a roofline performance perspective. It models LLM inference as alternating memory-bound and compute-bound phases, and approximates each phase with a compact piecewise-linear function defined over features proportional to FLOPs and memory I/O (e.g., operations and data moved per request). Given a co-batched step, LLMVisor decomposes the observed batch latency into additive per-request shares by solving this piecewise-linear model. The design emphasizes computational simplicity so that inference and attribution can run at microsecond-scale overhead within the scheduler. The authors implement and evaluate LLMVisor across different model sizes (Llama 3.1-8B, Qwen 2.5-14B/32B), GPU types (A100/H100), and tensor-parallelism/workload configurations.
AI.result: Across diverse settings, LLMVisor achieves near-perfect R-squared when predicting per-request latency contributions compared with ground truth. Relative error at the 90th and 99th percentiles is reduced by up to 2.5x and 3.3x, respectively, for prefill phases, and by up to 3.5x and 4.4x for decode phases, compared to a token-count-based baseline. The method remains robust in the presence of batching variability and sequence-length divergence among requests, and the computation fits within a microsecond-scale budget suitable for online use.
AI.conclusion: LLMVisor provides a practical solution to real-time, per-request latency attribution in co-batched, multi-tenant LLM inference. By exploiting a simple roofline-informed, piecewise-linear model over FLOP and memory-traffic features, it can decompose batch latency into accurate per-request shares with negligible overhead. This substantially outperforms naive token-count baselines, enabling more accurate accounting, billing, and control in large-scale LLM serving systems even under heterogeneous and dynamically changing workloads.

title: KGCaRe: Explainable Complex Conditional Question Answering using Automatic Knowledge Graph Construction and Context Retrieval with LLMs
summary:
Answering complex conditional questions using Large Language Models (LLMs) and Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) remains a challenge, particularly in domain-specific contexts where general-purpose LLMs and RAG tend to underperform. We hypothesize that augmenting RAG with unstructured and structured knowledge, extracted from both documents and knowledge graphs (KGs), can improve reasoning and answer accuracy for such tasks.
  To test this, we propose KGCaRe, a hybrid approach that combines neural retrieval with symbolic reasoning over LLM-generated KGs. KGCaRe constructs a KG from documents using a multi-prompt extraction strategy and stores it in a graph database. Simultaneously, the documents are embedded into a vector store to enable neural retrieval. KGCaRe performs innovative iterative graph traversal guided by the LLM to extract relevant triples, prune irrelevant information, and uses additional clue entities to traverse the graph again if the initial traversal does not provide satisfactory context to generate the answer. The relevant triples extracted from the KG in path form, along with semantically retrieved text passages, are then fed into custom KGCaRe prompts to generate answers to the complex conditional questions with explanations.
  We evaluate KGCaRe on two complex conditional QA datasets. Our results on these datasets show that KGCaRe consistently outperforms existing baselines, including Vanilla LLM, Code Prompt, Text Prompt, Think-on-Graph, Vanilla RAG, and HybridContextQA, across multiple LLMs such as Mistral, Mixtral, GPT-3.5, and GPT-4o. We publicly release the software pipeline that we developed to implement the proposed KGCaRe approach.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes KGCaRe, a hybrid RAG + knowledge-graph reasoning framework that builds an LLM-generated KG from documents and iteratively traverses it to answer complex conditional questions more accurately than existing methods.
AI.motivation: Standard LLMs and vanilla RAG struggle with complex conditional questions, especially in domain-specific settings where multi-hop reasoning and precise condition handling are needed. Existing approaches either rely solely on unstructured text retrieval or on pre-existing KGs, which are often incomplete or unavailable. The authors aim to leverage both unstructured documents and structured knowledge, automatically constructing and exploiting a task-specific KG to improve reasoning and answer quality.
AI.method: KGCaRe first constructs a knowledge graph from domain documents using an LLM with a multi-prompt extraction strategy, then stores this KG in a graph database while also embedding the original documents into a vector store. At query time, it combines neural retrieval and symbolic reasoning: the LLM guides iterative graph traversal to extract relevant triples, prunes irrelevant nodes/edges, and, if needed, uses additional clue entities for a second traversal when the first does not give enough context. The system then feeds the selected KG paths plus retrieved text passages into specialized prompts (KGCaRe prompts) to generate answers and explanations.
AI.result: On two complex conditional QA datasets, KGCaRe achieves consistent performance gains over several strong baselines, including pure LLM prompting (Vanilla LLM, Code Prompt, Text Prompt), graph-based reasoning (Think-on-Graph), standard RAG, and a prior hybrid approach (HybridContextQA), and this improvement holds across multiple backbone LLMs such as Mistral, Mixtral, GPT-3.5, and GPT-4o.
AI.conclusion: Automatically constructing and iteratively traversing an LLM-generated KG, then combining its structured paths with neural text retrieval, yields better reasoning and answer accuracy for complex conditional QA than existing LLM- and RAG-based techniques. The released software pipeline enables reproduction and extension of the KGCaRe framework for other domains and models.

title: Not Worth Another Token: Marginal Value Estimation for Efficient Deep Research Agents
summary: Long-horizon research agents solve open-ended tasks through iterative retrieval, aggregation, and synthesis, but context grows rapidly while the marginal value of additional evidence often declines. This leads to unnecessary token cost, higher latency, and noisier inputs for final report generation. We study marginal value estimation for context management in deep research agents and present the first systematic stage-aware comparison of pruning strategies across the pipeline. We evaluate lightweight heuristic criteria and a learned value model at pre-retrieval, post-retrieval, and pre-synthesis stages. Our results show that pruning effectiveness depends more on where pruning is applied than on the specific scoring rule: early pruning yields the largest end-to-end savings, while later pruning mainly refines the final synthesis context. Lightweight heuristics reduce token usage by up to 73% with little quality degradation, learned pruning remains competitive on selected trade-offs, and no single method dominates across quality, efficiency, and faithfulness. These findings provide practical guidance for designing efficient long-horizon agentic systems.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates how to efficiently manage and prune context in long-horizon research agents, showing that when pruning is applied matters more than how, and that simple heuristics can drastically cut token costs with minimal quality loss.
AI.motivation: Long-horizon research agents fetch and process large amounts of information over multiple steps, causing context windows to grow quickly. This leads to high token costs, latency, and noisy inputs, while extra evidence often adds diminishing value. There is a need to understand how to estimate the marginal value of context and prune it effectively across the agent pipeline.
AI.method: The authors perform a systematic, stage-aware comparison of different pruning strategies in deep research agents. They study both lightweight heuristic criteria and a learned value model, applying them at three key stages: pre-retrieval, post-retrieval, and pre-synthesis. They then measure their impact on token usage, quality, efficiency, and faithfulness of the final research outputs.
AI.result: They find that pruning location in the pipeline is more important than the exact scoring rule: pruning earlier (e.g., before retrieval) produces the largest end-to-end savings in tokens and latency, while later pruning mainly fine-tunes the context used for final synthesis. Lightweight heuristic pruning can reduce token usage by up to 73% with little degradation in output quality. Learned pruning strategies remain competitive on some quality–efficiency trade-offs, but no single method is best on all metrics.
AI.conclusion: Effective context management in long-horizon research agents hinges on stage-aware pruning rather than relying on a universally superior scoring method. Simple heuristics, applied early in the pipeline, can deliver major efficiency gains with limited impact on quality, while later-stage pruning helps refine synthesis inputs. The work offers practical design guidance for building efficient, high-performing long-horizon agentic systems and underscores the need to match pruning strategy and placement to desired trade-offs among quality, efficiency, and faithfulness.

title: Comparing British and American Audio Description of Movies
summary: Narrating the visual component of movies is known as audio description. It is a narrative technique designed to enable blind and visually impaired individuals to follow the story. However, it is far more constrained than most narratives: the descriptions not only need to convey the story in the movie, but they must also fit into gaps between dialogue and they need to conform to guidelines that exist in each region. In this work, we compare audio description created in the United Kingdom against audio description created in the United States. We use guidelines written for these two regions, alongside the impressions from a practitioner in the field, to motivate specific hypotheses about the differences. We test these hypotheses against our pre-existing corpus, which provides both human-authored American and British audio description for each of 206 movies. Results provide quantitative evidence to uphold all tested hypotheses, including differences in lexicon, the use of the progressive aspect, the use of passive constructions, the use of subjective adjectives and modifiers, when characters are named, how scenes are cued, and degree of overlap with movie dialogue and music. Our work offers a quantitative lens into the narrative technique of audio description.

AI.tldr: The paper quantitatively compares British and American audio description (AD) for films, confirming systematic stylistic and structural differences shaped by regional guidelines and practice.
AI.motivation: Audio description is vital for blind and visually impaired audiences but is heavily constrained and regionally regulated. Practitioners believe that US and UK AD differ in various linguistic and narrative ways, yet these claims lacked large-scale quantitative evidence. The authors aim to empirically test and characterize these regional differences to better understand AD as a narrative technique and to inform guidelines and practice.
AI.method: The authors formulate hypotheses about US–UK AD differences based on regional guidelines and expert practitioner impressions. They then use a pre-existing corpus containing parallel human-authored American and British AD tracks for 206 movies. Using corpus linguistics and quantitative analysis, they measure features such as lexical choice, progressive aspect usage, passive constructions, subjective adjectives/modifiers, character-naming practices, scene cueing strategies, and overlap with dialogue and music, and statistically test the hypotheses.
AI.result: All formulated hypotheses are supported. Quantitative analysis reveals systematic differences between US and UK AD in lexicon, frequency of progressive aspect, prevalence of passive voice, degree of subjectivity in adjectives and modifiers, timing and manner of naming characters, strategies for cueing scenes, and how much the AD overlaps with existing dialogue and music in the film.
AI.conclusion: Regional guidelines and practices produce distinct narrative styles in audio description in the US and UK, affecting multiple linguistic and structural dimensions. The study demonstrates that AD is not a monolithic technique but varies systematically by region, and it establishes a quantitative foundation for understanding and potentially refining AD guidelines and training. It positions corpus-based analysis as a useful tool for improving accessibility narratives.

title: CAP: A Scalable Benchmark for Evaluating Cross-Site Browser Agents with Complex Actions and Perception
summary: Large language models are increasingly deployed as autonomous agents that interact with the web through browsers. While recent progress has been driven by benchmarks that evaluate end-to-end task success, these evaluations largely overlook two fundamental sources of difficulty in real web browsing: complex actions over rich user interfaces and visual perception of dynamically rendered content, especially in workflows that span multiple websites. We introduce CAP, a scalable benchmark for evaluating browser agents on cross-site, human-like web tasks that require non-trivial UI interactions and visual understanding. Specifically, we adopt a decomposition-and-recomposition pipeline that first abstracts each website into a structured site card capturing user-facing functions, complex execution operations, and perceptual requirements, and then recomposes these components into realistic cross-site workflows. Each task is therefore grounded in multiple specific operations on each website, enabling fine-grained diagnosis. Built on this framework, we construct 420 tasks across 108 real-world websites and 24 domains under careful quality control. Experiments on state-of-the-art browser agents using our verifiable agent-as-a-judge evaluation framework show low success rates and reveal that perception-heavy interactions remain a major bottleneck, exposing substantial gaps between current agents and real-world web browsing demands.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces CAP, a benchmark for testing web-browsing language agents on realistic, cross-site tasks requiring complex UI actions and visual understanding, and shows current agents perform poorly, especially on perception-heavy interactions.
AI.motivation: Existing browser-agent benchmarks mainly test end-to-end task success but fail to capture two key challenges of real web use: (1) executing complex, fine-grained interactions on rich, modern web interfaces and (2) visually perceiving and interpreting dynamically rendered content, particularly when tasks span multiple sites. The authors aim to provide a more diagnostic and realistic evaluation setting for such agents.
AI.method: The authors design CAP, a benchmark built via a decomposition-and-recomposition pipeline. First, they analyze each website and create a structured 'site card' that encodes its user-facing functions, complex operations (e.g., multi-step UI sequences), and perceptual requirements (visual cues, layout, etc.). Then, they systematically recombine these components across sites into realistic, cross-site workflows. They also introduce an agent-as-a-judge, verifiable evaluation framework to automatically assess task success of browser agents on CAP.
AI.result: Using CAP, the authors evaluate state-of-the-art browser agents on 420 tasks covering 108 real-world websites across 24 domains. The agents achieve low success rates overall. Detailed analysis shows that tasks requiring heavy visual perception and complex interactions are especially challenging, indicating that these aspects are primary failure modes.
AI.conclusion: CAP exposes a significant gap between current browser agents and the demands of realistic web browsing. The benchmark’s cross-site, operation-grounded design supports fine-grained diagnosis of agent abilities and highlights perception-heavy UI interactions as major unsolved challenges. This suggests that improving visual understanding and interaction planning is crucial for advancing autonomous web-browsing agents.

title: SWE-Bench ProMax: Benchmarking Agents on Large-Scale Multilingual Code Refactoring
comment: Published as a conference paper at COLM 2026
summary: As AI coding agents take on increasingly complex, long-horizon software engineering tasks, existing benchmarks are rapidly saturating and their evaluation quality has come under serious scrutiny: a recent audit found that nearly 60% of unsolved SWE-bench Verified instances contain flawed tests -- either overly narrow tests that reject correct solutions or overly broad tests that check unstated requirements -- and that frontier models can verbatim reproduce gold patches from training data. Code refactoring, which requires coordinated, behavior-preserving changes across many files, offers a substantially harder and more realistic test of agent capability, yet remains underserved by current benchmarks. We introduce SWE-Bench ProMax, an expert-curated, multilingual code refactoring benchmark of 170 instances drawn from real commits across seven programming languages (Python, Java, TypeScript, Go, C, C++, and Rust). Every instance undergoes rigorous, multi-stage curation that directly addresses the quality problems identified in prior benchmarks: issue descriptions are rewritten from scratch to provide precise, unambiguous specifications, and test suites are manually reviewed to remove overly narrow and overly broad tests. Tasks with insufficient complexity or limited cross-file scope are filtered out, yielding a benchmark of challenging, large-scale refactoring tasks that average 11.4 modified files and 261.6 lines of code per instance, substantially exceeding the scale of existing benchmarks. Experiments with frontier models under two agent scaffolds show that the best model achieves only 41.2% resolve rate, confirming that SWE-Bench ProMax presents a meaningful and unsaturated challenge for current AI coding agents. Our benchmark is available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/swe-bench-promax/SWE-Bench-ProMax.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces SWE-Bench ProMax, a rigorous, multilingual benchmark for large-scale code refactoring tasks that remains unsaturated for current AI coding agents.
AI.motivation: Existing software engineering benchmarks for AI coding agents are saturated and flawed: many test cases are incorrect or misaligned with specifications, and models can memorize gold patches from training data. Moreover, current benchmarks under-represent realistic, complex refactoring tasks that span many files and must preserve behavior. The authors aim to provide a harder, cleaner, and more realistic evaluation setting focused on large-scale, behavior-preserving code refactoring across multiple languages.
AI.method: The authors construct SWE-Bench ProMax, a curated benchmark of 170 refactoring instances sampled from real-world commits in seven programming languages (Python, Java, TypeScript, Go, C, C++, Rust). Each instance passes a multi-stage curation pipeline: (1) issue descriptions are rewritten from scratch to be precise and unambiguous, (2) test suites are manually audited to remove overly narrow and overly broad tests, and (3) low-complexity or limited-scope tasks are filtered out based on cross-file impact and size. The resulting tasks are characterized by larger numbers of modified files and lines of code than existing benchmarks. They then evaluate frontier AI coding models under two different agent scaffolds on this benchmark to measure performance and difficulty.
AI.result: The curated benchmark contains 170 challenging refactoring tasks averaging 11.4 modified files and 261.6 lines of code per instance, which is substantially larger in scope than prior datasets. When evaluated on SWE-Bench ProMax, the best-performing frontier model reaches only a 41.2% resolve rate, indicating that current AI coding agents struggle with these tasks and that the benchmark is far from saturated.
AI.conclusion: SWE-Bench ProMax provides a high-quality, unsaturated, and more realistic benchmark for evaluating AI coding agents on complex, behavior-preserving refactoring tasks across multiple programming languages. By addressing flaws in prior benchmarks—such as poor test quality, ambiguous specifications, and limited task complexity—the benchmark exposes substantial headroom for improvement in agent capabilities and offers a robust platform for future research and development.

title: Estimating Uncertainty in Galaxy Morphology Classification
summary: Astronomers classify galaxy morphology to investigate cosmic evolution. While deep foundation models are increasingly utilized in Galaxy Morphology Classification (GMC), little work has been done on evaluating the uncertainty of GMC results. Uncertainty evaluation is important because astronomical data are inherently noisy due to instrumental and environmental limitations. Also, the continuous evolution of galaxies creates intrinsic morphological ambiguity. However, current foundation models operate as deterministic point estimators, failing to quantify the uncertainty. To overcome this limitation, we propose UEGMC, a post-hoc framework of Uncertainty Estimation for Galaxy Morphology Classification. It categorizes uncertainty in GMC into distinct types by model parameters, astronomical data, reference standards, or intrinsic physical ambiguities, thereby facilitating better classification. Our framework can directly predict uncertainties from representations extracted from the frozen backbones of foundation models, without computationally expensive sampling, therefore enabling fine-grained uncertainty evaluations. Our experimental results demonstrate that UEGMC provides competitive uncertainty quantification performance compared with previous methods.

AI.tldr: They introduce UEGMC, a post-hoc framework to estimate different types of uncertainty in galaxy morphology classification using frozen foundation model features, achieving competitive uncertainty quantification without expensive sampling.
AI.motivation: Galaxy morphology classification is key to studying cosmic evolution, but data are noisy and galaxy shapes are intrinsically ambiguous. Existing deep foundation models for this task act as deterministic classifiers and provide no measure of confidence or uncertainty about their predictions. This is problematic for scientific use, where understanding data quality, model reliability, and intrinsic ambiguity is crucial. The paper is motivated by the need for principled, fine-grained uncertainty estimation specifically tailored to galaxy morphology classification.
AI.method: The authors propose UEGMC, a post-hoc uncertainty estimation framework that operates on top of existing galaxy morphology foundation models. They freeze the backbone of a pre-trained foundation model and use its extracted representations as inputs to an uncertainty predictor. UEGMC disentangles and categorizes uncertainty into multiple types associated with model parameters, observational data quality, reference standards, and intrinsic physical ambiguity in galaxy morphology. It directly predicts uncertainty values from the feature representations without relying on computationally intensive sampling-based methods such as Monte Carlo or ensembles, enabling efficient and fine-grained uncertainty estimation.
AI.result: Experiments show that UEGMC achieves uncertainty quantification quality comparable to or better than existing uncertainty estimation methods for galaxy morphology classification. It provides detailed, type-specific uncertainty estimates while remaining computationally efficient, since it only requires a frozen backbone and a lightweight post-hoc head rather than retraining or heavy sampling.
AI.conclusion: UEGMC is an effective, efficient post-hoc framework for estimating multiple types of uncertainty in galaxy morphology classification built on top of foundation models. By leveraging frozen representations and direct prediction of uncertainties, it delivers fine-grained, competitive uncertainty quantification without expensive sampling. This makes foundation-model-based galaxy morphology analyses more reliable and scientifically usable in the presence of noisy data and intrinsic morphological ambiguity.

title: RA-FinBERT: Rule-aware LoRA adaptation for low-resource financial sentiment classification
comment: 12 pages, 6 figures, 2 tables. Fan Zhang and Jiaming Li are co-first authors. Corresponding author: Jiaming Li
summary: Financial sentiment analysis converts unstructured financial news into quantitative signals that can support market analysis and decision-making. Existing work on resource-efficient financial NLP has largely focused on compressing or adapting pretrained language models, with less attention to combining contextual representations with lightweight rule-derived features. This study develops Rule-Aware FinBERT (RA-FinBERT), a parameter-efficient framework that integrates low-rank adaptation (LoRA) with three continuous VADER-derived sentiment proportions (positive, negative, and neutral) and a source-level metadata feature. The standardized four-dimensional feature vector is directly concatenated with the 768-dimensional final-layer FinBERT [CLS] representation and passed through a lightweight classification head. This design introduces only 1,024 additional trainable weights relative to a structurally matched text-only FinBERT model. RA-FinBERT was evaluated against text-only FinBERT and a lightweight DistilBERT baseline for three-class sentiment classification of financial-news titles and descriptions. On the held-out test set, RA-FinBERT achieved 69.89% accuracy and a macro F1 score of 0.634, compared with 63.44% and 0.526 for text-only FinBERT. Neutral-class recall increased from 18.18% to 45.45%. The framework supports both CPU and GPU execution, offering a lightweight and practical approach to financial sentiment classification under constrained computational resources. These findings indicate that rule-derived sentiment information and source metadata can provide complementary signals to contextual FinBERT representations and improve performance with minimal additional model complexity.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes RA-FinBERT, a resource-efficient financial sentiment classifier that enhances FinBERT with a tiny set of rule-based sentiment and metadata features, achieving notably better accuracy and neutral-class detection with almost no added model complexity.
AI.motivation: Financial sentiment analysis is important for turning unstructured news into quantitative signals for markets, but resource-efficient methods have mostly focused on compressing or adapting large language models alone. Little work has explored combining these contextual models with simple rule-based sentiment signals and metadata, especially under tight computational constraints. The authors aim to show that such lightweight, rule-derived features can meaningfully improve performance with minimal additional parameters.
AI.method: The authors build Rule-Aware FinBERT (RA-FinBERT), which starts from FinBERT with LoRA-based low-rank adaptation and then augments its final-layer [CLS] representation (768 dimensions) with a 4D standardized feature vector. This vector consists of three continuous VADER sentiment proportions (positive, negative, neutral) computed from the text and one source-level metadata feature. The concatenated 772D vector is fed into a small classification head, adding only 1,024 trainable parameters compared with a structurally matched text-only FinBERT. They evaluate RA-FinBERT against a text-only FinBERT and a DistilBERT baseline on three-class sentiment classification (positive, negative, neutral) of financial news titles and descriptions, using both CPU and GPU settings.
AI.result: On the held-out test set, RA-FinBERT attains 69.89% accuracy and a macro F1 score of 0.634, outperforming text-only FinBERT, which scores 63.44% accuracy and 0.526 macro F1, and also outperforming the lightweight DistilBERT baseline. RA-FinBERT particularly improves neutral-class recall from 18.18% to 45.45%, a large gain in detecting neutral sentiment. These gains are achieved with only 1,024 extra trainable parameters beyond the text-only FinBERT structure.
AI.conclusion: The study concludes that augmenting contextual FinBERT representations with simple, rule-derived sentiment scores and source metadata yields complementary information that significantly boosts financial sentiment classification, especially for the neutral class, while keeping the model highly parameter- and resource-efficient. The RA-FinBERT framework is practical for deployment on both CPU and GPU in resource-constrained settings, demonstrating a promising direction for combining neural and rule-based signals in financial NLP.

title: Forgotten History or Test-of-Time? Retrospect and Prospect on RAG from an IR Perspective
summary:
Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) is widely regarded as a novel paradigm born from the limitations of large language models (LLMs)--a mechanism to ground their outputs in external knowledge. This view, however, is incomplete when considered within a broader historical context. In this paper, we argue that the core ideas underlying RAG are not new: foundational concepts such as integrating retrieval and language generation, knowledge augmentation, answer verification, and iterative query (or prompt) refinement had already been studied and instantiated in information retrieval (IR) and question answering (QA) research dating back to the early 2000s, well before the emergence of LLMs.
  We make this case by systematically tracing the intellectual lineage of modern RAG and Agentic RAG back to their classical IR and QA antecedents, and examining why this continuity has gone under-recognized -- a consequence of community fragmentation, shifting terminology, and the recency bias endemic to fast-moving fields. Rather than treating LLMs as the origin point of retrieval-augmented intelligence, we propose viewing them as a new interface layer atop a decades-old QA architecture. This reframing is not merely historical: by situating RAG within the longer trajectory of IR research, we surface underutilized prior work -- on user modeling, answer validation, and query refinement -- that can directly inform next-generation RAG design, reducing unintentional rediscovery and fostering genuine cross-community integration.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) is not a fundamentally new paradigm born with LLMs, but a modern interface on top of long-standing IR and QA ideas from the early 2000s.
AI.motivation: The community often treats RAG and Agentic RAG as novel constructs tightly coupled to LLMs, overlooking decades of prior work in IR and QA that already explored retrieval + generation, query refinement, and answer verification. This recency bias leads to reinvention, fragmented knowledge, and missed opportunities to leverage mature techniques.
AI.method: The authors conduct a historical and conceptual analysis: (1) tracing the intellectual lineage of modern RAG and Agentic RAG back to classical IR and QA research; (2) mapping core components of RAG (retrieval+generation integration, knowledge augmentation, verification, iterative refinement) to earlier systems; and (3) analyzing why this continuity has been under-recognized, focusing on community fragmentation and terminology shifts.
AI.result: They show that the essential mechanisms of RAG and Agentic RAG have clear antecedents in early 2000s IR/QA systems and frameworks. They demonstrate strong conceptual continuity between classical QA architectures and current RAG pipelines, and identify specific areas of prior work—user modeling, answer validation, query reformulation—that are directly applicable to improving modern RAG systems.
AI.conclusion: RAG should be seen not as a new paradigm introduced by LLMs, but as a reconfiguration of a long-standing QA architecture with LLMs serving as a powerful new interface layer. Recognizing this continuity can reduce redundant rediscovery, highlight rich prior work, and encourage cross-pollination between the IR, QA, and LLM communities to design more robust, effective next-generation RAG systems.

title: Fusion Training for Mathematical Generalization in Large Language Models
summary: Thinking Mode Fusion (TMF) enables large language models to support both concise responses and long-form reasoning by unifying a non-thinking mode and a thinking mode within a single model. However, its training dynamics, including the \emph{data ratio} and \emph{training schedule} between the two modes, remain underexplored. In this work, we present a systematic study of TMF by analyzing the effects of the training schedule and data ratio between thinking and non-thinking modes. Focusing on mathematical problem solving, we construct a benchmark with multiple thinking-to-non-thinking data ratios and three training schedules. Our results reveal an asymmetric interaction between the two modes: increasing the ratio of non-thinking supervision reduces the accuracy of the thinking mode. We further show that different training schedules modulate this trade-off and that the optimal schedule depends on the data ratio. Finally, we quantify a negative correlation between non-thinking and thinking mode supervision, highlighting an inherent tension between these two modes. These findings provide practical guidance for designing effective TMF training settings. All code and data are released to support further research at: \href{https://github.com/caocongfeng/Fusion-Bench.git}{\textbf{Fusion Bench}}.

AI.tldr: The paper systematically studies how to best train a single LLM to support both short, direct answers (non-thinking mode) and long-form chain-of-thought reasoning (thinking mode), focusing on data ratio and training schedule between the two modes.
AI.motivation: Thinking Mode Fusion lets one model produce both concise and step-by-step responses, but it is unclear how much training data to allocate to each mode and how to schedule training so that one mode does not harm the other. Understanding this interaction is important for building practical multi-mode LLMs.
AI.method: The authors focus on math problem solving and build a benchmark (Fusion Bench) with multiple predefined ratios of thinking vs non-thinking supervision and three different training schedules. They train models under these controlled settings and systematically compare performance of both modes, analyzing interactions, trade-offs, and correlations between them.
AI.result: They find an asymmetric interaction: increasing the proportion of non-thinking (concise) supervision degrades the accuracy of the thinking mode. Different training schedules change the severity of this trade-off, and which schedule works best depends on the chosen data ratio. They also quantify a negative correlation between thinking and non-thinking supervision performance, indicating inherent tension between them.
AI.conclusion: There is an inherent trade-off between supporting strong chain-of-thought reasoning and concise answering within a single model; more non-thinking supervision tends to hurt the thinking mode. Training schedules can partially manage this trade-off, and the paper’s empirical results offer practical guidance on choosing data ratios and schedules when training TMF models. The released Fusion Bench resources enable further systematic research on Thinking Mode Fusion.

title: TRACE-Memory: Public-Conditioned Retrieval and Utility-Aware Evidence Admission for Personalized Generation
comment: 9 pages, 4 figures, and 6 tables. Submitted to the 41st AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence (AAAI 2027)
summary: Personalized generation systems retrieve user history by request--memory relevance and inject it into the model context. Yet relevant history may concern the wrong preference aspect, duplicate public information, or provide insufficient support. We argue that personal memory should be used only when it adds utility beyond a public-only response. We propose TRACE-Memory, a two-stage framework for selective personalization. Stage 1 queries for user-specific information missing from the request and public context, then retrieves a coverage-oriented candidate pool. Stage 2 admits a compact subset of source-traceable evidence units, or the empty set, according to response-level incremental utility. We progressively train the query-generation and evidence-admission policies through structured SFT initialization, reduced-space stage-wise GRPO warm-up, and nested multi-sample Joint GRPO. Across 4,500 Controlled and Natural tasks from Goodreads, Amazon Reviews, and Reddit, TRACE-Memory consistently outperforms random and lexical memory use, improves over semantic retrieval, remains competitive with frontier-LLM memory pipelines as local generator capacity increases, and conditions evidence admission on public-context sufficiency, supporting selective rather than default personalization.

AI.tldr: TRACE-Memory proposes a selective personalization framework that only uses personal memory when it adds utility over public context, via a two-stage retrieval and evidence admission process optimized with structured SFT and GRPO variants.
AI.motivation: Existing personalized generation systems naively retrieve and inject user history based solely on request-memory relevance, which can surface the wrong preference aspects, duplicate public information, or offer little real support. There is a need for a principled way to decide when and how personal memories should be used so that personalization is beneficial rather than noisy or redundant.
AI.method: TRACE-Memory introduces a two-stage framework: (1) a query-generation stage that identifies user-specific information missing from the request and public context, then retrieves a coverage-oriented pool of candidate memories; and (2) an evidence-admission stage that selects a compact subset (possibly empty) of source-traceable evidence units based on their incremental utility to the final response. The policies for query generation and evidence admission are progressively trained using structured supervised fine-tuning (SFT) for initialization, followed by reduced-space, stage-wise GRPO for warm-up, and finally a nested multi-sample Joint GRPO optimization.
AI.result: On 4,500 controlled and natural tasks drawn from Goodreads, Amazon Reviews, and Reddit, TRACE-Memory outperforms random, lexical, and semantic memory retrieval baselines, stays competitive with memory pipelines built on stronger frontier LLMs as the local generator model improves, and demonstrates that its evidence admission is sensitive to whether the public context alone is sufficient to answer the query.
AI.conclusion: Selective personalization that conditions on the incremental utility of personal memories, rather than default inclusion based on relevance alone, yields better and more robust performance. TRACE-Memory offers a practical framework that decides when to use personal memory, how much to use, and which pieces to admit, achieving consistent gains over simpler memory retrieval strategies while avoiding unnecessary personalization when public context is adequate.

title: Consilience for Verifier-Free Test-Time Scaling
summary:
Test-time scaling often uses an external verifier, such as compilers and test cases in coding or trained value functions in robotics applications, to obtain high-quality rollouts. Verifier-free test-time scaling (or VF-TTS) is gaining extensive attention as a mechanism to enhance Large Language Model (LLM) reasoning, primarily because we do not have access to such high-quality verifiers in many real-world applications. Among existing VF-TTS methods, confidence-based VF-TTS methods, which compute and rank rollouts solely by confidence, are particularly promising. Such methods introduce near-zero overhead for sample evaluation and require minimal access to internal model states, making the methods highly flexible across models and tasks.
  In this paper, we demonstrate a critical limitation of existing confidence-based VF-TTS methods by showing that such methods catastrophically break down on complex tasks. We observe a very interesting phenomenon: uniformly high confidence frequently indicates a failure to explore, favoring confidently wrong answers. To address this, our core insight is that robust cognitive search requires a specific confidence trajectory pattern: such methods perform exploratory branching at the beginning, as manifested by low initial confidence, and converge to a high final confidence solution. To implement this insight, we introduce consilience, a novel selection framework that explicitly evaluates the temporal asymmetry of confidence in reasoning. We operationalize this via a combinatorial metric that actively penalizes high initial confidence while strictly demanding final certainty. Extensive experiments covering both graduate-level mathematics problems and free-form code generation demonstrate that consilience effectively outperforms existing baselines, validating our novel perspective on completion confidence.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that existing verifier-free test-time scaling methods that rely purely on confidence fail on complex reasoning tasks and proposes a new framework, consilience, which evaluates the temporal pattern of confidence over a reasoning trajectory to improve selection of high-quality LLM outputs.
AI.motivation: Verifier-free test-time scaling is attractive because many real-world tasks lack strong external verifiers, and confidence-based methods are especially practical due to low overhead and weak access requirements. However, their behavior on complex reasoning tasks is poorly understood, and there is a need to identify and fix their failure modes in order to make test-time scaling broadly reliable and robust.
AI.method: The authors empirically analyze confidence-based VF-TTS methods and identify a pathology where uniformly high confidence often corresponds to lack of exploration and confidently wrong answers. Based on this, they propose consilience, a new selection framework that explicitly models the temporal asymmetry of confidence in a reasoning trajectory. Consilience uses a combinatorial metric that penalizes high initial confidence (encouraging early exploration) while requiring high final confidence (ensuring convergence) and then selects rollouts according to this pattern.
AI.result: On challenging benchmarks involving graduate-level mathematics reasoning and free-form code generation, consilience consistently outperforms existing confidence-based VF-TTS baselines. The experiments show that incorporating the shape of the confidence trajectory leads to better selection of correct and robust solutions than using static or uniformly high-confidence criteria.
AI.conclusion: Static, purely confidence-based verifier-free test-time scaling methods break down on complex tasks because they cannot distinguish genuine reasoning from overconfident but shallow exploration. Modeling confidence as a trajectory and enforcing a pattern of low initial and high final confidence improves cognitive search and yields better LLM reasoning performance. The consilience framework demonstrates that temporal structure in confidence is a valuable signal for robust test-time scaling without external verifiers.

title: What Keeps Agent Skills from Being Reusable? Evidence from 138K SKILL.md Files
summary: Under the current standard, Agent Skills are SKILL.md files that combine instructions with supporting resources, enabling Large Language Model (LLM) agents to reuse procedures beyond a single conversation. Yet many public skills appear to originate from a single task, repository, or conversation, even when they are shared as reusable components. We analyze this gap across 138,133 public SKILL.md files from 20,556 repositories using a two-tier defect taxonomy grounded in the official specification and best-practice guidance. We find that 91.8% of skills contain at least one detected defect, with stable estimates across lenient and strict thresholds (88.8-94.6%). The dominant failures are ordinary packaging problems rather than exotic attacks: weak routing metadata, bloated or non-actionable bodies, and poor resource organization. A deterministic routing stress test over 20,000 skills shows the functional impact: skills with valid routing metadata are retrieved more reliably from startup descriptions than skills with routing defects. Defect rates vary by platform and provenance: specification-aware skills contain fewer defects, while AI-marked skills show more safety and portability problems. Lightweight enforcement and repair experiments support a quality-assured generation workflow combining spec-aware prompting, lightweight linting, automated repair, and safety gating.

AI.tldr: The paper empirically audits over 138k public SKILL.md files for LLM agents, finds that over 90% have specification or quality defects (mostly mundane packaging/metadata issues), shows that routing metadata quality measurably affects retrieval in a stress test, and proposes a lightweight quality-assurance workflow (spec-aware prompting, linting, automated repair, safety checks) to improve skill generation and reuse.
AI.motivation: Although SKILL.md-based agent skills are intended to be reusable components for LLM agents, many appear to be ad-hoc artifacts from single tasks or repos rather than robust, general-purpose skills. There is little empirical understanding of how well public skills comply with the specification or support safe, reliable reuse. The authors want to systematically characterize defects, their impact on retrieval/routing, and how to improve skill quality at scale.
AI.method: The authors collect 138,133 public SKILL.md files from 20,556 repositories and design a two-tier defect taxonomy derived from the official SKILL specification and best-practice guidelines. They implement automated detectors for multiple defect types (e.g., routing metadata issues, content/actionability problems, resource organization flaws) and measure defect prevalence under lenient and strict thresholds. They run a deterministic routing stress test on 20,000 skills, comparing retrieval success for skills with valid vs. defective routing metadata when given startup descriptions. They stratify defect rates by platform/provenance and run small-scale enforcement and repair experiments using spec-aware prompting, linting, automated fixes, and safety gating to assess a proposed quality-assured generation workflow.
AI.result: 91.8% of analyzed skills have at least one detected defect, with robustness checks showing 88.8–94.6% defect rates under different thresholds. Most issues are not adversarial but mundane packaging problems like weak or missing routing metadata, overly long or non-actionable instruction bodies, and disorganized or inappropriate supporting resources. The routing stress test shows that skills with valid routing metadata are more reliably retrieved from startup descriptions than skills with routing defects, demonstrating functional consequences. Defect rates differ across platforms and provenance: skills written with awareness of the SKILL specification tend to have fewer issues, whereas AI-generated or AI-marked skills have more safety and portability defects. Enforcement and repair experiments indicate that combining spec-aware prompting, automated linting, targeted repairs, and safety checks can meaningfully reduce defect rates with modest overhead.
AI.conclusion: Public SKILL.md-based agent skills are currently low-quality in aggregate, with pervasive but mostly ordinary packaging and metadata defects that undermine reliable routing and reuse. However, these issues are diagnosable and fixable: simple, deterministic checks plus spec-aware generation practices substantially improve compliance and safety. The authors conclude that the SKILL ecosystem should adopt lightweight quality-assurance workflows—centered on specification-based taxonomies, linting, automated repair, and safety gating—to make skills more reusable, portable, and dependable for LLM agents.

title: Decoding-Level Taboo: A Diagnostic Stress Test for LLM Robustness
summary:
Large language model evaluations typically focus on performance under nominal conditions, creating an illusion of capability where models comfortably walk a narrow, highly optimized generation corridor. In real-world deployments, however, complex system prompts, safety guardrails, and structural constraints continuously force models off this nominal path, driving a divergence between benchmark scores and deployment performance. To address this issue, we introduce Decoding-Level Taboo, a zero-prompt diagnostic stress test that intervenes directly in logit space at runtime, forcing models out of their nominal paths. By dynamically masking primary candidate tokens at word boundaries, Taboo forces machine circumlocution.
  Evaluating Taboo across several open-weight model families reveals that off-path robustness is heavily influenced by both parameter scale and post-training instruction alignment, with robustness generally improving with model size and alignment. Beyond the results presented in this paper, Taboo provides a novel primitive for generating diverse synthetic datasets, stress-testing runtime safety guardrails, and auditing model reliability prior to real-world deployment.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Decoding-Level Taboo, a stress-test that perturbs language model decoding in logit space, forcing them off their usual generation paths to measure robustness and reveal deployment-time weaknesses unnoticed by standard benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Current LLM evaluations mostly test models in ideal, nominal prompting conditions, which overstates their reliability because real-world deployments involve complex prompts, safety layers, and structural constraints that push models away from their optimized generation patterns. There is a need for a systematic way to probe how models behave when taken off their preferred decoding paths and to quantify their robustness under such perturbations.
AI.method: The authors propose Decoding-Level Taboo, a zero-prompt diagnostic technique that operates directly at decoding time in logit space. At word boundaries, the method dynamically masks out the model’s top candidate tokens (the primary choices), forcing the model to avoid its usual next-word preferences and instead generate alternative continuations, effectively inducing machine circumlocution. They then apply this intervention to several open-weight model families of varying sizes and alignment levels to measure performance degradation and behavioral changes under off-path decoding.
AI.result: Experiments across multiple open-weight LLM families show that robustness to the Taboo perturbation varies significantly with both parameter count and the extent of post-training instruction alignment. In general, larger and better-aligned models maintain coherence and task performance better when their preferred tokens are masked, indicating greater off-path robustness compared to smaller or less-aligned models.
AI.conclusion: Decoding-Level Taboo is an effective diagnostic stress test for probing LLM robustness under non-nominal decoding conditions. It reveals that off-path robustness tends to improve with model size and instruction alignment, highlighting an important dimension of capability not captured by standard benchmarks. The technique also serves as a general primitive for generating diverse synthetic data, evaluating runtime safety guardrails, and auditing model behavior before real-world deployment.

title: Hierarchical Self-Improvement: A Framework for Task-Specific Evolvable Agent Harnesses
summary: Modern LLM agents are often improved by modifying prompts, tools, or workflows manually, while the executable scaffold surrounding the model---the \emph{harness}---is typically treated as a fixed artifact after deployment. This work studies an alternative where the harness is \emph{task-specific and continuously evolvable}: each task family maintains its own harness, which is hot-swapped across iterations through a fixed task-injection seam and rewritten using environment feedback. We introduce \textbf{Hierarchical Self-Improvement (HSI)}, a framework in which a single frozen LLM $M$ operates across three hierarchical scopes: a task harness $H$ that executes tasks, an evolver that rewrites $H$, and a meta-evolver that rewrites the evolver's strategy code under a frozen outer anchor. A thinking-on/off design isolates the contribution of harness evolution by disabling reasoning during task execution while enabling it during self-modification. HSI is bounded by two factors: a \emph{feedback-fidelity bound}, since evolution requires informative reward signals to guide selection, and a \emph{backbone capability bound}, since harness redesign cannot overcome limitations of the frozen model. On BALROG with DeepSeek-V4-Flash-Preview as the frozen backbone, HSI achieves consistent gains over the initial harness on moderate-difficulty tasks ($+39.3$ on BabyAI, $+33.0$ on Crafter, $+25.0$ on TextWorld, and $+15.0$ on MiniHack, all in raw \% Progress), while obtaining strong held-out generalization on BabaIsAI sub-suites ($0.98$ best-test on BreakStop and $1.00$ on GoTo from a $20\%$ unseen split). On tasks beyond the backbone's capability (NLE), harness evolution provides no improvement. These results demonstrate task-specific harness evolution as a viable axis for improving frozen LLM agents under clear empirical limits. Code is available at https://github.com/TailinZhou/hsi.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Hierarchical Self-Improvement (HSI), where a frozen LLM continuously rewrites its own task-specific harness and the strategy that updates it, yielding significant performance gains on several benchmark environments while being limited by feedback quality and the base model’s capability.
AI.motivation: Most improvements to LLM agents focus on manual prompt, tool, or workflow engineering, while the surrounding executable harness is treated as static after deployment. The authors want a way for agents to autonomously and continually adapt that harness to specific task families, without fine-tuning the LLM itself, and to understand when such self-improvement works and when it fundamentally cannot help.
AI.method: They introduce HSI, a framework with three hierarchical scopes all powered by a single frozen LLM: (1) a task harness H that interfaces with the environment and executes tasks; (2) an evolver that rewrites the harness H using environment feedback via a fixed task-injection seam; and (3) a meta-evolver that rewrites the evolver’s own strategy code while maintaining an outer anchor. Reasoning is disabled during normal task execution (“thinking off”) and enabled during self-modification (“thinking on”) to isolate the effect of harness evolution. The framework is analyzed under two theoretical bounds: feedback-fidelity (quality of reward signals) and backbone capability (limits of the frozen LLM). They evaluate on BALROG benchmarks using DeepSeek-V4-Flash-Preview as the frozen backbone.
AI.result: On moderate-difficulty tasks, HSI substantially improves over the initial harness in raw percentage progress: +39.3 on BabyAI, +33.0 on Crafter, +25.0 on TextWorld, and +15.0 on MiniHack. It also shows strong held-out generalization within the BabaIsAI suite, achieving 0.98 best-test accuracy on BreakStop and 1.00 on GoTo with 20% of levels held out. On very hard tasks (NLE) that exceed the backbone LLM’s inherent competence, harness evolution yields no improvement, empirically confirming the backbone capability bound.
AI.conclusion: Task-specific, continuously evolvable harnesses provide a powerful and practical axis for improving frozen LLM agents, enabling them to autonomously refine their execution and adaptation strategies within a hierarchical self-improvement loop. However, the benefits are constrained by the informativeness of environmental feedback and the inherent capabilities of the underlying LLM, implying that harness evolution complements but cannot replace backbone model quality. The framework and code demonstrate a viable path toward more adaptive agentic systems without model retraining.

title: From Values to Benchmarks: Evaluating Large Language Models for Governmental Use in Dutch
summary: Large language models are increasingly being deployed in governmental settings, yet few existing evaluation frameworks jointly reflect the values of public administration and the linguistic requirements of non-English contexts. We present the "Grip on LLMs" framework, a systematic evaluation suite for Dutch governmental use developed in collaboration with domain experts from a major Dutch municipal organisation. Through an advisory board process, user research, and a survey of the users of a civil-servant chatbot, we identify six evaluation dimensions (factuality, honesty, social bias, energy consumption, cost, and training data transparency) and operationalise them into a benchmark suite covering more than 30 multilingual and Dutch-specific models. Our results reveal that no single model excels across all dimensions, and that trade-offs are unavoidable: higher quality consistently comes at greater environmental impact and financial cost, while bias remains largely independent of both. We further find that factuality (whether a model answers correctly) and honesty (whether a model acknowledges what it does not know) are governed by distinct properties, with high factuality not implying high honesty. To make these findings actionable for non-technical audiences, we release a publicly accessible, user-friendly model overview designed for the full range of stakeholders involved in governmental LLM selection, from engineers to policymakers.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a practical evaluation framework and benchmark (“Grip on LLMs”) for assessing large language models specifically for Dutch governmental use, covering multiple dimensions beyond accuracy and highlighting trade-offs between quality, cost, and environmental impact.
AI.motivation: Large language models are being adopted by governments, but existing evaluations rarely align with public-sector values (e.g., accountability, sustainability, fairness) or address non-English languages like Dutch. Public administrations need a structured, comprehensible way to compare LLMs that reflects their own priorities and usage contexts, so they can choose models responsibly and transparently.
AI.method: The authors co-designed an evaluation framework with domain experts from a large Dutch municipal organisation. Using an advisory board, user research, and a survey of civil-servant chatbot users, they distilled six key evaluation dimensions: factuality, honesty, social bias, energy consumption, cost, and training data transparency.
