We evaluated 4,238 scenarios across multiple domains and complexity tiers. Measurement validation met rigorous psychometric standards. Agreement among five independent model families was nearly perfect, with an intraclass correlation coefficient of 0.997 and a kappa of 0.971. Known-groups validity demonstrated large separation between tiers, with an eta-squared of 0.587 and all pairwise comparisons significant at p less than .001. Factor analysis revealed a dominant complexity construct, with loadings between 0.87 and 0.96 across three frameworks, while interactivity formed a weaker secondary dimension at 0.34. Discriminant validity was limited by a strong relationship between complexity and text length that persisted after controlling for tier, yielding a partial correlation of 0.86. This constrains construct purity but does not undermine the instrument's tier-grading function. Model analyses showed a negative association between throughput and schema pass rate (r = -0.967, p = .007, n = 5), suggesting a speed-quality trade-off, though largely driven by one high-throughput model. Llama 4 Maverick generated scenarios fastest at 134 per minute versus 25 for DeepSeek Chat V3.2, but underproduced complex-tier scenarios, whereas DeepSeek Chat V3.2 balanced domain coverage with high schema compliance. The system demonstrated strong psychometric properties, enabling reliable classification into Simple, Moderate, and Complex tiers and providing the measurement infrastructure needed for downstream cognitive assessment of AI systems

AI.tldr: The paper presents an automated, LLM-based pipeline to generate and psychometrically validate decision-making scenarios, achieving highly reliable classification into Simple, Moderate, and Complex tiers.
AI.motivation: Cognitive decision-making research needs many decision scenarios with precisely controlled complexity, but manual creation is slow, inconsistent, and subject to human bias. There is no scalable, standardized way to generate and validate large banks of scenarios across domains and complexity levels for assessing both humans and AI systems.
AI.method: The authors built an automated pipeline that uses large language models (LLMs) to generate structured decision scenarios and then evaluate their complexity. They defined a composite complexity framework grounded in established task-complexity theories, applied it to 4,238 generated scenarios spanning multiple domains and three complexity tiers (Simple, Moderate, Complex), and conducted psychometric validation. This included inter-model agreement analyses across five LLM families, known-groups validation across tiers, factor analysis to examine latent complexity dimensions, and tests of discriminant validity (especially vs. text length). They also compared LLMs’ generation speed, schema compliance, and distribution of complexity tiers.
AI.result: The complexity ratings showed extremely high agreement across five independent LLM families (ICC = 0.997, kappa = 0.971). Known-groups validity was strong, with large, statistically significant separation between the three complexity tiers (η² = 0.587; all pairwise p < .001). Factor analysis indicated a dominant complexity factor with high loadings (0.87–0.96) across three theoretical frameworks and a weaker secondary factor related to interactivity (loading ≈ 0.34). Discriminant validity was constrained because complexity correlated strongly with text length (partial r = 0.86 even after controlling for tier). In model-level analyses, there was a strong negative correlation between generation throughput and schema pass rate (r = -0.967, p = .007, n = 5), suggesting a speed–quality trade-off. Llama 4 Maverick generated scenarios fastest (134/min) but produced fewer complex-tier scenarios, while DeepSeek Chat V3.2 generated more balanced and schema-compliant outputs at slower speed (25/min).
AI.conclusion: The automated LLM-based pipeline can reliably generate and grade decision scenarios into Simple, Moderate, and Complex tiers with robust psychometric support. While the complexity construct is partially confounded with text length, this does not impair the tool’s practical use for tier classification. The system provides scalable measurement infrastructure for downstream cognitive assessment of AI systems and potentially for human decision-making research, though future work should address discriminant validity and disentangle complexity from length.

title: Business Arena: Benchmarking LLM Agents in a Realistic Marketplace
summary: Running a business is a challenging form of intelligent work. Operators must infer opportunities from partial signals, commit capital under uncertainty, adapt to delayed outcomes in a changing market, and satisfy regulatory obligations before trading legally. Frontier LLM agents can increasingly complete complex workflows, yet business-related capabilities are rarely evaluated in existing agent benchmarks. We introduce \textbf{Business Arena}, a controlled environment where an AI agent runs a cross-border shop, buying from suppliers and selling to buyers over a long horizon. We ground the arena in real Alibaba.com sourcing data and market conditions calibrated from authoritative sources. Delayed and coupled consequences make individual business decisions difficult to judge, but their combined outcome is measurable through profit. Because profit alone cannot explain why an agent succeeds or fails, we compare agents with human-designed strategies to estimate available opportunity, use skill-level metrics to reveal underlying strengths and weaknesses, and trace realized gains and losses to the actions that produced them. We use mechanism ablations to establish that strong results reflect genuine business intelligence rather than neglect or simulator-specific shortcuts. We evaluate 15 frontier models and find a ninefold difference in mean final net worth. Even the best model falls behind human-designed strategies, indicating that business operation remains challenging for LLM agents. Skill-level analysis reveals operating styles, from margin-focused premium sellers to high-turnover wholesalers and customer-service specialists, while action-level attribution identifies the sourcing, pricing, and recovery decisions that create or destroy value. Together, Business Arena takes a first step toward a realistic and trustworthy testbed for evaluating end-to-end business agents.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Business Arena, a realistic benchmark where AI agents run a cross-border online shop, enabling end-to-end evaluation of business capabilities of LLM agents via profit and skill-level metrics.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM agent benchmarks rarely test real-world business capabilities such as running a company over time, despite frontier LLMs increasingly handling complex workflows. Business operation involves long-horizon, uncertain, and regulated decision-making, which is underexplored yet commercially important. There is a need for a realistic, trustworthy testbed that goes beyond toy tasks and can reveal why agents succeed or fail rather than only measuring surface-level outcomes.
AI.method: The authors build Business Arena, a controlled simulation environment where an AI agent operates a cross-border shop that buys from suppliers and sells to buyers over a long horizon. The environment is grounded in real Alibaba.com sourcing data and market conditions calibrated from authoritative sources. They design metrics: overall profit and net worth; comparisons with human-designed baseline strategies to estimate achievable opportunity; skill-level metrics capturing strengths and weaknesses (e.g., sourcing, pricing, customer service, recovery); and action-level attribution of gains and losses to specific decisions. They perform mechanism ablations to ensure strong performance cannot be achieved through neglecting tasks or exploiting simulator artifacts. They then evaluate 15 frontier LLM models within this environment.
AI.result: In Business Arena, different LLM agents show large performance variation, with up to a ninefold difference in mean final net worth across 15 frontier models. Even the best-performing model underperforms carefully designed human strategies. The analysis reveals diverse operating styles among models, including margin-focused premium sellers, high-turnover wholesalers, and customer-service-oriented agents. Action-level attribution highlights which concrete sourcing, pricing, and recovery decisions generate or destroy value. Ablation studies indicate that strong performance corresponds to genuine business competence rather than shortcutting or exploiting quirks of the simulator.
AI.conclusion: Business Arena provides an initial realistic, end-to-end benchmark for evaluating the business-operation abilities of LLM agents. The environment and metrics expose both overall profitability and fine-grained skills and decision-level contributions. Current frontier models still lag behind human-designed strategies, suggesting that running a business remains a challenging task for LLM agents. The benchmark can guide future research on more capable and reliable business agents by revealing specific behavioral patterns, strengths, and weaknesses.

title: Theory-Guided Deception Detection: A RAG-Based Artificial Intelligence Exploration
summary: The current work developed seven Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) models based on leading deception theories and compared how deception judgments were made relative to baseline models. Across 700 statements drawn from five published deception datasets, four large language models (gpt-4o, claude-sonnet-4-6, ollama/llama3, deepseek-v4-flash), and two run-types (RAG vs. baseline), a total of 39,200 deception judgments were rendered. Detection accuracies were consistent with typical human accuracies and not statistically different across RAG (54.5%) and baseline models (54.6%). RAG-based models (57.0%) were less truth-biased than baseline models (59.7%), but the effect size was quite small. Theoretical perspective mattered little for accuracy yet mattered substantially for response bias, which ranged from highly lie-biased (the verifiability approach, 32.2%) to highly truth-biased (truth-default theory, 88.1%). Content effects and model effects further moderated the results. Theory-guided AI judgments are unreliable with current parameters, yet they might show promise with additional datasets, model testing, and theory-to-data matching.

AI.tldr: The paper evaluates seven theory-guided RAG deception-detection models against baseline LLMs and finds that, with current settings, they match human-like but low accuracy and mainly shift response biases rather than improve detection.
AI.motivation: To test whether grounding large language models in established deception theories via Retrieval-Augmented Generation can improve automated lie detection beyond baseline LLM performance and human-level accuracy, and to understand how different theoretical frameworks influence not just accuracy but also truth/lie response biases.
AI.method: The authors built seven RAG models, each aligned with a different leading deception theory, and compared them to non-RAG baselines. They used 700 statements from five existing deception datasets and four LLM backbones (gpt-4o, claude-sonnet-4-6, ollama/llama3, deepseek-v4-flash). For each statement–model–run-type combination, the system produced deception judgments, totaling 39,200 decisions. They then statistically compared accuracies, truth-bias levels, and the moderating effects of content and model type across conditions.
AI.result: Overall detection accuracy was around chance-plus, similar to human norms (~54–55%), and there was no statistically significant difference between RAG (54.5%) and baseline (54.6%) setups. RAG-based models were slightly less truth-biased (57.0% truth responses) than baselines (59.7%), but with a very small effect size. Different theoretical RAG variants produced markedly different response biases—from strongly lie-biased (verifiability approach, 32.2% truth responses) to strongly truth-biased (truth-default theory, 88.1%). Specific datasets (content) and backbone models further moderated accuracy and bias outcomes.
AI.conclusion: At present, embedding deception theories into LLMs via RAG does not yield more accurate deception detection than baseline models; it primarily changes response bias patterns rather than improving correctness. Theory choice strongly shapes whether models tend to call more lies or more truths but does not robustly raise accuracy above typical human levels. Thus, theory-guided AI deception judgments are unreliable with current parameters, although the approach could become more promising with better datasets, systematic model evaluation, and closer alignment between theoretical assumptions and the empirical data used for testing.

title: MedCalc-R1: Knowledge-Guided Reward Framework for Medical Mathematical Reasoning
summary: In Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) frameworks for mathematical reasoning tasks, floating-point results are typically evaluated using a tolerance-based reward. However, this strategy suffers from challenges such as difficulty in threshold calibration, unstable training dynamics, and limited accuracy, especially in clinical scenarios. To address these limitations, we propose a knowledge-guided hybrid reward framework (\textsc{MedCalc-R1}). Specifically, we introduce a knowledge verification reward mechanism that enforces explicit generation of computational formulas, which are further validated by an external verifier to enhance interpretability and reasoning reliability. Furthermore, we design a hybrid soft-hard reward scheme combining a hard constraint based on clinical safety thresholds with a soft, precision-sensitive reward that progressively guides learning within the acceptable range. Experimental results demonstrate that our method significantly outperforms existing baselines in both reasoning accuracy and generalization capability, validating the effectiveness and applicability in safety-critical domains.

AI.tldr: The paper presents MedCalc-R1, a knowledge-guided hybrid reward framework that improves reinforcement learning for mathematical reasoning in safety-critical clinical scenarios by enforcing formula verification and combining hard clinical thresholds with soft precision rewards.
AI.motivation: Existing RLVR approaches for mathematical reasoning typically rely on tolerance-based rewards for floating-point outputs. These methods suffer from difficult threshold tuning, unstable training, and limited accuracy, especially where clinical safety is crucial. There is a need for a reward design that is both interpretable and reliable, and that better aligns with domain knowledge and safety constraints.
AI.method: The authors propose MedCalc-R1, a knowledge-guided hybrid reward framework. First, they introduce a knowledge verification reward that requires the RL agent to explicitly generate the underlying computational formulas, which are then checked by an external verifier to ensure correctness and improve interpretability. Second, they design a hybrid soft-hard reward structure: a hard component enforces clinical safety thresholds, while a soft, precision-aware component provides graded feedback within the safe range to gradually refine model predictions.
AI.result: Experiments show that MedCalc-R1 achieves higher reasoning accuracy and better generalization than existing RLVR baselines on mathematical reasoning tasks in clinical contexts. The improvements are consistent across evaluations, indicating that the framework yields more stable and reliable training outcomes in safety-critical settings.
AI.conclusion: By integrating explicit formula verification with a hybrid soft-hard reward scheme grounded in clinical safety knowledge, MedCalc-R1 overcomes key limitations of tolerance-based RLVR rewards. The framework enhances interpretability, stability, and accuracy, demonstrating its practical value for safety-critical mathematical reasoning tasks in medicine and potentially other domains requiring verifiable, high-stakes computations.

title: PolicyKG: An Agentic LLM Pipeline for Translating Institutional Policies into SHACL Knowledge Graphs
comment: 23 pages, 3 figures, 4 tables. Under review at IJCKG 2026, Bangkok, Thailand
summary:
Institutional policies stay in natural language while the systems that check compliance demand machine-readable constraints. Bridging that gap is still done by hand.
  PolicyKG closes the loop. It is an LLM pipeline that reads a policy PDF, classifies each sentence as an obligation, permission, or prohibition, lifts the label into first-order deontic logic, and emits SHACL constraints. Four stages run on a LangGraph state machine with per-stage validators. The piece that matters most is the Corpus Adapter: a YAML vocabulary registry that grounds LLM predicates in a target ontology. Retargeting to a new domain means swapping the registry, not retraining a model.
  On the Asian Institute of Technology Policies and Procedures corpus (1,663 sentences, 443 rules), PolicyKG reaches 86.9% deontic classification accuracy (Cohen's kappa = .709). Three annotators independently re-label a 50-item sample and agree at Fleiss' kappa = .844. SHACL shape correctness on a 69-shape subset is F1 = .866. The FOL path handles 79.2% of rules; the rest go through a direct NL-to-SHACL fallback.
  We audited every one of the 443 rules for second- or higher-order constructs. An automated regex checklist flagged none, and a first-author pass on the 92 FOL-fallback cases confirmed the same. The exact upper 95% Clopper-Pearson bound on the true HOL rate is 0.67%. This is an audit finding for one corpus, not a proof of FOL sufficiency for institutional policy.
  Swapping the AIT registry for a GDPR registry raises exact property alignment from 1/15 to 11/15 (Fisher's exact p < .001; Cohen's h = 1.53). On the LexDeMod lease-contract benchmark (N = 200), Macro F1 drops to .370 because lease English uses "shall be entitled" for permission -- exactly the vocabulary mismatch registry swap is meant to fix. Repeated runs produce hash-identical SHACL outputs.

AI.tldr: PolicyKG is an LLM-based pipeline that converts natural-language institutional policies into machine-readable SHACL constraints via deontic logic, using a pluggable vocabulary registry to adapt across domains.
AI.motivation: Institutional policies are written in natural language, but automated compliance-checking systems require precisely structured, machine-readable rules. Currently, the transformation from prose policies to formal constraints is manual, labor-intensive, error-prone, and hard to adapt across domains. The paper aims to automate this translation, quantify how well first-order logic suffices for typical institutional policies, and provide a reusable mechanism to adapt the system to new policy domains without retraining models.
AI.method: The authors design PolicyKG, a four-stage LLM-based pipeline orchestrated with a LangGraph state machine and per-stage validators. The stages: (1) read and segment policy PDFs into sentences; (2) classify each sentence as obligation, permission, or prohibition (deontic classification); (3) lift the deontic-labeled text into first-order deontic logic (FOL) formulas; and (4) generate corresponding SHACL shapes as machine-readable constraints. A central component, the Corpus Adapter, is a YAML-based vocabulary registry that maps LLM predicates to a target ontology, enabling domain retargeting by swapping registries. The system includes a fallback path that directly maps natural language rules to SHACL when FOL lifting fails. They evaluate on the Asian Institute of Technology Policies and Procedures corpus, perform a detailed audit for higher-order logic constructs, test registry swapping with a GDPR registry, and benchmark on the LexDeMod lease-contract dataset.
AI.result: On the AIT corpus (1,663 sentences, 443 rules), PolicyKG achieves 86.9% accuracy for deontic classification with Cohen’s kappa of 0.709. Human annotators show high agreement on a 50-item sample (Fleiss’ kappa 0.844). For a 69-shape subset, SHACL shape correctness yields F1 = 0.866. The FOL-based path successfully handles 79.2% of the rules, with the remaining going through the direct NL-to-SHACL fallback. An audit of all 443 rules finds no second- or higher-order constructs; the upper 95% Clopper-Pearson bound on the true higher-order logic rate is 0.67%. Swapping from an AIT to a GDPR registry substantially improves property alignment from 1/15 to 11/15 (Fisher’s exact p < .001; Cohen’s h = 1.53), illustrating the impact of the vocabulary adapter. On the LexDeMod lease-contract benchmark (N=200), Macro F1 drops to 0.370, attributed to vocabulary mismatch such as the phrase “shall be entitled” for permission. The system produces hash-identical SHACL outputs across repeated runs, indicating determinism.
AI.conclusion: PolicyKG demonstrates that an LLM-driven, ontology-grounded pipeline can automatically convert natural-language institutional policies into formal SHACL constraints with reasonably high accuracy, and that most rules in at least one real-world corpus can be captured with first-order deontic logic. The YAML-based Corpus Adapter offers a practical way to retarget the system to new domains by reconfiguring vocabulary mappings instead of retraining models, though performance on out-of-domain corpora reveals sensitivity to domain-specific phrasing that the registry is intended to mitigate. The audit results suggest a very low empirical incidence of higher-order constructs in the examined corpus, but the authors stress this is an empirical finding, not a universal proof. Overall, the work closes much of the gap between human-readable institutional policies and machine-readable compliance constraints while highlighting the importance of domain-specific vocabulary alignment.

title: UniMoMo: Expert Merging-Based MoE Acceleration for Large Recommendation Models
summary: Sparse mixture-of-experts (MoE) layers expand recommendation capacity through conditional computation, yet a trained checkpoint still stores and routes over its full expert bank. We study a deployment problem: convert that checkpoint to a smaller standard MoE under an explicit expert budget, without adding a compression-specific online module. To address this, we introduce UniMoMo, a post-training compression framework formulated as a constrained graph coarsening problem. Rather than relying on parameter distance, UniMoMo groups experts based on their functional similarity, using an unlabeled calibration set to measure how similarly experts respond to shared recommendation states. To prevent performance degradation, we introduce a layer-adaptive protection mechanism that restricts the merging of high-traffic experts based on their routing exposure. Across Amazon Beauty, KuaiRec, and TenRec with 2, 4, and 6 MoE blocks, the final four-expert checkpoints obtain source-relative five-run mean NDCG@10 ratios of 99.92%--102.30% and measured A100 speedups of 1.28$\times$--1.63$\times$. An aggressive two-expert, top-1 operating point obtains ratios of 98.36%--104.24% and speedups of 1.47$\times$--2.21$\times$. These endpoint results evaluate the complete conversion-and-adaptation workflow and show that a trained recommendation MoE can be exported at multiple serving budgets.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes UniMoMo, a post-training compression framework that merges experts in sparse MoE recommendation models to meet an expert budget while maintaining accuracy and improving speed.
AI.motivation: Sparse MoE layers improve recommendation capacity via conditional computation but are expensive at deployment because the full bank of experts must still be stored and routed, even when a smaller expert budget is desired. Existing approaches often require extra online modules or rely on parameter-level similarity, which may not reflect functional behavior. There is a practical need to convert a trained, large MoE checkpoint into smaller, standard MoE models tailored to different serving budgets without retraining or complex runtime changes.
AI.method: The authors cast MoE compression as a constrained graph coarsening problem. Each expert is a node; edges represent functional similarity based on how experts respond to the same recommendation states from an unlabeled calibration set. UniMoMo clusters/merges experts according to this functional similarity while respecting an explicit expert-budget constraint. A layer-adaptive protection mechanism limits merging of high-traffic experts, determined by routing exposure, to avoid harming performance. The framework works post-training, without additional online compression modules, and yields smaller MoE checkpoints compatible with standard serving.
AI.result: On three recommendation benchmarks (Amazon Beauty, KuaiRec, TenRec) with models containing 2, 4, and 6 MoE blocks, UniMoMo compresses to four-expert models that retain or slightly improve ranking quality, achieving 99.92%–102.30% of the original NDCG@10 across five runs, while delivering 1.28×–1.63× speedups on an A100 GPU. A more aggressive configuration with only two experts and top-1 routing still achieves 98.36%–104.24% NDCG@10 ratios and 1.47×–2.21× speedups. These results cover the end-to-end conversion plus adaptation process and demonstrate that multiple deployment operating points are feasible from a single trained MoE model.
AI.conclusion: UniMoMo enables practical post-training compression of recommendation MoE models by merging experts based on functional similarity under an explicit expert budget, while protecting critical high-traffic experts. It delivers substantial inference speedups with negligible or even positive impact on NDCG@10 across several datasets and architectures. The approach allows a single large MoE checkpoint to be exported into multiple smaller, budget-aware MoE variants for flexible deployment, without needing specialized online compression modules or full retraining.

title: Business Truth, not SQL Accuracy: A Rule-Gated 7B Analytics Agent Outperforms a Direct-Prompted 32B Baseline
comment: 20 pages, 7 figures, 11 tables. Benchmark, code, run records, pre-registration and one-command reproduction: https://github.com/k-w-lee/query_proof
summary: LLM analytics agents are evaluated on SQL syntax accuracy, but production failures look different: questions with two valid business definitions, questions the warehouse cannot answer, deprecated columns after a schema change, and queries that execute successfully while returning the wrong business number. No execution-match metric can score them. This paper introduces WarehouseReliabilityBench, 400 frozen tasks over two synthetic warehouses in which roughly half the correct responses are a clarification, an abstention or a refusal, with pinned denominators and a pre-registered paired bootstrap fixing each claim verb before the numbers existed. QueryProof, a 7B agent, uses rules derived from a semantic layer and physical catalog to determine its behaviour, and gates every answer on deterministic post-execution checks. On an 80-task synthetic test split evaluated once, QueryProof outperforms a direct-prompted 32B baseline by +0.237 [+0.112, +0.375] Business Truth Rate at 71.0% lower cost per correct answer; against a cost-matched few-shot baseline the accuracy gain holds but the cost difference does not resolve. This compares systems rather than model sizes: the 32B baseline receives none of the scaffolding. False success falls from 0.754 to 0.351 of returned answers, and no wrong number was returned on an answerable task (0 of 24), though 13 answers went to questions requiring clarification or abstention. Removing the routing layer changes little (0.562 against 0.537), so the result does not depend on escalation. Routing tuned on validation over-abstains on test, and the fitted confidence model loses to the heuristic it replaced. Resampling template families rather than tasks widens both accuracy intervals to include zero, so the effect's direction is better supported than its magnitude. The gain tracks the deterministic layer, though no component ablation was run.

AI.tldr: Paper proposes WarehouseReliabilityBench to evaluate LLM analytics agents on realistic warehouse reliability rather than just SQL accuracy, and introduces QueryProof, a 7B agent with semantic rules and post-execution checks that improves business-truth accuracy and reduces harmful failures vs larger baselines at lower cost.
AI.motivation: Existing evaluations of LLM analytics agents mostly focus on SQL syntax or execution-match metrics, which miss realistic failure modes in production such as ambiguous business definitions, unanswerable questions, schema drift, and superficially successful but numerically wrong queries. There is a need for a benchmark and methods that capture these reliability and safety aspects in data warehouses.
AI.method: 1) Construct WarehouseReliabilityBench: 400 frozen tasks over two synthetic warehouses, with many tasks whose correct behaviour is to clarify, abstain, or refuse; use pinned denominators and a pre-registered paired bootstrap to fix claims before results exist. 2) Propose QueryProof, a 7B LLM-based analytics agent using rules derived from a semantic layer and physical catalog to decide when to answer, clarify, or abstain, and applying deterministic post-execution checks on each query result. 3) Compare QueryProof against direct-prompted and few-shot 32B baselines without scaffolding, analyzing Business Truth Rate, cost per correct answer, false success rate, and behavior of routing and confidence components.
AI.result: On an 80-task synthetic test split evaluated once, QueryProof beats a direct-prompted 32B baseline by +0.237 Business Truth Rate with confidence interval [+0.112, +0.375] and achieves 71.0% lower cost per correct answer; compared to a cost-matched few-shot 32B baseline, the accuracy gain remains but the cost advantage disappears. QueryProof cuts the fraction of false successes from 0.754 to 0.351 and returns no wrong numeric answer on answerable tasks (0/24), though it sometimes abstains or asks for clarification when it could have answered (13 such cases). Ablations show that removing the routing layer has minor impact (accuracy 0.562 vs 0.537), routing tuned on validation over-abstains on test, and a learned confidence model underperforms a heuristic. Resampling by template families widens confidence intervals to include zero, so the direction of improvement is clearer than its exact magnitude. Gains appear aligned with the deterministic checking/semantic layer rather than escalation, although no detailed component ablation was done.
AI.conclusion: WarehouseReliabilityBench provides a more realistic and safety-oriented benchmark for analytics agents by emphasizing clarification, abstention, and business-truth correctness rather than mere SQL syntax or execution success. QueryProof, a 7B system that integrates semantic-layer rules and deterministic post-execution validation, can outperform larger LLMs without scaffolding in terms of business truth, harmful failure reduction, and cost efficiency. However, the precise effect size is uncertain, routing and confidence components require further tuning, and more granular ablations are needed to isolate which deterministic elements drive the gains.

title: A QUBO-Inspired Computational Framework for Airport Landside Bottleneck Diagnosis and Dynamic Dispatch Optimization
summary: Airport landside traffic centers connect terminal arrivals with taxis, ride-hailing vehicles, private cars, buses, metro services, parking facilities, and terminal-area roadways. Peak arrivals can create coupled congestion across passenger queues, vehicle queues, pickup berths, storage areas, and access roads. This study proposes a QUBO-inspired computational framework for bottleneck diagnosis and dynamic dispatch in this setting. Shanghai Pudong International Airport and Hangzhou Xiaoshan International Airport serve as case airports. A five-minute state model links passenger arrivals, vehicle supply, pickup berth service, vehicle storage, and road capacity. Bottleneck diagnosis uses service intensity, road demand saturation, bottleneck frequency, queue severity, shadow-price leverage, and a composite congestion severity index. Two dispatch schemes are tested under consistent demand inputs: finite-action model predictive control and quadratic-unconstrained-binary-optimization-inspired simulated annealing. In the strong-peak baseline scenario, the QUBO-inspired method reduces the final passenger queue from 3445 to 2477 passengers at Shanghai Pudong and from 2053 to 1482 passengers at Hangzhou Xiaoshan. Case results indicate different dominant bottlenecks. Shanghai Pudong is more affected by road saturation, whereas Hangzhou Xiaoshan is more affected by pickup berth service. Robustness tests under demand, supply, service, road-capacity, modal-share, and random-noise perturbations show retained queue-reduction benefits under the tested uncertainty levels.

AI.tldr: The paper develops and tests a QUBO-inspired optimization and control framework to diagnose and mitigate coupled congestion in airport landside traffic centers, significantly reducing passenger queues under peak conditions at two major Chinese airports.
AI.motivation: Airport curbside and landside areas face complex, tightly coupled congestion among passengers, vehicles, berths, storage areas, and roads, especially during peak arrivals. Traditional, siloed approaches (e.g., focusing only on curbside management or only on road capacity) struggle to capture these interactions and to dynamically respond to rapidly changing conditions. There is a need for an integrated, data-driven framework that can both identify which subsystem is the true bottleneck at any moment and compute effective real-time dispatch decisions that reduce total congestion and passenger delays.
AI.method: The study builds a five-minute resolution state model of airport landside operations, capturing interactions between passenger arrivals, vehicle supply (taxis, ride-hailing, private cars, etc.), pickup berth service capacity, vehicle storage capacity, and road capacity. For diagnosis, it defines several indicators such as service intensity, road demand saturation, bottleneck frequency, queue severity, shadow-price leverage, and a composite congestion severity index to identify systemic bottlenecks. For control, it compares two dynamic dispatch schemes under the same demand: (1) a finite-action model predictive control (MPC) approach, and (2) a quadratic-unconstrained-binary-optimization (QUBO)-inspired simulated annealing method that searches over discrete dispatch decisions. The framework is calibrated and applied to Shanghai Pudong and Hangzhou Xiaoshan airports, and its robustness is tested via scenario perturbations in demand, supply, service, road capacity, modal split, and random noise.
AI.result: Under a strong-peak arrival scenario, the QUBO-inspired simulated annealing dispatch yields substantial reductions in final passenger queues: from 3445 to 2477 at Shanghai Pudong and from 2053 to 1482 at Hangzhou Xiaoshan, relative to the baseline. The analysis reveals that the dominant bottlenecks differ between the two airports: Shanghai Pudong is mainly constrained by road saturation, while Hangzhou Xiaoshan is constrained more by pickup berth service capacity. Robustness experiments demonstrate that these queue-reduction benefits persist under a variety of perturbations to key parameters and stochastic elements, indicating that the framework performs well despite uncertainty.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that a QUBO-inspired dynamic dispatch framework, integrated with a detailed, short-interval landside state model and systematic bottleneck diagnostics, can effectively mitigate coupled congestion in airport landside traffic centers. It not only reduces passenger queues under peak-demand conditions but also reveals airport-specific bottleneck structures, such as road saturation vs. pickup berth limitations. The demonstrated robustness under multiple scenarios suggests that the approach is promising for practical deployment and could be adapted to other multi-modal, capacity-constrained transport hubs beyond the case airports studied.

title: ComboShoppingBench: Evaluating LLM Agents for Budget-Constrained Basket Shopping with Coupons
summary: Real-world shopping often requires constructing a basket of complementary items rather than retrieving a single product. Such combo-shopping tasks arise in device setup, meal preparation, event planning, and group takeout ordering, requiring joint reasoning about item compatibility, availability, store-level requirements, delivery fees, coupons, and budgets. Evaluation is challenging because multiple baskets may satisfy the same request, making exact-match metrics unsuitable, whereas semantic evaluation alone cannot detect infeasible orders, invalid coupon combinations, or incorrect payments. We introduce ComboShoppingBench, an agentic shopping benchmark for open-ended yet verifiable basket construction in a simulated commerce and takeout environment. During task synthesis, an exploration agent constructs a feasible and semantically coherent basket of purchasable products; this witness guides the generation of coupons, budget constraints, user queries, and aligned evaluation rubrics. During evaluation, LLM judges assess semantic satisfaction, response quality, and claim faithfulness, while deterministic validation checks product-ID validity, budget compliance, and coupon optimality. Experiments with diverse LLM agents demonstrate that even strong agents struggle on ComboShoppingBench, highlighting substantial room for improvement in reliable, constraint-aware combo shopping.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces ComboShoppingBench, a benchmark for evaluating AI agents on realistic multi-item, constraint-heavy shopping tasks in simulated commerce and takeout settings.
AI.motivation: Most shopping benchmarks and retrieval tasks focus on selecting a single item, but real-world shopping often involves assembling baskets of multiple complementary items under complex constraints (compatibility, availability, store-level policies, fees, coupons, budgets). Existing evaluation methods are inadequate: exact-match metrics fail because many different baskets can satisfy a request, while purely semantic evaluation cannot reliably detect infeasible orders, invalid coupon use, or incorrect payment calculations. The authors are motivated to create a benchmark that reflects real-world combo-shopping complexity and supports objective, verifiable evaluation of agent performance.
AI.method: The authors build ComboShoppingBench, a simulated commerce and takeout environment for basket-construction tasks. They use an exploration agent during task synthesis to construct a feasible, semantically coherent basket of purchasable products; this basket acts as a witness that guides the automatic generation of associated coupons, budget constraints, user queries, and detailed evaluation rubrics aligned with the witness solution. For evaluation, they combine LLM-based judges, which rate semantic satisfaction, response quality, and faithfulness of claims, with deterministic validators that check product ID validity, budget and store constraints, and coupon correctness/optimality. They then run experiments using diverse LLM-based shopping agents within this environment.
AI.result: The experiments show that a variety of LLM agents, including strong state-of-the-art models, perform poorly on ComboShoppingBench. They often fail to satisfy constraints such as budgets, coupon compatibility, product availability, and payment correctness, even when their responses may look semantically appropriate. This indicates that current LLM agents struggle significantly with reliable, constraint-sensitive combo-shopping tasks in realistic settings.
AI.conclusion: ComboShoppingBench provides a challenging, realistic benchmark for evaluating agentic shopping systems on multi-item, constraint-rich tasks. The combination of open-ended, semantically flexible tasks with deterministic feasibility checks enables more faithful measurement of agent capabilities than either exact-match or purely semantic metrics alone. The poor performance of existing LLM agents on this benchmark underscores that there is substantial room to improve models and tooling for robust, constraint-aware shopping and decision-making agents.

title: Avalon-ToM-Bench: Evaluating Fine-Grained Theory of Mind via Asymmetric Game Mechanics
summary: Theory of Mind (ToM) is essential for agent interactions, yet existing evaluations either rely on static scenarios that oversimplify mental-state reasoning or interactive settings that provide limited diagnostic insight. We present Avalon-ToM-Bench, a fine-grained benchmark that operationalizes ToM through the asymmetric-information mechanics of The Resistance: Avalon. Rather than evaluating end-to-end gameplay, it decomposes ToM into a 2$\times$2 taxonomy -- epistemic versus motivational reasoning crossed with inference versus action -- using human-crafted, perspective-constrained queries. Benchmarking 28 LLMs reveals three insights: 1) Reasoning, not knowledge. Models show strong game-rule comprehension but markedly weaker ToM abilities, isolating failures to social reasoning rather than missing domain knowledge. 2) Expression, not representation. Mechanistic analyses via linear probing and activation steering show that models frequently represent correct mental-state inferences in their hidden states but fail to express them during generation -- linear probes recover 77-82% accuracy versus 62-70% from the models' own chain-of-thought. 3) Policy, not deliberation. Dedicated reasoning training yields substantial improvements whereas test-time chain-of-thought provides only marginal gains (+11.0 versus +1.1 points on average), suggesting that robust ToM depends on a learned reasoning policy rather than increased inference-time deliberation.

AI.tldr: Avalon-ToM-Bench is a fine-grained benchmark based on The Resistance: Avalon to evaluate Theory of Mind (ToM) in LLMs, revealing gaps between internal mental-state representation and expressed reasoning, and highlighting the importance of trained reasoning policies over test-time deliberation.
AI.motivation: Existing ToM evaluations for agents are either static and oversimplified or interactive but not diagnostically precise. There is a need for a benchmark that can precisely decompose and probe different facets of ToM reasoning in language models, disentangling social reasoning ability from domain knowledge and offering interpretability into how ToM is internally represented versus externally expressed.
AI.method: The authors design Avalon-ToM-Bench, a benchmark leveraging the asymmetric information structure of The Resistance: Avalon. They decompose ToM into a 2×2 taxonomy: epistemic vs. motivational reasoning and inference vs. action. They create human-crafted, perspective-constrained queries targeting each cell of this taxonomy. They then evaluate 28 LLMs on these tasks, analyze internal representations using linear probing and activation steering to detect mental-state information in hidden states, and compare different training and inference setups including dedicated reasoning training and test-time chain-of-thought prompting.
AI.result: Across 28 LLMs, the study finds that models understand the game rules well but struggle with ToM-specific social reasoning. Linear probes and activation steering indicate that correct mental-state inferences are often encoded in hidden representations, achieving around 77–82% accuracy, while models’ own chain-of-thought outputs perform worse at about 62–70% accuracy. Additionally, models benefit significantly more from specialized reasoning training (+11.0 points on average) than from added test-time chain-of-thought prompting (+1.1 points).
AI.conclusion: Avalon-ToM-Bench exposes a substantial gap between language models’ internal encoding of others’ mental states and their ability to articulate and act on those inferences. ToM limitations stem less from missing domain knowledge and more from deficiencies in social reasoning and learned reasoning policies. Improving ToM in LLMs likely requires training better reasoning policies rather than simply increasing inference-time deliberation or relying on general knowledge acquisition.

title: Smart Compaction: Predicting Compaction Utility from Lakehouse Table Metadata
summary: Open lakehouse table formats accumulate small data files over time, which degrades query performance. Deciding when compaction is worthwhile remains threshold-driven, but which metadata features actually determine compaction utility is not well understood. We present an open simulation framework that generates 2,376 Apache Iceberg tables spanning three orders of magnitude in file size, extracts 17 metadata features from manifest files without reading data, and trains XGBoost to predict the continuous file-reduction ratio (R2 = 0.998, RMSE= 0.013). The binary compaction decision turns out to be trivially separable by a single partition-level threshold max_files_per_partition> 4, requiring no learned model. Cross-schema validation on 96 TPC-H tables confirms generalisation without retraining (R2 = 0.976). A query benchmark reveals that compaction benefits metadata-heavy queries but can slow full-scan aggregations by reducing task parallelism. All code and data are publicly available.

AI.tldr: They build a simulation and ML-based analyzer for Apache Iceberg compaction, finding that simple metadata thresholds can replace complex models and that compaction helps metadata-heavy queries but can hurt full scans.
AI.motivation: Open table formats for data lakehouses, like Apache Iceberg, accumulate many small files, which slows queries. Existing compaction policies rely on heuristics and thresholds, but it is unclear which metadata features truly indicate whether compaction will be beneficial, and whether ML can meaningfully improve compaction decisions.
AI.method: They design a simulation framework that creates 2,376 synthetic Iceberg tables covering three orders of magnitude in file size. From each table’s manifest metadata, they extract 17 features without scanning data. They then train an XGBoost model to predict a continuous file-reduction ratio (how much compaction will reduce file count). They study both regression performance and the induced binary compaction decision and validate the model across schemas (including 96 TPC-H tables) without retraining. Finally, they run a query benchmark to measure performance impacts of compaction on different query types.
AI.result: The XGBoost model predicts the file-reduction ratio very accurately (R2=0.998, RMSE=0.013) on the simulated tables and generalizes well to TPC-H tables (R2=0.976) without retraining. However, the actual binary decision of whether to compact is almost trivially determined by a simple partition-level rule: compaction is useful when max_files_per_partition > 4. This rule works without any learned model. The query benchmark shows that compaction is beneficial for metadata-heavy queries but can slow down full-scan aggregation queries due to decreased task-level parallelism.
AI.conclusion: For Apache Iceberg table compaction, sophisticated ML modeling of metadata provides little added value over a simple threshold rule derived from metadata: a single partition-level max_files_per_partition > 4 is sufficient for deciding when to compact. Compaction decisions can therefore be automated cheaply using only manifest metadata. However, compaction is not universally beneficial—while it helps metadata-heavy queries, it may hurt full-table aggregations by reducing parallelism. The simulation framework, model, and datasets are released openly to support further work on data layout optimization and compaction policies.

title: Matryoshka Language Model Suites
summary: Training a language model suite classically requires training each model separately and serving them independently. We improve both training and inference efficiency by stacking sub-models of increasing size into a single nested architecture trained end-to-end. This Matryoshka training framework reduces the total parameter count of the suite, enables low-cost distillation from the largest to all smaller sub-models at every training step, and is well-suited for speculative decoding as the draft model is contained within the verifier. We validate our approach by training a Matryoshka suite comprising 500M, 1.5B, and 3B sub-models. Our suite is on par with independently trained baselines on benchmark performance and validation and out-of-domain perplexities, while using 36% less training compute and improving the throughput of speculative decoding by 14-26%. We also ablate key architectural choices, offering guidance for building strong Matryoshka LM suites.

AI.tldr: They propose a single “Matryoshka” nested language model that contains multiple sub-model sizes, achieving similar performance to separately trained models with less compute and faster speculative decoding.
AI.motivation: Conventional LM suites (e.g., 0.5B, 1.5B, 3B) require training and serving each model independently, which is compute-inefficient and complicates distillation and speculative decoding. The authors want a more efficient way to train and deploy multiple model sizes that still match the performance of independently trained models.
AI.method: They design a nested architecture where smaller sub-models are literally contained within larger ones (like Matryoshka dolls). All sub-models (500M, 1.5B, 3B) share parameters in a structured way and are trained end-to-end. This allows low-cost online distillation from the largest to all smaller models at every training step and makes speculative decoding easier because the draft model is a strict sub-model of the verifier. They also run ablations on architectural choices for this nested structure.
AI.result: A Matryoshka suite with 500M, 1.5B, and 3B sub-models matches independently trained baselines on benchmarks and both validation and out-of-domain perplexities, while reducing training compute by 36% and improving speculative decoding throughput by 14–26%.
AI.conclusion: Nested, Matryoshka-style training can replace separately trained LM suites, delivering similar performance with substantially lower training compute and more efficient inference via speculative decoding. Architectural design choices for nesting matter, and their ablations provide guidance for practitioners building such suites.

title: SkillReason: Reasoning-Enhanced Agent Skill Retrieval for Implicit User Requests
summary: Large language model agents increasingly rely on reusable skills to extend their capabilities beyond parametric knowl- edge. However, retrieving the appropriate skill from a large- scale library remains challenging because realistic user re- quests are often concise and underspecified, stating only the task goal while leaving the required capabilities and execu- tion steps implicit. Existing benchmarks provide limited cov- erage of such requests. To address this gap, we introduce SkillReason-Bench, a large-scale cross-domain benchmark containing 3,729 queries and a retrieval corpus of 61,228 skills spanning nine domains. We further propose SkillRea- son, a two-stage framework that uses chain-of-thought rea- soning as training-time supervision for skill retrieval. In Stage I, capability reasoning traces generated by a stronger teacher provide explicit supervision through contrastive learning, re- trieval distribution alignment, and language modeling, en- couraging the retriever to internalize capability reasoning in its query representation. In Stage II, a retrieval-guided GRPO objective encourages the model to explore reasoning trajecto- ries better suited to its own capabilities and more effective for retrieval. At inference, SkillReason directly encodes the orig- inal query without autoregressive CoT generation, preserv- ing efficient query-only retrieval. Extensive experiments on SkillReason-Bench, SkillRet, and SRA-Bench show that Skill- Reason achieves state-of-the-art performance across all three benchmarks, demonstrating that reasoning-enhanced training better bridges the semantic gap between high-level task goals and skill capabilities.

AI.tldr: Introduces SkillReason-Bench and SkillReason, a reasoning-enhanced framework for retrieving reusable skills for LLM agents from large libraries given underspecified user queries, achieving SOTA on multiple benchmarks.
AI.motivation: LLM agents increasingly depend on external, reusable skills or tools, but realistic user queries are short and underspecified, making it hard to retrieve the right skills from large libraries. Existing benchmarks poorly capture this setting, limiting progress on retrieval methods that can infer implicit capabilities and steps from high-level goals.
AI.method:
1) Construct SkillReason-Bench, a large-scale benchmark of 3,729 queries and 61,228 skills across nine domains, where queries are concise high-level goals and skills encode capabilities.
2) Propose SkillReason, a two-stage skill retrieval framework that uses chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning only at training time.
   - Stage I: Use a stronger teacher model to generate capability reasoning traces (CoT) for queries. Train the retriever with (a) contrastive learning, (b) retrieval distribution alignment, and (c) language modeling over these traces so that the query encoder implicitly internalizes capability reasoning in its representations.
   - Stage II: Apply a retrieval-guided GRPO (a policy optimization style) objective so the model explores its own reasoning trajectories that are well matched to its capabilities and beneficial for retrieval quality.
3) At inference, perform efficient query-only retrieval: directly encode the user query without generating CoT, relying on the reasoning-enhanced representation learned during training.
AI.result: SkillReason obtains state-of-the-art performance on three benchmarks: the newly proposed SkillReason-Bench, plus existing SkillRet and SRA-Bench. Results show improved alignment between high-level, underspecified task goals and the capabilities of skills in large libraries, outperforming prior retrievers that lack explicit reasoning-based training signals.
AI.conclusion: By supervising skill retrieval with chain-of-thought style capability reasoning during training—while keeping inference efficient and CoT-free—SkillReason more effectively bridges the semantic gap between users’ high-level task descriptions and the underlying skills an LLM agent should use. The new SkillReason-Bench benchmark further establishes a realistic evaluation setting for underspecified queries across multiple domains, and experiments confirm that reasoning-enhanced training is a powerful paradigm for large-scale skill retrieval.

title: Mismatch Matters: On-Policy Distillation Beyond Token Agreement
summary: On-policy distillation (OPD) has emerged as a core component of modern LLM post-training pipelines, yet we reveal a failure mode: degenerate agreement, where students exploit repetitive loops to achieve near-perfect token agreement with the teacher despite globally flawed responses. We therefore shift our focus from agreement to teacher-student mismatch, and find that mismatch tokens can be mainly categorized into two types: student-excess tokens and student-deficit tokens. Student-excess tokens are generated by the student but assigned near-zero probability by the teacher; their log-ratio corrections grow unbounded and destabilize the update. Student-deficit tokens, in contrast, are preferred by the teacher but rarely sampled by the student; their absence blocks the transfer of the teacher's reasoning patterns. To tackle these mismatch directions, we propose TIDE (Token-level Independent Deficit-Excess correction), which applies bounded Hellinger shaping to suppress the most severe sampled excesses and an analytic teacher top-$K$ injection to restore deficient probability mass without requiring deficit tokens to be sampled. Across mathematical reasoning benchmarks with multiple Qwen3 teacher-student pairs, TIDE consistently outperforms standard OPD and recent token-selection and reward-shaping baselines. Moreover, the gains of TIDE are more pronounced under strong teacher-student mismatch, where it improves Avg@8 from 6.9% to 20.3%, reduces average response length by a factor of 3.6, and substantially reduces formatting failures. Code is available at https://github.com/yzc-666/TIDE

AI.tldr: The paper identifies a critical failure mode in on-policy distillation for LLMs, where students achieve high token-level agreement with teachers via degenerate looping, and introduces TIDE, a token-level correction method that handles teacher-student probability mismatches (excess and deficit tokens) to stabilize training and improve reasoning performance.
AI.motivation: On-policy distillation (OPD) is widely used in post-training LLM pipelines to transfer knowledge from a strong teacher model to a smaller or cheaper student. However, the authors observe that optimizing for token-level agreement can lead to a degenerate behavior: students learn to exploit repetitive loops that match the teacher’s tokens locally but produce globally incorrect or low-quality responses. This shows that naive OPD can fail even when agreement metrics look excellent. The motivation is therefore to understand and fix this failure mode by examining where and how teacher and student token distributions diverge, so that distillation actually transfers reasoning ability instead of superficial agreement patterns.
AI.method: The authors analyze teacher-student token mismatches during OPD, categorizing them into two directions: (1) student-excess tokens—tokens that the student frequently generates but the teacher assigns near-zero probability to, causing unbounded log-ratio corrections and unstable updates; and (2) student-deficit tokens—tokens that the teacher strongly prefers but that the student rarely or never samples, preventing the student from ever learning the teacher’s reasoning moves. Based on this, they propose TIDE (Token-level Independent Deficit-Excess correction). TIDE uses: (a) bounded Hellinger shaping on sampled tokens to dampen the influence of extreme student-excess tokens, preventing update explosions; and (b) an analytic teacher top-K injection, which explicitly injects probability mass for the teacher’s top-K preferred tokens into the update rule, so that the student can learn about deficit tokens even when they are not sampled in the student’s trajectory. The approach is applied within the OPD framework on mathematical reasoning tasks for several Qwen3 teacher–student model pairs.
AI.result: Empirically, on mathematical reasoning benchmarks and across multiple Qwen3 teacher-student configurations, TIDE outperforms standard OPD as well as recent token-selection and reward-shaping baselines. The performance benefits are especially large when there is strong teacher-student mismatch (e.g., capability or distributional gaps). In such mismatched settings, TIDE increases Avg@8 accuracy from 6.9% to 20.3%, shortens average response length by a factor of 3.6, and greatly reduces formatting failures in the students’ outputs. These results show that handling excess and deficit tokens explicitly leads to better transfer of reasoning capabilities and more stable training dynamics.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that naive on-policy distillation, which optimizes for token-level agreement, is vulnerable to degenerate agreement loops and fails to reliably transfer teacher reasoning. By reframing the problem around teacher-student mismatches, particularly excess and deficit tokens, the authors design TIDE, a principled token-level correction scheme. With bounded Hellinger shaping for student-excess tokens and analytic top-K injection for student-deficit tokens, TIDE stabilizes OPD and significantly improves reasoning performance, efficiency, and formatting reliability across diverse teacher-student pairs. The authors argue that future distillation methods should explicitly address these mismatch dimensions rather than relying solely on agreement-based objectives.

title: The Scaffolding Matters More Than the Interface: A Controlled Comparison of MCP and CLI Tool Use Across Seven Agent Scaffoldings, Five Language Models, and One Software Task
comment: 29 pages, 4 figures, 8 tables. Companion methodology paper: arXiv:2606.11869. Dataset and measurement harness (open source, GPL-3.0): https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21851992
summary:
How much an AI coding agent costs to run can depend more on the agent scaffolding that drives it than on the interface through which it
  reaches its tools. We set out to measure the cost of tool use over the Model Context Protocol (MCP) against tool use over an ordinary
  command-line interface (CLI), a difference on which published estimates disagree by more than an order of magnitude while resting on
  practitioner reports that cannot be reproduced. We ran one fixed software task -- six operations against a private online git repository --
  across seven agent scaffoldings and five language models, and we verified completion by inspecting the repository state rather than trusting
  the agent's self-report. The dominant effect was the scaffolding. Two of the seven ship no MCP support at all; they completed every run using
  only the CLI, which shows that MCP is unnecessary for this class of work, and they were 5.0x to 28x cheaper than the five scaffoldings that
  do support MCP, comparing CLI runs alone with no MCP server attached anywhere. The effect was largest for a small 27-billion-parameter model
  running locally, whose cost varied 139x across scaffoldings while it completed the task under all of them. The comparison we set out to make
  proved unstable: thirteen strictly paired MCP-to-CLI ratios span 0.43x to 29x, with outliers on both sides. The two interfaces separate on
  the cost of failure, where 12.9 per cent of the money spent on MCP runs bought no completed work against 2.2 per cent on CLI runs, but not on
  its frequency: failures were equally common in both, in the original runs and in their repetitions alike. Agents frequently ignored the
  interface they were assigned, so comparisons that do not verify actual behaviour measure an unknown mixture. The harness, the task, the
  verification and the complete dataset are released as open source.

AI.tldr: The paper empirically measures how much AI coding agents cost to run under different agent scaffoldings and interfaces (MCP vs CLI), finding that scaffolding choice dominates cost and reliability, while MCP vs CLI effects are inconsistent and smaller than claimed in prior reports.
AI.motivation: Prior estimates of the cost of AI agents using tools over the Model Context Protocol (MCP) versus standard command-line interfaces (CLI) disagree by more than an order of magnitude and are based on non-reproducible practitioner anecdotes. There is a need for a controlled, reproducible empirical study that isolates the effect of the interface (MCP vs CLI) from the effect of the agent scaffolding and verifies task completion objectively rather than trusting the agent’s self-report.
AI.method: The authors designed a fixed, realistic software-engineering task: six concrete operations against a private online git repository. They ran this same task across seven different agent scaffoldings and five different language models, in both MCP and CLI configurations where supported. Task success was verified by inspecting the final state of the git repository, not by trusting model/agent self-reports. They measured monetary cost and success/failure across many runs and compared costs: (1) across scaffoldings for the same model and interface, and (2) between MCP and CLI for strictly paired configurations. All code, harness, task definitions, verification logic, and data were released as open source for reproducibility.
AI.result: The main finding is that the choice of agent scaffolding dominates cost variance, far more than the MCP vs CLI interface distinction. Two of the seven scaffoldings do not support MCP at all, yet successfully completed every run via CLI only and were 5.0x–28x cheaper than the five MCP-supporting scaffoldings, even when comparing pure CLI runs with no MCP server attached. For a local 27B-parameter model, cost varied by 139x across scaffoldings while still completing the task in all cases, showing extreme sensitivity to scaffolding design. The MCP vs CLI ratio proved unstable: 13 strictly paired comparisons ranged from 0.43x to 29x, with large outliers in both directions. MCP runs wasted more money on failed attempts (12.9% of MCP spend produced no successful completion vs 2.2% for CLI), but failure rates by count were similar between interfaces. Agents often ignored their assigned interface, meaning that naive log-based comparisons without verifying actual behaviour can be misleading.
AI.conclusion: For this specific class of software-engineering tasks, MCP is not necessary: robust agents can complete work purely via CLI. The dominant determinant of operational cost is the agent scaffolding, not whether tools are accessed via MCP or CLI. Interface-level cost comparisons are highly unstable and can be confounded if experiments do not verify what interfaces the agents actually used. MCP appears to incur higher waste in terms of money spent on failed runs, but not a higher failure frequency. The authors advocate for careful, verifiable experimental setups and release their harness, tasks, verification, and data as open source to enable reproducible benchmarking of agent cost and behaviour.

title: Agentic Auto-Research is Fuzz Testing
summary: Autonomous research agents can generate experiments faster than researchers can validate them. Researchers have responded by scaling the proposer and ranking more samples with a learned judge or human reviewers. We argue that this *generate-and-rank* paradigm misses the problem of sparse feedback. Within a declared research problem, an agent follows the control loop of a greybox fuzzer: it proposes a candidate, executes it, observes feedback, and chooses what to try next. A fuzzer rarely finds a bug, but coverage makes partial progress observable on every execution. Fuzzers then use that signal to mutate inputs and allocate effort, rather than only to rank completed runs. Auto-research needs the same two capabilities. First, each experiment should expose a cheap, dense signal of epistemic progress before final scientific validation is available. Second, that signal should determine the next intervention so that the agent searches rather than repeatedly samples. Because the optimized progress signal is guidance rather than a verdict, final validation must still decide what counts as a discovery using evidence protected from adaptive reuse. We propose controlled tests of whether candidate signals predict validated progress, whether feedback-directed search yields more validated discoveries per unit cost than repeated sampling, and whether protected validation reduces false discoveries. Feedback architecture, not only generation, is a central bottleneck in auto-research.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that current "generate-and-rank" autonomous research systems are limited by sparse feedback and proposes a feedback-directed search framework, inspired by greybox fuzzing, where experiments emit dense progress signals used to guide subsequent experiments, with final validation held out to prevent overfitting and false discoveries.
AI.motivation: Autonomous research agents can now generate experimental ideas much faster than humans can validate them, causing a bottleneck at the evaluation stage. Existing approaches respond by scaling proposal generation and ranking (e.g., with learned judges or human reviewers), but this doesn’t fix the underlying issue that scientific feedback is sparse and delayed: most experiments are inconclusive and true breakthroughs are rare. The authors note that in analogous domains such as software fuzzing, systems make progress by exploiting dense, cheap signals about partial progress (like code coverage) on every run, which allows for efficient exploration despite rare ultimate rewards (bugs). They are motivated to bring similar feedback-rich, search-driven mechanisms to automated science so that auto-research agents can explore research spaces more intelligently and not just produce and rank many candidate experiments.
AI.method: Conceptually, the paper reframes auto-research as a feedback-driven control loop akin to a greybox fuzzer: within a fixed research problem, the agent repeatedly (1) proposes an experiment or intervention, (2) executes it, (3) observes a dense progress signal, and (4) adapts the next experiment based on that signal. The authors define two key requirements: (a) each experiment must yield a cheap, dense proxy signal for epistemic progress before full scientific validation, and (b) this signal must be used for adaptive search, not only for ranking completed experiments. To test their ideas, they propose controlled evaluations along three axes: (1) identify and test candidate progress signals by checking whether they predict ultimate, fully validated scientific gains; (2) compare feedback-directed search against simple repeated sampling in terms of validated discoveries per unit cost; and (3) assess whether separating the optimized progress signal from a protected validation set reduces false discoveries due to adaptive overfitting. The work is methodological and architectural rather than introducing a particular algorithmic implementation, focusing on how to structure feedback and evaluation in auto-research systems.
AI.result: As this is an abstract, concrete empirical results are not detailed. Instead, the paper’s primary outcome is a conceptual framework and a set of proposed tests. The authors articulate the limitations of the generate-and-rank paradigm under sparse feedback and crystallize the analogy between auto-research and greybox fuzzing. They formalize the idea that a dense epistemic progress signal can and should guide exploration and that final scientific validation must be held out from this adaptive process. They then outline experimental protocols to measure whether proposed progress signals correlate with validated advances, whether feedback-directed search is more sample-efficient than naive sampling, and whether protected validation mitigates false positives. The contribution is thus a research agenda and feedback architecture, rather than reported quantitative gains.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that the core bottleneck in autonomous research is not merely in generating more candidate experiments but in designing effective feedback architectures. Auto-research systems should emulate fuzzers by obtaining dense, cheap measures of epistemic progress on each experiment and using these signals to adaptively steer the search space, while reserving separate, non-adaptive validation to determine true discoveries and avoid overfitting. The authors argue that progress in automated science will depend crucially on developing and rigorously testing such feedback mechanisms—specifically, verifying the predictive value of progress proxies, showing that feedback-directed search improves validated discovery rates, and ensuring that protected validation reduces false discoveries. Feedback design, rather than just scaling generation and ranking, is positioned as central to advancing auto-research.

title: Branch2Skill: Efficient Skill Evolution Through Reasoning Trees
summary: Skill evolution improves agent skills through feedback over time, with failed trajectories often providing informative signals by revealing incomplete or misleading behaviors. However, existing methods mainly rely on single trajectories, where early reasoning errors can propagate through subsequent steps and weaken the feedback available for skill refinement. Consequently, improving skills requires repeated cycles of rollout, diagnosis, and update, incurring substantial token costs. To address this challenge, we introduce Branch2Skill, an efficient framework that transforms a single reasoning tree into dense supervision for skill evolution. For each task or problem, Branch2Skill performs Monte Carlo tree search under a fixed budget to obtain diverse reasoning trajectories, then compares an elite path with sibling alternatives sharing the same prefixes to extract step-wise evidence about which reasoning patterns to retain, revise, or avoid. Finally, Branch2Skill distills multi-step evidence into reusable updates, allowing one reasoning tree to provide supervision across multiple reasoning steps and reducing the need for repeated rollout-update cycles. Across six benchmarks covering reasoning and agentic tasks, Branch2Skill consistently improves task performance while enhancing skill evolution efficiency. For example, with GPT 5.5 as the target model, Branch2Skill uses 73.2% fewer tokens than SkillOpt, while achieving superior performance. These results demonstrate that reasoning trees can support not only more effective trajectory search, but also richer supervision for more efficient skill improvement. Code will be published.

AI.tldr: Branch2Skill converts a single Monte Carlo search reasoning tree into dense, step-wise supervision signals to make LLM agent skill evolution more efficient and less token-expensive than trajectory-based methods.
AI.motivation: Existing skill evolution methods in LLM agents typically learn from individual trajectories. Early reasoning errors in these trajectories propagate forward, corrupting later steps and weakening feedback quality. As a result, these methods must repeatedly perform expensive cycles of rollout, diagnosis, and parameter updates to improve skills, leading to large token costs and inefficiencies. The authors aim to better exploit the rich structure of reasoning trees—rather than just single paths—to obtain denser and more reliable supervision signals from the same interaction budget.
AI.method: Branch2Skill builds a reasoning tree for each task using Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) under a fixed budget, generating multiple diverse reasoning trajectories. Within this tree, it identifies an elite (high-quality) path and systematically compares each of its steps to sibling branches that share the same prefix. These comparisons reveal which local reasoning choices lead to better or worse outcomes. The framework then converts this step-wise, branch-level evidence into supervision signals that indicate which reasoning patterns to keep, revise, or avoid. Finally, it distills these multi-step, multi-branch signals into reusable skill updates for the target model, so that a single reasoning tree supervises many steps simultaneously, reducing the number of external rollout–update cycles required.
AI.result: On six benchmarks spanning both reasoning and agentic tasks, Branch2Skill consistently improves performance over baselines while using fewer tokens for skill evolution. In particular, when adapting GPT 5.5, the method achieves better task performance than the prior SkillOpt approach while consuming 73.2% fewer tokens, indicating significantly higher data- and token-efficiency. These empirical results support that leveraging reasoning trees for supervision yields more effective and economical skill improvement than relying on isolated trajectories.
AI.conclusion: Branch2Skill shows that the structural information in reasoning trees can be harnessed not only for search but also for learning. By transforming a single MCTS reasoning tree into dense, step-wise supervision, it enables more efficient and effective skill evolution for LLM agents, substantially cutting token usage while improving performance across diverse benchmarks. This suggests that future skill-improvement frameworks should more fully exploit tree-structured reasoning signals rather than depending on repeated, isolated trajectory rollouts. Code will be released to facilitate further research and application.

title: Towards Expert-level Medical AI for Real-time Video Consultations
summary: Audio-visual interaction is the standard for patient-physician consultations, enabling natural communication and effective assessment of illness through non-verbal cues. While text-based AI has shown promise, it discards essential perceptual dimensions and limits patients who cannot articulate symptoms in writing. Early efforts to extend medical AI to audio-visual interaction have demonstrated feasibility but not reached clinician-level performance. Here, we provide the first demonstration of expert-level AI in real-time clinical video consultations using AMIE (Articulate Medical Intelligence Explorer) in a video configuration. AMIE (Video) is a Gemini-based multi-agent system integrating low-latency dialogue, clinical reasoning, and real-time audio-visual perception. To guide development, we established a taxonomy and automated evaluations for clinical audio-visual cues in telehealth settings. In a randomized Objective Structured Clinical Examination (OSCE) study with 30 primary care physicians (PCPs), 15 patient actors and 100 clinical scenarios, we compared AMIE (Video), its text-only counterpart AMIE (Text), and PCPs consulting via video. Clinical evaluators rated AMIE (Video) on par or better than PCPs in history-taking, diagnosis, management, and physical observation and examination. Patient actors preferred AMIE's approach to assessing and explaining conditions, while PCPs were preferred for rapport and partnership building. In modality ablation, patient actors preferred AMIE (Video)'s interface over text chat for communicative effectiveness, convenience, and feeling understood. Limitations remain in fine anatomical precision, subtle affective nuances, and high-frequency movements. While further research is needed before real-world translation, these results mark an important milestone toward AI systems capable of augmenting care across the sensory complexity of clinical practice.

AI.tldr: The paper presents AMIE (Video), a Gemini-based multi-agent AI system that conducts real-time audio-visual clinical video consultations and achieves expert-level performance comparable to primary care physicians in a controlled OSCE setting.
AI.motivation: Current patient-physician consultations rely heavily on audio-visual interaction and non-verbal cues. Existing text-based medical AI ignores these perceptual dimensions and disadvantages patients who struggle to describe symptoms in writing. Early audio-visual medical AI systems have shown only feasibility, not clinician-level quality. The authors aim to build and rigorously evaluate an AI system that can operate in realistic telehealth video consultations and reach expert-level performance, potentially expanding access to high-quality care.
AI.method: The authors develop AMIE (Video), a Gemini-based multi-agent system that combines low-latency dialogue, structured clinical reasoning, and real-time audio-visual perception to participate in clinical video consultations.
