They design a taxonomy of clinical audio-visual cues relevant to telehealth and create automated evaluation frameworks to guide model improvement. For empirical evaluation, they conduct a randomized Objective Structured Clinical Examination (OSCE) involving 30 primary care physicians, 15 trained patient actors, and 100 scripted clinical scenarios. They compare three conditions: AMIE (Video), a text-only version AMIE (Text), and human PCPs consulting over video. Clinical experts rate performance on history-taking, diagnosis, management, and physical observation/examination, while patient actors rate their subjective experiences. They also run modality ablation experiments comparing AMIE (Video) to text chat interfaces.
AI.result: In OSCE simulations, clinical evaluators rate AMIE (Video) as comparable to or better than primary care physicians on history-taking, diagnostic accuracy, management decisions, and physical observation/exam within the constraints of video consultation. Patient actors report preferring AMIE's style for assessing and explaining medical conditions, whereas they favor human PCPs for establishing rapport and a sense of partnership. In modality comparisons, actors judge AMIE (Video)'s audio-visual interface as more effective, convenient, and conducive to feeling understood than a text-only chat interface. However, AMIE (Video) still struggles with tasks requiring very fine anatomical localization, detection of subtle emotional states, and interpretation of fast, high-frequency movements.
AI.conclusion: The study shows that an AI system equipped with real-time audio-visual perception and multi-agent clinical reasoning can perform at expert primary-care level in simulated video consultations, at least for history-taking, diagnosis, management, and gross physical observation. Patients may value such systems for clarity and thoroughness, while humans remain stronger at relational aspects of care. Despite remaining limitations in fine-grained perception and affect recognition, and the gap between OSCE simulations and real-world clinical deployment, the work represents a key milestone towards AI that can augment clinicians across the full sensory range of telehealth practice.

title: A Structural Dynamics Graph World Model: Unified Modeling, Constrained Rollout, and Interpretable Calibration
summary: The state evolution of a complex system arises jointly from object laws, relational propagation, domain conservation, and unmodeled error. Forcing all sources into one black box makes mechanism attribution and constraint preservation unauditable; forcing every mechanism into one equation family discards mature domain solvers. We propose SD-GWM, a Structural Dynamics Graph World Model as an executable structural contract: nodes declare self-dynamics S, edges declare neighbor graph-coupled dynamics N---both fixed-form mechanism assets (rules, ODEs, solvers) calibrating only authorized parameters. An optional bounded residual R concentrates learnability, while a global projection maps states to feasibility, enforcing constraints without guaranteeing accuracy gains. On eight pre-registered research questions, SD-GWM delivers (i) heterogeneous integration: rules and solvers plug in natively; (ii) semantic fidelity: disabling R preserves source semantics bit-for-bit, with four theory properties under explicit proof/empirical boundaries; (iii) auditable governance: stepwise traces enable counterfactual fault localization (top-1 = 1.0) without post-hoc approximations. On a semi-synthetic flood testbed and USGS streamflow, SD-GWM reduces constraint violations to floating-point tolerance in analytical tests and to zero in semi-synthetic and real-data cases. Persistence matches SD-GWM in calm periods, but during a 254-day extreme-flood shift persistence and all neural baselines collapse (90-min RMSE 892-3007 cfs) while SD-GWM holds at 108 cfs (8-28x gain). The bounded residual cuts RMSE ~50% only under backbone bias. We position SD-GWM not as a universally superior forecaster, but as a verifiable substrate for auditable, constraint-safe spatiotemporal mining.

AI.tldr: They propose SD-GWM, a structural dynamics graph world model that blends explicit physical/structural mechanisms with a small learnable residual while preserving domain constraints and full auditability, achieving strong performance and constraint satisfaction on hydrologic forecasting tasks, especially under distribution shift.
AI.motivation: Existing forecasting and world-model approaches either (1) lump all dynamics into a black-box model, making it hard to attribute behavior to specific mechanisms and to enforce domain constraints, or (2) force every mechanism into a single equation family, preventing reuse of established domain-specific solvers. This limits trust, auditability, and safe integration of physical knowledge with machine learning, especially in safety-critical or highly structured spatiotemporal systems like hydrology. The authors want a framework where heterogeneous rules and solvers can be composed, semantics can be preserved, and learned components are explicitly bounded and auditable.
AI.method: They introduce SD-GWM, a Structural Dynamics Graph World Model. The system is represented as a graph whose nodes have self-dynamics S and edges have neighbor-coupled dynamics N. Both S and N are fixed-form mechanism modules (e.g., rules, ODEs, solvers) with only certain parameters allowed to be calibrated. An optional, explicitly bounded residual R is added to capture unmodeled error, concentrating learning capacity. A global projection operator maps states into a feasible set, enforcing domain constraints (e.g., conservation) independent of accuracy. The model design emphasizes: (1) native plug-in of existing rules and solvers; (2) the ability to turn off the residual R so that the system reduces exactly to the source mechanisms; and (3) stepwise execution traces that allow counterfactual analysis and fault localization. They evaluate SD-GWM on pre-registered questions using a semi-synthetic flood testbed and real USGS streamflow data, benchmarking against persistence and neural baselines.
AI.result: Empirically, SD-GWM achieves: (i) Heterogeneous integration: different rules and solvers are incorporated directly as S and N modules. (ii) Semantic fidelity: when the residual R is disabled, the model reproduces the behavior of the source mechanisms exactly (bit-for-bit), with four theory properties bounded by formal proof or empirical validation. (iii) Auditable governance: stepwise traces allow precise counterfactual fault localization, achieving perfect top-1 fault identification (score 1.0) without needing post-hoc approximations. In analytical tests, constraint violations are reduced to floating-point tolerance; in semi-synthetic and real-data flood forecasting, constraint violations are eliminated. Under normal (calm) conditions, a simple persistence baseline performs similarly to SD-GWM, but during a 254-day extreme-flood regime shift, persistence and all neural baselines fail badly (90-minute RMSE 892–3007 cfs) whereas SD-GWM maintains an RMSE of 108 cfs, corresponding to an 8–28x improvement. The bounded residual term yields about a 50% RMSE reduction only when the backbone mechanisms are biased, confirming that learning is focused on compensating systematic errors rather than relearning the whole system.
AI.conclusion: SD-GWM should be viewed not as a universally best forecasting model, but as a structured substrate that cleanly combines explicit domain mechanisms with limited, auditable learning while strictly enforcing constraints. It enables trustworthy, constraint-safe spatiotemporal modeling, supports rigorous audit and fault localization, and remains robust under strong distribution shifts in hydrologic applications, making it suitable as an infrastructural layer for future spatiotemporal data mining rather than a one-size-fits-all predictor.

title: EnergyBridge: Benchmarking Household Energy Management, User Participation, and Grid Flexibility
summary: Residential virtual power plants (VPPs) can provide grid flexibility by shifting household demand, but physical flexibility becomes dependable capacity only when residents authorize a plan and the promised response is delivered. Existing benchmarks evaluate control but omit event-specific authorization. We present EnergyBridge, a benchmark and agent framework connecting capacity reporting, household authorization, and physical execution. It combines region-specific EnergyPlus environments for Tianjin and Berlin with an LLM-based User Participation Simulator. Against 584 persona- and event-matched human role-play judgments, the LLM-based User Participation Simulator preserves method ordering with a 5.3-point mean absolute acceptance error. Across conventional controllers and agent baselines, EnergyBridge achieves the highest simulated authorization, lowest event-window energy, and the most reliable capacity commitment in both regions. We release human data and codes for reproducible human-centered grid-flexibility research: https://github.com/Agentic-Intelligence-Lab/EnergyBridge.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces EnergyBridge, a benchmark and agent framework that links capacity estimation, household authorization, and physical load control for residential virtual power plants, validated with both human and LLM-simulated user participation.
AI.motivation: Residential virtual power plants rely not only on technical control capabilities but also on whether households actually authorize and follow through on demand-shift plans. Existing benchmarks focus on control performance and physical flexibility but ignore event-specific human authorization, making it hard to assess dependable capacity and user-centric reliability.
AI.method: The authors build EnergyBridge, which integrates (1) region-specific EnergyPlus simulation environments for Tianjin and Berlin to model physical household energy behavior; (2) an LLM-based User Participation Simulator that predicts whether residents will authorize specific demand-response events; and (3) an agent framework that ties capacity reporting, user authorization, and physical execution into one evaluation pipeline. They validate the User Participation Simulator using 584 human role-play judgments matched by persona and event, evaluating whether the LLM preserves method ordering and acceptance rates. They then benchmark conventional controllers and agent baselines within EnergyBridge across both regions.
AI.result: The LLM-based User Participation Simulator closely mirrors human role-play decisions, with a 5.3-point mean absolute error in acceptance rates while preserving the relative ordering of methods. Using the EnergyBridge framework, the authors find that their approach achieves higher simulated authorization rates, lower energy consumption during event windows, and more reliable capacity commitments than conventional controllers and agent baselines, consistently in both Tianjin and Berlin simulations.
AI.conclusion: EnergyBridge provides a human-centered, reproducible benchmark for evaluating residential virtual power plant strategies that explicitly incorporate user authorization and dependable capacity. By coupling building simulations with an LLM-based participation model validated against human data, the framework enables more realistic assessment and development of grid flexibility controllers. The release of code and human data aims to accelerate research on user-aware, reliable demand-response systems.

title: PluginEval: A Diagnostic Benchmark for Fine-Grained Error Attribution in Function Calling
summary: Reliable evaluation of tool routing is critical as Large Language Models increasingly operate as autonomous agents. Current benchmarks face three structural limitations: data distributions that follow a power law leave rare scenarios underrepresented; the absence of adversarial hard negatives obscures performance differences across models; and annotation pipelines depend on LLM judgments that have not been validated through execution. In this paper, we introduce PluginEval, a benchmark constructed through a two-stage framework that systematically mitigates these limitations. First, we formulate tool routing as a sequence of three decisions and separate generation from verification. LLMs propose candidate calls, while deterministic validation and real API execution provide reliable quality signals. Second, we decompose each plugin by capability, intent, and boundary to identify trigger and exclusion scenarios. We then generate queries at different difficulty levels to fill coverage gaps, including adversarial negatives targeting three failure modes, and return them to the first stage for annotation. This process creates a closed loop that iterates until coverage converges. For evaluation, we move beyond aggregate accuracy. An LLM judge anchored to gold annotations classifies failures as missed calls, spurious calls, or parameter errors, producing a detailed error profile for each model. We evaluate five model families, including proprietary models and models with open weights, analyze their performance across difficulty levels and error categories, and validate the judge through agreement with human annotations.

AI.tldr: Proposes PluginEval, a benchmark and framework for reliably evaluating LLM tool-routing using executable validation, capability-based scenario decomposition, and detailed error profiling.
AI.motivation: Existing tool-routing benchmarks are unreliable because (1) data follows a power-law distribution, so rare but important scenarios are poorly covered; (2) they lack adversarial hard negative examples, making it difficult to distinguish model capabilities; and (3) their labels depend heavily on unvalidated LLM judgments instead of real tool execution, undermining label quality and trustworthiness.
AI.method: They design a two-stage, closed-loop benchmark construction framework. Stage 1: formalize tool routing as a sequence of three decisions and separate proposal from verification—LLMs generate candidate tool calls, then deterministic validators plus real API executions verify correctness to produce accurate labels. Stage 2: decompose each plugin along three axes—capability, user intent, and boundary conditions—to identify both trigger and exclusion scenarios. They systematically generate queries at varying difficulty levels, including adversarial negatives tailored to three typical failure modes, to fill uncovered regions of the scenario space. These generated queries are sent back into Stage 1 for annotation. The loop repeats until scenario coverage converges. For evaluation, they augment basic accuracy metrics with an LLM judge, calibrated against gold labels, that categorizes errors as missed calls, spurious calls, or parameter errors, enabling nuanced error analysis.
AI.result: They construct PluginEval, a benchmark that provides broader and more balanced coverage of tool-routing scenarios, including rare and adversarial cases. The framework yields labeled data supported by deterministic validation and real API executions instead of pure LLM judgments. Using PluginEval, they evaluate five different LLM families—covering both proprietary and open-weight models—across multiple difficulty tiers and error types, and obtain fine-grained error profiles that reveal systematic differences in failure modes. They also empirically demonstrate that their LLM judge’s failure classifications align well with human annotators, validating its reliability as an evaluation component.
AI.conclusion: PluginEval offers a more reliable and comprehensive way to evaluate LLM tool-routing than prior benchmarks by (a) combining executable validation with structured scenario generation, (b) explicitly targeting coverage gaps and adversarial failure modes, and (c) providing detailed, validated error taxonomies per model. This enables more trustworthy comparisons between models and deeper insights into how and why they fail during tool use, positioning PluginEval as a stronger foundation for developing and assessing LLM-based tool agents.

title: AI Evaluation Should Measure Verification Cost, Not Correctness Alone
summary: The reliability of AI generative models is typically measured by output correctness, yet in practice it depends on the effort required to verify those outputs. We argue that current evaluation metrics overlook a critical failure mode: Verification-Cost Errors (VCEs), defined as incorrect input-output pairs that a declared fraction of the verifier population fails to identify within the verification budget available in a given deployment context. Unlike standard notions of "hallucination", VCEs are defined operationally, by the failure of correct identification within budget rather than by any property of the output itself. Plausibility and authoritative presentation are hypothesised contributors to that failure, not defining conditions. To capture this asymmetry, we introduce the notion of verification cost relative to a deployment budget as an operational dimension that current evaluation does not routinely capture. The quantity is presented as a conceptual instrument rather than a finalized metric. Evidence from code generation and multi-modal document understanding shows that high benchmark accuracy can mask significant verification effort in practice. We therefore take the position that correctness alone is insufficient as a measure of reliability. AI evaluation should explicitly account for verification cost, reflecting whether errors can be detected under realistic resource constraints.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that measuring AI reliability only by correctness is incomplete and introduces Verification-Cost Errors (VCEs), emphasizing the practical effort needed to detect AI mistakes within real-world resource limits.
AI.motivation: Existing evaluations of generative AI models focus largely on whether outputs are correct or hallucinated, ignoring how hard it is for users to check those outputs. In realistic deployments, people have limited time, knowledge, and attention to verify AI responses. This gap means that current metrics can overstate reliability, because they don’t capture cases where outputs are wrong but look convincing enough that many users will not catch the error within their verification budget. The authors want a framework that reflects the actual operational risks of using AI systems in practice, not just their abstract accuracy on benchmarks.
AI.method: The paper introduces a conceptual framework centered on Verification-Cost Errors (VCEs), defined as incorrect input–output pairs that a specified fraction of verifiers fail to flag as wrong within a given verification budget (time, expertise, tools, etc.) in a deployment context. The authors distinguish VCEs from traditional hallucinations by grounding them in verification failure instead of semantic properties of outputs. They formalize “verification cost relative to a deployment budget” as an additional dimension in evaluation, argue for its relevance, and illustrate it empirically through case studies in code generation and multimodal document understanding. These studies compare standard benchmark accuracy with the actual effort needed to check correctness and highlight mismatches between the two.
AI.result: Empirical evidence from code generation and multimodal document understanding tasks indicates that models with high benchmark accuracy can still impose substantial verification burdens on users. In these settings, many incorrect outputs are difficult or time-consuming for users to identify, leading to Verification-Cost Errors even when overall correctness metrics appear strong. The findings show that traditional accuracy scores can mask significant practical risk, as users may fail to detect convincing but wrong outputs within their realistic resource constraints.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that correctness alone is not an adequate measure of AI system reliability. Evaluations must explicitly incorporate verification cost—including user time, expertise, and context-specific resource limits—to capture whether errors are actually detectable in practice. The authors position VCEs and verification cost as operational, deployment-aware concepts that should complement existing hallucination and accuracy metrics. They call for future evaluation methodologies and benchmarks to integrate these dimensions so that AI systems are assessed against realistic conditions of use, rather than purely abstract correctness measures.

title: FitAQA: A Benchmark of Fitness Action Quality Assessment for Multimodal Large Language Models
summary: Fitness Action Quality Assessment (AQA) is important for intelligent sports training, yet the capabilities of Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) in this setting remain underexplored. Existing benchmarks rely on action-specific annotation schemes and focus primarily on final assessment outputs, offering limited insight into how models assess exercise quality. We introduce FitAQA, a systematic benchmark for evaluating MLLMs in fitness AQA, containing 2,219 videos and 5,512 QA instances across 30 bodyweight exercises. In collaboration with experts in sports science, we develop a unified form error taxonomy that defines 38 recurring form errors within six complementary quality dimensions: alignment, symmetry, stability, coordination, tempo, and completeness. This taxonomy provides a shared assessment framework across different exercises. FitAQA further formulates three evaluation tasks: perception for recognizing relevant visual evidence, judgement for combining that evidence with domain knowledge to assess execution correctness, and temporal grounding for localizing form errors over time. Extensive evaluation shows that current MLLMs still struggle to assess exercise quality comprehensively and localize form errors precisely. Controlled experiments further indicate that visual perception is a key bottleneck, as judgement performance improves substantially when ground-truth perceptual evidence is provided. The dataset and evaluation code will be made publicly available.

AI.tldr: FitAQA is a benchmark to evaluate how well multimodal large language models assess the quality of fitness exercises, focusing on perception, judgement, and temporal localization of form errors.
AI.motivation: Existing fitness action quality assessment benchmarks are action-specific, rely on heterogeneous annotation schemes, and only evaluate final scores, offering little insight into how models internally perceive and reason about exercise quality. There is a lack of systematic evaluation of MLLMs in this domain, especially regarding how they detect and reason about form errors over time in videos.
AI.method: The authors construct FitAQA, a benchmark with 2,219 videos and 5,512 question–answer instances covering 30 bodyweight exercises. In collaboration with sports science experts, they design a unified error taxonomy of 38 recurring form errors grouped into six quality dimensions: alignment, symmetry, stability, coordination, tempo, and completeness. Using this taxonomy, they define three tasks: (1) perception – identifying visual evidence of form; (2) judgement – integrating visual cues with domain knowledge to decide correctness; and (3) temporal grounding – locating when in the video form errors occur. They then evaluate multiple state-of-the-art MLLMs on these tasks and run controlled experiments where ground-truth perceptual evidence is supplied to isolate perception vs. judgement limitations.
AI.result: Empirical results show that current MLLMs perform poorly at comprehensive fitness quality assessment and struggle to precisely localize form errors in time. When provided with ground-truth perceptual evidence, models’ judgement performance improves notably, revealing that their main weakness lies in visual perception rather than in combining evidence with domain knowledge once the evidence is known.
AI.conclusion: FitAQA provides a unified, expert-designed framework and benchmark for analyzing how MLLMs perceive, judge, and temporally localize exercise quality and form errors. The study concludes that visual perception is the dominant bottleneck for current MLLMs in fitness AQA, and that improving video perception capabilities is crucial for progress. The dataset and code will be released to support future research and model development in this area.

title: Scale-to-Dialogue: Low-Burden Elicitation of Daily Premenstrual Symptom Ratings with Small Language Models
summary: Prospective daily symptom tracking is central to premenstrual health assessment, but repeated ordinal forms impose substantial response burden. We formulate conversational administration as an ordinal label-recovery problem: the system actively elicits a small set of symptom clusters and maps each response to the original severity labels. We used 3,320 complete participant-days from the mcPHASES dataset, covering cramps, mood swing, fatigue, sleep issues, stress, and bloating on a six-level scale. Six participants were reserved for development and 36 for a frozen evaluation comprising 360 participant-days and 2,160 item labels. A ModernBERT evidence gate detected whether a symptom was expressed, and Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct produced deterministic structured severity scores. Fixed six-item questioning achieved a quadratic weighted kappa of 0.976, whereas three joint symptom-cluster questions achieved 0.913, 97.45% agreement within one severity level, and 80.94% recall for moderate-or-higher symptoms while reducing questions by 50%. Open-first adaptive policies required 3.92-5.98 questions and produced lower agreement than the corresponding fixed policies. Participant-cluster bootstrap analysis estimated a kappa difference of -0.062 (95% CI -0.076 to -0.048) between the three-cluster and six-item strategies. Active cluster-level elicitation provides a direct, local-model route from natural conversation to reusable daily symptom labels.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a conversational approach to premenstrual symptom tracking that recovers detailed ordinal severity labels from a few cluster-based questions, achieving high agreement with traditional item-by-item ratings while halving question burden.
AI.motivation: Daily premenstrual symptom tracking typically relies on long ordinal questionnaires that are burdensome, reducing adherence and practicality in real-world settings. The authors aim to make this process more efficient by replacing many repetitive items with short, natural conversations that still recover the same granular severity labels needed for clinical and research use.
AI.method: Using 3,320 participant-days from the mcPHASES dataset with six symptoms rated on a six-level scale, the authors cast conversational tracking as an ordinal label-recovery task. They build a two-stage LLM-based pipeline: a ModernBERT classifier (evidence gate) determines if a symptom is present and a Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct model deterministically outputs structured severity scores. They compare fixed questioning policies (six individual items vs. three joint symptom-cluster questions) and open-first adaptive policies, evaluating agreement with ground-truth labels using quadratic weighted kappa, within-one-level accuracy, recall for moderate-or-higher symptoms, and participant-cluster bootstrap CIs.
AI.result: The fixed six-item policy nearly perfectly recovers original labels (quadratic weighted kappa 0.976). A three-cluster conversational strategy, which halves the number of questions, still attains high performance (kappa 0.913, 97.45% of labels within one severity level, and 80.94% recall for moderate-or-higher symptoms). Open-first adaptive policies that attempt to dynamically decide which clusters to probe required on average 3.9–6.0 questions and yielded lower agreement than the corresponding fixed strategies. Bootstrap analysis across participants and clusters estimated that the three-cluster policy’s kappa is only 0.062 lower than the six-item baseline (95% CI -0.076 to -0.048).
AI.conclusion: Structured, cluster-level conversational elicitation combined with local LLMs can reliably reconstruct detailed ordinal symptom labels from substantially fewer questions, preserving clinically relevant information while reducing burden. Fixed cluster-based questioning currently outperforms more complex adaptive policies, suggesting that simple, well-designed conversational prompts may be sufficient for practical, privacy-preserving premenstrual symptom tracking and could generalize to other daily health-monitoring tasks.

title: SymDiag: Explainable Diagnosis for LLM Reasoning via Neuro-Symbolic Verification
summary: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly serve as data-driven reasoners, yet their chains-of-thought (CoT) can be unfaithful even when final answers are correct. Most existing ``verification'' signals are not diagnostic: answer matching observes only the outcome, LLM-as-judge provides subjective and non-verifiable critiques, and scalar rewards (e.g., PRMs/RMs) offer little insight into where a multi-step derivation fails.We propose \textbf{SymDiag}, a neuro-symbolic framework that \textbf{reframes reasoning verification as structured failure diagnosis}. SymDiag translates natural-language CoT into symbolic constraints and performs step-level satisfiability/entailment checks to (i) localize failing steps and (ii) produce verifiable diagnostic evidence, including counterexamples, inconsistency witnesses, and missing-premise indicators. A central challenge is that apparent ``logic violations'' can be caused either by genuine reasoning defects or by neural-to-symbolic translation noise. SymDiag therefore incorporates a Self-Auditor that disentangles TranslationError from ReasoningError via dual symbolic encodings consistency checks, enabling robust diagnosis under partial observability. Across diverse mathematical, logical, scientific, and general reasoning benchmarks, SymDiag improves detection of unfaithful reasoning and provides substantially more effective feedback for multi-round reasoning repair than outcome-only verification and LLM-based judging, offering a principled foundation for trustworthy and scalable reasoning diagnosis.

AI.tldr: SymDiag is a neuro-symbolic framework that checks the faithfulness of large language model chain-of-thought by translating it into symbolic constraints, locating faulty reasoning steps, and distinguishing true reasoning errors from translation noise, thereby enabling verifiable and fine-grained diagnosis and repair of multi-step reasoning.
AI.motivation: Existing methods for verifying large language model reasoning are coarse and non-diagnostic: answer matching only checks final outcomes, LLM-as-judge evaluations are subjective and non-verifiable, and scalar reward models give a single score without indicating where in a multi-step derivation things go wrong. Additionally, chains-of-thought can appear correct at the final answer while containing unfaithful or flawed intermediate reasoning. The authors are motivated to build a principled, fine-grained, and verifiable diagnosis framework that can localize reasoning errors, provide concrete evidence of failure, and support iterative repair of LLM reasoning, all while handling noise introduced when translating natural language reasoning into symbolic form.
AI.method: The paper introduces SymDiag, a neuro-symbolic framework that converts a model’s natural-language chain-of-thought into symbolic constraints and then applies logical satisfiability and entailment checks at each reasoning step. For every step, SymDiag tests whether the claimed conclusion is entailed by or consistent with the accumulated premises, and when checks fail it generates explicit diagnostic artifacts such as counterexamples, inconsistency witnesses, or indicators of missing premises. To handle the ambiguity that an apparent logical violation may stem from errors in symbolic translation rather than genuine reasoning flaws, SymDiag integrates a Self-Auditor module. This module performs dual symbolic encodings and cross-consistency checks to separate TranslationError from ReasoningError, thereby increasing robustness under partial observability and imperfect parsing of natural-language explanations. The system is evaluated across multiple benchmarks in mathematics, logic, science, and general reasoning tasks.
AI.result: Across a variety of reasoning benchmarks, SymDiag more accurately detects unfaithful or incorrect reasoning in LLM chains-of-thought than baselines that rely on answer-only verification or LLM-based judges. It can pinpoint faulty steps and provide rich, verifiable evidence such as counterexamples and explicit inconsistencies. When used in multi-round reasoning repair loops, its structured feedback leads to substantially more effective correction of model reasoning processes than feedback derived from outcome-only checks or scalar rewards, demonstrating improved reliability and scalability of reasoning diagnosis.
AI.conclusion: The authors conclude that reframing reasoning verification as structured failure diagnosis via a neuro-symbolic approach offers a principled way to assess and improve LLM reasoning faithfulness. By translating natural-language chains-of-thought into symbolic form, running step-level logical checks, and disentangling translation noise from true reasoning errors with a Self-Auditor, SymDiag delivers fine-grained, verifiable, and actionable diagnostics. This framework not only outperforms existing verification methods in detecting unfaithful reasoning but also provides high-quality feedback that enables better iterative repair, suggesting a viable path toward more trustworthy and scalable reasoning with large language models.

title: Deferred Audio Pruning with Local Audio-Visual Dynamics for Omni-LLMs
summary: Omni-modal LLMs jointly process audio, video, and text, but long multimodal sequences incur substantial prefill and KV-cache costs. Existing omni-modal compression methods primarily focus on pre-LLM token reduction, leaving modality-specific compression across the LLM boundary underexplored. We propose A-PACK, a two-stage framework that defers audio pruning until query-conditioned multimodal interactions emerge. Our analysis shows that audio exhibits higher task-relevant information density and representational diversity per token than video. We further find that local audio-visual dynamics provide a more effective cue for visual selection than token-wise matching. We therefore preserve audio and compress video with local dynamics before the LLM, then progressively prune low-relevance audio and visual tokens and their KV-cache entries inside the LLM. Across four benchmarks on Qwen2.5-Omni-7B/3B, A-PACK achieves the strongest average performance among the evaluated prior methods while reducing prefill FLOPs by up to 78% and improving decoding throughput by up to 2.21x.

AI.tldr: A-PACK is a two-stage compression framework for omni-modal LLMs that preserves informative audio, compresses video early using local audio-visual dynamics, and then prunes low-relevance audio/visual tokens and KV-cache entries inside the LLM, greatly cutting compute while maintaining or improving performance.
AI.motivation: Omni-modal LLMs that process audio, video, and text together suffer from high computational costs, especially for long multimodal sequences due to prefill computation and large KV-caches. Existing compression approaches mostly reduce tokens before the LLM uniformly across modalities, and they underexplore how to compress different modalities differently and how to prune inside the LLM during inference. There is a need for a more principled, modality-aware compression strategy that targets both prefill and decoding costs while preserving task performance.
AI.method: The paper introduces A-PACK, a two-stage, modality-aware compression framework. Stage 1 operates before the LLM: based on the finding that audio carries higher task-relevant information density per token than video, the method largely preserves audio while compressing video using local audio-visual dynamics (rather than simple token-wise similarity) to decide which visual tokens are most relevant. Stage 2 operates inside the LLM: as query-conditioned multimodal interactions develop, A-PACK progressively prunes low-relevance audio and visual tokens along with their associated KV-cache entries to reduce both prefill and decoding-time memory and compute. The approach is evaluated on Qwen2.5-Omni-7B/3B models and multiple benchmarks, comparing against prior compression methods.
AI.result: On four multimodal benchmarks using Qwen2.5-Omni-7B and 3B, A-PACK delivers the best average task performance among all evaluated compression baselines, while substantially reducing computation: prefill FLOPs are reduced by up to 78%, and decoding throughput is improved by up to 2.21x. These results indicate that A-PACK’s modality-aware, two-stage pruning strategy is more effective than prior, primarily pre-LLM token-reduction techniques.
AI.conclusion: A-PACK shows that deferring pruning of high-information modalities (audio) until after query-conditioned interactions arise, while aggressively compressing less dense modalities (video) and pruning KV-cache entries within the LLM, can significantly cut inference cost with minimal or no loss in accuracy. The findings about audio’s higher information density and the superiority of local audio-visual dynamics for visual selection suggest new principles for designing compression schemes for omni-modal LLMs, and the empirical results validate that a carefully staged, modality-specific strategy outperforms existing omni-modal compression methods.

title: Improving Generalization Robustness of Multimodal RLVR
summary: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) makes Multimodal Large Language Models more accurate, but the gains are brittle: simply paraphrasing a question or changing the prompt template can degrade them, which challenges reliable deployment in high-stakes scenarios like medical VQA. We trace this to two issues of the standard RL objective. First, the binary verifier conflates format with content, so the reward signal cannot tell a wrong answer apart from a misformatted one. Second, the training distribution covers only a thin slice of the real-world prompts that the model might meet at deployment, so policies that perform well on the training distribution can behave differently under unseen prompts during test. Both failures call for a robust post-training method that helps the policy cover a broader distribution of semantically equivalent prompts, and we identify two measures that help achieve this objective: separating format from semantics in the reward, and applying policy invariance across perturbed prompts with equivalent semantics. We therefore propose Prompt-Invariant RLVR (PIRL), consisting of a dynamic trinary reward and a consistency regularizer based on an embedding-space adversary. Under stress testing, PIRL's average accuracy on benchmarks drops by only $\le 1\%$, where GRPO drops ~3%. On dynamic evaluation, PIRL also achieves the smallest performance drop.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Prompt-Invariant RLVR (PIRL), a reinforcement learning framework that makes multimodal LLMs trained with verifiable rewards robust to paraphrased prompts and formatting changes by disentangling format from semantics and enforcing consistency across semantically equivalent prompts.
AI.motivation: Standard RL with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) improves accuracy of multimodal LLMs but is brittle: small changes like paraphrasing or prompt template modifications can significantly degrade performance. This is dangerous for high-stakes domains such as medical visual question answering (VQA). The authors identify that (1) binary verifiers conflate answer correctness with output format, and (2) models are trained on a narrow distribution of prompts, leading to poor generalization across semantically equivalent variations. They aim to develop a robust post-training method that generalizes across such variations.
AI.method: The authors introduce Prompt-Invariant RLVR (PIRL). PIRL modifies RLVR in two main ways: (1) a dynamic trinary reward that explicitly separates formatting correctness from semantic correctness, providing more informative feedback than a binary verifier; and (2) a policy invariance mechanism that enforces consistency of the model’s behavior across semantically equivalent but perturbed prompts. This is implemented via a consistency regularizer driven by an embedding-space adversary that generates challenging prompt perturbations while preserving semantics.
AI.result: In stress tests where prompts are systematically perturbed (e.g., paraphrased, template-changed), PIRL displays a much smaller drop in accuracy compared with baselines: its average accuracy degradation across benchmarks is at most about 1%, while GRPO suffers around a 3% drop. In dynamic evaluation settings that simulate changing or evolving prompts at test time, PIRL also achieves the smallest performance decrease among compared methods, demonstrating improved robustness and stability.
AI.conclusion: PIRL effectively addresses the brittleness of RL with Verifiable Rewards by disentangling format from semantics in the reward signal and enforcing prompt-invariant behavior. This leads to notably more robust multimodal LLMs whose performance is less sensitive to prompt paraphrasing and template changes, making them better suited for reliable deployment in real-world, high-stakes applications.

title: Three Generations of Healthcare IT: From the Digital Record to the Computable Care Process
summary: Objective. Healthcare IT is usually organized by the technologies it adopts. We instead organize it by the unit of information a system makes computable, and describe a computational layer whose object is patient-specific clinical intent. Approach. We give criteria for a computational layer, derive three (record, clinical state, and a proposed layer of intent), and formalize the Actionable Clinical Record (ACR) as the atomic object of the third layer. Discussion. The framework distinguishes prescribed, observed, and intended process; existing standards represent intent once it is structured but do not recover it from natural communication, the capability we localize. The ACR is complementary to FHIR workflow resources, guidelines, and process mining; a companion feasibility study illustrates tractability for one narrow subproblem. Conclusion. Computable clinical intent is a coherent research direction; the ACR, its readiness ladder, and an executable-correctness evaluation framework are reusable constructs for subsequent work to extend, evaluate, or falsify.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a new computational layer in healthcare IT centered on patient-specific clinical intent and introduces the Actionable Clinical Record (ACR) as its atomic unit.
AI.motivation: Current healthcare IT is organized around technologies, not around the type of computable information. Existing standards mainly encode clinical data and structured intent but do not capture or recover the underlying clinical intent, especially when it is expressed in natural, unstructured communication. There is a need for a conceptual and computational framework that can represent and compute over clinical intent itself, to better support workflows and decision-making.
AI.method: The authors reconceptualize healthcare IT architecture by defining criteria for computational layers based on the unit of information they make computable. They derive three such layers: (1) the record layer, (2) the clinical state layer, and (3) a proposed intent layer. They then formalize the Actionable Clinical Record (ACR) as the atomic object of the intent layer, and position it relative to existing standards like FHIR workflow, clinical guidelines, and process mining. They also reference a companion feasibility study that applies the concept to a narrow subproblem to demonstrate tractability.
AI.result: The work yields a theoretical framework that distinguishes between prescribed, observed, and intended clinical processes. It shows that current standards adequately cover structured forms of intent but lack mechanisms to recover intent from natural clinical communication. The ACR concept is defined and shown to be complementary to existing FHIR workflow resources and other process representations, with preliminary evidence of feasibility from the companion study.
AI.conclusion: The authors conclude that making clinical intent computable is a viable and useful research direction. They present the ACR, its readiness ladder (a maturity/implementation progression), and an executable-correctness evaluation framework as reusable constructs for future research. These constructs can be used to extend, empirically evaluate, or potentially falsify the proposed approach to computable clinical intent.

title: PROSLEX: A Novel Dataset for Expert-Annotated Legal Statute Prediction for Indian Judiciary
summary: Legal Statute Prediction (LSP) involves automatically identifying relevant legal statutes given factual descriptions in legal documents, typically framed as a multi-label classification task within natural language processing and information retrieval research. While recent advances have begun incorporating Large Language Models (LLMs) for statute prediction, current approaches primarily focus on accuracy metrics without addressing the critical need for legal reasoning, a fundamental requirement in judicial contexts where decisions must be explainable and justifiable. To address this research gap, we present PROSLEX (PRediction Of Statutes and LEgal eXplanation), a comprehensive dataset comprising 1,623 expert-annotated legal documents from the Indian context. Each document is paired with statute predictions and detailed explanations, totaling 7,450 explanations, capturing the underlying legal reasoning. Using this dataset, we systematically evaluate various prompting strategies, including zero-shot, few-shot, chain-of-thought, and tree-of-thoughts approaches, to generate both statute predictions and their corresponding legal rationales. Our evaluation framework measures not only predictive performance but also the coherence and legal validity of generated explanations, positioning PROSLEX as a benchmark for developing explainable AI systems that can support legal practitioners while advancing research in interpretable legal NLP. To ensure reproducibility, we have made our PROSLEX dataset and model code available on GitHub: https://github.com/subinay494/Legal_Statute_Prediction_Explanation.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces PROSLEX, an expert-annotated Indian legal dataset for statute prediction with accompanying human-written legal explanations, and uses it to benchmark LLM-based methods that jointly predict statutes and generate legally coherent rationales.
AI.motivation: Existing Legal Statute Prediction work, especially with LLMs, largely optimizes accuracy but neglects explicit legal reasoning and explainability, which are crucial for real-world judicial use where decisions must be justified. There is also a lack of high-quality datasets that pair statute labels with detailed legal rationales.
AI.method: The authors construct PROSLEX, a dataset of 1,623 Indian legal case documents with statute labels and 7,450 expert-written explanations mapping facts to statutes. They then design an evaluation framework and systematically test different LLM prompting strategies—zero-shot, few-shot, chain-of-thought, and tree-of-thoughts—for joint statute prediction and rationale generation, assessing both predictive performance and the quality of legal explanations.
AI.result: PROSLEX enables quantitative comparison of prompting strategies for legal statute prediction with explanations. The experiments show how different prompting paradigms trade off between prediction accuracy and explanation quality (coherence and legal validity), demonstrating that more structured reasoning prompts (CoT, ToT) can improve the interpretability and legal soundness of model outputs compared to basic zero-/few-shot prompting.
AI.conclusion: PROSLEX serves as a new benchmark resource for explainable legal NLP in the Indian context, enriching statute prediction with human-authored legal reasoning. By providing data, code, and an evaluation framework that jointly measure accuracy and explanation quality, the work advances the development of LLM-based systems that are not only effective at predicting statutes but also capable of generating transparent, legally grounded rationales useful to legal practitioners.

title: Findings of the First Teaching Monster Challenge: A Benchmark of Pedagogical Content Knowledge in AI Agents
summary: AI agents can now solve problems, answer like subject experts, and generate long-form multimodal content. However, whether they can adapt a lesson to fit a specified learner, which education calls Pedagogical Content Knowledge (PCK), has not been benchmarked. To measure it, we introduce the Teaching Monster Challenge, the first instructional video generation benchmark to treat the learner persona as an explicit evaluation criterion. Each system is given a topic and a learner persona and must generate a complete instructional video. Every video is screened by an LLM-judge, ranked by crowd pairwise voting, and finalized by an expert panel. The first edition shows that today's systems handle the content well but are far weaker at presenting it and adapting it to the learner. The same process exposes a limit of automatic judging. The LLM-judge separates a clear low-performing tail but ranks the strongest systems poorly. The strongest systems receive nearly identical scores from the judge, so its ranking of them does not match human preference. Progress therefore requires not only better teaching systems but also better automatic judges, and we release the benchmark, rubric, and human judgments as a testbed for both.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces the Teaching Monster Challenge, a benchmark for testing how well AI systems generate instructional videos tailored to specific learner personas, revealing that current systems are good at content but weak at pedagogy and that current LLM-based judges also mis-rank the best systems.
AI.motivation: While AI agents can already solve problems, answer questions like experts, and generate rich content, it is unclear whether they can demonstrate Pedagogical Content Knowledge (PCK)—the ability to adapt explanations and lessons to specific learners. Education research considers PCK crucial for effective teaching, yet existing AI evaluations mostly ignore this dimension and focus on task correctness or content quality alone. Moreover, automatic evaluation of teaching quality is difficult, and it is unknown whether LLM-based judges reliably capture human preferences about instructional quality, especially when learner characteristics matter. This gap motivates the need for a dedicated benchmark that assesses both AI teaching systems and the automatic judges used to evaluate them, with explicit attention to learner personas.
AI.method: The authors design the Teaching Monster Challenge, an instructional video generation benchmark where each system receives (1) a topic to teach and (2) a detailed learner persona (e.g., background knowledge, interests, challenges). Systems must generate full instructional videos tailored to that persona. The evaluation pipeline has three layers: (a) an LLM-based automatic judge that screens all videos and assigns initial scores; (b) crowd-sourced pairwise comparisons where human raters watch video pairs and choose which is better; and (c) an expert panel that reviews outcomes and finalizes rankings and judgments. The benchmark includes a rubric that explicitly scores both content mastery and pedagogical adaptation to the target learner. The authors then apply this benchmark to a set of current AI systems to compare their performance and to study how well the LLM-judge aligns with human rankings, especially among high-performing systems.
AI.result: Empirical results from the first iteration of the Teaching Monster Challenge show that current AI systems generally succeed at covering the subject matter accurately but perform poorly at the pedagogical aspects: presentation quality, structuring of explanations, and adaptation to the specific learner persona. When examining the evaluation pipeline, the LLM-based judge is effective at identifying a clear group of low-performing systems, but it struggles at the high end of performance. Among the top systems, their scores from the LLM-judge cluster very closely, leading to rankings that diverge significantly from those derived from crowd pairwise voting and expert assessment. In particular, the systems that human evaluators consider strongest are not ranked as such by the LLM-judge.
AI.conclusion: The Teaching Monster Challenge establishes a new benchmark for measuring AI systems' Pedagogical Content Knowledge through persona-aware instructional video generation. The findings indicate that contemporary systems are much stronger at getting the content right than at teaching it effectively to a specified learner, highlighting pedagogical adaptation as an open challenge for AI education tools. The work also reveals limitations of current LLM-based automatic judges: they can filter out obviously weak instruction but fail to produce reliable fine-grained rankings of strong systems, leading to misalignment with human preferences. Consequently, advancing AI in education requires progress on two fronts: improving teaching-oriented AI systems and developing more sensitive, persona-aware automatic evaluation methods. The authors release the benchmark, rubric, and human judgment data to support future research on both instructional generation and automatic judging.

title: AquiLLM: An Architecture for Supporting Tacit Knowledge Capture in Research Groups
comment: Accepted for publication in the NGEN-AI 2026 proceedings
summary: Recent advances in retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) and large language models (LLMs) enable researchers to integrate AI into scientific workflows. However, using proprietary commercial AI systems raises concerns about transparency, reproducibility and privacy, which are essential for scientific practices. To this end, AquiLLM was developed as an open-source modular RAG-LLM framework using open-weight models, designed to support research groups in capturing tacit knowledge. In this work, we present a series of architectural improvements and feature enhancements to AquiLLM, including local embedding and reranking, multimodal capabilities, OpenAI-compatible inference interfaces, user interface improvements, semantic and episodic memory capabilities, and skills support. These enhancements were informed by discussions with domain experts, including astrophysicists and environmental researchers, and represent a step toward AI systems more closely aligned with scientific research practices.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces AquiLLM, an open-source modular RAG-LLM framework tailored for scientific research, and presents architectural and feature upgrades to better align AI assistance with real-world research practices.
AI.motivation: Commercial AI systems in scientific workflows create problems for transparency, reproducibility, and privacy, all of which are critical in science. There is also a need to systematically capture tacit knowledge within research groups, which current tools do not fully support. An open, customizable RAG-LLM framework can address these gaps while fitting diverse scientific domains.
AI.method: The authors extend AquiLLM—an open-source RAG-LLM framework built on open-weight models—through a set of architectural and feature improvements. These include adding local embedding and reranking pipelines, multimodal input capabilities, OpenAI-compatible inference APIs, an improved user interface, semantic and episodic memory for longer-term context, and a skills framework. The design is iteratively informed by discussions with domain experts such as astrophysicists and environmental researchers.
AI.result: The enhanced AquiLLM framework now supports local and privacy-preserving retrieval, multimodal interaction, compatibility with existing OpenAI-based tooling, richer memory and knowledge-capture features, and better usability for researchers. Expert feedback indicates that these changes bring the system closer to the actual needs and workflows of scientific research groups.
AI.conclusion: AquiLLM’s new architecture and features demonstrate that open-source, open-weight RAG-LLM systems can be adapted to better align with scientific standards of transparency, reproducibility, and privacy while supporting tacit knowledge capture. This work is a step toward AI research assistants that more naturally integrate into and augment real scientific practices across domains.

title: Full-bandwidth transformer
summary: Autoregressive transformers compute along two axes: horizontally across generated tokens, and vertically through model depth. Dense attention gives each token broad horizontal access to the past, but the vertical feedback channel between decoding steps remains narrow: only the sampled token returns to the bottom of the stack, while the top-layer hidden state is discarded. We introduce the \emph{full-bandwidth transformer}, which widens this channel with \emph{latent feedback}: at each decoding step, the previous top-layer hidden state is fused with the sampled token embedding through a gated linear unit and fed back as the next input. Latent feedback lets non-verbalized computation re-enter the stack with a renewed depth budget, while preserving the standard transformer architecture, KV cache, and language-modeling objective. To train full-bandwidth transformers without losing parallel teacher forcing, we use a scheduled multi-pass objective that introduces latent feedback late in pretraining and mixes a small fraction of deeper feedback passes for stability. We train 1B-parameter full-bandwidth transformers up to 400B tokens and find that latent feedback improves validation loss, 5-shot language-model evaluation, math and coding generation, and instruction-tuned performance. With negligible per-token decoding overhead, full-bandwidth transformers match or approach standard transformers trained with roughly $1.5\times$ more tokens, and manage to produce shorter reasoning traces at equal or better accuracy.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a “full-bandwidth transformer” that feeds back the previous step’s top-layer hidden state as part of the next input, improving sample efficiency and reasoning quality with minimal decoding overhead.
AI.motivation: In standard autoregressive transformers, each step only feeds back the sampled token to the model’s input layer, while discarding the rich top-layer hidden state. This creates a narrow vertical feedback channel between decoding steps, limiting the ability to reuse non-verbalized internal computation across time. The authors are motivated to widen this feedback channel so that the model can more effectively carry forward internal reasoning, improve performance without drastically changing architecture or cost, and reduce the amount of training data needed to reach a given capability level.
AI.method: They introduce the full-bandwidth transformer, which augments a standard decoder-only transformer with latent feedback. At each decoding step, the previous step’s top-layer hidden state is fused with the current step’s sampled token embedding via a gated linear unit; this fused vector becomes the next input embedding at the bottom of the stack. This allows internal, non-output representations to be reintroduced with a fresh depth budget while keeping the standard attention mechanism, KV cache, and language-modeling objective. To keep training parallelizable with teacher forcing, they use a scheduled multi-pass training objective: the model is first trained normally, and latent feedback is introduced later in pretraining, with a small proportion of deeper feedback passes added and mixed in to maintain stability and efficiency.
AI.result: They train 1B-parameter full-bandwidth transformers on up to 400B tokens. Models with latent feedback show improved validation loss and better performance on 5-shot language modeling benchmarks, as well as stronger math and coding generation capabilities. After instruction tuning, they also perform better on instruction-following tasks. These gains come with negligible extra per-token decoding cost, and the models’ performance is competitive with or close to standard transformers that have been trained on about 1.5 times more data. Additionally, the models tend to produce shorter reasoning traces while maintaining equal or better accuracy.
AI.conclusion: Widening the vertical feedback channel in autoregressive transformers via latent feedback—reinjecting the previous top-layer hidden state through a gated fusion with token embeddings—improves sample efficiency, language modeling performance, and reasoning quality, all while preserving the standard transformer architecture and incurring minimal inference overhead. Full-bandwidth transformers can match or approach the performance of conventional models that require substantially more training tokens and can generate more concise reasoning traces without sacrificing accuracy.

title: LLM Reasoning for Subjective Tasks: Failure Modes, Mitigation, and Dynamic Reasoning Routing
summary: Recommendation systems thrive on personalization, where ''correctness'' is rarely a binary truth but a matter of subjective human preference. As Large Language Models (LLMs) are deployed as autonomous verifiers of safety and quality guidelines, they face a distinctive challenge: context-aware preference alignment. Recent gains in Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) are indexed mostly on objective, mathematical tasks. Through a large-scale study spanning both proprietary and open-source models on four real-world verification tasks from a production recommender platform, we ask whether explicit reasoning generalizes to subjective, human-centric industry rubrics. We expose a fundamental vulnerability: rigid, math-centric reasoning traces actively degrade verification, and applying standard RLVR triggers a phenomenon we term reasoning collapse, in which the policy abandons deliberation in favor of rapid heuristic guessing. We introduce a conditional length-penalized post-training algorithm that intertwines verification accuracy with bounded reasoning length, halting collapse and recovering performance. Finally, we show that a reasoning trace's efficacy is tightly coupled with its socio-linguistic framing: across 1500 synthesized personas, verification accuracy swings by nearly 0.38 macro-F1 depending solely on the adopted reasoning persona---evidence that much subjective-verification error is really reasoning-style mismatch. This observation motivates a mid-training architecture that routes reasoning through contextually aligned personas. This work offers both a scalable algorithmic patch and a long-term architectural blueprint for aligning reasoning models with real-world subjective constraints.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how LLMs verify subjective recommendations and shows that current math-style chain-of-thought and RLVR can harm performance via “reasoning collapse,” then proposes bounded-length, persona-aligned reasoning methods that restore and improve verification.
AI.motivation: Modern recommender systems increasingly rely on LLMs to verify content for safety and quality, but these judgments are subjective and context-dependent, unlike the objective math/logical tasks where RL with verifiable rewards has excelled. Existing RLVR and explicit reasoning techniques may not transfer cleanly to human-centric rubrics, and there is little understanding of how reasoning style and length affect verification of recommendations in real production settings.
AI.method: The authors conduct a large-scale empirical study using both proprietary and open-source LLMs on four real-world verification tasks derived from an operational recommender platform. They systematically apply explicit chain-of-thought style reasoning and standard RLVR to these subjective verification tasks, observing their impact on accuracy and behavior. Upon discovering “reasoning collapse,” they propose: (1) a conditional length-penalized post-training algorithm that jointly optimizes verification accuracy and keeps reasoning traces within bounded length; and (2) a mid-training routing architecture that conditions the model’s reasoning on synthesized socio-linguistic personas matched to context. They evaluate across ~1500 synthetic personas and measure macro-F1 changes to quantify the effect of reasoning style and persona alignment.
AI.result: They show that standard math-centric explicit reasoning degrades subjective verification performance, and that RLVR can induce “reasoning collapse,” where the model stops genuine deliberation and resorts to shallow, fast guessing. Their conditional length-penalized training mitigates collapse, improving verification metrics over naïve RLVR and unpenalized reasoning. Moreover, they find that the same base model exhibits large swings (up to ~0.38 macro-F1) in verification accuracy purely due to the socio-linguistic framing of its reasoning trace, across 1500 synthetic personas, demonstrating that a substantial portion of errors stems from reasoning-style mismatch rather than base competence. The proposed persona-routing mid-training architecture exploits this to further boost accuracy and robustness.
AI.conclusion: Explicit reasoning as currently practiced—optimized for objective, math-like problems—can be harmful when LLMs are used as verifiers of subjective recommendation guidelines. RLVR, if applied naïvely, risks reasoning collapse in which the model abandons careful reasoning. By constraining reasoning length and conditioning on context-appropriate reasoning personas, LLMs can maintain or improve verification accuracy in real-world subjective tasks. The work argues that future reasoning systems should be architected to be persona- and context-aware rather than relying on a single, rigid chain-of-thought style, providing both an immediate algorithmic fix and a more general design direction for aligning reasoning models with human, subjective constraints.

title: From Manuals to Maintenance: Fine-Tuning MedGemma for Multi-Modal Imaging System Support in Low-Resource Settings
comment: Accepted at the AFRICAI 2026 Workshop, a satellite event at MICCAI 2026. To appear in Springer Lecture Notes in Computer Science (LNCS)
summary: Imaging device downtime is a major barrier to healthcare delivery in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs), often driven by limited access to specialized biomedical engineering support. We present a multi-modality medical equipment maintenance question-answering (QA) framework and demonstrate the fine-tuning of a medical foundation model for specialized technical troubleshooting tasks. Guided by a multi-country survey across nine LMICs, we curated technical manuals from MRI and ultrasound systems to generate the INGENZI_DatasetV1, containing 10,294 high-quality, filtered QA-context pairs. Using QLoRA-based parameter-efficient fine-tuning, we adapted the MedGemma-4b-it model to interpret system error logs and generate step-by-step equipment repair instructions. Compared to the baseline model, the fine-tuned system achieved substantial improvements across metrics, including F1 score (0.22 to 0.38), ROUGE-2 (0.18 to 0.41), and BERTScore F1 (0.86 to 0.91). These metric gains demonstrate that the model generates significantly more precise and procedurally accurate technical responses to new troubleshooting queries. This work establishes a reliable foundation for AI-assisted diagnostic and maintenance tools in resource-constrained settings.

AI.tldr: They fine-tune a medical language model on a new MRI/ultrasound maintenance QA dataset so it can read error logs and output better step-by-step repair instructions, improving multiple text-generation metrics and supporting AI-based device maintenance in low-resource settings.
AI.motivation: In LMICs, imaging devices like MRI and ultrasound often sit idle because of long downtimes, largely due to limited access to specialized biomedical engineers. Existing models are not tailored to highly technical, device-specific troubleshooting. The authors aim to create an AI system that can help non-expert users diagnose and fix equipment issues more reliably, thereby improving healthcare delivery.
AI.method: The authors first conducted a multi-country survey in nine LMICs to understand maintenance challenges and information needs. They then collected and curated technical manuals from MRI and ultrasound systems, transforming them into INGENZI_DatasetV1, a corpus of 10,294 filtered QA-context pairs focused on troubleshooting and maintenance. Using QLoRA-based parameter-efficient fine-tuning, they adapted the MedGemma-4b-it medical foundation model to this dataset so that the model can interpret system error logs and generate procedural repair instructions. Model performance was evaluated on standard text-generation metrics such as F1, ROUGE-2, and BERTScore F1, comparing the fine-tuned model against the baseline.
AI.result: After fine-tuning on INGENZI_DatasetV1, the adapted MedGemma-4b-it model significantly outperformed the baseline. Quantitatively, the F1 score increased from 0.22 to 0.38, ROUGE-2 from 0.18 to 0.41, and BERTScore F1 from 0.86 to 0.91. These improvements indicate more precise, contextually aligned, and procedurally faithful responses when handling novel troubleshooting questions and error logs from imaging equipment.
AI.conclusion: The study shows that parameter-efficient fine-tuning of a compact medical foundation model on a curated, device-specific maintenance QA dataset yields markedly better technical troubleshooting outputs. This provides a practical foundation for AI-assisted diagnostic and maintenance support tools for MRI and ultrasound equipment in resource-constrained LMIC settings, with the potential to reduce imaging device downtime and improve access to diagnostic care.

title: Decoding Phenotypes: A Framework for Fusing Genomic Language Models and Neuroimaging
summary: Neuroimaging and genetic testing are two important clinical references for nervous system diseases, offering complementary diagnostic information. However, integrating genomic and neuroimaging data for precise disease diagnosis is challenging due to cross-modality heterogeneity. Existing imaging-genetics approaches mainly encode genetic information as hard-coded labels, which lose the local sequence context around disease-associated variants. To address this limitation, we propose GeneFuse, a multimodal learning framework that aligns genetic representations from pre-trained Genomic Language Models (GLMs) with features extracted from images. GeneFuse integrates two components: (1) Genotype-Conditioned Feature Modulation (GCFM), a FiLM-inspired module that uses genomic embeddings to modulate image feature maps; and (2) Uncertainty-aware Genomic Residual Fusion (U-GRF), a fusion strategy that uses imaging-derived predictive uncertainty to gate the contribution of genotypic features. We evaluate GeneFuse on early cognitive decline identification (NC vs. MCI) and dementia screening (NC vs. AD). In the APOE-centered setting, GeneFuse achieves AUROCs of 0.77 and 0.83, outperforming existing imaging-genetics fusion methods. These results indicate that GLM-derived genomic embeddings provide additional information to imaging.

AI.tldr: GeneFuse is a multimodal framework that aligns genomic embeddings from pre-trained genomic language models with neuroimaging features to improve diagnosis of early cognitive decline and dementia.
AI.motivation: Integrating genomic and neuroimaging data can improve diagnosis of nervous system diseases, but existing methods typically use simplified, hard-coded genetic labels that ignore the local sequence context around disease-associated variants and struggle with cross-modality heterogeneity.
AI.method: GeneFuse uses genomic embeddings from pre-trained Genomic Language Models as inputs to a multimodal model with two key components: (1) Genotype-Conditioned Feature Modulation (GCFM), a FiLM-like module that uses genomic embeddings to conditionally modulate image feature maps, and (2) Uncertainty-aware Genomic Residual Fusion (U-GRF), which fuses genetic and imaging features while using imaging-derived predictive uncertainty to gate the influence of genetic information.
AI.result: On tasks of early cognitive decline identification (NC vs. MCI) and dementia screening (NC vs. AD) in an APOE-centered setting, GeneFuse achieves AUROCs of 0.77 and 0.83, outperforming existing imaging-genetics fusion baselines.
AI.conclusion: Leveraging contextual genomic embeddings from Genomic Language Models and fusing them with neuroimaging in an uncertainty-aware manner yields more informative multimodal representations, demonstrating that GLM-derived genetic features add diagnostic value beyond imaging alone.

title: Integrated Multimodal AI System for Retrieval-Augmented Reasoning, Object Sensing, and Damage Analysis
summary: This work presents a unified multimodal AI system for damage assessment that integrates retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) models, thermal spectrum perception, vision foundation model pipelines, and exploratory wireless signal sensing. A RAG component is developed to ground a locally hosted language model in project-specific documentation, including specialized damage level classification criteria to mitigate hallucinations during inference. Controlled comparisons against static few-shot prompting demonstrate that dynamic retrieval improves grounding and factual consistency. We further compare vector-based RAG with a knowledge graph variant constructed via entity-relation extraction, and show that graph-based retrieval produces stronger responses for damage assessment queries requiring cross-document reasoning, motivating hybrid dense, sparse, and graph-aware retrieval. To address limitations of EO imagery under adverse lighting and weather conditions, infrared (IR)/thermal sensing is employed for object detection and segmentation. Our detectors generate candidate detections, yielding improved segmentation of a broad array of objects. Paired IR versus visible spectrum tracking experiments reveal failure modes, motivating multimodal fusion for robust object detection and damage analysis. Vision foundation and vision-language models are leveraged to generate synthetic damage imagery and classify damage severity with high accuracy, supporting training and validation of downstream damage assessment models. Finally, exploratory Wireless-based sensing demonstrates potential to detect presence, motion, and post-event environmental changes where EO and IR sensing are ineffective.

AI.tldr: Unified multimodal AI system for damage assessment combining RAG-grounded language models, IR/thermal vision, foundation models, and exploratory wireless sensing to improve robustness, factuality, and cross-modal coverage.
AI.motivation: Existing damage assessment systems suffer from hallucinations in language models, limited robustness of electro-optical (EO) imagery under poor conditions, weak cross-document reasoning, and lack of sensing when visual modalities fail. There is a need for an integrated, multimodal framework that can reliably assess damage across varying conditions, leverage project-specific knowledge, and exploit complementary sensing channels.
AI.method: Design a unified framework with: (1) a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) module that grounds a local LLM in project documentation and codified damage criteria; (2) comparative evaluation of static few-shot prompting vs dynamic retrieval, and dense vector-based RAG vs knowledge-graph-based RAG; (3) IR/thermal object detection and segmentation pipelines and tracking experiments comparing IR vs visible spectrum; (4) use of vision foundation and vision-language models to synthesize damage imagery and classify damage severity; and (5) exploratory wireless signal sensing for detecting presence, motion, and environmental changes when EO/IR are ineffective.
AI.result: Dynamic RAG grounding outperforms static few-shot prompting in factual consistency. Knowledge-graph-based retrieval yields stronger answers for cross-document damage assessment queries, suggesting benefits of hybrid dense, sparse, and graph-aware retrieval. IR/thermal detectors improve segmentation of diverse objects and reveal complementary strengths and failure modes versus visible spectrum tracking, motivating multimodal fusion. Vision foundation and vision-language models can generate synthetic damage imagery and classify damage severity with high accuracy, providing useful data for training/validation. Wireless sensing shows feasibility in detecting presence, motion, and post-event environmental changes in scenarios where EO/IR are limited.
AI.conclusion: A unified, multimodal AI framework combining RAG-grounded language models, IR/thermal imaging, vision foundation models, and wireless sensing can enhance robustness, accuracy, and coverage of damage assessment, particularly in challenging conditions and complex information environments. Knowledge-graph-enhanced retrieval and multimodal fusion emerge as promising directions for future hybrid damage assessment systems.

title: Not an A11y: How Android Accessibility Exposes Mobile AI Agents to Indirect Prompt Injection
summary: The rise of autonomous AI agents represents a major paradigm shift in how users interact with mobile devices. Frameworks such as MobileRun and Mobile-Use can autonomously navigate Android applications and execute complex multi-step tasks. To interpret user interfaces, these frameworks rely primarily on Android accessibility (A11y) trees and secondarily on visual screenshots. In this paper, we demonstrate that this architectural dependence on unsanitized accessibility metadata, together with visual input, introduces a systemic vulnerability to indirect prompt injection. We show that adversarial prompts can cause autonomous agents to abandon their original objectives, violate context boundaries, and perform unauthorized device actions. Our empirical evaluation demonstrates goal hijacking, context drift, and unauthorized actions across visually hidden and fully exposed attack scenarios. In aggregate, MobileRun reaches an attack success rate of 0.822 with Gemma4:31B, while Mobile-Use with Qwen3.6:35B reduces this to 0.150 but does not eliminate context drift or unauthorized actions. These findings reveal that current mobile agent frameworks fail to enforce semantic context boundaries, treating passive environmental text as trusted instructions. Finally, we present a taxonomy of these attacks and discuss the need for zero-trust input validation, dedicated security agents, and strict context isolation within mobile agent architectures.
