AI.tldr: The paper shows that autonomous mobile AI agents that rely on Android accessibility trees and screenshots are systematically vulnerable to indirect prompt injection, enabling attackers to hijack goals and trigger unauthorized actions.
AI.motivation: Autonomous AI agents on mobile devices (e.g., MobileRun and Mobile-Use) can control apps and perform complex tasks for users. They interpret app interfaces mainly through Android accessibility metadata and screenshots. As these agents become more capable, any systemic vulnerability in how they consume interface text could lead to serious security risks, such as goal hijacking or unauthorized device actions. The authors are motivated to investigate whether treating accessibility text as trusted instructions exposes these systems to prompt injection attacks and to quantify how severe and widespread this vulnerability is.
AI.method: The authors analyze the architectures of mobile agent frameworks like MobileRun and Mobile-Use, focusing on their dependence on Android accessibility (A11y) trees and visual screenshots as input. They then design indirect prompt injection attacks by embedding adversarial instructions into accessibility metadata and UI content, including both visually hidden and visible text. Using large language models (Gemma4:31B for MobileRun and Qwen3.6:35B for Mobile-Use), they empirically evaluate how often these agents deviate from their intended tasks, cross context boundaries, and perform unauthorized actions under various attack scenarios. They systematically categorize the observed attack behaviors into a taxonomy.
AI.result: Experiments show that adversarial prompts embedded in Android accessibility metadata and UI text can reliably cause autonomous mobile agents to deviate from their original objectives, violate context boundaries, and execute unauthorized device actions. MobileRun, when paired with Gemma4:31B, exhibits a high attack success rate of 0.822 across tested scenarios. Mobile-Use, combined with Qwen3.6:35B, reduces the measured attack success rate to 0.150, indicating some increased robustness, but still suffers from context drift and unauthorized actions. The attacks are successful both when malicious text is visually hidden and when it is fully visible, demonstrating a systemic vulnerability.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that current mobile autonomous agent frameworks are fundamentally vulnerable because they treat environmental text—especially Android accessibility metadata—as trustworthy instructions instead of untrusted input. This leads to a failure to enforce semantic context boundaries and makes the systems susceptible to indirect prompt injection, enabling goal hijacking and unauthorized actions. The authors propose a taxonomy of these attacks and argue for architectural changes such as zero-trust input validation for all UI text, the introduction of dedicated security agents to scrutinize instructions, and strict context isolation mechanisms within mobile agent pipelines to mitigate these risks.

title: Depth-Aware Implicit Neural Representation Priors for 3D Gravity Inversion
summary: Gravimetry images subsurface density contrasts associated with geological structures, geothermal systems, and intrusive bodies. Recovering a three-dimensional density model from gravity observations is highly ill-posed because of its non-uniqueness, limited data coverage, and the attenuation of the gravity field with depth. Classical inversion methods rely on explicit regularization and parameter tuning, whereas supervised deep-learning approaches require representative gravity--density pairs that are rarely available. This paper proposes an unsupervised depth-aware implicit neural representation for 3D gravity inversion. The density volume is represented by multiple coordinate-based neural networks assigned to overlapping depth slabs and optimized directly from the observed gravity measurements through the sensitivity matrix. Slab-specific Fourier features, physics-based depth gains, and scheduled regularization provide structural priors without requiring labeled density models. Experiments on four synthetic scenarios show that the proposed method provides better overall performance in terms of RMSE, PSNR, and SSIM than the evaluated conventional and neural baselines. It also recovers more compact and spatially coherent density bodies, improves the separation of nearby anomalies, preserves internal structures, and reconstructs their vertical extent better. These results indicate that the proposed depth-aware formulation helps to mitigate the depth ambiguity inherent in gravity inversion. In the field experiment, where no ground-truth density model was available, the method produced compact, separated, and vertically coherent anomalies consistent with the observed gravity pattern.

AI.tldr: An unsupervised, depth-aware implicit neural representation is proposed for 3D gravity inversion, yielding more accurate and geologically plausible density reconstructions than classical and neural baselines, without needing labeled training data.
AI.motivation: Gravity inversion to recover 3D subsurface density is highly ill-posed due to non-uniqueness, limited coverage, and depth attenuation of the gravity field. Classical inversions demand careful regularization and parameter tuning, while supervised deep learning needs large sets of representative gravity–density pairs, which are rarely available in real settings. There is a need for a method that can incorporate strong structural priors and mitigate depth ambiguity without relying on labeled ground-truth models.
AI.method: The authors introduce an unsupervised depth-aware implicit neural representation for 3D gravity inversion. The subsurface density is parameterized by multiple coordinate-based neural networks, each responsible for an overlapping depth slab. These networks are trained directly from observed gravity data through the physics-based sensitivity matrix, without labeled density targets. The approach uses slab-specific Fourier features to encode spatial variation, depth-dependent gains derived from the physics of gravity attenuation, and a scheduled regularization scheme to inject structural priors and stabilize training over time.
AI.result: On four synthetic test scenarios, the method outperforms conventional inversion and neural baselines across RMSE, PSNR, and SSIM metrics. It produces density models that are more compact and spatially coherent, better separates closely spaced anomalies, preserves internal structures, and more accurately reconstructs the vertical extent of density bodies, indicating a reduction in depth ambiguity. In a real field application lacking ground-truth density, the recovered anomalies are compact, separated, and vertically coherent, and they agree qualitatively with the observed gravity patterns.
AI.conclusion: The proposed depth-aware implicit neural representation provides an effective unsupervised framework for 3D gravity inversion, mitigating depth ambiguity and improving structural fidelity without requiring labeled density models. Its ability to produce compact, coherent, and geologically plausible anomalies, and to outperform existing baselines on multiple metrics, suggests it is a promising tool for practical gravity-based subsurface imaging in both synthetic and field settings.

title: Reading is not Reasoning: Bridging the Agentic Policy Gap in Vision-Text Compression
summary: Multi-step language-model agents repeatedly process growing interaction histories, leading to substantial context costs. Vision--text compression reduces these costs by rendering history as images, but the resulting modality shift creates a marked capability gap. Through controlled evaluations of history recovery, matched-state decisions, and complete trajectories, we show that this gap cannot be explained by OCR quality alone. Visual-history agents exhibit systematic drift in action selection, query formulation, stopping, and evidence use, revealing an agentic policy gap. We introduce \textbf{CAPS}, a two-stage \textbf{C}ross-modal \textbf{A}gentic \textbf{P}olicy \textbf{S}elf-distillation framework that uses the same model's stronger text-history policy to supervise its visual-history counterpart. Offline trajectory self-distillation transfers successful text-policy behavior to visual-history inputs, while online policy self-distillation provides dense supervision on states visited by the visual-history policy during reinforcement learning. On SearchQA, CAPS improves over AgentOCR by 5.0\% and 3.4\% with 3B and 7B backbones, respectively. On full-history ALFWorld, the corresponding gains are 15.6\% and 14.5\%. Across settings, CAPS reduces average memory-context cost by up to 63.3\% and peak cost by up to 83.4\% relative to matched text-history policies. These results show that explicit cross-modal policy self-distillation can preserve agent capability under vision--text compression. Our code will be made publicly available in a future release.

AI.tldr: The paper tackles the high context cost of multi-step language-model agents by compressing interaction history into images, then closing the resulting performance gap via cross-modal policy self-distillation, enabling visual-history agents to match text-history capabilities with far lower memory use.
AI.motivation: Multi-step LM agents repeatedly re-read long and growing text histories, which is expensive in context length and computation. Vision–text compression can shorten these histories by turning text into images, but this introduces a modality shift: agents given visual histories perform worse than those given text histories. Existing work often attributes this primarily to OCR issues, but the authors observe systematic behavioral differences (action choice, query formulation, stopping decisions, evidence use) that suggest a deeper policy mismatch between text- and vision-conditioned agents. They are motivated to understand and close this ";agentic policy gap"; so that vision–text compression can reduce context cost without sacrificing agent performance.
AI.method: The authors first run controlled experiments comparing agents with text histories versus those with visually rendered histories, measuring history reconstruction, matched-state decision behavior, and full trajectory outcomes to isolate where performance diverges and to show the gap is not just due to OCR errors. They then propose CAPS, a two-stage cross-modal agentic policy self-distillation framework. In the offline stage, they perform trajectory-level self-distillation, using trajectories from the stronger text-history policy as supervision targets to train the same backbone model to act on visual-history inputs. In the online stage, during reinforcement learning, they add policy self-distillation: the text-history policy provides dense supervision on the specific states visited by the visual-history policy, ensuring behavior alignment under the visual modality. This combination transfers the agentic behavior learned with text histories into the visual-history setting.
AI.result: On the SearchQA benchmark, CAPS yields performance improvements over a strong visual-history baseline (AgentOCR) of 5.0 percentage points for 3B-parameter backbones and 3.4 points for 7B models. On the more challenging, full-history ALFWorld environment, the gains are larger: 15.6 and 14.5 percentage points for 3B and 7B models, respectively. At the same time, CAPS maintains the compression benefits of vision–text history: relative to text-history policies with matched backbones, it reduces average memory context cost by up to 63.3% and peak context cost by up to 83.4%. The evaluations also confirm that the pre-existing visual-history agents exhibited systematic drifts in action selection, query formulation, stopping behavior, and evidence use that are mitigated by CAPS.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that the performance gap between text-history and visual-history agents is fundamentally an agentic policy gap rather than merely an OCR or perception issue. Explicit cross-modal agentic policy self-distillation—using a model’s own text-history policy to supervise its visual-history variant—can successfully transfer decision-making behavior across modalities. CAPS substantially restores agent capabilities under vision–text compression while providing large reductions in memory context usage, demonstrating that effective, low-cost multi-step agents can be built without sacrificing performance. The authors plan to release code to facilitate further research in cross-modal policy alignment and compressed-history agents.

title: CoRe-UIE: Rethinking Coexisting and Region-wise Degradation for Underwater Image Enhancement
summary: Underwater images often suffer from diverse and coexisting degradations, including color distortion, scattering haze, texture attenuation, and uneven illumination. These degradations vary across regions and may coexist locally, making conventional uniform restoration difficult to adapt to different degradation patterns. To address this problem, we propose Coexisting and Region-wise Degradation for Underwater Image Enhancement (\textbf{CoRe-UIE}), a degradation-oriented expert collaboration framework. CoRe-UIE combines a content-preserving shared expert with four shared-backbone routed experts for color correction, scattering suppression, texture recovery, and illumination protection. The routed experts share the same architecture but have independent parameters, and are assigned to different regions through input-derived degradation cues and region-adaptive Top-\(k\) routing. We further introduce a Hilbert--Schmidt Independence Criterion (HSIC)-based representation constraint to reduce statistical dependence among expert features and alleviate redundant expert responses. Experiments on UIEB, LSUI, and U45 demonstrate that CoRe-UIE achieves competitive quantitative performance and visually balanced enhancement under diverse underwater degradation conditions.

AI.tldr: A framework (CoRe-UIE) for underwater image enhancement that uses multiple specialized experts routed region-wise to handle coexisting degradations, with an independence constraint to reduce redundancy, achieving strong performance on several benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Underwater images suffer from multiple, spatially varying degradations—color distortion, haze, texture loss, and uneven illumination—that often coexist in different regions of the same image. Conventional methods typically assume a more uniform degradation and thus struggle to adapt to these complex, region-wise variations. There is a need for an enhancement method that can flexibly and locally adapt to different degradation types within the same image while preserving content and avoiding over-correction.
AI.method: The authors propose CoRe-UIE, a degradation-oriented expert collaboration framework. It uses a content-preserving shared expert plus four routed experts, each specializing in a particular degradation factor: color correction, scattering suppression, texture recovery, and illumination protection. All routed experts share the same network architecture but have separate parameters. A routing mechanism assigns different image regions to different experts based on degradation cues derived from the input and a region-adaptive Top-k routing strategy, enabling multiple experts to collaborate on each region if needed. Additionally, they introduce a Hilbert–Schmidt Independence Criterion (HSIC)-based representation constraint to make the expert feature representations more statistically independent, thereby reducing overlap and redundancy in the experts’ responses.
AI.result: On three underwater image enhancement benchmarks (UIEB, LSUI, and U45), CoRe-UIE attains competitive or superior quantitative metrics compared with existing methods, and visual evaluations show more balanced and natural enhancement across diverse and coexisting underwater degradations.
AI.conclusion: By explicitly modeling coexisting and region-wise degradations via specialized routed experts and enforcing representation independence among them, CoRe-UIE can adaptively and collaboratively enhance underwater images, leading to improved quantitative performance and visually balanced results across varied underwater conditions.

title: Context Is Not Authority: Structured Runtime Governance for Financial Market Agents
comment: 15 pages, 1 figure, 9 tables. Qiangqiang Liu and Yichi Zhang are corresponding authors
summary: Financial agents can turn correct context into an unauthorized effect: a customer-facing commitment, trade, or deployed policy. We present SAGE-Fin, a finance-specific authority-handoff contract that makes the proposed effect, not merely its text, the object of runtime control. SAGE-Fin compiles proposals into typed, adapter-bound candidates; records missing or stale institutional obligations as coverage debt; contracts authority under current market, account, policy, and dialogue state; and requires an exact-artifact receipt whose nominal type matches the consuming response, execution, or policy adapter. Evidence and workflow progress cannot substitute for effect authority, and prior authorization is rechecked after state changes. Across an authored 616-case catalog, five deterministic specifications yield 3,080 outputs; a label-isolated harness obtains 616/616 binary reference-prototype parity, including 3/3 named response-gate fixtures, while 22 tests cover selected paths. These results establish executable conformance, not independent safety accuracy. Separately, SAGE-Fin's response gate processed real customer-facing production requests at a confidential digital-asset platform. An operational team independent of the implementation team reached a strongly positive post-deployment conclusion on practical usefulness and workflow fit, and end-user feedback was also strongly positive. Disclosure permits only the review's independence, stakeholder classes, assessed dimensions, and directional conclusion, so this is qualitative field corroboration rather than an aggregate effect estimate. Three distinct de-identified predecessor failures, with independently confirmed 0/3 interception, ground repeated-emission drift, stale account evidence, and missing escalation state without estimating prevalence or treatment effect.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces SAGE-Fin, a contract system for financial AI agents that controls actual effects (like commitments or trades) rather than just their text, ensuring that any customer-facing or transactional action is explicitly authorized at runtime.
AI.motivation: Financial AI agents can take contextually correct information and still produce unauthorized real-world effects, such as binding commitments, trades, or policy changes. Existing guardrails and logging often focus on text output or evidence/workflow artifacts, not on the concrete external effects that result. There is a need for a domain-specific authority-handoff and execution model that is tightly integrated with financial institutions’ obligations, account states, policies, and dialogue context, to prevent drift, stale-state actions, and missing escalations.
AI.method: The authors design SAGE-Fin, an authority-handoff contract specialized for finance. It compiles model proposals into typed, adapter-bound candidate effects; tracks missing or outdated institutional obligations as "coverage debt"; and determines whether authority is valid under the current market, account, policy, and dialogue state. The system requires an exact-artifact receipt whose type matches the downstream adapter (response, execution, or policy), and it revalidates prior authorizations after any state change. They construct a 616-case catalog of scenarios and run five deterministic specifications to generate 3,080 outputs, validating parity between a reference and prototype implementation with a label-isolated test harness. Additional unit tests exercise selected code paths. They also deploy a response-gate module in a production digital-asset platform and gather structured qualitative feedback from an independent operational team and end users. Finally, they analyze three real historical failure cases (de-identified) to show how SAGE-Fin’s design targets specific failure modes, without quantifying prevalence or treatment effect.
AI.result: In the synthetic catalog, SAGE-Fin achieves 616/616 binary parity between the reference and prototype implementations across 3,080 outputs, including full agreement on three named response-gate fixtures. Twenty-two additional tests cover key execution paths. This demonstrates executable conformance of the implementation to its specifications, though not the overall safety performance relative to ground truth. In production, SAGE-Fin’s response gate successfully processed real customer-facing requests at a confidential digital-asset platform. An independent operational team judged it to have strong practical usefulness and good workflow fit, and end-user feedback was also strongly positive. The three historical failure cases (repeated-emission drift, stale account evidence, and missing escalation state) are shown to be conceptually intercepted by SAGE-Fin, but without quantified impact.
AI.conclusion: SAGE-Fin provides a structured, finance-specific runtime contract that ties AI agents’ authority directly to the concrete effects they attempt to trigger, rather than to their textual outputs or evidentiary artifacts. By enforcing typed, adapter-bound proposals, tracking coverage debt, and revalidating authority after state changes, it aims to prevent unauthorized or stale actions in financial workflows. The work demonstrates that the implementation conforms to its formal specifications and that the system is practically usable and valued in at least one real-world deployment, but it does not claim or measure overall safety improvements or incident reduction rates. Instead, it offers a principled mechanism and qualitative field corroboration that such an effect-centric authority model fits real financial operations and addresses clinically observed failure patterns.

title: DualCert: A Solver for the Traveling Salesman Problem with Constraint-Coupled Learning
summary: Large traveling salesman problem (TSP) instances require a solver to allocate limited computation while preserving the validity of its outputs. Existing neural--operations-research (OR) hybrids predict guidance without requiring learned transitions to satisfy constraints discovered during search. DualCert introduces \emph{constraint-coupled learning}, in which current degree equations and dynamically separated subtour-elimination constraints (SECs) define each learned transition. At each refinement, the degree equations and selected, strictly satisfied SEC equations, with positive slacks, define an iterate-dependent primal-slack Karush--Kuhn--Tucker (KKT) manifold. Repaired dual variables and violated SEC rows define a local cost field. An exact constrained mirror-descent step maps each finite state to a positive state on the same manifold. Where selected rows and deterministic ties remain fixed, implicit differentiation maps parameter perturbations into the manifold tangent space and reuses the forward constraint operator for the local-cost-field derivative. The terminal edge state allocates computation across Held--Karp ascent, candidate-graph edge tests, and tour construction under a fixed budget. Deterministic verification recomputes original costs and accepts only verified candidate-graph lower bounds and edge decisions. On 1,000 held-out TSP1000 instances, DualCert attains a mean tour-cost gap of \(0.0573\%\) from Lin--Kernighan--Helsgaun version 3 (LKH-3) reference tours in \(9.55\) batch-amortized seconds per instance. It returns a verified candidate-graph lower bound for every instance and achieves \(81.46\%\) edge-decision coverage. The mean gap is \(67.1\%\) smaller than the reported NeuroLKH mean gap. Thus, optimization constraints govern learning, while deterministic verification preserves output validity.

AI.tldr: DualCert is a neural-OR hybrid for large TSPs that couples learning directly to optimization constraints and then deterministically verifies all outputs, achieving very small optimality gaps under strict validity guarantees.
AI.motivation: Neural approaches to combinatorial optimization, like TSP, can guide search efficiently but often ignore the exact constraints that arise during classical optimization, and they may produce unverified or invalid outputs. There is a need for methods that (1) exploit learning for speed and guidance, (2) remain tightly grounded in the underlying mathematical programming constraints, and (3) provide deterministic guarantees or verifiable correctness of outputs.
AI.method: DualCert introduces constraint-coupled learning: every learned transition is constructed to satisfy the current degree constraints and dynamically generated subtour-elimination constraints (SECs). At each refinement step, the method forms an iterate-dependent primal-slack KKT manifold from degree equations and strictly satisfied SEC equations. It defines a local cost field using repaired dual variables and violated SECs, then performs an exact constrained mirror-descent step that keeps the state on this manifold while improving the objective. Implicit differentiation is used to map parameter changes into the tangent space of this manifold, allowing efficient gradient computation with reuse of the constraint operator. The final edge state dictates how computation is allocated among Held–Karp ascent, candidate-graph edge tests, and tour construction. A deterministic verification phase recomputes original costs and accepts only those lower bounds and edge decisions that can be fully verified.
AI.result: On 1,000 held-out TSP instances of size 1000, DualCert achieves a mean optimality gap of 0.0573% relative to LKH-3 tours, using 9.55 batch-amortized seconds per instance. It produces a verified candidate-graph lower bound for every instance and covers 81.46% of edge decisions. Its mean gap is reported to be 67.1% smaller than that of NeuroLKH, a prior neural-guided TSP solver.
AI.conclusion: By embedding optimization constraints directly into the learning process and pairing this with deterministic verification, DualCert yields high-quality TSP solutions that are both accurate and provably valid. This architecture demonstrates that optimization constraints can effectively govern learning in neural-OR hybrids, improving reliability and performance over previous neural methods while keeping strong guarantees on solution validity.

title: A Multi-Scale Temporal Framework with Dynamic Fusion for EEG-Based Emotion Recognition
comment: The paper has been accepted at: IEEE | 2026 9th International Conference on Pattern Recognition and Artificial Intelligence (PRAI 2026)
summary: Mixed emotions represent a clinically relevant but still underexplored target for automatic emotion recognition. EEG provides millisecond-level access to neural activity, yet most EEG pipelines analyze the signal through a single temporal window, thereby fixing the temporal structure available to the model. This study introduces a multi-scale temporal framework for EEG-based emotion recognition. The EEG waveform is decomposed into windows of one or several durations, processed by a shared attention-based encoder, and integrated through a dynamic fusion module that assigns sample-specific weights across temporal scales. The framework is evaluated under a subject-independent protocol in binary and three-class settings, with the three-class task including the mixed affective category. The best results are 65.22% for the two-class task and 45.43% for the three-class task. Both are obtained with three-scale dynamic-fusion configurations and remain substantially above the full-signal baseline. The best-performing temporal scales differ between the two tasks. Dynamic fusion outperforms concatenation in the highest-scoring two-class configuration and slightly exceeds it in the highest-scoring three-class configuration, although these multi-scale settings require substantially more computation than the full-signal baseline.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a multi-scale temporal EEG framework with dynamic fusion for automatic recognition of pure and mixed emotions, achieving better accuracy than a full-signal baseline in both binary and three-class tasks.
AI.motivation: Mixed emotions are clinically important but underexplored in automatic emotion recognition. Existing EEG-based approaches usually use a single temporal window, which fixes the temporal structure and may miss information occurring at different time scales, especially for complex or mixed affective states.
AI.method: The authors design a multi-scale temporal framework for EEG-based emotion recognition. They segment the EEG waveform into multiple window durations (temporal scales). Each windowed segment is processed by a shared attention-based encoder. Then, a dynamic fusion module assigns sample-specific weights to the outputs from different temporal scales, effectively learning which scales are most informative for each instance. They evaluate this framework in a subject-independent setting on binary (two-class) and three-class emotion recognition tasks, where the three-class task includes a mixed-emotion category. They compare multi-scale dynamic fusion to a full-signal baseline and to simple concatenation of multi-scale features.
AI.result: Using three temporal scales with dynamic fusion yields the best performance: 65.22% accuracy for the binary emotion classification and 45.43% for the three-class task including mixed emotions. These results are significantly better than the full-signal (single-window) baseline. The optimal set of temporal scales differs between the binary and three-class tasks, and dynamic fusion performs better than feature concatenation in the best two-class configuration and slightly better in the best three-class configuration. However, these multi-scale settings incur much higher computational cost compared with the baseline.
AI.conclusion: Multi-scale temporal modeling with dynamic, sample-specific fusion improves EEG-based emotion recognition, including for mixed affective states, compared with using a single full-signal window. The attention-based encoder plus dynamic fusion can adaptively emphasize the most informative temporal scales for each sample. Although the approach is computationally more expensive, it provides a promising direction for capturing the complex temporal dynamics underlying pure and mixed emotions in EEG signals.

title: Who Bridges Safety? Identifying and Targeting Cross-Lingual Shared Safety Pathways
summary: Uncovering the internal mechanisms underlying the safety capabilities of large language models (LLMs) is crucial for developing trustworthy artificial intelligence. Currently, mechanistic interpretability studies on multilingual safety are largely confined to local components, such as isolated neurons. However, this static and fragmented perspective overlooks the synergy among components and fails to elucidate how safety signals dynamically propagate within the model to drive safety decisions ultimately. In this work, we move beyond isolated neurons to identify and target the cross-layer functional pathways formed during safety signal propagation, thereby uncovering the mechanisms driving the cross-lingual safety gap. Specifically, we first identify monolingual safety pathways and validate their impact on refusing harmful requests. Subsequent cross-lingual analyses reveal a sparse subset of cross-lingual shared safety pathways, confirming that this intersection acts as the internal bridge transferring safety capabilities from high-resource (HR) languages to non-high-resource (NHR) languages. Building on these mechanistic findings, we propose a pathways-targeted alignment method based on the cross-lingual shared safety pathways. Experimental results show that updating only a small fraction of pathway parameters significantly improves safety in NHR languages while largely preserving the model's general capabilities.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies cross-layer safety pathways in multilingual LLMs, showing how shared pathways transfer safety from high-resource to low-resource languages and proposing a pathway-targeted alignment method that boosts non-high-resource language safety with minimal impact on general abilities.
AI.motivation: To develop trustworthy multilingual LLMs, we need to understand how safety behavior (like refusing harmful requests) emerges internally. Existing mechanistic interpretability mostly inspects isolated neurons, which misses how safety signals propagate through layers and across languages, and cannot explain cross-lingual safety gaps between high-resource and non-high-resource languages.
AI.method: The authors move from single neurons to cross-layer functional pathways that carry safety signals. They: (1) identify monolingual safety pathways associated with refusals to harmful requests; (2) validate their causal impact on safety behavior; (3) perform cross-lingual analysis to find a sparse intersection of safety pathways shared between high-resource and non-high-resource languages; and (4) design a pathways-targeted alignment method that updates parameters only on these shared safety pathways to enhance safety in non-high-resource languages.
AI.result: They find that safety is implemented not by isolated neurons but by cross-layer pathways whose activation and parameters affect refusal behavior. A sparse subset of these pathways is shared across languages and acts as an internal bridge transferring safety capabilities from high-resource to non-high-resource languages. Updating only a small fraction of parameters on these shared pathways leads to substantial safety improvements in non-high-resource languages while preserving most of the model’s general performance.
AI.conclusion: Safety behavior in multilingual LLMs is driven by structured, cross-layer safety pathways, some of which are shared across languages and mediate transfer from high-resource to non-high-resource languages. Targeting these shared safety pathways during alignment is an efficient way to close cross-lingual safety gaps with minimal interference to overall capabilities, demonstrating the practical value of mechanistic insights for safer multilingual AI.

title: Different Feedback, Different Updates: Selective Self-Learning from User Interactions for Large Language Models
summary: User feedback offers natural supervision for persistent LLM improvement, but a single message may support multiple behavioral changes with different scopes of generalization. We introduce SLIFT, a selective self-learning framework built on a task-relative view of user feedback. SLIFT decomposes each feedback message into atomic components and interprets each component relative to the original task as Fix, Spec, or Null: requirements for task validity, compatible condition-specific refinements, or content with no reliable positive update direction. To incorporate each change at the appropriate scope, SLIFT trains two complementary LoRA adapters on a shared frozen backbone: a Generalist that consolidates Fix requirements into default behavior through feedback-conditioned self-distillation, and a Specialist that observes only the task and Generalist response to supply residual guidance for applicable, unmet Spec refinements. Null components induce no positive update. Across backbones, SLIFT achieves strong performance on both MemoryBench and WildFB, with targeted analyses further examining its underlying mechanisms. We release our code at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/SLIFT.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes SLIFT, a selective self-learning framework that decomposes user feedback into different types and trains two LoRA adapters (Generalist and Specialist) to integrate corrections at appropriate levels of generalization, improving LLM behavior on feedback-driven benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing methods that use user feedback to improve LLMs often treat each feedback message as a single signal, failing to distinguish between corrections that should generalize broadly, refinements that apply only in specific contexts, and feedback that is noisy or ambiguous. This can lead to overgeneralization, mis-generalization, or learning from unreliable signals. The authors are motivated to create a framework that can selectively learn from feedback, mapping each part of the feedback to an appropriate learning scope, so that LLMs can continually improve from natural user interactions without degrading performance elsewhere.
AI.method: SLIFT first decomposes each user feedback message into atomic components. Each component is interpreted relative to the original task as one of three types: (1) Fix: requirements necessary for the task to be valid or correct; (2) Spec: compatible, condition-specific refinements or preferences that should not necessarily generalize universally; (3) Null: feedback content that does not provide a reliable positive update direction (e.g., noisy, irrelevant, or contradictory suggestions). To integrate these different components, SLIFT uses a frozen backbone LLM with two LoRA adapters. The Generalist adapter is trained to consolidate Fix requirements into the model's default behavior via feedback-conditioned self-distillation: the model learns to produce corrected outputs that respect Fix constraints as the new norm. The Specialist adapter only observes the task and the Generalist’s output and learns to provide residual guidance to satisfy applicable Spec refinements that the Generalist does not yet fulfill. Null components are explicitly prevented from inducing positive updates. This architecture separates general corrections from context-specific refinements, enabling more precise and reliable self-learning from feedback.
AI.result: Across multiple backbone models, SLIFT achieves strong empirical performance on MemoryBench and WildFB, two benchmarks that measure a model’s ability to use and benefit from user feedback and memory-like corrections. The results show that SLIFT can improve both general behavior (via the Generalist) and task-specific refinements (via the Specialist), outperforming baselines that do not separate feedback into different scopes or that update the model monolithically. Targeted analyses further investigate how SLIFT’s decomposition of feedback and dual-adapter design contribute to its gains, providing evidence that selectively learning Fix vs. Spec components leads to more robust and controllable behavior changes.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that user feedback is inherently multi-faceted and should not be treated as a single undifferentiated learning signal. By adopting a task-relative view of feedback and decomposing it into Fix, Spec, and Null components, SLIFT enables selective self-learning that respects the appropriate generalization scope for each feedback element. The dual-adapter architecture—Generalist for broad corrections and Specialist for residual, context-specific refinements—allows LLMs to improve continually from natural feedback without overgeneralization or degradation on other tasks. The positive results on MemoryBench and WildFB support the effectiveness of this approach, and the released code facilitates further research on structured feedback-driven learning for LLMs.

title: RAVEN-Eval: Rubric-Guided Automatic Evaluation for AI Video Generation Models Based on LMM Preference Judgement
summary: AI video generation has advanced rapidly and entered widespread commercial use. As a result, quality differences among videos produced by state-of-the-art AI video generation models~(AIVGMs) have become increasingly difficult to discern using conventional evaluation criteria, such as visual fidelity and semantic instruction following. Meanwhile, human evaluation now requires more expertise and sustained attention, substantially increasing annotation costs. This calls for automated evaluation that can reliably distinguish fine-grained differences among advanced AIVGMs with minimal human intervention. To address this challenge, we present RAVEN-Eval, a rubric-guided automated evaluation framework for AIVGMs, built primarily on the LMM-as-a-judge paradigm. Through an automatic task curation and quality-filtering pipeline, RAVEN-Eval curates 150 text-to-video~(T2V) tasks and 100 image-to-video~(I2V) tasks, and systematically collects more than 4,500 AIGVs. At its core, RAVEN-Eval adopts rubric-guided automated LMM preference judgement, in which LMM judges conduct pairwise comparisons according to task-specific rubrics. It further introduces an anchor-based model insertion approach to reduce the evaluation cost of incorporating new models. Finally, we evaluate 20 high-performance AIVGMs, as well as the judging capabilities of 13 LMM judges, and establish the RAVEN-Eval Leaderboards. Overall, RAVEN-Eval paves a scalable path for automatic and trustworthy evaluation of rapidly evolving AIVGMs.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces RAVEN-Eval, an automated, rubric-guided evaluation framework using large multimodal models (LMMs) as judges to distinguish fine-grained quality differences among advanced AI video generation models (AIVGMs).
AI.motivation: Existing evaluation of AI video generation models relies on visual fidelity metrics, semantic alignment, and costly, expertise-heavy human annotation, which are no longer sufficient or scalable when state-of-the-art models produce similarly high-quality outputs. There is a need for a reliable, low-cost, automated evaluation system that can capture subtle, fine-grained differences between advanced text-to-video and image-to-video models while minimizing human intervention.
AI.method: RAVEN-Eval constructs a benchmark via an automatic task curation and quality-filtering pipeline, resulting in 150 text-to-video and 100 image-to-video tasks and over 4,500 generated videos. It uses rubric-guided, task-specific criteria and employs large multimodal models as judges to perform pairwise preference comparisons between video outputs from different generators. Additionally, it proposes an anchor-based model insertion strategy, where new models are evaluated relative to fixed anchor models to reduce the number of required comparisons and thus the evaluation cost.
AI.result: Using RAVEN-Eval, the authors evaluate 20 strong AI video generation models and systematically compare their performance. They also assess 13 different LMMs in their role as judges, analyzing their reliability and capabilities. The framework produces ranked leaderboards for both video generation models and LMM judges, demonstrating that rubric-guided LMM-as-a-judge evaluation can differentiate fine-grained quality differences among high-performing systems.
AI.conclusion: RAVEN-Eval provides a scalable, rubric-driven framework for automatic evaluation of AI video generation models, reducing dependence on expensive human annotation while maintaining trustworthy, fine-grained model comparisons. By combining curated tasks, LMM-based pairwise judgement, and anchor-based insertion for new models, it establishes a practical path toward continuous, automated benchmarking of rapidly evolving AI video generation systems, along with insights into the judging quality of different LMMs.

title: Motif 3: Technical Report
summary: We introduce Motif 3, a decoder-only Mixture-of-Experts language model with 314 billion total parameters and 13.2 billion activated per token. Each sparse MoE layer contains 384 routed experts, with eight selected per token. This fine-grained sparsity provides substantial expert capacity while limiting computation. Motif 3 is built around Grouped Differential Latent Attention (GDLA), which integrates grouped differential attention with the compressed key-value representation of Multi-head Latent Attention. The architecture further incorporates modified manifold-constrained hyper-connections, Expert Specific PolyNorm activations, and multi-token prediction to improve optimization stability, expert specialization, and inference efficiency. We pretrain Motif 3 on approximately 12.5 trillion tokens spanning web documents, STEM, code, mathematics, multilingual content, and domain-specialized corpora. Expert-balancing and numerical-stabilization techniques support stable training at scale, while selective MXFP8 computation and communication, memory-efficient fused kernels, and window-aware context parallelism enable training with context lengths up to 256K tokens. Our post-training pipeline combines general supervised fine-tuning, six specialist teachers trained with reinforcement learning, a software-engineering teacher trained with supervised fine-tuning, and Multi-teacher On-Policy Distillation. The resulting unified model consolidates complementary capabilities in reasoning, coding, tool use, professional work, long-context understanding, calibrated abstention, and instruction following. Across a broad evaluation suite, Motif 3 demonstrates competitive performance against leading open weight models, including strong results on long-horizon agentic tasks, mathematical reasoning, scientific knowledge, and hallucination-sensitive evaluation.

AI.tldr: Motif 3 is a 314B-parameter sparse Mixture-of-Experts language model that activates only 13.2B parameters per token, using a novel attention and training pipeline to achieve strong performance, especially on long-context and reasoning-heavy tasks.
AI.motivation: To scale language models to very large capacities without prohibitive computational cost, while improving reasoning, coding, long-context understanding, and reducing hallucinations. The authors aim to leverage fine-grained MoE sparsity, advanced attention mechanisms, and a sophisticated post-training pipeline to build a unified, high-capability model competitive with leading open-weight systems.
AI.method: They design a decoder-only sparse Mixture-of-Experts model with 314B total parameters where each MoE layer has 384 experts and routes each token to 8 experts. The core is Grouped Differential Latent Attention (GDLA), combining grouped differential attention with compressed key-value representations from Multi-head Latent Attention. They add manifold-constrained hyper-connections, Expert Specific PolyNorm activations, and multi-token prediction to stabilize training and improve expert specialization and efficiency. Training uses ~12.5T tokens across diverse domains and employs expert-balancing and numerical stabilization. Efficiency comes from selective MXFP8 compute/communication, fused kernels, and window-aware context parallelism to support 256K context. Post-training includes general SFT, multiple specialist RL-trained teachers, a supervised software-engineering teacher, and Multi-teacher On-Policy Distillation to merge capabilities into one model.
AI.result: Motif 3 attains strong, competitive performance versus top open-weight models. It excels particularly on long-horizon agentic tasks, mathematical reasoning, scientific knowledge benchmarks, long-context understanding, tool use, and hallucination-sensitive evaluations, while maintaining robust coding and professional-task performance.
AI.conclusion: Fine-grained sparse MoE architecture combined with GDLA, careful optimization techniques, and a multi-teacher distillation pipeline can deliver a unified large language model with very large total capacity but moderate per-token compute. This design yields competitive or strong performance across a wide range of complex tasks, especially those requiring long context and reliable reasoning, suggesting such architectures are a promising direction for scalable, high-capability open models.

title: MELLON - Multimodal Enhanced LLM for Online Navigation
summary: Web navigation agents are capable of addressing various types of tasks on different websites. Current baselines on web navigation are either unimodal or lack strong reasoning abilities given multimodal inputs. Focusing on the WebShop benchmark, a real-world website simulation, we explore the alignment of text and images, as well as multimodal reasoning and planning abilities, to enhance the performance of web navigation agents. We propose three innovative multimodal enhancements: Multimodal Enhanced LLM for Online Navigation (MELLON), VQAgent, and Multimodal Ranker. MELLON demonstrates a significant improvement in task completion accuracy, with a 9.26% increase after just one epoch of training. Our findings suggest the necessity of further exploration into multimodal approaches, with a focus on more extensive training and alignment strategies to enhance the effectiveness of web navigation agents.

AI.tldr: The paper enhances web navigation agents on the WebShop benchmark by introducing three multimodal methods that better align text and images, significantly boosting task completion accuracy.
AI.motivation: Existing web navigation agents are limited: many are unimodal (often text-only) or, when multimodal, lack strong reasoning and planning abilities over combined text–image inputs. On realistic e-commerce-style sites, agents must understand both product images and descriptions and reason over them to complete complex user tasks. The authors aim to close this gap and improve real-world web navigation performance.
AI.method: They focus on the WebShop benchmark, a simulated real-world shopping website, and introduce three multimodal enhancements. (1) MELLON (Multimodal Enhanced LLM for Online Navigation): a multimodal extension of an LLM-based web agent trained to jointly process page text and images for navigation and decision-making. (2) VQAgent: likely a module or agent that uses vector-quantized or discrete embeddings to better capture visual information for downstream reasoning in navigation. (3) Multimodal Ranker: a model that ranks candidate actions or items by jointly using visual and textual cues, guiding the agent toward more promising navigation choices. They train these components and integrate them in the web navigation pipeline to test their effect on WebShop tasks.
AI.result: MELLON achieves a notable 9.26% absolute increase in task completion accuracy after only one epoch of training on WebShop, indicating that better multimodal alignment and reasoning substantially improves web navigation performance. The abstract implies that the other components (VQAgent and Multimodal Ranker) also contribute to performance gains, though detailed metrics are not given here.
AI.conclusion: The study concludes that multimodal approaches—especially those that tightly integrate text–image alignment with explicit reasoning and planning—are crucial for advancing web navigation agents. Even relatively modest training of such models can yield sizable performance improvements, and further work on larger-scale training and more sophisticated alignment strategies is needed to fully realize their potential on real-world web tasks.

title: RISE-RL: Rubric-Informed Selective Exploration for Open-Ended Reinforcement Learning
summary: Aligning Large Language Models (LLMs) for open-ended tasks is challenging because responses must satisfy multidimensional criteria without following a single correct generation trajectory. Existing rubric-based reinforcement learning (RL) methods compress fine-grained criterion-level feedback into scalar rewards, making persistent capability gaps difficult to target under limited on-policy exploration. We propose $\textbf{RISE-RL}$ (Rubric-Informed Selective Exploration), which uses repeatedly missed rubric criteria to elicit privileged trajectories that are difficult to discover through unguided exploration alone. RISE-RL retains only trajectories whose complete-rubric reward exceeds the mean reward of natural rollouts, and then re-evaluates them under the original prompt to emphasize behaviors that remain weakly supported by the natural policy. The resulting guidance signal is optimized through a separate auxiliary objective and removed once its additional benefit diminishes. Experiments with 4B and 14B models across writing, chat, health, and science show that RISE-RL achieves the highest mean score on every evaluated benchmark under guidance-free evaluation. Compared with standard Rubric-RL, it improves the average score by 1.3 points at the 4B scale and $\textbf{3.3 points at the 14B scale}$, including a $\textbf{6.0-point}$ gain on CreativeWriting-V3. It also improves creative-writing diversity and yields gains on objectively scored medical and scientific benchmarks. These results indicate that selective internalization through reward filtering and policy support shaping is effective for open-ended reinforcement learning.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes RISE-RL, a reinforcement learning method that better aligns large language models on open-ended tasks by selectively exploring and internalizing rubric criteria that models consistently miss, improving performance and diversity across multiple benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Aligning LLMs on open-ended tasks is difficult because there is no single correct answer and outputs must satisfy multiple rubric criteria simultaneously. Existing rubric-based RL methods collapse fine-grained feedback into a scalar reward, which makes it hard to focus learning on persistent weaknesses and to discover rare but valuable trajectories under limited on-policy exploration. The authors want an RL approach that can systematically target repeatedly missed rubric criteria and overcome the limitations of unguided exploration.
AI.method: The authors introduce RISE-RL (Rubric-Informed Selective Exploration). First, they use a detailed rubric that scores multiple criteria for model responses. They identify criteria that the current policy repeatedly fails to satisfy and use these as a signal to elicit privileged trajectories that are unlikely to appear via standard exploration. Among all generated trajectories, they filter and retain only those whose full-rubric reward is above the mean reward of natural (unguided) rollouts. These filtered trajectories are then re-evaluated under the original prompt to highlight behaviors that are still weakly supported by the base policy. This guidance signal is optimized with a separate auxiliary objective, alongside the main RL objective. The guidance is gradually removed once it stops providing additional benefit, yielding a policy that has selectively internalized the previously missing capabilities without relying on ongoing guidance at inference time.
AI.result: On 4B and 14B parameter models evaluated on writing, chat, health, and science tasks, RISE-RL achieves the highest mean score on all benchmarks under guidance-free evaluation. Relative to standard Rubric-RL, it improves average scores by 1.3 points at 4B and 3.3 points at 14B, with a notable 6.0-point gain on the CreativeWriting-V3 benchmark. It also increases diversity in creative-writing tasks and improves performance on objectively scored medical and scientific benchmarks, indicating benefits beyond subjective or stylistic metrics.
AI.conclusion: Selective internalization of rubric criteria via reward filtering and policy support shaping is an effective strategy for open-ended RL alignment of LLMs. By focusing exploration and learning on repeatedly missed rubric dimensions and using privileged but filtered trajectories, RISE-RL overcomes some limitations of scalar-reward rubric RL, leading to stronger, more diverse, and more broadly applicable performance without requiring extra guidance at inference time.

title: ChronoState: Hidden Elapsed-Time Conditioning for Temporal-State Action Selection in Frozen-Backbone Language Models
comment: Submitted to SPIE Defense and Commercial Sensing 2027
summary: Temporal decisions in language-model systems often depend on both symbolic task state and elapsed wall-clock time, such as cache expiration, job completion, quota resets, deadlines, or stale sessions. We study whether elapsed time can be supplied as a non-token, system-side scalar and composed with visible symbolic state by a frozen-backbone language model. We introduce ChronoState, a compositional temporal-state benchmark in which symbolic state appears in the prompt, elapsed seconds tau are supplied through a hidden chronometric-injection channel, and the model selects a forced-choice temporal action. Here, "hidden" means hidden from the user-visible token sequence, not from model computation. Using Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct as a frozen bf16 backbone with a 31-dimensional sinusoidal-plus-log time encoding, gated FiLM residual modulation, and a rank-8 LoRA action surface, hidden-time CI reaches 0.9305 +/- 0.0134 accuracy and 0.9410 +/- 0.0103 balanced accuracy. No-time and shuffled-time controls fall to 0.5511 +/- 0.0042 and 0.3323 +/- 0.0097, respectively, with high shuffled-time wrong-state consistency supporting causal dependence on the injected scalar within the trained distribution. Generalization remains strong for held-out templates, durations, and multi-constraint compositions, but held-out quota-family transfer is weak at 0.5065 +/- 0.0559, while a fair prompt+LoRA timestamp baseline reaches 0.9893 +/- 0.0052. Thus, ChronoState supports a narrow conclusion: hidden elapsed time can be composed with symbolic task state under direct supervision, but does not establish autonomous time tracking, broad unseen-family abstraction, or superiority over prompt-injected timestamps.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates whether language models can use elapsed time provided as a hidden scalar (not as tokens) together with symbolic state to make temporal decisions, introducing the ChronoState benchmark and showing that such hidden-time conditioning works under supervision but doesn’t replace explicit timestamp prompts or yield broad generalization.
AI.motivation: Many real-world LLM applications depend on temporal logic that combines symbolic state (e.g., cache flags, quotas, job states) with actual elapsed wall-clock time. Existing systems typically inject time as text tokens, which is indirect, brittle, and may be suboptimal for precise temporal control. The authors want to know if elapsed time can instead be provided as a direct, non-linguistic scalar signal that the model composes with the symbolic task state, without retraining the full backbone. They specifically seek to understand if such a design enables robust, causal dependence on time and good generalization to new temporal scenarios.
AI.method: The authors propose ChronoState, a benchmark where the prompt contains the symbolic task state while the elapsed time τ is passed through a hidden, non-token channel into the model. They freeze the Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct backbone (bf16), encode τ using a 31-dimensional sinusoidal-plus-log time representation, and inject this into the model via gated FiLM (Feature-wise Linear Modulation) residual modulation. A rank-8 LoRA layer is trained as the action surface for forced-choice temporal decisions (e.g., whether to expire a cache or reset a quota). They compare several conditions: (1) hidden injected time (CI), (2) no-time control, and (3) shuffled-time control, and they also build a baseline where time is given via prompt tokens plus LoRA. Performance is evaluated via accuracy and balanced accuracy, including tests on held-out templates, durations, multi-constraint compositions, and a held-out quota-family transfer setting.
AI.result: With hidden-time chronometric injection, the modified model achieves 0.9305 ± 0.0134 accuracy and 0.9410 ± 0.0103 balanced accuracy on ChronoState. Removing time information reduces performance to 0.5511 ± 0.0042, while shuffling the injected time yields 0.3323 ± 0.0097 and shows high consistency of wrong answers with the wrong time, indicating a causal role for the injected scalar signal. Generalization is strong for unseen templates, new durations, and compositions involving multiple temporal constraints. However, transfer to a held-out quota-family task is weak at 0.5065 ± 0.0559. A baseline that provides time via textual timestamps in the prompt plus a LoRA head performs better, at 0.9893 ± 0.0052 accuracy.
AI.conclusion: The experiments show that a frozen LLM backbone can meaningfully use a hidden, continuous time signal when combined with symbolic state, achieving strong in-distribution and some out-of-distribution generalization under direct supervision. The model’s decisions depend causally on the injected time scalar. However, this mechanism does not confer autonomous time tracking, does not yield strong abstraction to unseen temporal task families (e.g., new quota types), and offers no advantage over simply encoding time in the prompt as text tokens. ChronoState therefore supports a limited but clear conclusion: hidden-time conditioning is feasible and effective for trained scenarios, but it is not yet a superior or broadly general alternative to prompt-based timestamps.

title: TRACE: TRajectory Attribution for Automated Context Engineering
summary:
Production AI agents fail when their context sources -- system prompts, knowledge bases, tool descriptions, and procedural skills -- contain errors or gaps. Current maintenance relies on manual log review and ad-hoc debugging, creating a scalability bottleneck as interaction volume grows.
  We present TRACE (TRajectory Attribution for Automated Context Engineering), an automated feedback loop that mines historical agent trajectories to diagnose and remediate context failures. Our key insight is that trajectories are rich with implicit dissatisfaction signals -- user corrections, rephrasing, abandonment cues -- that reveal precisely where context sources failed, without explicit feedback collection. Unlike model fine-tuning, TRACE operates on the context layer, enabling rapid iteration without retraining.
  We make four contributions: (1) a trajectory mining framework that systematically extracts diagnostic information from historical agent executions; (2) multi-component causal attribution that extends textual gradients from monolithic prompt optimization to heterogeneous context sources (skills, knowledge bases, tools, prompts); (3) exploratory verification, where agents actively read context sources to distinguish content gaps requiring CREATE from stale content requiring UPDATE, achieving 96% operation accuracy; and (4) a reusable simulation methodology and verifiable benchmark addressing the absence of open datasets for context debugging, with a six-category fault taxonomy, ground truth annotations, and a cross-layer verification protocol.
  On 60 dissatisfaction traces spanning three complexity tiers (up to 16 execution nodes), TRACE achieves 72.7% root cause attribution and 82% end-to-end fix effectiveness, showing that over 80% of context-layer failures can be automatically diagnosed and remediated by mining historical trajectories, an overlooked resource in production systems.

AI.tldr: TRACE is a method that automatically analyzes past AI agent interactions to find and fix problems in their prompts, tools, and knowledge sources, improving reliability without retraining models.
AI.motivation: Production AI agents often fail because their surrounding context—system prompts, tools, knowledge bases, and skills—contains errors or missing information. Maintaining and debugging this context currently requires manual log inspection and ad-hoc fixes, which does not scale as interaction volume and system complexity grow. There is a need for an automated, systematic way to diagnose and repair context-layer failures using existing interaction data, without expensive model fine-tuning or explicit user feedback collection.
AI.method: TRACE introduces an automated feedback loop that mines historical agent trajectories (multi-step executions) for implicit dissatisfaction signals such as user corrections, rephrasings, and abandonment. It uses a trajectory mining framework to extract diagnostic information; a multi-component causal attribution mechanism that generalizes textual gradient ideas to heterogeneous context sources (prompts, tools, skills, knowledge base entries); and an exploratory verification phase where agents actively read and probe context sources to decide whether missing or stale content requires CREATE or UPDATE operations. The authors also design a reusable simulation methodology and benchmark with a six-category fault taxonomy, ground-truth annotations, and a cross-layer verification protocol to rigorously evaluate context debugging performance.
AI.result: In experiments on 60 dissatisfaction traces across three complexity levels (up to 16 execution nodes per trace), TRACE attains 72.7% accuracy in identifying the root cause of context failures and 82% effectiveness in implementing fixes that resolve the issues end-to-end. Exploratory verification achieves 96% accuracy in distinguishing between content creation versus update operations. These results indicate that more than 80% of context-layer failures can be automatically diagnosed and repaired by leveraging historical trajectories, without model retraining.
AI.conclusion: Mining historical agent trajectories provides a powerful, underused signal for automated context engineering in production AI systems. TRACE demonstrates that context-layer failures—arising from prompts, tools, skills, and knowledge sources—can be accurately attributed and largely remediated through an automated feedback loop that operates entirely on the context layer. This approach scales better than manual debugging, avoids the costs and risks of model fine-tuning, and is supported by a reusable, verifiable benchmark for future work on context debugging and maintenance.

title: CIDER: A Dataset of Contextual Disclosure Boundaries for Privacy Preference Alignment
summary: Aligning large language models (LLMs) with human privacy preferences requires capturing individuals' disclosure boundaries beyond general privacy norms. However, a gap remains in eliciting such nuanced preferences to evaluate alignment in realistic settings. We introduce CIDER, a dataset of 14,850 human annotations from 169 users, forming 1,650 contextual disclosure boundary sets across 60 interpersonal communication scenarios involving information sharing that violates privacy norms. Each boundary represents a real user's disclosure decisions over 9 sharing variants in a scenario, for a given communication role and AI-mediated condition. We formulate a task in which models predict a user's disclosure decision from historical boundaries, with varying levels of contextual information. Across 12 open and proprietary models, in-context personalization improves prediction accuracy by up to 11.41 percentage points using only 6 historical examples. Larger models such as GPT-5.4 (with medium reasoning effort) and Claude Sonnet 4.6 are better at leveraging semantic context to understand user-specific, context-dependent disclosure preferences for more accurate predictions, while smaller models tend to rely on structured heuristics based on disclosure granularity and identifiability. Personalization generally improves prediction accuracy, but the improvement is often accompanied by imbalanced shifts in false-positive and false-negative rates across models, with only Claude Sonnet 4.6 achieving balanced improvements in both. Our findings reveal both the promise and limitations of inference-time personalization for privacy preference modeling and position CIDER as a resource for advancing personalized privacy alignment.

AI.tldr: The paper presents CIDER, a dataset and benchmark for modeling individual privacy disclosure boundaries, and evaluates how well different large language models can be personalized in-context to predict user-specific disclosure decisions.
AI.motivation: Existing work on privacy and LLM alignment mostly relies on general privacy norms, but real people have nuanced, context-dependent disclosure boundaries that vary by interpersonal scenario, communication role, and AI mediation. There is no standard way or dataset to elicit and evaluate such fine-grained, user-specific privacy preferences in realistic communication settings. This limits our ability to align LLMs with individual privacy expectations and to understand how personalization at inference time can help.
AI.method: The authors design 60 interpersonal communication scenarios involving norm-violating information sharing. For each scenario they define 9 sharing variants differing in aspects like level of detail, identifiability, and channel. They recruit 169 users who provide 14,850 annotations that form 1,650 disclosure boundary sets, where each boundary set is a single user’s allow/deny decisions over the 9 variants under specified communication roles and AI-mediated conditions. They then formulate a prediction task where a model must predict a user’s disclosure decision on new instances, given varying amounts of historical decisions (in-context personalization). They benchmark 12 open and proprietary LLMs, systematically varying context size and type, and analyze accuracy, error patterns, and false-positive/false-negative trade-offs.
AI.result: In-context personalization using a small number of historical disclosure examples (as few as 6) improves LLM prediction accuracy of user decisions by up to 11.41 percentage points. Larger, more capable models such as GPT-5.4 (medium reasoning effort) and Claude Sonnet 4.6 better exploit semantic and contextual cues to capture user-specific, context-dependent privacy preferences, while smaller models rely more on superficial, structured heuristics like disclosure granularity and identifiability. Personalization consistently boosts overall accuracy but often skews the balance between false positives (over-sharing) and false negatives (over-withholding). Among the tested models, only Claude Sonnet 4.6 manages to improve both types of errors in a balanced way.
AI.conclusion: The study shows that inference-time personalization via in-context learning can substantially enhance LLM alignment with individual privacy disclosure preferences, but it also introduces nuanced risks, particularly asymmetric shifts in false-positive and false-negative rates that can manifest as over- or under-sharing. CIDER provides a realistic, user-grounded benchmark for future research on personalized privacy alignment. The authors conclude that while personalization is promising for capturing fine-grained disclosure boundaries, careful evaluation and model design are needed to avoid harmful error patterns and to achieve balanced, trustworthy privacy behaviors in AI systems.

title: From Relevance to Execution Utility: Reward-Aware Dynamic Execution Gating for Skill-Based LLM Agents
summary: Agent skills are increasingly used to equip large language model (LLM) agents with reusable procedural knowledge. Although recent work has substantially improved skill retrieval due to the increasing skill libraries, retrieving a plausible skill bundle does not guarantee that executing it is worthwhile. Since every skill-conditioned rollout is computationally expensive, deciding whether a retrieved bundle should be executed has become an increasingly important challenge. To this end, we introduce the Reward-Aware Dynamic Execution Gate (RADEG), a lightweight, retriever-agnostic decision layer between skill retrieval and agent execution. RADEG learns a low-cost surrogate model that predicts the execution utility of a query--bundle pair before the expensive rollout is launched. To obtain informative supervision while controlling for task difficulty, we locally perturb each retrieved bundle by deleting, adding, or replacing one skill, producing matched same-query rollouts that isolate the effect of bundle composition on verifier reward. During deployment, RADEG updates only a warm-started logistic head as new verifier feedback becomes available, enabling inexpensive adaptation of the execute/skip boundary without retraining either the retriever or the agent. Under a query-level held-out evaluation on 288 collected rollouts, RADEG substantially reduces unnecessary agent executions while preserving a large fraction of the downstream verifier reward. It consistently outperforms relevance-based and random gating across different execution budgets, demonstrating that execution-aware surrogate modeling provides a practical and cost-effective complement to skill retrieval.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes RADEG, a lightweight decision layer that predicts whether executing a retrieved skill bundle is worthwhile for an LLM agent, reducing unnecessary expensive executions while maintaining most reward.
AI.motivation: As LLM agents rely more on large libraries of reusable skills, retrieving a seemingly relevant bundle of skills does not ensure that executing them will yield sufficient benefit. Each skill-conditioned rollout is computationally expensive, so naively executing every retrieved bundle can waste significant resources. There is a need for a mechanism that can cheaply predict, before execution, whether a given retrieved skill bundle is likely to produce enough reward to justify its computational cost.
AI.method: The authors introduce Reward-Aware Dynamic Execution Gate (RADEG), a retriever-agnostic, lightweight gating layer inserted between skill retrieval and agent execution. RADEG trains a low-cost surrogate model to estimate the execution utility (expected verifier reward) of a query–skill-bundle pair. To obtain supervision that isolates the effect of bundle composition, they perform local perturbations on each retrieved bundle—deleting, adding, or replacing a single skill—to create matched same-query rollouts whose reward differences reflect the impact of skill configuration. During deployment, RADEG uses a warm-started logistic head that is updated online as new verifier feedback is observed, dynamically adjusting the execute/skip threshold without retraining the retriever or the base agent.
AI.result: In a query-level held-out evaluation using 288 collected rollouts, RADEG substantially cuts down on unnecessary agent executions while retaining a large portion of the downstream verifier reward. Across a range of execution budgets, RADEG consistently surpasses relevance-based gating and random gating baselines in terms of reward-efficiency trade-off, indicating that its reward-aware surrogate predictions better capture when execution is worthwhile.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that execution-aware surrogate modeling, instantiated as RADEG, is an effective and practical complement to existing skill retrieval systems for LLM agents. By inserting a learned, low-cost gate that predicts the value of executing a retrieved skill bundle, systems can significantly reduce computational overhead while preserving most of the achievable reward. RADEG’s retriever-agnostic design and inexpensive online adaptivity make it suitable for real-world deployments where skill libraries and task distributions evolve over time.

title: Agentic Router: An Execution-Grounded Continual Learning Approach With Memory
summary: Large language model (LLM) agents provide a promising interface for command-line-based network operations, but a plausible command may still fail or introduce operational risk after execution. Existing approaches mainly focus on command generation or final configuration correctness, and do not use execution-grounded experience to jointly improve candidate coverage and action selection. We propose an execution-grounded dual-path consequence-aware agent for CLI-based SONiC operations, which generates multiple complete actions, predicts their execution consequences, and selects the final action through utility- and risk-aware reranking. The proposal-side path abstracts reusable operational lessons into retrievable guidance to improve feasible-action coverage without modifying the proposal LLM, while the selection-side path adapts the consequence predictor through session-level LoRA updates using real SSH feedback to improve conditional selection quality. Experiments over multi-turn SONiC operation sessions with different Qwen3 proposal models show that the framework improves feasible-action coverage and top-1 execution success, and that the two adaptation paths provide complementary gains over interaction.

AI.tldr: They build an LLM-based network operations agent that not only proposes CLI commands but also predicts their execution consequences and uses that to choose safer, higher-utility commands, adapting over time from real SSH feedback.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM agents for network device operations can generate plausible CLI commands, but these commands may still fail or be risky when executed. Prior work focuses on command generation or final configuration correctness and lacks a mechanism to learn continuously from actual execution feedback to both broaden the set of feasible actions and improve which action is chosen.
AI.method: They design a dual-path, execution-grounded, consequence-aware agent for SONiC CLI operations. The proposal path generates multiple full candidate actions and uses a retrieval-like abstraction of past operational lessons as guidance to enlarge the pool of feasible actions, without changing the base proposal LLM. The selection path predicts the consequences of executing each candidate and re-ranks them based on a utility and risk model, updating the consequence predictor using LoRA at the session level with real SSH feedback to tailor it to current conditions.
AI.result: In multi-turn SONiC operation experiments using different Qwen3 models as the proposal LLM, their framework increases both the coverage of feasible actions among generated candidates and the top-1 execution success rate. They also show that the proposal-side retrieval guidance and the selection-side adaptive consequence prediction provide complementary improvements when used together across interactions.
AI.conclusion: Integrating execution-grounded consequence prediction and experience reuse into an LLM agent for CLI-based network operations yields safer and more effective automation: it generates more feasible commands, chooses better ones to execute, and adapts online to operational feedback. The dual-path design—separating proposal enhancement from selection adaptation—allows complementary improvements without altering the underlying proposal LLM.

title: Structure-Preserving Uncertainty Propagation in First-Order Proof Search
comment: 79 pages, 6 figures. Executable binaries, documentation, examples, and public samplers: https://github.com/tammet/gkreasoner
summary:
GK is a query-directed first-order prover that extends ordinary resolution-based proof search with explicit positive and negative claims, numerical confidence values, and prioritized default rules with exceptions. It works directly with non-ground clauses, including equality and function terms. Candidate proofs are found by bounded first-order proof search; exception conditions of defaults are checked by further bounded searches, recursively when exceptions themselves depend on defaults. This avoids requiring a finite global grounding, while allowing incomplete searches to be reported as such.
  This paper adds structure-preserving quantitative reporting to that framework. Retained proof histories are used in two calculations.
