AI.conclusion: Prescribed optimization pipelines function as capability-dependent scaffolding: for weaker or medium-strength optimizers, explicit structure and constraints are necessary for effective self-improvement, but as optimizer capability increases, these prescriptions become less critical. In the proposed OEO framework, a sufficiently powerful model can autonomously design the route from measurable feedback to persistent improvement within fixed external constraints. This reframes the role of hand-designed pipelines: essential boundaries (objective, resources, safety limits) remain external, while the internal optimization strategy can be open-ended and model-driven when using frontier-scale optimizers.

title: Hallucination-Free GUI Grounding via Regression-Free Layout-Aware Matching
summary: GUI agents are shifting from metadata-dependent large language models to purely visual multimodal large language models (MLLMs) that operate directly on screenshots. The core task, GUI grounding, requires translating abstract user instructions into precise element coordinates. This task faces a persistent dual obstacle: conventional grounding models lack the semantic richness to interpret abstract instructions, while end-to-end MLLMs suffer from coordinate hallucinations caused by deficient fine-grained perception. We propose a regression-free framework where a frozen MLLM performs instruction parsing and a dedicated grounding model handles precise localization without learning any coordinate regression. A frozen MLLM first elaborates the abstract instruction into a structured visual description rich in layout cues. These descriptions are then fed to a novel Layout-Aware GUI Grounding Model, which performs regression-free localization by matching against layout-prior candidates, inherently suppressing hallucinations and avoiding expensive fine-tuning. The grounding model is trained with only Text/Icon binary labels, requiring no coordinate regression parameters. On ScreenSpot-Pro, our method achieves over 20% improvement in grounding accuracy over end-to-end systems; on Mind2Web, it raises success rate and element selection rate by more than 15%. These results demonstrate that decoupling instruction understanding from layout-aware localization effectively resolves the core challenges of GUI interaction.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a regression-free GUI grounding framework that decouples instruction understanding (via a frozen MLLM) from precise element localization (via a layout-aware grounding model), significantly improving grounding accuracy and reducing hallucinations.
AI.motivation: Existing GUI grounding approaches either use conventional models that lack semantic richness for understanding abstract user instructions, or end-to-end MLLMs that directly predict coordinates but often hallucinate due to weak fine-grained perception and require expensive fine-tuning. There is a need for a method that can understand complex instructions while reliably and accurately localizing GUI elements without coordinate hallucinations or heavy supervision.
AI.method: The authors introduce a regression-free two-stage framework. First, a frozen multimodal large language model (MLLM) parses the high-level user instruction and elaborates it into a structured visual description that includes rich layout cues about the target element. Second, they propose a Layout-Aware GUI Grounding Model that consumes these descriptions and performs localization by matching them against a set of layout-prior candidate regions instead of regressing coordinates directly. The grounding model is trained using only binary Text/Icon labels for candidates, with no coordinate regression parameters, and it leverages layout priors to avoid hallucinations and circumvent expensive end-to-end fine-tuning of the MLLM.
AI.result: On the ScreenSpot-Pro benchmark, the proposed framework improves GUI grounding accuracy by more than 20% compared to end-to-end MLLM-based systems. On the Mind2Web benchmark, it increases both overall task success rate and element selection rate by more than 15% over state-of-the-art baselines, indicating better instruction following and more accurate element localization in practical GUI interaction tasks.
AI.conclusion: Decoupling semantic instruction understanding from spatial localization, and replacing direct coordinate regression with layout-aware candidate matching, effectively addresses the core challenges in GUI grounding. By using a frozen MLLM for instruction parsing and a lightweight, regression-free grounding model trained with simple binary labels, the method suppresses coordinate hallucinations, eliminates the need for expensive fine-tuning, and substantially improves performance on GUI interaction benchmarks such as ScreenSpot-Pro and Mind2Web.

title: Open Evaluation Agent: Efficient and Promptable Evaluation of Visual Generative Models
comment: Journal extension of our ACL 2025 paper (arXiv:2412.09645). 12 pages. Code: https://github.com/Vchitect/Evaluation-Agent
summary: Recent advances in visual generative models have enabled high-quality image and video generation, but evaluating these models often demands sampling hundreds or thousands of images or videos, which is computationally expensive. Existing evaluation methods also rely on rigid pipelines that overlook specific user needs and provide numerical results without clear explanations. Mimicking how humans quickly form impressions of a model's capabilities from only a few samples, we propose the Evaluation Agent framework, which employs human-like strategies for efficient, dynamic, multi-round evaluations, offering detailed, user-tailored analyses. Given a natural-language evaluation request, the agent decomposes it into sub-aspects, generates targeted prompts, samples images or videos from the evaluated model, invokes suitable evaluation tools, and iteratively updates its plan from the observed evidence, covering both predefined benchmark dimensions and open-ended user concerns. The framework is thus efficient, promptable, explainable, and scalable across models and tools. Experiments show that Evaluation Agent reduces evaluation time to 10% of traditional methods while delivering comparable results. We further introduce Open Evaluation Agent (Open-EA) by constructing EA-CoT-10K, a corpus of history-conditioned step-level instruction-tuning records derived from multi-round evaluation rollouts, and training EA-3B from Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct as a local planning backbone that preserves the structured reasoning, tool invocation, and summary protocol of the API-based agent while reducing dependence on proprietary backbones. Experiments validate the API-based agent on established T2I/T2V benchmarks and open-ended queries, and evaluate Open-EA on four in-domain and three out-of-domain T2V generator families, showing partial cross-family transfer of the learned policy.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Evaluation Agent, an agentic framework that evaluates visual generative models (image/video) efficiently and interactively from natural-language requests, and introduces Open-EA, an open, smaller planning backbone trained on a new EA-CoT-10K corpus.
AI.motivation: Evaluating modern text-to-image (T2I) and text-to-video (T2V) generative models is expensive and inflexible. Traditional evaluation requires sampling large numbers of images/videos and uses rigid, benchmark-centric pipelines. These pipelines (1) are computationally costly, (2) ignore user-specific evaluation needs, and (3) output opaque numerical scores without explanations. Humans, by contrast, can rapidly form qualitative judgments from only a few examples and adjust what they inspect based on early impressions. The authors aim to design an evaluation framework that is more human-like: efficient with few samples, interactive, user-promptable, and capable of giving interpretable, tailored feedback while remaining compatible with existing tools and benchmarks.
AI.method: They propose the Evaluation Agent framework: an agent that performs multi-round, tool-augmented evaluation of generative models guided by natural-language requests. Given a user query, the agent (1) decomposes the high-level request into sub-aspects (e.g., fidelity, temporal consistency, text alignment, style), (2) designs targeted prompts for each aspect, (3) queries the target generative model to sample a small set of images/videos, (4) selects and calls appropriate evaluation tools/metrics (e.g., quality, alignment, diversity measures), and (5) iteratively updates its evaluation plan using the intermediate evidence, similar to human exploratory analysis. The agent aims to cover both standard benchmark dimensions and open-ended user concerns. To reduce dependence on proprietary LLMs, they also build Open Evaluation Agent (Open-EA): they collect EA-CoT-10K, a dataset of multi-round evaluation trajectories with step-level reasoning and tool calls, and fine-tune a 3B-parameter model (EA-3B) based on Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct to imitate the API-based agent’s structured reasoning, tool invocation patterns, and summarization protocol as a local planning backbone.
AI.result: Empirically, Evaluation Agent cuts evaluation time down to about 10% of traditional large-sample pipelines while maintaining comparable quantitative evaluation outcomes on standard T2I/T2V benchmarks. The API-based agent is validated on both established benchmarks and open-ended evaluation requests, demonstrating that it can adapt to user-specified criteria and still produce meaningful metric-based assessments. For Open-EA, experiments across four in-domain and three out-of-domain T2V model families show that the learned policy partially transfers across generator families, indicating the EA-3B planner can generalize beyond the specific models seen during data collection, though not perfectly.
AI.conclusion: The work demonstrates that an agentic, human-like evaluation framework can significantly improve efficiency and flexibility in assessing visual generative models without sacrificing performance on standard benchmarks. Evaluation Agent provides a promptable, explainable, and scalable way to evaluate diverse T2I/T2V models by dynamically decomposing user requests, adaptively designing probes, and orchestrating existing tools. Open-EA shows that much of this behavior can be captured by a small, open planning model trained on EA-CoT-10K, reducing reliance on large proprietary LLMs and enabling more accessible, reproducible evaluation systems. The partial cross-family transfer suggests promising but not yet complete generalization of the learned evaluation policy across different generator architectures.

title: Adaptive Semantic Capacity Allocation for Parallel Generative Recommendation
summary: Autoregressive semantic ID recommenders are constrained by expensive beam-search decoding, which limits the practical length of item identifiers. Parallel generation methods alleviate this bottleneck by predicting all semantic ID tokens simultaneously, enabling longer IDs. However, existing semantic ID methods still rely on manually predefined and homogeneous ID structures, where both the number of semantic slots and the codebook size of each slot are treated as fixed hyperparameters. This ignores the heterogeneous capacity demands of different semantic subspaces and may allocate prediction capacity to slots with limited utility. We show that uniformly expanding semantic slots can provide limited gains, indicating redundant capacity in homogeneous semantic IDs. We propose InforID, a lightweight adaptive semantic target construction framework for parallel generative recommendation. InforID allocates a fixed capacity budget across candidate semantic slots, thereby jointly determining the effective ID length and slot-specific codebook sizes. Experiments demonstrate improved recommendation accuracy under comparable capacity budgets while preserving one-step parallel prediction.

AI.tldr: The paper addresses limitations of autoregressive semantic ID recommenders and proposes InforID, an adaptive semantic target construction framework that optimizes semantic ID capacity allocation for parallel generative recommendation.
AI.motivation: Existing semantic ID recommenders either suffer from expensive beam-search decoding or rely on rigid, homogeneous ID structures where slot counts and codebook sizes are fixed hyperparameters. This ignores heterogeneous capacity demands across semantic subspaces, leading to inefficient capacity allocation and limited gains from uniformly expanding semantic slots.
AI.method: The authors design InforID, a lightweight adaptive semantic target construction framework for parallel generative recommendation. InforID distributes a fixed overall capacity budget across candidate semantic slots, effectively learning both the number of active slots (ID length) and the codebook size per slot. This allows the model to tailor capacity to more informative semantic subspaces while maintaining one-step parallel generation.
AI.result: Experiments show that, under the same or comparable total capacity budgets, InforID achieves higher recommendation accuracy than existing semantic ID methods that use manually predefined and homogeneous ID structures. The method retains the efficiency benefits of parallel, one-step prediction while better utilizing semantic capacity.
AI.conclusion: InforID provides a more flexible and efficient way to construct semantic IDs for parallel generative recommendation by adaptively allocating capacity across slots rather than relying on fixed, homogeneous ID structures. This adaptive design reduces redundant capacity, improves recommendation accuracy, and preserves fast one-step parallel prediction, making it more suitable for practical systems.

title: Model Discovery Agent: LLM-assisted Bayesian experiment design for data-efficient discovery of mechanistic world models
summary: Predicting the answer to interventional ``what if'' questions --- the outcome of an action never taken --- requires a \emph{mechanistic}, causal model, not a curve fit; and learning such a model requires \emph{experiments}, because passive data leaves its mechanisms unidentified. Experiments are expensive, so the central problem is \emph{data efficiency}. We present the Model Discovery Agent (MDA), which couples a large language model (LLM), used as a \emph{proposer} of candidate structures, with standard Bayesian machinery --- sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) for parameter and structure posteriors, simulation-based inference (SBI) for intractable likelihoods, and value-of-information (VoI) for experiment design --- to discover latent mechanistic world models from few interventions. MDA operates in the M-open setting: when the truth lies outside the current hypothesis class, a predictive check flags the inadequacy and the proposer expands the hypothesis space with a new model whose parameters are then identified by designed experiments. We show that \emph{discovery and design reinforce}: the design step identifies the mechanism the discovery step proposes, and the identified mechanism improves predictions, enabling further discoveries from the remaining unexplained residuals. On three different benchmarks --- covering physics (\DPbench, \citep{wiemann2026discoverphysics}), chemistry (\CHEMbench, \citep{kabra2026autoscilab}) and biology (\HHbench, a new partially observed single-neuron electrophysiology benchmark we create) --- we show that MDA sets a new SOTA in terms of data-efficient model learning and reliable interventional forecasting ability.

AI.tldr: They propose Model Discovery Agent (MDA), a system that uses an LLM plus Bayesian tools to efficiently learn mechanistic causal models from few experiments and achieve strong interventional predictions across physics, chemistry, and biology benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Interventional “what if” questions require mechanistic causal models rather than pure predictive curve fitting, but such models are hard to learn because they need costly experiments and standard approaches are data-inefficient and often assume the true model is within a fixed hypothesis class. The authors want a method that can efficiently discover and refine mechanistic world models with minimal interventions, even when the true data-generating process lies outside current model classes.
AI.method: MDA couples a large language model acting as a structural proposer with Bayesian inference and experimental design tools. Sequential Monte Carlo is used to maintain posteriors over model structures and parameters; simulation-based inference handles intractable likelihoods; and value-of-information criteria guide which experiments to perform next. The system works in an M-open setting by performing predictive checks; when existing models fail, the LLM proposes new candidate mechanisms, which are then tested and identified via designed experiments, iteratively expanding and refining the hypothesis space.
AI.result: Across three benchmarks—DPbench for physics, CHEMbench for chemistry, and a new HHbench for partially observed single-neuron electrophysiology—the MDA framework achieves state-of-the-art performance in learning accurate mechanistic models with few interventions and in reliably forecasting outcomes under novel interventions. The experiments demonstrate that the cycle of discovery (model proposal and expansion) and design (targeted experiments) mutually reinforce each other, leading to faster and more accurate mechanism identification than baselines.
AI.conclusion: MDA shows that integrating LLM-based model structure proposal with principled Bayesian inference and value-of-information-driven experiment design enables data-efficient discovery of mechanistic causal models, even in M-open settings. The iterative interaction between discovering new candidate mechanisms and designing informative experiments leads to reliable interventional predictions and sets a new performance bar on diverse scientific benchmarks, suggesting a promising paradigm for automated scientific model discovery.

title: Second-Order Muon Done Right: A Principled Marriage of Spectral Geometry and Curvature
summary: Muon's polar update is exact for an unweighted spectral geometry. We introduce GO-MUON, which uses a matched data-dependent geometry and reuses it across several optimization steps. Conditioned on any positive-definite left and right maps, its raw update exactly solves the corresponding weighted spectral oracle; this statement is independent of how the maps are estimated or how recently they were refreshed. For softmax cross-entropy, we quantify when the observed-label backward factor approaches the model Fisher and generalized Gauss--Newton factor. We also show that four-step refresh nearly preserves the tracking delay of slowly changing geometry while increasing stationary factor noise, making lazy geometry a compute--statistics tradeoff rather than a denoising mechanism.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces GO-MUON, an optimization method that reuses a data-dependent geometry across multiple steps, providing exact polar updates for weighted spectral oracles under broad conditions, and analyzes its behavior for softmax cross-entropy and under lazy (infrequent) geometry refresh.
AI.motivation: To improve and generalize Muon's polar update by extending it from unweighted to weighted spectral geometries, enabling efficient reuse of data-dependent curvature information across multiple optimization steps and clarifying the statistical-computational tradeoffs of infrequent geometry updates.
AI.method: The authors define GO-MUON, which conditions Muon's polar update on arbitrary positive-definite left and right maps to form a matched weighted spectral geometry. They prove that, under these conditions, the raw update exactly solves the corresponding weighted spectral oracle, regardless of how the maps are estimated or refreshed. They then specialize the analysis to softmax cross-entropy to relate the backward factors to the model Fisher and generalized Gauss-Newton matrices, and study the effects of refreshing the geometry every four steps on tracking delay and noise characteristics.
AI.result: They show that GO-MUON's polar update is an exact solver for any weighted spectral oracle induced by positive-definite left/right maps, independent of the refresh scheme. For softmax cross-entropy, they derive conditions under which the observed-label backward factor approximates the model Fisher and generalized Gauss-Newton factors. Empirically or theoretically (not fully specified in the abstract), they find that a four-step geometry refresh maintains nearly the same tracking delay for slowly changing geometries but increases the stationary noise in the curvature factors.
AI.conclusion: GO-MUON generalizes Muon's polar update to a broad class of weighted spectral geometries, enabling lazy (infrequent) geometry updates that trade off computational savings against increased curvature noise rather than serving purely as a denoising mechanism. This reframes geometry reuse as a compute-statistics tradeoff while preserving exactness with respect to the chosen spectral oracle.

title: AirFlow: Context Preserving and Multi-Rate State Modeling for Air Quality Forecasting
summary: Accurate air quality forecasting is essential for public health and urban environmental management, but remains challenging because pollutant channels differ in periodicity and distribution drift, while their concentration trajectories contain both multi-scale dependencies and rapid changes. Recent methods have improved spatial dependency learning and meteorological covariate modeling. However, pollutant channels are still passed through the same normalization rule and temporal backbone, using a shared latent representation for channel-specific distributions and changes at different rates. To address this limitation, we propose AirFlow, a pollutant-aware dual-stream framework that operates on station multivariate observations without additional graph propagation or predefined signal decomposition. Specifically, AirFlow designs two novel blocks: (1) a statistic-guided normalization routing mechanism that selects a normalization path for each pollutant according to its 24-hour autocorrelation and distribution drift; and (2) a hierarchical dual-stream state model that combines multi-scale state space propagation with learnable response coefficients, where gated bidirectional cross-attention exchanges information and adaptively fuses the resulting representations. Experiments on real-world data from multiple cities show that AirFlow achieves the best performance in 34 of 36 metrics comparisons, with reductions of up to 11.11% root mean square error over the state-of-the-art baseline. AirFlow also requires only 0.0483M parameters and 0.0215G FLOPs, achieving high forecasting accuracy with low computational overhead.

AI.tldr: AirFlow introduces a pollutant-aware dual-stream forecasting framework that customizes normalization and temporal modeling per pollutant, achieving more accurate and efficient air quality predictions than prior methods.
AI.motivation: Existing air quality forecasting models struggle because different pollutants exhibit heterogeneous temporal patterns: they vary in periodicity, experience distribution drift, and show both long-range dependencies and abrupt changes. Yet most methods treat all pollutant channels identically—using a single normalization strategy and a shared temporal backbone—which fails to capture channel-specific behaviors and change rates. There is also a desire to avoid heavy graph-based models or hand-crafted signal decompositions while still effectively leveraging multivariate station observations. This motivates a new architecture that is explicitly pollutant-aware and can adapt its processing to each pollutant’s statistical and temporal characteristics, while remaining computationally efficient.
AI.method: The paper proposes AirFlow, a pollutant-aware dual-stream framework for multivariate air quality time-series from monitoring stations. It introduces two main components. (1) A statistic-guided normalization routing mechanism: for each pollutant channel, the system computes statistics such as 24-hour autocorrelation and measures of distribution drift, then uses these to route the channel through one of multiple candidate normalization paths, allowing pollutant-specific normalization instead of a single shared rule. (2) A hierarchical dual-stream state model: temporal dynamics are modeled using a multi-scale state space propagation in two parallel streams, each with learnable response coefficients. Gated bidirectional cross-attention connects the two streams, enabling them to exchange information, reconcile different temporal scales, and adaptively fuse their representations into a shared prediction, all without explicit graph propagation or pre-defined signal decomposition.
AI.result: On real-world multi-city air quality datasets, AirFlow outperforms prior methods across nearly all evaluation settings. It achieves the best scores in 34 out of 36 metric comparisons and attains up to an 11.11% reduction in root mean square error relative to the strongest baseline. Despite its improved accuracy, the model is lightweight, using only about 0.0483 million parameters and 0.0215 gigaflops of computation, indicating that the gains do not come at the cost of high computational complexity.
AI.conclusion: Channel-agnostic treatment of pollutants in air quality forecasting is suboptimal because pollutants follow distinct temporal and distributional patterns. By introducing statistic-guided normalization routing and a hierarchical dual-stream state model with cross-attention, AirFlow tailors its processing to each pollutant while maintaining an efficient architecture. The empirical results demonstrate that pollutant-aware design significantly enhances prediction accuracy and efficiency, suggesting that future air quality forecasting systems should explicitly model channel heterogeneity instead of relying on shared representations and uniform normalization.

title: CARD: Controlled Agentic Reddit Discussions for Credit Card Simulation
summary: Online credit card discussions provide a natural setting for studying how consumers communicate about financial products. Simulating these discussions requires more than just generating individual comments, the generated threads should also match how real users express themselves and interact with others. We introduce CARD, a framework for generating realistic credit card discussion threads. Given a credit card post and its matched real thread, CARD uses non-verbatim guidance on reply structure, comment function, stance, tone, and conversational variation. A planner organizes these controls, a writer generates the discussion, and a calibration loop updates comments' populations that contribute to differences between the generated and real thread distributions. We evaluate CARD on real Reddit credit card discussions using lexical, semantic, behavioral, and structural metrics. CARD matches the distributions of real credit card discussions better than simulation baselines across multiple LLMs and also demonstrates smaller effect sizes and distribution distances across metrics. These results show that structured planning and targeted revision can generate the realism of simulated credit card discussions.

AI.tldr: A framework (CARD) for generating realistic, full discussion threads about credit cards, not just individual comments, using structured planning and calibration to mimic real Reddit conversations.
AI.motivation: Existing text generation methods often create isolated, out‑of-context comments and fail to capture how people actually interact in multi‑turn financial discussions. For research, product testing, and simulation, we need synthetic discussion threads that resemble real consumer conversations in content, interaction patterns, tone, and stance.
AI.method: They propose CARD, a pipeline with (1) a planner that encodes guidance about reply structure, comment roles (e.g., ask, answer, challenge), stance, tone, and stylistic variation using a real reference thread; (2) a writer model (LLM) that generates an entire synthetic thread following this plan; and (3) a calibration loop that compares distributions of properties in the generated thread to those in the real thread and iteratively updates or re‑samples comments to better match lexical, semantic, behavioral, and structural characteristics.
AI.result: On Reddit credit card discussions, CARD produces simulated threads whose distributions across lexical content, semantics, user behavior patterns, and reply structures more closely match real data than several baseline simulation methods, and shows reduced effect sizes and distribution distances between real and synthetic threads across multiple underlying LLMs.
AI.conclusion: Structured control over conversation properties plus an iterative calibration process substantially improves the realism of synthetic online credit card discussions, suggesting that CARD is a useful framework for generating high‑fidelity conversational data for financial communication research and related applications.

title: CEAA: A Cognitive Embodied Agents Architecture for Interactive Computing Systems
summary: The development of embodied Intelligent Virtual Agents (IVAs) that have cognitive capabilities in real-time interactive virtual environments remains a challenge, even with today's advancements in technology. Existing architectures are often focused on either the implementation of low-level reactive control systems that are constrained by commercial game engines, or high-level representations of reasoning models that can be difficult to implement in virtual worlds. This paper builds on that notion and proposes a modular cognitive architecture for deploying embodied IVAs. This architecture builds on existing, pre-established frameworks such as the Sense-Think-Act paradigm and the Belief-Desire-Intention cognitive model, among others, and aims to provide a reusable implementation-oriented framework as a template for deploying IVA "brains" in interactive 3D computing systems. The proposed architecture contributes by providing a modular, implementation-oriented framework for the deployment of embodied, cognitive-capable IVAs and bridges the gap between high-level agent reasoning models with real-time embodied execution, for scalable, adaptive, and explainable agents in complex interactive virtual environments.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a modular, implementation-oriented cognitive architecture to deploy embodied Intelligent Virtual Agents (IVAs) that can operate in real time in complex 3D virtual environments.
AI.motivation: Despite technological progress, it remains difficult to create embodied IVAs with genuine cognitive capabilities that work robustly and in real time in interactive virtual environments. Current approaches either focus on low-level reactive control constrained by game engines or high-level reasoning models that are hard to implement practically. There is a need to bridge these two extremes with a reusable, practical architecture.
AI.method: The authors design a modular cognitive architecture that integrates and operationalizes established frameworks like the Sense-Think-Act paradigm and the Belief-Desire-Intention (BDI) model. The architecture is conceived as an implementation-oriented, reusable template for building the "brains" of IVAs that can be embedded into interactive 3D systems. The design emphasizes modularity, real-time operation, and compatibility with existing virtual environment technologies.
AI.result: The result is a proposed architecture that demonstrates how high-level reasoning frameworks can be connected to real-time embodied execution for IVAs. While the abstract does not give empirical evaluation details, it claims that the architecture supports scalable, adaptive, and explainable behavior in complex interactive virtual environments.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that its modular cognitive architecture successfully bridges the gap between abstract agent reasoning models and their real-time embodied deployment in virtual worlds. It offers a reusable template for implementing cognitive-capable IVA "brains" that can be scaled and adapted across different 3D interactive systems, improving the practical deployment of intelligent, explainable agents in virtual environments.

title: ArchAgent v2: A Case Study with the Data Prefetching Championship
summary:
Agentic artificial intelligence has shown great promise in automating algorithm design, but scaling similar techniques to computer microarchitecture discovery remains challenging due to vast search spaces, strict hardware budgets, and long simulation times. In this work, we present ArchAgent v2, a framework which scales automated microarchitecture search to multi-level data prefetching. While the original ArchAgent successfully discovered single-level cache replacement policies in competition settings, it does not scale to multi-level prefetching where the design space and degrees of freedom are larger. To overcome this, we introduce two new additions to ArchAgent: a cascaded evolutionary search that subdivides the design space by sequentially evolving and freezing prefetchers at individual cache levels, and a hardware-realizability feedback loop that embeds real-time size-estimation directly into the evolution process.
  Evaluated under identical rules of the 4th Data Prefetching Championship (DPC4), ArchAgent v2 automatically designs a three-level prefetcher that outperforms the winning hand-designed solution, further demonstrating automated agentic discovery as a useful tool for computer architects. Our discovered policy achieves a 3.8\% geometric mean IPC speedup over the baseline overall and a 0.3\% improvement over the prior champion, BertiGO. On low-bandwidth single-core configurations, our policy yields a 4.6\% performance speedup compared to only 2.6\% for BertiGO. However, multi-core evolution still remains a significant challenge due to simulation latency impeding evolution speed. Finally, our profiling of an ArchAgent evolution of over 12,000 candidate designs provides key insights into how automated evolutionary agents explore and synthesize complex microarchitectural logic.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces ArchAgent v2, an automated AI framework that scales microarchitecture search to design multi-level data prefetchers, outperforming the human-designed state-of-the-art in a standard benchmark competition.
AI.motivation: While agentic AI has been effective in automating algorithm design, extending it to complex hardware microarchitecture discovery is difficult because of extremely large design spaces, tight hardware constraints, and slow simulations. Existing systems like the original ArchAgent work only for simpler problems (e.g., single-level cache replacement) and cannot scale to multi-level prefetching, a more intricate and higher-dimensional design task critical for modern processors.
AI.method: The authors propose ArchAgent v2 with two main innovations: (1) a cascaded evolutionary search strategy that decomposes the problem by sequentially evolving prefetcher designs for each cache level and then freezing them, thereby reducing the effective search dimensionality; and (2) a hardware-realizability feedback loop that integrates real-time hardware size estimation into the evolutionary process to ensure the discovered designs stay within strict area and resource budgets. They then run large-scale evolutionary experiments, exploring over 12,000 candidate designs under the formal rules of the DPC4 competition.
AI.result: Under the 4th Data Prefetching Championship (DPC4) rules, ArchAgent v2 automatically discovers a three-level prefetcher that beats the previous human-designed winning solution, BertiGO. The learned design delivers a 3.8% geometric-mean IPC speedup over the baseline and a 0.3% IPC improvement over BertiGO overall, with larger gains (4.6% vs. 2.6% for BertiGO) in low-bandwidth single-core settings. The system also generates extensive evolutionary traces (over 12,000 candidates) that the authors analyze to understand how the agent searches the design space.
AI.conclusion: ArchAgent v2 demonstrates that agentic AI and evolutionary search can successfully scale from simpler cache policies to complex multi-level data prefetcher design, surpassing a top human-engineered microarchitecture in a standard competition benchmark while respecting hardware constraints. However, the study also highlights remaining challenges, notably the difficulty of extending this approach to multi-core settings due to slow simulation times, and uses large-scale evolution logs to offer insight into how automated agents synthesize sophisticated microarchitectural logic.

title: SHE: Trajectory-driven Safety Harness Evolution for LLM Agents
summary: The safety of large language model (LLM) agents depends not only on model weights but also on the agent harness that manages context, memory, tools, permissions, and runtime control. Existing safety mechanisms often treat the harness as a fixed deployment artifact, limiting their ability to evolve with emerging risks. Moreover, coupled functions across harness components obscure safety responsibility attribution, making localized evolution difficult. We propose Safety Harness Evolution (SHE), a framework that learns evolving safe boundaries from rollout trajectories. SHE decomposes the harness into four artifacts with explicit safety responsibilities, including the System Prompt, Rule Bank, Safety Memory, and Tool Policy, defining clear functional boundaries for localized evolution. Based on this decomposition, SHE introduces an attribution-guided evolution loop that converts trajectory failures into structured diagnoses, learns artifact-specific boundary refinements, and selects evolved harnesses through safety-utility validation. Experiments on Agent-SafetyBench demonstrate that SHE effectively enhances safety through harness evolution, achieving a 3.1x ASR reduction compared with static SafeHarness, while also improving benign utility. The evolved harness further generalizes to unseen risks on the held-out AgentHarm benchmark and transfers across agent models without additional evolution.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Safety Harness Evolution (SHE), a framework that adaptively improves the safety of LLM-based agents by evolving their surrounding harness rather than changing model weights.
AI.motivation: Safety of LLM agents is determined not only by model parameters but also by the surrounding agent harness (prompts, tools, memory, permissions, control). Existing safety methods largely treat this harness as a static, monolithic object, which: (1) cannot easily adapt to new or emerging risks, and (2) has tightly coupled components that blur safety responsibilities, making it hard to diagnose failures or update specific parts. The authors aim to create a structured, evolvable safety harness that can learn from deployment trajectories and improve safety over time while preserving utility.
AI.method: They propose Safety Harness Evolution (SHE), which: (1) Decomposes the agent harness into four explicit safety artifacts—System Prompt, Rule Bank, Safety Memory, and Tool Policy—each with clear safety responsibilities and functional boundaries; (2) Runs agents and collects rollout trajectories on safety benchmarks, then uses an attribution-guided procedure to turn observed failures into structured diagnoses that identify which artifact(s) are responsible; (3) Performs artifact-specific boundary refinement, i.e., learning or editing only the implicated components (e.g., updating rules, system prompt constraints, safety memory entries, or tool permissions); (4) Validates candidate evolved harnesses via a safety-utility evaluation loop, selecting those that both reduce attack success rate and maintain or improve benign task performance; (5) Tests generalization across benchmarks and models to evaluate whether evolved harnesses transfer without further adaptation.
AI.result: On Agent-SafetyBench, SHE significantly reduces the attack success rate (ASR) of LLM agents by a factor of 3.1× compared with a strong static baseline (SafeHarness) while simultaneously improving benign task utility. The harnesses evolved via SHE generalize to unseen risks when evaluated on the held-out AgentHarm benchmark, and the same evolved harness configuration can be transferred to different underlying agent models without additional evolution, retaining safety gains.
AI.conclusion: Structuring the agent harness into separate, responsibility-specific safety artifacts and evolving these components based on trajectory feedback is an effective path to improving LLM agent safety. SHE shows that harness-level evolution can substantially reduce vulnerability to attacks and even enhance benign performance, while generalizing to new risk settings and different models. This suggests that future safety work should treat the harness as a first-class, adaptive object rather than a fixed deployment detail, enabling more modular, diagnosable, and transferable safety mechanisms for LLM agents.

title: DSLE: A Learning Environment for Dark Souls Boss Encounters
comment: AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence and Interactive Digital Entertainment, 2026
summary: We introduce the Dark Souls Learning Environment (DSLE), a containerized platform that presents all 22 boss encounters of Dark Souls: Remastered as game-playing agent benchmarks through a Gymnasium-style interface. DSLE combines real-time combat, high-dimensional visual input, and sparse terminal rewards, with each environment step being a real action executed against the running game. To support controlled comparison, we define DSLE-5, a representative five-boss subset, spanning a melee fight, a spatially constrained arena, an environmental-hazard fight, a multi-target fight, and a fast final-boss fight, that we recommend as the starting suite for agents built on DSLE. On DSLE-5 we evaluate a random policy, an expert system, an evolutionary baseline, and PPO and DQN agents trained from visual input. The expert system and the evolutionary baseline each defeat the Asylum Demon, the game's tutorial boss (63% and 43% peak win rates), but none of the five methods defeats the other four DSLE-5 bosses; PPO and DQN show no measurable learning (at most 0.33% win rate on the tutorial boss, 0% elsewhere) within a budget that already costs tens of wall-clock hours per run. A broader study running the evolutionary baseline across all 22 encounters under advantaged all level-50 stats yields wins on only a handful of additional early-game bosses and leaves the rest unwon. The failure cases range from sub-10-second deaths in cramped, multi-target encounters to minute-long stalemates that inflict almost no damage, and we report them through survival time and damage dealt rather than win rate alone.

AI.tldr: The paper presents DSLE, a Dark Souls: Remastered boss-fight benchmark suite for reinforcement learning, and shows that several standard methods perform very poorly on it.
AI.motivation: Standard RL benchmarks often lack the difficulty, real-time control, sparse rewards, and complex dynamics of challenging commercial games. Dark Souls bosses are known for demanding combat requiring precise timing, strategy, and adaptation, making them an attractive yet underexplored testbed for evaluating the limits of current RL agents.
AI.method: They build DSLE, a containerized environment that wraps 22 Dark Souls: Remastered boss encounters into Gymnasium-style interfaces, where each environment step corresponds to a real in-game action with high-dimensional visual observations and sparse terminal rewards. They also define DSLE-5, a recommended subset of five diverse bosses, and evaluate multiple baselines: a random policy, an expert-system controller, an evolutionary algorithm, and PPO and DQN agents trained directly from pixels. They measure performance through win rates, survival time, and damage dealt.
AI.result: On the DSLE-5 subset, only the expert system and evolutionary baseline occasionally defeat the tutorial boss (Asylum Demon) with 63% and 43% peak win rates, respectively; no method defeats the other four bosses. PPO and DQN show effectively no learning, achieving at most 0.33% win rate on the tutorial boss and 0% on others within training budgets that already take tens of wall-clock hours. Extending the evolutionary baseline to all 22 bosses at advantaged stats yields victories on only a few early-game encounters, with most bosses remaining unbeaten. Failure cases span very quick deaths in hard multi-target or cramped fights to drawn-out stalemates, prompting the use of richer metrics than win rate alone.
AI.conclusion: DSLE exposes a class of RL tasks that are drastically harder than common benchmarks, revealing a significant gap between current methods and the ability to master complex, real-time commercial game combat. The environment serves both as a challenging new benchmark suite and as evidence that progress in sample efficiency, exploration, long-horizon credit assignment, and robust control is needed for agents to handle such tasks. The authors advocate using DSLE-5 as a standard starting point and emphasize that future work should focus not only on win rates but also on intermediate metrics like survival time and damage dealt.

title: GENCO - A Unified Neural Solver Embedded in a Development Framework for Steady-State Grid Analysis
summary:
Foundation models are transforming business workflows and boosting productivity, yet they remain largely absent from engineering domains such as power system analysis, where strict physical consistency must be enforced.
  We present GENCO (GEometric Neural Corrective Optimizer), a unified neural solver for steady-state transmission grid analysis that handles power flow (PF), optimal power flow (OPF), and state estimation (SE) within a single architecture and shared network representation. To support advances in neural power system solvers, we introduce the open-source GridFM Development Framework, which standardizes synthetic data generation and training in a low-code environment. We also release large-scale datasets with millions of PF and OPF scenarios across diverse grid topologies to support reproducible benchmarking.
  We evaluate GENCO on the PFDelta and OPFData benchmarks against state-of-the-art neural solvers and classical solvers, including Newton-Raphson and IPOPT, as well as on real-world Hydro-Québec SCADA data. For large-scale PF, GENCO recovers the full AC operating state, including voltage magnitudes and reactive power that DC-PF cannot provide, while matching DC-PF-level active power-balance residuals. It achieves up to 30x speedups over Newton-Raphson at only 2x the runtime of DC-PF. For OPF, it achieves up to 85x speedups over IPOPT while improving feasibility, optimality, and runtime over DC-OPF. For SE, GENCO is more robust than classical weighted least squares to noisy measurements and network parameter errors, and always returns a high-quality estimate even when weighted least squares fails to converge.
  Together, the unified architecture and development framework provide a new approach to large-scale steady-state grid analysis, lowering the barrier to entry for power system engineers and marking a step toward Grid Foundation Models.

AI.tldr: GENCO is a unified neural solver and framework for fast, physically consistent steady-state power system analysis (PF, OPF, SE), achieving large speedups over classical methods while maintaining or improving accuracy and robustness.
AI.motivation: Foundation models greatly enhance productivity in many domains but are underused in power systems because grid analysis must strictly obey physical laws and is traditionally solved with iterative optimization methods. Existing neural solvers are often task-specific (PF, OPF, or SE) and lack common infrastructures and standardized datasets, making it difficult to build scalable, general-purpose models and to compare approaches fairly. The authors aim to bridge this gap and move toward foundation-model-style tools for power grids.
AI.method: They design GENCO, a geometric neural corrective optimizer that shares a single architecture and network representation across three tasks: power flow, optimal power flow, and state estimation. GENCO learns to iteratively correct states or decisions so that they satisfy AC power flow physics and operational constraints. To support training and evaluation, they build the GridFM Development Framework, a low-code environment that standardizes synthetic grid data generation and training processes, and they create and release large-scale datasets with millions of PF and OPF scenarios over varied grid topologies. They train and benchmark GENCO using these datasets and the PFDelta and OPFData benchmarks, as well as real SCADA data from Hydro-Québec.
AI.result: On large-scale power flow, GENCO reconstructs the full AC operating point (including voltages and reactive power) while keeping active power-balance residuals comparable to fast but approximate DC-PF. It yields up to 30x speedup over the Newton-Raphson AC-PF solver with only about 2x the runtime of DC-PF. For OPF, it provides up to 85x speedup over the nonlinear solver IPOPT and simultaneously improves feasibility, optimality, and runtime compared with DC-OPF approximations. For state estimation, GENCO is more robust than classical weighted least-squares estimators in the presence of noisy measurements and parameter errors and reliably converges to high-quality solutions even when weighted least squares fails.
AI.conclusion: A single, shared neural architecture (GENCO) can effectively solve multiple steady-state grid analysis tasks (PF, OPF, SE) with substantial computational gains and robustness advantages over classical solvers, while respecting AC physics. Combined with the GridFM Development Framework and released datasets, this approach lowers the barrier for applying machine learning in power systems and constitutes a step toward “Grid Foundation Models” that generalize across tasks and network topologies.
